docs.text:
Military Traditions · Bhāratīya Jñāna Paramparā

War, armies, weapons, fortification, war ethics and the martial arts of South Asia

docs.title: Preface
docs.text:
This is Volume 20 of the series Bhāratīya Jñāna Paramparā: Yuddha and Dhanurveda: Military Traditions. It covers both the military history and military thought of the subcontinent and the warrior’s training, ethics and arts. Its subject is war in South Asia from the fortified towns of the Indus civilisation to the sepoy armies of the East India Company: how armies were raised, paid, armed and led; what the classical texts — the Arthaśāstra, the epics, the dharmaśāstras and the late manuals called dhanurveda — say about war; how forts were built and taken, how navies fought, how rulers gathered intelligence; how the ethics of war were argued over and how they were, and were not, observed; and what became of the warrior’s arts, from wrestling and archery to kaḷarippayaṟṟu, silambam and gatka.

The book tries to be fair to every tradition that shaped warfare in the subcontinent. Vedic chariot-fighters, Mauryan and Gupta armies, the Cōḻa fleet, Rajput clans, Turkic and Afghan cavalry, the Delhi sultans, Vijayanagara, the Mughals, the Ahoms, the Marathas, the Sikhs, Mysore, the Gorkhas and Dogras of the Himalaya, the hired Purbiya and Afghan soldiers of the military labour market, and the sepoys of the Company each receive attention on their own terms. Military history in India has often been written to praise one community or blame another; the aim here is to describe what armies did, using the evidence and the work of historians such as P. C. Chakravarti, Sarva Daman Singh, Jos Gommans, Dirk Kolff, Kaushik Roy and Thomas Trautmann, whose books are cited in the text and collected in the select bibliography.

Primary texts are quoted in the original only where both the wording and the reference can be confirmed; elsewhere they are paraphrased, with a reference to a standard edition or translation. Several popular claims are discussed only to be set aside: that the epics describe nuclear weapons or aircraft, that the Buddhist monk Bodhidharma carried kung fu from India to China, that any Indian martial art is “the mother of all martial arts”, that an unbroken written science of dhanurveda survives from Vedic times, and that the rockets of Tipu Sultan were the origin of modern rocketry. Dates are given as the range accepted in current scholarship, with traditional dates labelled as such; army sizes and casualty figures are given only where a source can be named, and with the caution that ancient and medieval numbers deserve. The series dedication speaks of an unbroken tradition of knowledge. For the arts of war the continuity this volume finds is of a different kind: not a single science handed down from the Vedic age, but practical knowledge that was learned, borrowed, written down late and rewritten many times.

The chapters on the martial arts describe practices and the claims made for them; they are not manuals. Nothing in this volume should be used as instruction in striking vital points or in any other technique that can injure, and claims about the healing power of marma or varmam treatment are reported as traditional claims, not as established medicine. No survey of this size can be complete, and every quotation should be checked against a critical edition before scholarly use. Four maps locate the passes and battlefields, the forts, the naval actions and the battles of the Company’s wars; a glossary of the principal technical terms and a chronology are provided at the end.

Nikhil Kumar Rajput Ramanujan College, University of Delhi Guru Pūrṇimā, 2026

docs.title: Chapter 1: Introduction: War, Warriors and the Study of Indian Military Traditions
1.1 The Scope of This Volume
docs.text:
War has been part of South Asian history for as long as there is evidence for that history, and the subcontinent has produced a large literature about it: hymns that praise victorious chariot-fighters, an epic whose central event is an eighteen-day battle, a treatise on statecraft that devotes whole books to campaigns, sieges and secret operations, codes of law that set out how a king should fight, Persian chronicles of conquest, Marathi and Rajasthani ballads of heroes, and the reports of Greek, Chinese, Arab, Portuguese and British observers. Alongside the literature stand the physical remains — forts, hero-stones, weapons in museums — and a number of living practices, from wrestling in earthen pits to the sword-and-shield exercises of Kerala and Punjab.

This volume surveys that material. Its title joins two Sanskrit words. Yuddha means battle or war in general. Dhanurveda, literally “knowledge of the bow”, is the traditional name for the science of arms, counted in some later lists as one of the four “subsidiary Vedas” (upaveda). The two words mark the two halves of the subject. One half is collective and political: how states raised and paid armies, how campaigns and sieges were conducted, how wars were justified and limited. The other half is individual: how warriors were trained, what weapons they used, what ideals they were taught, and what became of the warrior’s arts when the world that sustained them changed.

The book is organised as follows. Chapters 2 to 7 deal with early India and with the classical sources: the history of warfare to about 600 CE, the texts that discuss war (and how late or early they are), archery and the dhanurveda manuals, weapons and military technology, the elephants, horses and chariots on which Indian armies depended, and the theory of strategy, battle arrays and intelligence. Chapters 8 and 9 narrate the history of war from the early medieval kingdoms through the Turkic conquests, the Delhi Sultanate, Vijayanagara, the Mughals, the Ahoms, the Marathas, the Sikhs and Mysore. Chapters 10 and 11 treat fortification and naval warfare. Chapter 12 examines the ethics of war — dharmayuddha — as the texts state it, with the exceptions the texts themselves allow, and as it was practised. Chapters 13 to 16 turn to the warrior: education and martial culture, wrestling and unarmed combat, the regional martial arts, and women in war. Chapter 17 follows the hired soldiers of the military labour market from the fifteenth century to 1857, and Chapter 18 the regular armies that Mysore, the Marathas, Hyderabad, the Sikh kingdom, Nepal and other states built between 1740 and 1849. Chapter 19 describes the colonial conquest, the sepoy armies of the East India Company and the disarming of Indian society, and Chapter 20 the modern revival of the martial arts, the much-discussed question of Indian influence on the martial arts of other Asian countries, and the conclusions of the volume.

docs.title: 1.2.1 Texts
docs.text:
The written sources for Indian warfare are rich but uneven, and each kind has its own biases. The Vedic hymns, composed in their core between about 1500 and 1200 BCE, are poetry addressed to gods; they mention chariots, bows, forts and battles, but they are not descriptions of campaigns (Singh 1965; Jamison and Brereton 2014). The two Sanskrit epics, the Mahābhārata and the Rāmāyaṇa, grew over several centuries, roughly between 400 BCE and 400 CE, and their battle books combine conventions of heroic poetry with much that is fantastic (Brockington 1998). They are invaluable for ideals and vocabulary but cannot be read as eyewitness accounts of a historical war.

The Arthaśāstra attributed to Kauṭilya is the single most important Sanskrit source on military organisation. Tradition identifies its author with Cāṇakya, minister of Candragupta Maurya, c. 300 BCE; but the text as we have it is a composite work, and Patrick Olivelle, its most recent translator, dates it between about 50 BCE and 300 CE (Olivelle 2013). Its value lies in its practical, administrative outlook, but it is a manual of what a king should do, not a record of what any particular king did. The dharmaśāstras, above all the Mānava Dharmaśāstra (Manusmṛti, c. 2nd century CE), state rules for the conduct of kings and of war (Olivelle 2005). The texts that call themselves dhanurveda, and the military chapters of encyclopaedic Purāṇas such as the Agni Purāṇa, are in their present form medieval or later, as Chapter 3 explains.

From the thirteenth century onwards Persian chronicles and administrative manuals — histories of the Delhi sultans, Bābur’s memoirs, Abū’l-Faẓl’s Āʾīn-i Akbarī — provide detailed narrative and statistical material, with the biases of court historians (Thackston 1996; Blochmann 1873). Regional literatures add Tamil war poetry, Rajasthani heroic poetry, Marathi chronicles (bakhar) and ballads (povāḍā), Assamese buraṅjī chronicles, and Sikh accounts. Foreign observers — Megasthenes and the Alexander historians, Chinese pilgrims, Arab geographers, Marco Polo, Portuguese and Dutch merchants, British officers — describe what they saw, often with misunderstanding but sometimes with precision.

docs.title: 1.2.2 Inscriptions and material evidence
docs.text:
Inscriptions are the most reliable source for early and medieval India. Aśoka’s Thirteenth Rock Edict describes the Kaliṅga war in the emperor’s own words (Hultzsch 1925); royal eulogies (praśasti) such as Samudragupta’s Allahabad pillar inscription or the Aihoḷe inscription of Pulakeśin II list conquests; copper-plate grants and temple inscriptions record military officers, gifts to soldiers and the deaths of heroes. Thousands of hero-stones (vīrakal, pāliyā, naṭukal) commemorate individual warriors who died defending cattle, villages or their lords.

Archaeology provides fortifications, weapons and depictions of warfare in sculpture and painting. Museum collections of arms and armour in India and abroad are rich for the period after about 1500 and thin for earlier centuries, since iron rusts and wood and leather perish (Elgood 2004; Egerton 1880).

docs.title: 1.2.3 Living practice
docs.text: The martial arts that are still practised are a further source, but a difficult one. Practitioners often trace their arts to gods, sages or remote antiquity. Historians cannot simply accept such genealogies, nor can they dismiss them; they have to compare oral tradition with dated evidence. Phillip Zarrilli’s study of kaḷarippayaṟṟu, which combines fieldwork with historical research, is a model of how this can be done (Zarrilli 1998); Joseph Alter’s ethnography of North Indian wrestling is another (Alter 1992).

docs.title: 1.3 The Archaeology of War
docs.text:
Archaeology contributes in several ways to the study of Indian warfare, though battlefield archaeology, which has transformed the study of some European battles, has scarcely begun in India. Fortifications are the most visible archaeological evidence: the walls of Harappan cities, the ramparts of early historic towns, and the thousands of medieval and early modern forts discussed in Chapter 10. Weapons are found in hoards and burials. The “copper hoards” of the Ganges–Yamuna region, dating to the second millennium BCE, include flat axes, harpoons and swords with distinctive antenna-shaped hilts, whose purpose — weapons, ritual objects or both — is debated. The megalithic burials of the Deccan and south India, from the early first millennium BCE onwards, contain many iron weapons, including swords, daggers, spearheads and arrowheads, as well as horse equipment. Sculpture, coins and painting provide images of soldiers, weapons and battles. Skeletal remains with signs of violent injury have been studied at a few sites, but such evidence is scarce.

The interpretation of archaeological evidence for war requires caution. Walls may have been built for prestige or flood protection as well as defence; weapons in graves may be symbols of status rather than evidence of use; and images follow artistic conventions. Combined with texts and inscriptions, however, archaeology provides an indispensable check on literary accounts, and it is the only source for the long periods and the many communities that left no written record.

docs.title: 1.4 Historiography
docs.text:
Modern study of Indian warfare began in the colonial period. Gustav Oppert’s On the Weapons, Army Organisation, and Political Maxims of the Ancient Hindus (1880) collected Sanskrit passages on weapons and argued, on weak evidence, that the ancient Indians had known gunpowder (Oppert 1880). E. Washburn Hopkins’s long study of the warrior class in the Sanskrit epic (1889) remains useful for its thorough collection of epic material (Hopkins 1889). In the first half of the twentieth century Indian scholars wrote general accounts of ancient Indian warfare: V. R. Ramachandra Dikshitar’s War in Ancient India (1944) and P. C. Chakravarti’s The Art of War in Ancient India (1941) are the most substantial (Dikshitar 1944; Chakravarti 1941). Chakravarti in particular read the Sanskrit sources critically, compared them with Greek accounts, and was willing to say where Indian armies had been weak. Sarva Daman Singh’s Ancient Indian Warfare, with Special Reference to the Vedic Period (1965) is the standard study of the early material (Singh 1965).

These writers worked partly in reaction to colonial stereotypes of an unwarlike or militarily backward India, and nationalist writing sometimes overcorrected, presenting every Indian defeat as the result of treachery and every text as evidence of scientific foresight. More recent scholarship has asked different questions. Dirk Kolff showed that north Indian soldiering between 1450 and 1850 formed a vast “military labour market” in which peasants became soldiers for pay and identities such as “Rajput” were often acquired through service rather than fixed by birth (Kolff 1990). Jos Gommans placed Mughal warfare in the context of the arid frontier, the horse trade and the movement of armies along the “high roads” of empire (Gommans 2002). Thomas Trautmann traced the history of the war elephant from its Indian origins to its spread across Eurasia (Trautmann 2015). Kaushik Roy has written comprehensive surveys of warfare in South Asia and of the relationship between Hindu thought and the ethics of war (Roy 2004, 2011, 2012). Peter Jackson’s study of the Delhi Sultanate, Stewart Gordon’s of the Marathas and Seema Alavi’s of the Company’s sepoys are among many regional and period studies used in this volume (Jackson 1999; Gordon 1993; Alavi 1995).

docs.title: 1.5 The Geography of War
docs.text:
The geography of the subcontinent shaped its wars in ways that remained remarkably constant over three thousand years. Figure 1.1 shows the passes of the north-west and some of the battlefields named in the narrative chapters; the forts, the coasts and the Company’s wars have maps of their own (Figures 10.10, 11.2 and 19.2).

Figure 1.1. Mountain passes and some battlefields of South Asia from 326 BCE to 1761 named in Chapters 2, 8 and 9. The inset enlarges the corridor north of Delhi where the battles of Tarain, Pānīpat and Karnal were fought. Positions are plotted by latitude and longitude; those of the Hydaspes crossing, Samugarh, Talikota (Rakshasa–Tangadi) and the Bolan Pass are approximate, Kurukṣetra is the traditional site of the epic battle, and Dhauli marks the site of Aśoka’s edicts in Kaliṅga, not a battlefield. The frame is that of the map in Volume 12, extended northward to 35\(^\circ\)N; the coastline is simplified, islands other than Sri Lanka are omitted, and no rivers or political boundaries are shown.

docs.title: 1.5.1 The north-western passes and the arid corridor
docs.text:
To the north, the Himalaya formed a barrier that armies crossed only with great difficulty; no major invasion of India came across the high Himalaya in the period covered by this book. To the north-west, however, the mountains of Afghanistan and Baluchistan are crossed by passes — the Khyber, the Kurram, the Gomal, the Bolan — that led from the Iranian plateau and Central Asia into the Indus valley. Through them came the Achaemenid Persians, Alexander, the Indo-Greeks, Śakas, Kuṣāṇas and Hūṇas, the Ghaznavids and Ghurids, the Mongols, Tīmūr, Bābur, Nādir Shāh and Aḥmad Shāh Durrānī. They also carried trade, pilgrims and ideas, and above all horses (Chapter 6).

Beyond the passes, an arid and semi-arid zone stretches from the Punjab and Sindh through Rajasthan and Gujarat and into the western Deccan. Jos Gommans has argued that this “arid zone” was the key to Indian military history in the medieval and early modern periods: it supported pastoral peoples who bred horses and camels, supplied mobile cavalry, and formed a corridor along which conquerors from Central Asia could move into the heart of India and down into the Deccan (Gommans 2002). The capitals of north Indian empires — Delhi, Agra, Lahore — lay where this arid corridor met the fertile Ganges plain.

docs.title: 1.5.2 The Ganges valley
docs.text: The Ganges plain, with its dense agricultural population and its great rivers, was the economic core of most north Indian empires, from Magadha and the Mauryas to the Guptas, the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughals. Its wealth paid for armies, and its peasant population supplied soldiers (Kolff 1990). Its rivers were both obstacles and highways: armies crossed them on bridges of boats, and the rivers carried supplies and river fleets. Control of the middle Ganges, with its capitals at Pāṭaliputra, Kanauj and later Delhi and Agra, was the prize of many wars.

docs.title: 1.5.3 Forests and hills
docs.text: To the south and east of the Ganges plain lay the forests and hills of central India, eastern India and the north-east. These were the homelands of peoples whom Sanskrit texts called āṭavika, “forest dwellers”, and the habitat of the wild elephants that kings captured for war (Trautmann 2015). Forest peoples served kings as soldiers, guides and elephant-catchers, and they also raided settled lands and resisted conquest; Aśoka’s Thirteenth Rock Edict contains a warning to them. Armies found the forests difficult to penetrate, and many of the longest-lasting independent states — the Gonds of central India, the Ahoms of Assam, the hill kingdoms of the north-east — drew strength from forest and hill terrain.

docs.title: 1.5.4 The Deccan and the south
docs.text: The Deccan plateau, with its flat-topped hills and its long dry season, was the land of hill forts and of cavalry warfare. Its northern edge, along the Vindhya and Satpura ranges and the Narmada river, formed a frontier between north and south that several north Indian empires failed to cross: Harṣa was stopped on the Narmada by Pulakeśin II, and the Mughals needed nearly a century (from the 1590s to 1687) to subdue the Deccan sultanates and never finally defeated the Marathas. The far south, with its rich river deltas, its long coastline and its ancient Tamil kingdoms, developed military traditions of its own, including the naval expeditions of the Cōḻas (Chapter 11).

docs.title: 1.5.5 The monsoon and the campaigning season
docs.text: The monsoon governed the calendar of war. From June to September the rains turned roads to mud, swelled rivers, spread disease and made campaigning difficult. Campaigns therefore normally began after the rains, in October or November, when the harvest was in and grain and fodder were available, and ended before the next monsoon. The festival of Daśahrā, at the end of the rains, marked in many kingdoms the beginning of the campaigning season (Chapter 13). Armies caught by the monsoon could suffer disaster: the Mughal general Mīr Jumla’s army in Assam in 1662–63 was devastated by rain and disease (Chapter 9).

docs.title: 1.5.6 The coasts
docs.text: The subcontinent’s long coastline was the site of a maritime trade that linked India to the Persian Gulf, the Red Sea, East Africa, Southeast Asia and China for more than two thousand years. Coastal states taxed and protected this trade, and some — the Cōḻas, the sultans of Gujarat, the Zamorins of Calicut, the Marathas — built fleets. But the sea was also the route by which, from 1498, European ships armed with cannon arrived, and naval power proved to be one of the foundations of the East India Company’s eventual conquest.

docs.title: 1.6 War and the Economy
docs.text:
Armies were expensive, and every Indian theorist of the state recognised the connection between military power and wealth. The Arthaśāstra states that the army has its root in the treasury, and it devotes most of its length to the administration of revenue, trade, mines, forests and agriculture (Olivelle 2013). Medieval and early modern states devised a series of institutions to pay their armies: the assignment of revenue to military commanders (iqṭā in the Delhi Sultanate, amaram among the nāyakas of Vijayanagara, jāgīr under the Mughals), the payment of soldiers in cash, and the levying of tribute from subordinate rulers (Jackson 1999; Stein 1989; Richards 1993).

The demands of war shaped the economy in turn. Armies on campaign consumed huge quantities of grain and fodder, supplied by itinerant grain carriers and by the markets that travelled with them (Chapter 6); they employed artisans to make weapons, saddles, tents and uniforms; they drew on bankers to advance money against future revenue; and they devastated the lands through which they passed. In the eighteenth century, the competition among Indian states and the European companies to pay ever larger and more expensive armies — what historians call “military fiscalism” — placed great strain on the peasantry and the banking networks of India, and the state that could best mobilise money, the East India Company, won (Roy 2011). How the Indian states and the Company met these costs is examined in Section 18.12.

docs.title: 1.7 India in the History of War
docs.text:
Indian military history has often been studied in isolation, as if the subcontinent were a world of its own. In fact, India was part of the Eurasian world of war from the beginning. The horse and the chariot came to India from the steppes in the second millennium BCE, as they came to China, Mesopotamia and Egypt. The war elephant, perfected in India, spread to the Persian, Hellenistic and Carthaginian armies and to Southeast Asia (Trautmann 2015). The mounted archer of the steppes transformed Indian warfare as he transformed that of China, Iran and eastern Europe. Gunpowder, invented in China, reached India through Central Asia and the Ottoman and Persian world. The flintlock and the drilled infantry battalion came from Europe. Indian steel, Indian elephants, Indian textiles and Indian military ideas travelled outwards.

Seen in this light, many features of Indian warfare that are sometimes presented as unique are better understood as Indian versions of common patterns: the four-arm army, the hill fort, the ethic of the warrior aristocracy, the codes of fair fighting, the hero-stone, the reliance on mercenaries and on the military labour of peasants. What was distinctive was the particular combination of these elements, shaped by Indian geography, society and religion. Comparison with other parts of the world helps to identify what was genuinely Indian and to avoid both the exaggeration of Indian uniqueness and the neglect of Indian achievement.

docs.title: 1.8 A Note on Numbers
docs.text:
Readers of Indian military history soon meet very large numbers. The Mahābhārata says that nearly four million fighting men, horses, elephants and chariots met at Kurukṣetra. Greek writers report Nanda and Mauryan armies of hundreds of thousands. Xuanzang credits Harṣa with tens of thousands of elephants. Persian chronicles describe armies of a hundred thousand horsemen and more, and Bābur says that he defeated a hundred thousand men with twelve thousand.

Such numbers must be treated with caution. Epic numbers are poetic and symbolic. Foreign observers were often told what their hosts wished them to believe. Court chroniclers had every reason to exaggerate the size of the enemy and the scale of the victory. Even administrative figures, such as the numbers of horsemen that Mughal officers were supposed to maintain, often bore little relation to the numbers actually mustered. Large armies were certainly raised — the Mughal armies of the seventeenth century were among the largest in the world — but precise figures for particular battles are rarely reliable. This volume gives numbers only with their source, and readers are encouraged to treat them as indications of scale rather than counts.

docs.title: 1.9 Some Myths This Volume Does Not Repeat
docs.text:
Popular writing on Indian military traditions contains a number of claims that do not survive examination. They are listed here so that readers can recognise them; each is discussed further in the relevant chapter.

Divine weapons as ancient technology. The epics describe weapons invoked by spells (astra) that burn, flood or blind whole armies, and the Rāmāyaṇa describes the flying chariot Puṣpaka. These are literary and religious motifs. There is no textual or archaeological basis for the claim that they record nuclear weapons, guided missiles or aircraft (Chapter 4). An unbroken Vedic science of war. No treatise on dhanurveda survives from the Vedic period. The surviving texts with that name are medieval or later compilations, and several were attributed to ancient sages long after they were written (Chapter 3). Bodhidharma and kung fu. The legend that the Indian monk Bodhidharma taught martial exercises at the Shaolin monastery first appears in the seventeenth century, about eleven hundred years after his supposed lifetime; it is not history (Chapter 20). “The mother of all martial arts”. Kaḷarippayaṟṟu in its known form is documented from roughly the twelfth century onward, and no Indian art can be shown to be the source of all others (Chapter 15). Tipu Sultan’s rockets as the origin of rocketry. The iron-cased rockets of Mysore were effective weapons and they influenced William Congreve’s rockets in Britain. They did not originate rocketry, which was known in China centuries earlier (Chapter 5).

docs.title: 1.10 Periods and Dates
docs.text:
The periods used in this volume (Table 1.1) are conventional and approximate. Dates follow the mainstream scholarly consensus; where a traditional date differs, it is identified as traditional.

docs.title: 1.11 Recurring Themes
docs.text:
Several themes run through the chapters that follow.

Military labour.

For most of Indian history, armies were assembled from many sources: royal guards, the levies of subordinate chiefs, mercenary bands, forest peoples, nomadic cavalry and peasants who took up arms for a season. The ideal of a hereditary warrior caste, the kṣatriya, coexisted with a reality in which soldiers came from almost every social group. Kolff’s study of the north Indian military labour market is the clearest demonstration of this (Kolff 1990) (Chapter 17), and the same pattern can be seen in the epics’ references to hired soldiers (bhṛta) and in the Arthaśāstra’s list of troops drawn from different sources.

Frontiers and animals.

Indian warfare was shaped by geography. The arid zone running from Sindh and Rajasthan into the Deccan supported horse-breeding pastoralists and was the corridor of conquest from Central Asia (Gommans 2002). The forests of central and eastern India supplied elephants, which were captured rather than bred and were a royal monopoly (Trautmann 2015). Most good war-horses were imported, by land from Central Asia and by sea from Arabia and Persia (Digby 1971). The availability of these animals, more than any doctrine, explains much of Indian military history.

Ideal and practice.

The texts describe an ideal of righteous war (dharmayuddha) with rules protecting non-combatants and fallen enemies. They also describe, often in the same works, deception, night attacks, assassination and the use of spies. Chapter 12 examines both, as well as the evidence of what armies actually did.

Exchange.

Indian armies adopted new weapons, animals and methods wherever they found them: the chariot from the Bronze Age world, the elephant from their own forests, horse-archery and the stirrup-equipped cavalry of the steppe, gunpowder artillery from the Ottoman and Persian world, and European drill and flintlocks in the eighteenth century. In turn, Indian elephants, steel, textiles and ideas travelled outward. A purely nativist account of Indian military history misses most of what is interesting about it.

Caste, gender and community.

Military service, the right to bear arms and the honours of warriors were distributed unequally. The dharmaśāstras reserved warfare in principle for the kṣatriya, though they allowed others to fight in emergencies; epic stories such as those of Ekalavya and Karṇa show how birth could bar access to training (Chapter 13). Women appear as rulers and commanders, as defenders of forts, and as victims of war, including in the mass self-immolations (jauhar) of besieged Rajput forts, which this volume describes without romanticising (Chapter 16). Colonial recruitment policy later froze some communities into “martial races” and excluded others (Chapter 19).

docs.title: 1.12 Dhanurveda among the Branches of Knowledge
docs.text:
Indian scholars classified knowledge in many ways, and the science of arms found a place in several schemes. In some later lists the four Vedas are each paired with a “subsidiary Veda” (upaveda): medicine (āyurveda) with the Ṛgveda, the science of arms (dhanurveda) with the Yajurveda, music (gāndharvaveda) with the Sāmaveda, and either statecraft (arthaśāstra) or architecture (sthāpatyaveda) with the Atharvaveda. The best-known statement of this scheme is in the Prasthānabheda of the sixteenth-century Advaita scholar Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, which surveys the eighteen branches of knowledge (vidyāsthāna) and gives the science of arms a brief entry among them. Similar classifications appear in other late texts.

These schemes are important as evidence of how learned brahmins organised knowledge and how they sought to give practical arts the prestige of association with the Veda. They are not evidence that a body of military science was transmitted alongside the Vedas from the Vedic period. The Vedic texts themselves contain no treatise on arms, and dhanurveda becomes a familiar name for a body of learning only in later literature, notably the epics, where Droṇa and other teachers are masters of it. As Chapter 3 explains, the surviving texts of dhanurveda are medieval or later.

The Arthaśāstra offers a different classification. It recognises four sciences that a king must learn: philosophy (ānvīkṣikī), the three Vedas (trayī), economics (vārttā) and government (daṇḍanīti), the last including the use of force (AŚ 1.2–4) (Olivelle 2013). In this scheme the conduct of war belongs to the science of government, together with law, administration and foreign policy, rather than forming a separate science of its own.

docs.title: 1.13 Military Knowledge and the Indian Knowledge Systems
docs.text:
This volume is part of a series on Indian knowledge systems, and it is fair to ask in what sense the subject of this book is “knowledge”. Much military knowledge in India, as elsewhere, was practical: it was learned by doing, transmitted from teacher to pupil and from father to son, and rarely written down. The Arthaśāstra’s administrative theory, the epics’ reflections on the ethics of war, the technical literatures of elephants, horses and medicine, the metallurgical skill of the smiths who made crucible steel, the engineering of forts and their water systems, and the body knowledge of wrestlers and martial artists are all forms of knowledge, but of very different kinds.

Treating them as “Indian knowledge systems” has value if it encourages their serious study. It also carries a risk: the temptation to present every practice as a “science”, every text as older than it is, and every achievement as unique or unprecedented. The approach of this volume is to take Indian military knowledge seriously by subjecting it to the same historical and critical scrutiny that scholars apply to other traditions. That means dating texts, testing claims against evidence, comparing Indian practices with those of other societies, and acknowledging both achievements and failures. Respect for a tradition is better shown by understanding it accurately than by exaggerating it.

docs.title: 1.14 The Martial Arts
docs.text:
India has many living martial traditions: wrestling (kuśtī, earlier mallayuddha) across the north and west; kaḷarippayaṟṟu in Kerala; silambam and the vital-point art of varmakkalai in Tamil Nadu; gatka among Sikhs; huyen langlon (thang-ta) in Manipur; and many more local forms of stick, sword and shield play. They differ greatly in history, in social setting and in the evidence available for their past. Some are documented in medieval texts; others are known mainly from nineteenth- and twentieth-century descriptions and reconstructions.

Two cautions apply throughout. First, the claims made for these arts by modern promoters — that they are thousands of years old, that they are the source of other Asian martial arts, or that their knowledge of the body’s vital points (marma, varmam) has been confirmed by neuroscience — are reported here as claims and examined against the evidence. Second, this volume describes these arts historically. It does not give instruction in techniques intended to injure, and it treats the therapeutic claims of traditional vital-point medicine as traditional claims.

docs.title: 1.16 This Volume and the Series
docs.text: Military traditions touch many other fields of Indian knowledge, and several subjects mentioned in this volume are treated more fully elsewhere in the series Bhāratīya Jñāna Paramparā. The Arthaśāstra, the dharmaśāstras and the theory of kingship are discussed in Volume 18, Rājanīti and Dharmaśāstra. The epics and Purāṇas, whose battle narratives are used here, are the subject of Volume 7, Itihāsa–Purāṇa. The medical knowledge of wounds and vital points belongs to Volume 13, Āyurveda; metallurgy, including iron, steel and the chemistry of gunpowder, to Volume 14, Rasāyana; the architecture of forts and cities to Volume 16, Vāstu–Śilpa; maritime trade and seafaring to Volume 19, Vāṇijya and Samudra; the education of princes and the gymnasium to Volume 22, Manas and Śikṣā; and the relations between martial arts, dance and theatre to Volume 9, Saṅgīta–Nāṭya.

docs.title: 1.17 Conventions
docs.text: Sanskrit, Pali and Prakrit words are given in the International Alphabet of Sanskrit Transliteration (IAST); the anusvāra is written ṃ. Tamil and Malayalam words follow the standard scholarly transliteration (with ḻ, ṟ and ṉ) where they are technical terms, and familiar spellings for names of places and modern institutions. Persian and Urdu terms are given in a simplified transliteration. Dates are CE unless marked BCE. The glossary at the end of the volume explains the principal technical terms.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Chakravarti (1941) and Singh (1965): the best older studies of early Indian warfare.

  • Roy (2004): a survey of South Asian warfare to the present.

  • Gommans (2002) and Kolff (1990): the essential modern studies of Mughal warfare and the military labour market.

  • Trautmann (2015): the history of the war elephant.

  • Zarrilli (1998) and Alter (1992): studies of two living martial traditions.

docs.title: Chapter 2: Warfare in Early India, from the Harappans to the Age of Harṣa
2.1 Introduction
docs.text: This chapter surveys warfare in the subcontinent from the cities of the Indus civilisation to the early seventh century CE. It is a long period, and the evidence for it changes in kind as well as quantity. For the Harappan period we have only archaeology; for the Vedic period, hymns and ritual texts; for the age of the Buddha, religious literature composed and edited later; and from Alexander’s invasion onwards, Greek and Latin accounts, inscriptions, coins and an increasing body of Sanskrit and Tamil literature. Throughout, the reader should remember that warfare is easier to infer than to describe: we know far more about what weapons and arrays existed in principle than about how any particular battle was fought.

docs.title: 2.2 The Indus Civilisation
docs.text:
The mature Harappan civilisation (c. 2600–1900 BCE) built large planned towns. Many of them — Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Kalibangan, Dholavira, Lothal — had massive walls of mud-brick or stone around a raised “citadel” and sometimes around the lower town as well. Whether these walls were built mainly for defence is debated. They would certainly have impeded attackers, but they also protected against floods, controlled access to the town and expressed civic power. Archaeologists have found copper and bronze spearheads, arrowheads, knives and daggers, as well as sling-stones and clay balls; but they have found few weapons designed only for war, no clear evidence of destruction by large armies, and no depictions of battles. Gregory Possehl, summarising the evidence, concluded that the Indus civilisation shows remarkably little sign of organised warfare compared with contemporary Mesopotamia or Egypt (Possehl 2002). This does not mean that there was no violence, only that it is not visible in the record.

Two popular claims need correction. First, there is no convincing evidence of the domesticated horse or of the spoked-wheel chariot in the mature Harappan cities. Claims of “Harappan horse bits” or of horse figures on seals rest on misidentifications. Second, the discovery at Sinauli in western Uttar Pradesh (c. 2000–1800 BCE) of burials with solid-wheeled vehicles, swords and shields has been described by its excavators as evidence of “chariots”. The vehicles had solid wheels and there is no evidence of the horses that drew them; whether they were war chariots in the later sense is uncertain and remains under study.

docs.title: 2.3.1 War in the Ṛgveda
docs.text:
The hymns of the Ṛgveda (core c. 1500–1200 BCE) were composed by a society for which cattle were the chief form of wealth and raids for cattle were a normal form of conflict; one of the words for battle, gaviṣṭi, literally means “seeking cows”. The principal war-god is Indra, praised as the breaker of forts (purandara) and the winner of cattle, water and light. The most important military technology was the light, horse-drawn chariot (ratha) with spoked wheels, carrying a driver and a warrior armed with a bow (Singh 1965).

Sarva Daman Singh’s study of the Vedic evidence describes the chariot, the bow (dhanus, possibly composite), arrows tipped with horn or metal and sometimes poisoned, the quiver, body armour (varman), helmets (śiprā), spears and axes. The hymns refer to purs, usually translated “forts”; these were probably earthworks or palisaded enclosures rather than stone cities (Singh 1965). Battles were fought between tribes (jana) and between the Āryas and peoples they called Dāsa or Dasyu.

docs.title: 2.3.2 The Battle of the Ten Kings
docs.text: The best-known Vedic battle is the “battle of the ten kings” (dāśarājña), celebrated in hymns of the seventh book of the Ṛgveda, especially RV 7.18, 7.33 and 7.83 (Jamison and Brereton 2014). Sudās, king of the Bharatas, with the help of Indra and of his priest Vasiṣṭha, defeated a coalition of ten kings beside the river Paruṣṇī, identified with the Ravi in Punjab. The hymns say that the enemies tried to divert or cross the river and were drowned. The episode is one of the earliest named battles in the literature of the subcontinent, but it is known only from praise-poems composed by the victors’ priests, and its details — numbers, tactics, even the identity of all ten kings — cannot be reconstructed with confidence.

docs.title: 2.3.3 Later Vedic kingship
docs.text: In the later Vedic period (c. 1200–500 BCE) chiefdoms became kingdoms, settlement moved eastward into the Ganges valley, and iron came into general use, first for weapons and later for tools. The great royal rituals described in the Brāhmaṇas — the royal consecration (rājasūya) and the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) — contain martial elements: a mock cattle raid, a chariot drive, the year-long wandering of the sacrificial horse guarded by armed men. Among the king’s “jewels” (ratnin), the officials honoured during the consecration, are the army commander (senānī) and the charioteer (sūta) (Singh 1965; Thapar 2002).

docs.title: 2.4 Iron, Cities and the Rise of States
docs.text: The emergence of the first large states in the Ganges valley in the first millennium BCE — the period sometimes called the “second urbanisation” — was connected with changes in technology and economy that also transformed warfare. Iron, which came into widespread use in the early first millennium BCE, allowed the production of more and cheaper weapons as well as tools for clearing forest and cultivating the heavy soils of the middle Ganges plain. Agricultural surpluses supported growing towns, rulers and armies. Many towns of the period were surrounded by earthen ramparts and moats, and some, like Rājagṛha and Kauśāmbī, by massive walls; the fortified city became the centre of the state. Coinage, in the form of punch-marked silver coins, made it easier to pay soldiers and officials. The rise of Magadha, which possessed rich agricultural land, iron ores in the hills to the south, and forests full of elephants, illustrates how these factors combined (Thapar 2002; Trautmann 2015). The armies of the Mauryas and their successors were built on this economic foundation.

docs.title: 2.5 The Age of the Mahājanapadas and the Rise of Magadha
docs.text:
By the sixth and fifth centuries BCE Buddhist and Jain texts list sixteen great states (mahājanapada) across north India, some ruled by kings and some by assemblies of clans (gaṇa or saṅgha). Over the following two centuries Magadha, in south Bihar, absorbed its rivals. Its rise owed much to its position on the Ganges, its iron ores, its rich rice lands, and the forests to the south that supplied elephants (Thapar 2002; Trautmann 2015).

Jain canonical tradition describes the war of King Kūṇika (Ajātaśatru) of Magadha against the Vajjian confederacy and credits him with two remarkable devices: the mahāśilākaṇṭaka, apparently a machine for throwing large stones, and the rathamusala, a chariot fitted with a mace or blades. Whether these descriptions record real machines or exaggerate simpler devices is uncertain, but they show that siege and battlefield engines were imagined, and probably used, before the Mauryas.

Greek writers who accompanied or followed Alexander describe the army of the Nanda kings of Magadha, beyond the Beas, as very large; the figures they give (in one version 200,000 infantry, 20,000 cavalry, 2,000 chariots and 3,000 or more elephants) differ between authors and probably reflect rumour reaching Alexander’s camp rather than any count (McCrindle 1893). They are best treated as evidence that Magadha was known to field an army much larger than those of the Punjab kingdoms.

docs.title: 2.6 Alexander in the Punjab
docs.text:
Alexander of Macedon crossed the Hindu Kush in 327 BCE and campaigned in the north-west and Punjab until 325 BCE. The Greek and Latin historians, especially Arrian, writing in the second century CE from earlier memoirs, are the first detailed external accounts of Indian armies in battle (Chakravarti 1941; Roy 2004).

The best documented battle is that against Porus, ruler of the Paurava kingdom between the Jhelum (Hydaspes) and the Chenab, in 326 BCE (Figure 1.1). Porus held the far bank of the Jhelum with an army including infantry, cavalry, chariots and war elephants. Alexander made repeated feints along the river and then crossed by night upstream in a rainstorm. In the battle that followed, Alexander’s cavalry defeated Porus’s cavalry on the flank, while the Macedonian phalanx, armed with long pikes, held the elephants. Arrian and Curtius report that rain had made the ground slippery and muddy, hampering the Indian chariots and the archers, whose long bows had to be braced against the ground. The elephants, wounded and leaderless, eventually trampled friend and foe alike. Porus was wounded and captured, but Alexander restored him as ruler, now as an ally.

Several points emerge from the Greek accounts. Indian armies of the north-west fought as combined forces of four arms. The elephants were formidable against horses unused to them, but were vulnerable to disciplined infantry and to panic. Indian archers used long bows that were powerful but slow. And Indian commanders did not yet have a cavalry able to match Alexander’s veteran horsemen. Modern attempts to identify Porus’s deployment with a named vyūha from the Sanskrit texts are speculation; no Indian account of the battle survives. Alexander’s army refused to advance beyond the Beas in 326 BCE, and he withdrew down the Indus.

docs.title: 2.7.1 Candragupta and Seleucus
docs.text: Within a few years of Alexander’s departure, Candragupta Maurya (r. c. 321–297 BCE) overthrew the Nandas and established an empire that eventually extended from Afghanistan to Bengal and into the Deccan. Around 303 BCE he fought Seleucus, Alexander’s successor in the east. The outcome was a treaty by which Seleucus ceded territories in the north-west and received five hundred war elephants, which he later used in the wars of the successors in western Asia. Trautmann has shown that this transfer was a turning point in the spread of the war elephant beyond India (Trautmann 2015).

docs.title: 2.7.2 Megasthenes on the Mauryan army
docs.text:
Megasthenes, Seleucus’s envoy to Candragupta’s capital Pāṭaliputra, wrote an account of India that survives only in quotations by later authors, chiefly Strabo, Diodorus and Arrian. According to Strabo’s summary, the war office was administered by thirty officials divided into six boards of five, responsible respectively for co-operation with the navy, for transport and supply, for the infantry, the cavalry, the chariots and the elephants. Soldiers were paid from the royal treasury and their weapons kept in royal arsenals. Megasthenes also reported that farmers worked their fields undisturbed while battles were fought nearby, a statement often cited as evidence of restraint in Indian warfare, though it is an idealised generalisation (Chakravarti 1941). Pliny gives the strength of the Mauryan army as 600,000 infantry, 30,000 cavalry and 9,000 elephants; like other ancient figures, these numbers cannot be verified.

Megasthenes also divided the people of India into seven classes, a scheme that does not correspond exactly to the Indian varṇas. His fifth class was the soldiers: second in number only to the farmers, maintained with their horses and elephants at the king’s expense, and idle in peacetime while others made their weapons, tended their animals and drove their chariots (Chakravarti 1941; Thapar 1961). The picture of a professional, state-paid army agrees with the Arthaśāstra, though Megasthenes generalised from what he saw at the capital.

docs.title: 2.7.3 Aśoka and the Kaliṅga war
docs.text: Candragupta’s grandson Aśoka (r. c. 268–232 BCE) conquered Kaliṅga (coastal Odisha) in about the eighth year of his reign, c. 261 BCE. His Thirteenth Rock Edict, inscribed in several versions across the empire (though, significantly, not in Kaliṅga itself), records the cost in his own words: 150,000 people were deported, 100,000 killed, and many times that number died. Aśoka says that he felt remorse and that thereafter he regarded “conquest by dhamma” as the best conquest (Hultzsch 1925; Thapar 1961). The edict is a rare example of a ruler publicly regretting a war, but it should be read carefully: Aśoka did not disband his army, and in the same edict he warns the forest peoples on his borders that he has power as well as compassion. The figures, though given by the victor himself, are round numbers and may not be precise.

docs.title: 2.8 Between the Mauryas and the Guptas
2.8.1 Invaders and the cavalry revolution
docs.text: After the Mauryan empire broke up in the second century BCE, north-western India was ruled successively by Indo-Greek kings, Śakas (Scythians), Parthians and Kuṣāṇas, all of whom came from or through the steppe and Iranian world. They brought with them a style of warfare in which cavalry was decisive: horse-archers using powerful composite bows, and heavily armoured horsemen with long lances (Section 2.9). These centuries probably saw the final decline of the war chariot in north India, although chariots remained in literary convention and ceremony long after they had disappeared from the battlefield (Roy 2004).

docs.title: 2.8.2 Kaliṅga, the Deccan and the far south
docs.text:
The Hāthīgumphā inscription of Khāravela of Kaliṅga (probably first century BCE) is one of the earliest royal records of campaigns: it claims victories against Magadha and a confederacy of Tamil states, records an army sent westward in defiance of the Sātavāhana king Sātakarṇi, and describes the recovery of a Jina image taken from Kaliṅga by a Nanda king. In the Deccan the Sātavāhana kings fought the Śaka Kṣatrapas of western India for control of the ports and trade routes (Section 2.10); their coins show ships.

In the far south, the Tamil poems of the Caṅkam anthologies (core c. 1st–3rd centuries CE) describe warfare between the Cēra, Cōḻa and Pāṇṭiya kings and many smaller chiefs (Section 2.11) (Hart and Heifetz 1999). The battle of Veṇṇi, in which the Cōḻa king Karikāla defeated a coalition including the Cēra and Pāṇṭiya kings, is celebrated in several poems. The Tamil grammatical tradition classified war poetry by situation: veṭci (cattle raid), karantai (recovery of cattle), vañci (invasion), kāñci (resistance), uḻiñai (siege), nocci (defence of a fort), tumpai (pitched battle) and vākai (victory) (Hart and Heifetz 1999).

docs.title: 2.9 The Kuṣāṇa Empire
docs.text: The Kuṣāṇas, a branch of the Yuezhi people who had migrated from the borders of China to Bactria, built in the first and second centuries CE an empire that stretched from Central Asia across Afghanistan into the Ganges valley as far as Mathura and beyond. Under Kaniṣka (probably early second century CE), it was one of the great powers of Eurasia, alongside Rome, Parthia and Han China, and it controlled important stretches of the Silk Roads. Kuṣāṇa coins and sculpture show kings in the dress of steppe horsemen — long belted coats, trousers and boots — and some carry swords and maces. Their armies, built around cavalry, brought the military practices of the steppe deep into north India. The Kuṣāṇa period also saw intense cultural exchange, visible in the Gandhāra and Mathurā schools of art and in the spread of Buddhism to Central Asia and China (Thapar 2002).

docs.title: 2.10 The Western Deccan and the Śaka Kṣatrapas
docs.text:
The wars between the Sātavāhana kings of the Deccan and the Śaka rulers of western India, known by the title Kṣatrapa (“satrap”), are among the best documented of the early centuries CE, because both sides left inscriptions. The prize was the rich trade of the western coast, whose ports, such as Bharukaccha (Broach) and Kalyāṇa, exported Indian goods to the Roman world, and the routes that linked them to the interior.

An inscription of the queen mother Gautamī Balaśrī at the Buddhist caves of Nasik praises her son Gautamīputra Sātakarṇi (early second century CE) as the destroyer of Śakas, Yavanas and Pahlavas and the uprooter of the line of the Kṣaharāta ruler Nahapāna; coins of Nahapāna restruck by Gautamīputra confirm his victory. A generation later, the great rock inscription of the Śaka ruler Rudradāman at Junagadh in Gujarat (c. 150 CE) claims that he twice defeated Sātakarṇi, “lord of the Deccan”, but spared him because of a family relationship. The Junagadh inscription is also notable for being written in Sanskrit, and for recording the repair of a great reservoir damaged by a storm; the kings who fought these wars were also builders and administrators (Thapar 2002).

These inscriptions show the language of military glory that would become standard in Indian royal inscriptions: the king as conqueror of named enemies, protector of the social order, and merciful victor who restores defeated rivals.

docs.title: 2.11 Warfare in the Tamil Country
docs.text:
The Tamil poems of the Caṅkam anthologies give a picture of warfare unlike anything in Sanskrit literature: concrete, local, and seen from the viewpoint of the participants and their families (Hart and Heifetz 1999). The kings of the Cēra, Cōḻa and Pāṇṭiya lines, and many smaller chiefs (vēḷir), fought constantly. Wars often began with cattle raids, in which bands of warriors seized the herds of an enemy village and the owners pursued them to recover them; men who died in such fights were commemorated with hero-stones (naṭukal), which the poems describe being set up, decorated with peacock feathers and worshipped. Larger wars involved the siege of forts, protected by ditches, walls and gates studded with spikes, and battles fought with elephants, chariots, cavalry and infantry armed with spears, swords, bows and shields.

The poems describe the war drum (muracu), kept in its own shrine and worshipped, whose capture meant defeat; the garlands of flowers that identified the warriors of each side; the bards (pāṇar, poruṉar) who followed kings to war, praised their victories and received rich gifts; and the grief of mothers and wives. One celebrated theme is the king’s generosity: a king’s fame depended as much on his gifts to poets as on his victories. Another is the honour of death in battle: one poem refers to the custom of cutting with a sword the body of a king who had died of illness, so that he should not lose the heaven of heroes.

These poems are the most important early evidence for warfare in south India, and they preserve a tradition that remained distinct from the Sanskrit one for many centuries, though the two gradually merged.

docs.title: 2.12 Sri Lanka
docs.text:
The Pali chronicles of Sri Lanka, the Dīpavaṃsa and the Mahāvaṃsa, compiled in the fourth to sixth centuries CE from earlier traditions, tell of wars between the Sinhalese kings of Anurādhapura and rulers from south India. The most famous is the war of King Duṭṭhagāmaṇī (second century BCE according to the chronicle) against the Tamil king Eḷāra, who had ruled Anurādhapura for many years. The chronicle describes Duṭṭhagāmaṇī’s champions, his war elephant Kaṇḍula, the siege of a series of forts, and the final single combat in which Eḷāra was killed; it also records that Duṭṭhagāmaṇī ordered Eḷāra to be honoured with a monument (Geiger 1912). The chronicle is a religious history written to glorify Buddhist kings, and its accounts of these wars are shaped by that purpose; its treatment of the ethics of the war is discussed in Chapter 12.

Sri Lanka’s later wars lie outside the period of this chapter, and the rest of the volume returns to the island only in passing, so they are summarised here. The Cōḻas held the north of the island from the late tenth century until Vijayabāhu I drove them out around 1070 (Chapter 11); Parākramabāhu I of Polonnaruva (r. 1153–1186) sent expeditions to Burma and intervened in the civil wars of the Pāṇḍya kingdom. From the sixteenth century the European companies seized the coasts, and the hill kingdom of Kandy became the centre of resistance. Kandyan armies, fighting in forest and mountain country, destroyed Portuguese columns at Danture in 1594 and Randeniwela in 1630; Rājasiṃha II then allied with the Dutch, who expelled the Portuguese by 1658 and kept the coasts for themselves. The Dutch took and lost Kandy in the war of 1760–66, and the British garrison left in Kandy after its occupation in 1803 was destroyed. The kingdom fell only in 1815, when the British advanced with the support of disaffected Kandyan chiefs; its last king was exiled to Vellore (Section 10.17), and the rising of 1817–18 in Uva was suppressed with great severity (Silva 1981). These wars, like the hill wars of the Indian mainland, show how far terrain and seasons could offset the advantages of European arms.

docs.title: 2.13 The Gupta Age
docs.text:
The Gupta dynasty, founded in the early fourth century CE, built the largest north Indian empire since the Mauryas. Samudragupta’s long praise-inscription on the Allahabad pillar lists the kings he “uprooted” in the Ganges valley, those of the south whom he captured and released, and the frontier peoples and distant rulers who paid him homage (Thapar 2002). Gupta gold coins show the kings as archers, as horsemen, and in the act of killing lions, tigers and rhinoceroses: martial and hunting prowess was part of the royal image. Candragupta II (r. c. 375–415) defeated the Śaka rulers of western India and gained the ports of Gujarat.

In the mid-fifth century the Hūṇas (Huns) attacked the north-west, and Skandagupta claims in his Bhitari inscription to have defeated them. Their later invasions, described in the next section, accelerated the break-up of Gupta power. Like the Śakas before them, the Hūṇas fought as mounted archers.

docs.title: 2.14 The Hūṇas and Yaśodharman
docs.text:
The Hūṇa invasions of the late fifth and early sixth centuries were among the most destructive episodes of early Indian history. The Hūṇas who entered India were probably a branch of the Hephthalites or related groups who had established a power in Bactria and Afghanistan. Their kings Toramāṇa and Mihirakula ruled the north-west and parts of central India in the early sixth century; Mihirakula is remembered in Buddhist sources, including the account of Xuanzang, as a persecutor of Buddhism and destroyer of monasteries, and in Kalhaṇa’s history of Kashmir as a cruel king.

The Hūṇas were defeated by a coalition of Indian rulers. An inscription on a pillar at Sondhni near Mandasor in Malwa records that the Aulikara king Yaśodharman forced Mihirakula to pay him homage; the later Guptas also claimed victories. The Hūṇa episode hastened the fragmentation of north India into regional kingdoms, and some Hūṇa groups settled in India and were absorbed into the population, some of their descendants later claiming Rajput status. The episode illustrates both the vulnerability of north India to mounted invaders from the north-west and its capacity to absorb them.

docs.title: 2.15 The Early Seventh Century: Harṣa and Pulakeśin II
docs.text: By about 600 CE the political map of India was a pattern of regional kingdoms. Two of their rulers are particularly well documented. Harṣavardhana (r. 606–647) of Thanesar and Kanauj is the subject of a prose biography, the Harṣacarita of his court poet Bāṇa, and is described by the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang. Xuanzang’s account credits Harṣa with a very large army of elephants and cavalry built up in years of continuous campaigning; the figures he reports are those he was told at court. The Cāḷukya king Pulakeśin II of Bādāmi stopped Harṣa’s advance into the Deccan, probably on the Narmada, an event recorded in the Aihoḷe inscription of 634 (Thapar 2002). The Aihoḷe inscription says that Harṣa’s “joy” (harṣa) melted away when his elephants fell in battle. The pun works only because elephants were the decisive and the most prized arm of the age.

docs.title: 2.16 The Battle Books of the Mahābhārata as Cultural History
docs.text:
Even if the battle books of the Mahābhārata cannot be read as an account of a historical war, they are rich evidence for the ideals and imagination of warfare in the centuries of their composition (Brockington 1998; Hopkins 1889). They imagine war as a contest between heroes, each with his chariot, charioteer, banner, conch and named bow, fighting duels in which they exchange arrows and divine weapons while the common soldiers die in their thousands in the background. They describe the formal challenges and boasts that preceded combat, the honour paid to a worthy opponent, the shame of retreat, and the grief of the victors. They reveal anxieties about loyalty, as in Karṇa’s divided allegiance, and about the obligations of teachers and kinsmen on opposing sides, as in the cases of Bhīṣma and Droṇa. And they dramatise, again and again, the conflict between the rules of fair fighting and the will to win.

In this sense the epic is a source for the history of warrior values rather than of military operations. Its influence on later Indian ideas of war was enormous: it supplied the models of heroism, the vocabulary of arrays and weapons, and the moral dilemmas through which later generations thought about war, from medieval court poets to modern nationalists and filmmakers.

docs.title: 2.17 Military Administration in the Mauryan and Gupta States
2.17.1 The Arthaśāstra’s army
docs.text:
Whatever its precise date, the Arthaśāstra provides a picture of the military administration that a large Indian state of the early centuries was thought to need (Kangle 1960–1965; Olivelle 2013). The army was under a commander-in-chief (senāpati), with superintendents (adhyakṣa) for each arm — infantry, cavalry, chariots and elephants — and for the armoury, the stables and the elephant forests. Soldiers were paid from the treasury, and the text gives a scale of salaries for officials and soldiers, from the highest ministers and commanders to the trained foot-soldier. Weapons and armour were made in state workshops and kept in the royal armoury, to be issued when needed. Elephants, horses and their keepers, trainers and physicians were all under state control.

The text also recognises that armies were not only made up of the king’s regular troops; its classification of troops by source and reliability is discussed in Section 7.5. It also discusses the army’s camp-followers and supporting personnel: engineers to clear roads and build bridges, labourers to dig ditches and build ramparts, and physicians with surgical instruments, medicines, oils and bandages, accompanied by women with food and drink, to stand behind the battle line to care for the wounded and encourage the fighting men (AŚ 10.3) (Olivelle 2013).

docs.title: 2.17.2 Gupta officers
docs.text: Gupta inscriptions and seals name military and diplomatic officers whose titles suggest a developed military administration. The mahābalādhikṛta was a commander of forces; the mahādaṇḍanāyaka a high officer, apparently with military and judicial functions; the sāndhivigrahika was the minister of “peace and war”, responsible for relations with other states. Hariṣeṇa, who composed Samudragupta’s Allahabad inscription, held this last title, together with the offices of kumārāmātya and mahādaṇḍanāyaka (Thapar 2002). The offices of the sāndhivigrahika and of military commanders continue in the inscriptions of many later dynasties.

docs.title: 2.18 Military Medicine in Early India
docs.text:
Indian medicine developed a substantial body of knowledge about wounds, which must have been informed by the experience of war. The surgical treatise attributed to Suśruta, the Suśruta Saṃhitā, which reached its present form by c. 500 CE, devotes considerable attention to the extraction of foreign bodies (śalya), including arrowheads, from the body; it describes the signs by which a lodged arrowhead could be located, the instruments used to extract it, and the treatment of the wound afterwards. It also describes the marmas, the vital points where injury is especially dangerous (Chapter 14), the dressing of wounds, the setting of fractures and the stopping of bleeding. Although the Suśruta Saṃhitā is a medical, not a military, text, its surgery of wounds was relevant to soldiers, and the Arthaśāstra’s prescription that physicians should accompany the army shows that the connection was recognised.

The epics, too, describe the care of wounded warriors: physicians extracting arrows, and the wounded Bhīṣma, lying on his bed of arrows, refusing the surgeons who come to treat him. In later centuries, Mughal and Maratha armies employed surgeons, and the care of wounded soldiers is mentioned in chronicles; but systematic military medicine, with field hospitals and medical services, developed only in the colonial army of the nineteenth century.

docs.title: 2.19 The Fourfold Army and the Akṣauhiṇī
2.19.1 The four limbs
docs.text: Throughout the period covered in this chapter the standard Sanskrit description of an army is caturaṅga, “having four limbs”: chariots (ratha), elephants (hastin, gaja), cavalry (aśva) and infantry (patti, padāti). The formula appears in the epics, the Arthaśāstra and the Buddhist and Jain canons, and it gave its name to the board game caturaṅga, the ancestor of chess (Section 2.20). The relative importance of the four arms changed over time: the chariot was the elite arm of the Vedic and early epic warrior, the elephant became the decisive arm from the later first millennium BCE, and cavalry rose in importance from the period of the Śakas and Kuṣāṇas onwards. In addition to the four arms, real armies included engineers, labourers, scouts, porters, camp followers, physicians, cooks and the boatmen who managed river crossings, as the Arthaśāstra recognises.

docs.title: 2.19.2 The epic arithmetic
docs.text:
The Mahābhārata gives a scheme of military units in which each unit is three times the size of the one below it, beginning with the patti of one chariot, one elephant, three horsemen and five foot-soldiers (MBh 1.2.15–23) (Buitenen 1973–1978). Ten anīkinīs make an akṣauhiṇī. Table 2.1 sets out the arithmetic.

Table 2.1. The epic scheme of army units (Mahābhārata 1.2) Unit Chariots Elephants Horse Foot patti 1 1 3 5 senāmukha (3 patti) 3 3 9 15 gulma (3 senāmukha) 9 9 27 45 gaṇa (3 gulma) 27 27 81 135 vāhinī (3 gaṇa) 81 81 243 405 pṛtanā (3 vāhinī) 243 243 729 1,215 camū (3 pṛtanā) 729 729 2,187 3,645 anīkinī (3 camū) 2,187 2,187 6,561 10,935 akṣauhiṇī (10 anīkinī) 21,870 21,870 65,610 109,350

The epic says that eighteen akṣauhiṇīs fought at Kurukṣetra, eleven for the Kauravas and seven for the Pāṇḍavas. By the epic’s own arithmetic this means some two million foot-soldiers, more than a million horsemen, and nearly four hundred thousand chariots and as many elephants: numbers far beyond what any pre-modern state could have assembled or fed. The scheme is an exercise in idealised symmetry, a way of expressing vastness, not a record of real organisation. Other texts, including the Arthaśāstra, give quite different unit schemes (Kangle 1960–1965), and real armies were never composed in fixed ratios of chariots to elephants to horses.

docs.title: 2.20 From Caturaṅga to Chess
docs.text: The four-limbed army gave its name to India’s most widespread military-themed contribution to world culture. Chess is descended from an Indian board game called caturaṅga, whose pieces were the arms of the army. H. J. R. Murray’s A History of Chess (1913), which remains the fundamental study, concluded that the game originated in north-western India, probably in the sixth or early seventh century CE (Murray 1913). The earliest clear literary references are Indian and Persian. In the Harṣacarita, Bāṇa, praising the peace of Harṣa’s reign, plays on the double meaning of words for war and for the game: in that kingdom, he says, the only “armies” arrayed on squares were those of the board. A Middle Persian text of the Sasanian period, the Wizārišn ī čatrang (“The Explanation of Chess”), tells how an Indian king sent the game to the court of Khosrow I (r. 531–579) as a challenge, and how the minister Wuzurgmihr deciphered it and invented backgammon in reply. The story is legendary, but it shows that Persians believed the game had come from India.

docs.title: 2.20.1 The pieces
docs.text:
The names of the pieces trace the game’s journey (Table 2.2). The Sanskrit rājan (king) became the Persian shāh; the king’s counsellor or general (mantrin, senāpati) became the Persian farzīn and Arabic firz, which in Europe became the queen; the elephant (gaja, Persian pīl, Arabic al-fīl) became the Spanish alfil and the English bishop; the horse became the knight; the foot-soldier became the pawn; and the chariot became the Persian rukh, the rook, though the derivation of this word is uncertain. The word “chess” comes, through Old French, from shāh, and “checkmate” from the Persian shāh māt, “the king is helpless” (Murray 1913).

Table 2.2. The pieces of caturaṅga and their descendants Sanskrit Persian Arabic English rājan (king) shāh shāh king mantrin, senāpati (counsellor, general) farzīn firz queen gaja, hastin (elephant) pīl fīl bishop aśva (horse) asp faras knight ratha (chariot) rukh rukh rook padāti (foot-soldier) piyāda baidaq pawn

docs.title: 2.20.2 From Persia to the world, and back
docs.text:
After the Arab conquest of Iran, chess (shaṭranj) became a favourite game of the Islamic world, whose players and writers developed its theory and composed problems. It reached Europe through Muslim Spain and Sicily by the tenth and eleventh centuries, and spread eastward to Central Asia, China, Korea, Japan and Southeast Asia, where local variants developed. In late fifteenth-century Europe the queen and bishop acquired their long-range moves, producing the faster modern game. Al-Bīrūnī in the eleventh century described a four-handed form played with dice in India; Murray rejected the view that this was the original form (Murray 1913).

Chess remained popular in India in its own forms, played at the Mughal and other courts, and Indian rules differed from European ones until the nineteenth century, for example in the promotion of pawns and the king’s first move. In the 1850s the Bengali player Moheschunder Bannerjee played many games in Calcutta with the British player John Cochrane, and his style is remembered in the name “Indian Defence” given to a family of openings in which Black develops the bishop on the long diagonal. Mir Sultan Khan, a Punjabi player brought to England by his patron, won the British championship in 1929, 1932 and 1933. After independence chess became an organised sport; Viswanathan Anand became world champion in 2000 and held the undisputed title from 2007 to 2013, and D. Gukesh won the world championship in 2024. The game of the four-limbed army has returned to its homeland as a modern sport.

docs.title: 2.21 Greek and Latin Writers on Indian Warfare
docs.text:
Greek and Latin writers are among the earliest datable witnesses to warfare in India, and they are often quoted, sometimes uncritically. Their value and their limits differ. Herodotus wrote at second hand, about Indians from the Persian province in the north-west serving in the army of Xerxes. The historians of Alexander wrote centuries after the events, from the memoirs of his officers, which were themselves partisan; they magnify the difficulty of his victories and repeat the figures his officers gave. Megasthenes, who visited the Mauryan court around 300 BCE, survives only in quotation and paraphrase by later writers, who selected what interested them. All of them saw India through Greek categories, as when Megasthenes divided Indian society into seven “classes”, one of them the warriors (McCrindle 1877, 1893; Thapar 2002). Table 2.3 lists the principal writers.

Table 2.3. Greek and Latin writers on Indian warfare Writer and work Date Relevance and limits Herodotus, Histories 5th c. BCE Describes Indians in Xerxes’ army with cotton garments and cane bows and arrows tipped with iron; second-hand Ctesias, Indika c. 400 BCE Fragmentary; much is fabulous Megasthenes, Indika c. 300 BCE Lost; known through Strabo, Diodorus, Arrian and Pliny; describes the Mauryan war office, the warrior class and the royal army Diodorus Siculus, Library of History 1st c. BCE Preserves a summary of Megasthenes and an account of Alexander’s campaign Strabo, Geography, book 15 Late 1st c. BCE – early 1st c. CE The fullest summary of Megasthenes on administration and the army Quintus Curtius Rufus, History of Alexander 1st c. CE Rhetorical narrative of the campaign against Porus Pliny the Elder, Natural History, book 6 1st c. CE Gives figures for the armies of Indian kings, derived from Megasthenes and other sources; unverifiable Plutarch, Life of Alexander c. 100 CE Describes Porus and the army’s refusal to march on to the Ganges Arrian, Anabasis and Indica 2nd c. CE The most careful account of the Hydaspes battle; the Indica describes Indian infantry with long bows and cavalry

docs.title: 2.22 Assessment
docs.text:
The wars and campaigns discussed in this chapter, with their main sources, are listed in Table 2.4. Two features of that list matter for the rest of the book. The first is the character of the sources. Before the Mauryas almost every war is known from the poetry or the religious literature of the victors, and even after them the best evidence comes from royal inscriptions written to praise a conqueror and from foreigners who never saw a battle; no Indian account of a single battle of this period describes how it was fought. The second is the importance of contact. The horse and chariot, the mounted archer of the steppe and the Hellenistic and Kuṣāṇa styles of cavalry each came from outside, while the war elephant, perfected in the Ganges valley, went out from India to the Mediterranean; iron, by contrast, was probably worked in India from local beginnings. The texts examined in the next chapter were composed against this background, and they should be read in its light.
