docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Singh (1965): the standard study of Vedic warfare.

  • Chakravarti (1941): classical sources, Greek accounts and their interpretation.

  • Possehl (2002): the Indus civilisation, including the question of warfare.

  • Thapar (1961) and Hultzsch (1925): Aśoka and his inscriptions.

  • Hart and Heifetz (1999): translations of the Tamil poems of war and kingship.

  • Trautmann (2015): the elephant in Indian and Eurasian warfare.

  • Murray (1913): the classic history of chess and its Indian origin.

docs.title: Chapter 3: The Texts of War: Arthaśāstra, Epic, Nīti and Dhanurveda
3.1 Introduction
docs.text:
Readers who approach the subject through popular books often meet the statement that ancient India possessed a complete written “science of war”, the dhanurveda, handed down from the Vedic sages. The reality is more interesting and more complicated. Indian literature contains a great deal about war, but it is scattered across many genres — statecraft (arthaśāstra and nītiśāstra), law (dharmaśāstra), epic, Purāṇa, court poetry, technical treatises on elephants, horses and machines, and, from the thirteenth century, Persian manuals and chronicles. The texts that bear the name dhanurveda are late arrivals in this literature, and most of them are compilations whose dates are uncertain.

This chapter introduces the principal texts, with the best available estimates of their dates. Its purpose is to give readers a map of the sources used in the rest of the book and a sense of what kind of evidence each provides. Table 3.2, near the end of the chapter, summarises the discussion.

docs.title: 3.2.1 Date and authorship
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra, “the science of material gain” or statecraft, is a prose treatise in fifteen books. It names its author as Kauṭilya (or Kauṭalya), and tradition identifies him with Cāṇakya (also called Viṣṇugupta), the minister who helped Candragupta Maurya to power around 321 BCE. Modern scholarship, beginning with Thomas Trautmann’s statistical study of its vocabulary and style, has shown that the text is not the work of a single author of the Mauryan period (Trautmann 1971). It contains layers of different date. Olivelle, its latest editor and translator, argues that an original treatise was composed between about 50 BCE and 125 CE and revised into its present form between about 175 and 300 CE (Olivelle 2013). This volume therefore dates the Arthaśāstra c. 50 BCE–300 CE, and treats the attribution to a minister of Candragupta as traditional. Hartmut Scharfe’s investigations into the text’s political vocabulary support a similar view of its composite character (Scharfe 1993). Mark McClish has since argued that the text as we have it is the product of a redaction that reorganised an earlier treatise on government and brought it into line with brahmanical norms of law and kingship; on this reading the Arthaśāstra’s accommodation of dharma, discussed in Chapters 7 and 12, belongs largely to its later layer (McClish 2019).

The text was lost to modern scholarship until a manuscript was discovered in Mysore and published by R. Shamasastry, who translated it in 1915 (Shamasastry 1915). R. P. Kangle’s critical edition, translation and study (1960–1965) remains fundamental (Kangle 1960–1965); there are later translations by L. N. Rangarajan and Patrick Olivelle, and a selection by Mark McClish and Olivelle (Rangarajan 1992; Olivelle 2013; McClish and Olivelle 2012).

docs.title: 3.2.2 Military content
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra is not primarily a military treatise; most of it concerns administration, revenue, law and diplomacy. But its outlook is that of a ruler who expects to fight, and it contains more systematic military material than any other early Sanskrit work:

  • Book 2 (on the activities of superintendents) describes the construction of forts (2.3–4), the armoury and its superintendent (2.18), and the superintendents of horses (2.30), elephants (2.31–32), and chariots, infantry and the army commander (2.33). It specifies the training, feeding and medical care of horses and elephants, the classes of weapons and armour to be stored, and the qualities of a commander.

  • Book 7 sets out the “six measures” of foreign policy (ṣāḍguṇya): peace, war, staying quiet, marching, seeking shelter and the dual policy. It also defines three kinds of war (AŚ 7.6): open war (prakāśayuddha), concealed war (kūṭayuddha), involving surprise attacks and deception in the field, and “silent war” (tūṣṇīṃyuddha), the use of secret agents to kill or subvert enemy leaders.

  • Book 9 concerns preparations for a campaign: assessment of one’s own strength and the enemy’s, the right season for marching, and the six kinds of troops available, from hereditary and hired troops to forest peoples, whose relative reliability it discusses (Section 7.5).

  • Book 10 deals with war itself: the laying out of the camp, the march, the protection of the army, battlefields suitable for each arm, the functions of each arm, and the battle arrays (vyūha) (Chapter 7).

  • Books 12–14 deal with the weak king facing a stronger enemy, with the capture of forts by siege and subversion, and with secret practices, including poisons and magical recipes of doubtful efficacy.

The tone throughout is pragmatic. The Arthaśāstra advises the king to fight only when he can win, to prefer diplomacy and subversion to battle when they are cheaper, and to use deception freely. It is the most important single source for the institutions of war in early India, but it is a normative manual. It tells us what a learned theorist thought a king should do; it does not tell us that any particular king did it.

docs.title: 3.3.1 The Mahābhārata
docs.text:
The Mahābhārata, in its critical edition some 75,000 verses (about 100,000 in the traditional reckoning), grew over many centuries, roughly 400 BCE to 400 CE (Brockington 1998). Its central narrative is a war between two sets of cousins, the Pāṇḍavas and the Kauravas, culminating in an eighteen-day battle at Kurukṣetra. Several of its books are therefore military in content:

  • the Ādiparvan describes the education of the princes by Droṇa and the tournament in which they display their skills;

  • the Udyogaparvan describes the diplomacy that preceded the war, the embassies, the assembling of allies and the mustering of armies;

  • the battle books (Bhīṣma-, Droṇa-, Karṇa- and Śalyaparvan) describe the fighting day by day, with named arrays (vyūha), single combats, the use of divine weapons and the deaths of the great heroes;

  • the Sauptikaparvan describes the night massacre of the sleeping Pāṇḍava camp by Aśvatthāman;

  • the Śāntiparvan, after the war, contains Bhīṣma’s long instruction to Yudhiṣṭhira on the duties of kings (rājadharma), including rules for the conduct of war, and on conduct in emergencies (āpaddharma) (Fitzgerald 2004).

The epic’s battle descriptions are poetry, governed by heroic conventions: they focus on duels between champions, exaggerate numbers, and mix the plausible with the supernatural. Their value lies in the vocabulary and ideals of war they preserve, and in the moral arguments about war that run through the whole poem (Chapter 12). Alf Hiltebeitel’s study of the battle books shows how they are also shaped by ritual and mythic patterns (Hiltebeitel 1976).

docs.title: 3.3.2 The Rāmāyaṇa
docs.text: The Rāmāyaṇa of Vālmīki tells of Rāma’s war against Rāvaṇa, king of Laṅkā, in its sixth book, the Yuddhakāṇḍa. It describes the building of a causeway across the sea, the siege of Laṅkā, a city of walls, moats and gates, and a series of battles between Rāma’s army of monkeys and bears and the demons of Laṅkā. Its military details are fewer and more fantastic than those of the Mahābhārata, but the poem’s account of Rāma’s training by the sage Viśvāmitra, who gives him divine weapons, became a model for later descriptions of royal education.

docs.title: 3.4 Buddhist and Jain Literature
docs.text:
Buddhist and Jain texts are not usually thought of as sources for military history, but they contain much that bears on it. The Pali canon, compiled over several centuries and written down in Sri Lanka by tradition in the first century BCE, describes the kingdoms and republics of the Buddha’s time and their wars. In the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta, King Ajātasattu of Magadha sends his minister to ask the Buddha whether he can conquer the Vajjian confederacy; the Buddha replies indirectly that the Vajjis will not decline as long as they meet often in assembly, act in concord, respect their elders, their women and their shrines, and follow their ancient customs. The passage is a reflection on the strength of republican institutions in war, and Magadha’s later conquest of the Vajjis is attributed in the tradition to the use of a minister to sow dissension among them.

The Jātaka stories, which tell of the Buddha’s previous lives, contain many tales of kings, armies, sieges and archers, and they mention military training at Takkasilā (Taxila), the celebrated centre of learning in the north-west, where princes are said to have gone to learn the arts, including archery. These stories are folk tales in Buddhist dress and cannot be dated precisely, but they reflect the ideas of their time about kingship and war. Popular claims that Taxila was “the world’s first university” or a “military academy” founded in the seventh century BCE go far beyond this evidence; Taxila was a city where individual teachers taught pupils, not an institution of the later monastic kind.

Jain canonical texts, compiled and edited over many centuries, describe the wars of the Magadhan king Kūṇika (Ajātasattu) and, as Chapter 2 noted, credit him with machines of war. Jain literature also developed a distinctive treatment of war in the story of Bharata and Bāhubali, the two sons of the first Jina, Ṛṣabha: when their armies meet, the brothers agree to fight a series of single combats rather than sacrifice their soldiers, and Bāhubali, on the point of victory, renounces the world.

docs.title: 3.5 Court Poetry and Historical Writing
docs.text:
Sanskrit court poetry (kāvya) often describes war, especially in the conventional “conquest of the quarters” (digvijaya), in which the hero marches around India subduing the kings of each region. Kālidāsa’s Raghuvaṃśa (c. fourth to fifth century) describes such a campaign by King Raghu in its fourth canto. Bāṇa’s Harṣacarita (seventh century) describes the mustering and march of Harṣa’s army in vivid detail, with its elephants, horses, camels, baggage, camp followers and the damage it did to the fields. Bilhaṇa’s Vikramāṅkadevacarita (late eleventh century) celebrates the wars of the Cāḷukya king Vikramāditya VI. These works are panegyrics, but their authors were courtiers who had seen armies and campaigns, and their descriptions contain much realistic detail.

The most important work of Sanskrit historical writing, Kalhaṇa’s Rājataraṅgiṇī (“River of Kings”), a verse history of Kashmir completed in 1148–49, is unusual in its critical attitude to its sources and its frankness about the failings of kings. Its later books describe in detail the civil wars of Kashmir in the eleventh and twelfth centuries: the struggles of kings with the landholding ḍāmaras, the sieges of forts, the use of mercenaries, the plundering of temples, the role of women in politics and the sufferings of the people. It is one of the richest sources for medieval warfare anywhere in India.

docs.title: 3.6.1 Manu and the legal tradition
docs.text: The seventh chapter of the Mānava Dharmaśāstra (Manusmṛti, c. 2nd century CE) sets out the duties of a king. It covers the choice of a capital and the kinds of fort (MDh 7.70), the six measures of foreign policy, the four means (upāya) of conciliation, gifts, dissension and force, the conduct of a campaign, and the rules of fair fighting (MDh 7.90–93), which are discussed in Chapter 12 (Olivelle 2005). Later legal texts, such as the Yājñavalkya Smṛti, repeat and adapt these rules. Their interest is less in military technique than in the legitimacy of war and the obligations of the warrior.

docs.title: 3.6.2 Kāmandaka’s Nītisāra
docs.text: The Nītisāra (“Essence of Policy”) of Kāmandaka is a verse treatise on statecraft that acknowledges its debt to the Arthaśāstra and condenses much of its political doctrine. Its date is uncertain; most estimates place it between the fifth and eighth centuries CE. It treats the circle of states, the six measures, the qualities of ministers and envoys, espionage, the march and battle arrays. It was widely read, and it was translated into Old Javanese — a sign of the reach of Indian political literature in Southeast Asia.

docs.title: 3.6.3 The Tamil tradition
docs.text: In Tamil, the Caṅkam war poems (Chapter 2) preserve a non-Sanskrit vocabulary and ethic of war, and the Tirukkuṟaḷ treats kingship and the army systematically (Section 3.7).

docs.title: 3.7 The Tamil Kuṟaḷ on the Army
docs.text: The Tirukkuṟaḷ, a Tamil collection of 1,330 couplets probably composed around the fifth century CE, deserves a fuller word, because it is one of the few Indian texts outside Sanskrit to treat military matters systematically. Its second book, on poruḷ (wealth, polity), is devoted to kingship. Couplet 381 lists six things a king must possess — army, people, wealth, ministers, allies and fortress — and the book contains chapters on the fortress (araṇ), the excellence of the army (paṭaimāṭci) and the pride of the soldier (paṭaiccerukku). The couplets praise an army that does not flee, that is ancient and tested, and that is well led; they praise the soldier who counts as lost the days on which he received no wound, and who prefers death in battle to dishonour. The Kuṟaḷ combines these heroic values with a strong emphasis on justice, generosity and the avoidance of needless cruelty in kingship, and it remains one of the most widely read ethical works in Tamil.

docs.title: 3.8.1 The Agni Purāṇa
docs.text:
The Purāṇas are encyclopaedic texts that grew over many centuries, and several of them include chapters on kingship and war. The most important for this subject is the Agni Purāṇa, which contains a short group of four chapters on dhanurveda (248–251 in Rājendralāla Mitra’s edition; the chapter numbers differ slightly in other printed editions), together with chapters on royal duties, omens, the consecration of weapons and battle arrays (Mitra 1870–1879; Gangadharan 1984–1987). The Agni Purāṇa is a compilation whose present form is generally dated to the later first millennium CE or the early second; estimates range from about the eighth to the eleventh century, and some of its material may be older (Rocher 1986). It cannot be used as evidence for Vedic or Mauryan practice.

The Agni Purāṇa’s dhanurveda divides fighting into five kinds, by the way the weapon is used: with weapons released by a machine, released by the hand, released and then recovered, not released at all (the sword), and without weapons (wrestling). It then describes the archer’s stances, the drawing and loosing of the bow, target practice, and the handling of the noose, sword, mace and many other weapons. Chapter 4 sets out its teaching in detail (Section 4.7.2). The Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa, probably composed in Kashmir in the second half of the first millennium CE, also includes material on kingship, weapons and the training of princes.

docs.title: 3.8.2 Later dhanurveda texts
docs.text:
Several later texts call themselves dhanurveda or include sections on it:

  • The Dhanurveda attributed to Vasiṣṭha (Vasiṣṭha-Dhanurveda-Saṃhitā), printed in the early twentieth century, is a compilation of uncertain date. It shares material with the Agni Purāṇa and with medieval anthologies, and its attribution to the Vedic sage is traditional. It cannot be dated before the second millennium CE with any confidence.

  • The Śārṅgadhara-paddhati, a Sanskrit anthology compiled in 1363, includes a section of verses on archery.

  • The Kodaṇḍamaṇḍana, attributed to Maṇḍana, an architect at the court of Rāṇā Kumbhā of Mewar in the fifteenth century, is a treatise on archery.

  • The Nītiprakāśikā, published by Gustav Oppert in 1882, is attributed in its colophons to Vaiśampāyana, the narrator of the Mahābhārata (Oppert 1882). The attribution is traditional and the work is medieval; it lists weapons and arrays and was used by Oppert in his study of Indian weapons (Oppert 1880).

Other titles that appear in popular lists — a “Viśvāmitra Dhanurveda”, a “Hastavidyārṇava” of hand-to-hand combat, a “Yuddhatantradīpikā” — are either unpublished, unlocated or misdescribed. One example deserves correction: the Hastividyārṇava (“Ocean of Elephant Lore”) is an illustrated Assamese treatise on elephants, completed in 1734 by Sukumār Barkaith for the Ahom king Śiva Siṃha and his queen (Choudhury 1976). It is a work on the care, classification and medicine of elephants, not on unarmed combat.

The pattern is clear. A body of practical knowledge about arms certainly existed in early India; the epics and the Arthaśāstra presuppose it. But the written dhanurveda that survives is a relatively late and partial codification, and the idea of a complete ancient “Dhanurveda” text is a construction of later tradition.

docs.title: 3.9.1 Elephants and horses
docs.text: Specialised literatures on elephants (gajaśāstra, hastyāyurveda) and horses (aśvaśāstra, often associated with the name of Śālihotra or of the Pāṇḍava Nakula) deal with the breeding, classification, training and veterinary care of the animals on which armies depended. The Hastyāyurveda attributed to the sage Pālakāpya and the Kerala Mātaṅgalīlā are among the elephant texts; their dates are uncertain. Trautmann uses this literature, together with the Arthaśāstra, in his history of the war elephant (Trautmann 2015). Chapter 6 discusses it.

docs.title: 3.9.2 Machines
docs.text: The Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra, an architectural encyclopaedia attributed to King Bhoja of Mālwa (eleventh century), includes a chapter on mechanical devices (yantra) that mentions machines for the defence of forts alongside automata and water devices. The Yuktikalpataru, also attributed to Bhoja, discusses among other things ships and weapons; the attribution is uncertain and the text as transmitted may be later. Both works are better evidence for the learned imagination of courts than for the actual machines used in war, but they show that military engineering was considered a fit subject for Sanskrit learning.

docs.title: 3.9.3 The Mānasollāsa
docs.text: The Mānasollāsa (also called Abhilaṣitārthacintāmaṇi), compiled for the Cāḷukya king Someśvara III of Kalyāṇa around 1129–1131, is an encyclopaedia of the things a king should know and enjoy (Shrigondekar 1925–1961). Its sections on royal recreation include detailed accounts of wrestling (mallavinoda), of elephant-fights and of horsemanship, and its sections on government include military matters. It is one of the most important sources for the martial sports of the medieval Deccan (Chapter 14).

docs.title: 3.9.4 The Śukranīti
docs.text: The Śukranīti, attributed to Śukra, the preceptor of the demons, is often cited for its description of guns (nālika) and gunpowder. Lallanji Gopal showed in 1962 that the text in its present form is a nineteenth-century composition (Gopal 1962). It is therefore no evidence for ancient knowledge of firearms, a claim made in the nineteenth century by Oppert and repeated since.

docs.title: 3.10 Persian Manuals and Chronicles
docs.text:
From the thirteenth century, the courts of north India produced a large literature in Persian. Among the earliest relevant works is the Ādāb al-ḥarb wa’l-shajāʿa (“The Rules of War and Bravery”) of Fakhr-i Mudabbir, written at Delhi in the early thirteenth century, which discusses the duties of rulers and generals, the organisation of armies, arms, sieges and battle arrays in the tradition of Persian “mirrors for princes”. The chronicles of the Delhi Sultanate record campaigns and military reforms from the sultans’ point of view (Section 3.14) (Jackson 1999).

For the Mughal period, the memoirs of Bābur (written in Chagatai Turkish and later translated into Persian) give a soldier’s account of the battles of Pānīpat (1526) and Khanua (1527) (Thackston 1996). Abū’l-Faẓl’s Āʾīn-i Akbarī (completed c. 1598) describes the imperial army, the ranks (manṣab) of nobles, the arsenal, and the imperial stables of horses and elephants in statistical detail (Blochmann 1873). These works were written to glorify the dynasty, but their administrative information is of great value (Gommans 2002; Irvine 1903).

docs.title: 3.11 Regional Literatures
docs.text:
Regional literatures add other perspectives:

  • Rajasthani heroic poetry (rāso, vāt, khyāt) celebrates the deeds of Rajput warriors, often long after the events; the Pṛthvīrāj Rāso, in its surviving forms much later than its hero’s twelfth-century lifetime, is the most famous example (Talbot 2016).

  • Marathi chronicles (bakhar), such as the Sabhāsad Bakhar (1690s) on Śivājī, and ballads (povāḍā) preserve memories of the Maratha wars. The Ājñāpatra (1716), a statement of royal policy attributed to Rāmacandrapant Amātya, contains important chapters on forts and on the navy (Gordon 1993).

  • Assamese buraṅjī chronicles record the wars of the Ahom kingdom against the Mughals and others with unusual precision (Gait 1906).

  • Punjabi and Braj writings associated with the Sikh Gurus and their followers, including the compositions collected in the Dasam Granth, contain martial poetry and descriptions of battles (Dhavan 2011).

docs.title: 3.12 Inscriptions
docs.text:
Inscriptions are the most reliable source for the political and military history of early and medieval India, because they are contemporary and can usually be dated. Several kinds are relevant.

  • Royal eulogies (praśasti) list a king’s conquests and those of his ancestors. Samudragupta’s Allahabad pillar inscription, the Aihoḷe inscription of Pulakeśin II, and the long historical introductions (meykkīrtti) of Cōḻa inscriptions are examples. They are boastful and selective, but they record the names of enemies and battles and can often be checked against the inscriptions of the other side.

  • Grants of land on copper plates or stone often name the officers present, among them military commanders, and sometimes record grants to soldiers or to the families of men who died in battle.

  • Hero-stones commemorate individual warriors who died fighting (Chapter 13). They are the most abundant evidence for small-scale warfare and for the participation of ordinary people.

  • Temple inscriptions record gifts by soldiers and commanders and, in the Cōḻa period, the endowments made for regiments.

docs.title: 3.13 Foreign Observers
docs.text:
Foreign writers provide an outside view, often valuable precisely because they noticed what Indian writers took for granted. The most important include:

  • Greek and Latin authors: Arrian’s Anabasis and Indica, both drawing on the memoirs of Alexander’s officers and on Megasthenes; Strabo, Diodorus and Pliny, who preserve Megasthenes’ account of Mauryan India (Chakravarti 1941).

  • Chinese pilgrims: Faxian (early fifth century) and Xuanzang (seventh century), who describe the kingdoms they visited, including Harṣa’s army and court.

  • Arab and Persian geographers and scholars: the ninth- and tenth-century authors who described the Indian kingdoms of their time, and al-Bīrūnī, whose Kitāb al-Hind (c. 1030) is a remarkable account of Indian society and learning (Eaton 2019).

  • Travellers: Marco Polo, who visited south India in the 1290s; Ibn Baṭṭūṭa, who served Muḥammad bin Tughluq in the 1330s and 1340s; the Portuguese Domingo Paes and Fernão Nuniz, who described Vijayanagara and its army in the sixteenth century; and seventeenth-century European visitors to the Mughal court such as François Bernier and Niccolao Manucci, who described the Mughal army on the march.

  • European company records: from the seventeenth century, the letters and records of the Portuguese, Dutch, English and French companies contain a vast body of information on Indian armies, wars and military markets.

Each of these sources has its biases — Greek writers saw India through the lens of their own culture, travellers repeated what they were told, company servants judged Indian states by their usefulness to trade — but together they provide a check on Indian court literature and fill many of its gaps.

docs.title: 3.14 Persian Historical Writing
docs.text: The Persian chronicles of the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughal empire are the main narrative sources for the military history of north India from the thirteenth to the eighteenth century. Among the most important are Minhāj al-Sirāj Jūzjānī’s Ṭabaqāt-i Nāṣirī (1259–60), which covers the Ghurid conquest and the early sultanate; Ziyāʾ al-Dīn Baranī’s Tārīkh-i Fīrūz Shāhī (1357), with its account of ʿAlāʾ al-Dīn Khaljī’s reforms; Bābur’s memoirs; Abū’l-Faẓl’s Akbarnāma and Āʾīn-i Akbarī; and the many histories of the later Mughal period (Jackson 1999; Gommans 2002). Their authors were usually courtiers, and they wrote to glorify their patrons and to offer moral lessons; their accounts of battles follow literary conventions, and their figures for armies and casualties are often inflated. But they provide detailed chronologies, names, and much administrative information, and historians have learned to read them critically, comparing them with inscriptions, coins, regional sources and the accounts of foreign observers.

docs.title: 3.15 The Vocabulary of War
docs.text:
The languages of Indian warfare reflect its history. Sanskrit supplied a rich vocabulary of war, much of which passed into the regional languages. From the thirteenth century, Persian became the language of administration and of military affairs at the courts of the Delhi sultans, the Deccan sultanates and the Mughals, and many Persian and Turkic military terms entered Hindi, Urdu, Marathi, Bengali, Punjabi and other languages; some of them, such as sipāhī (sepoy), passed into English. Table 3.1 lists some common terms. It is not a list of exact equivalents — the institutions behind the words differed — but it shows how the two vocabularies existed side by side, and how readers moving between Sanskrit and Persian sources must translate not only words but concepts.

Table 3.1. Some military terms in Sanskrit and Persian English Sanskrit Persian (and Hindustani) army senā, bala, camū, daṇḍa lashkar, fauj soldier yodha, bhaṭa, sainika sipāhī infantry patti, padāti piyāda cavalry, trooper aśvāroha, sādin sawār; risāla (a cavalry unit) commander senāpati, daṇḍanāyaka sipahsālār, sardār war, battle yuddha, saṅgrāma, raṇa, samara jang, ḥarb, razm battle array vyūha ṣaff vanguard; centre agra; madhya, uras harāwal; qol wings pakṣa barānghār, juwānghār camp skandhāvāra, śibira lashkargāh, urdū fort durga qilʿa; Hindi gaṛh fort commander durgapāla qilʿadār bow; arrow dhanus, cāpa; bāṇa, śara kamān; tīr sword khaḍga, asi shamshīr; Hindi talwār shield carman, phalaka, kheṭaka sipar; Hindi ḍhāl armour kavaca, varman zirih (mail), jaushan gun; musket (late) nālika tūp; bandūq, tufang artillery park — tūpkhāna elephant gaja, hastin, nāga fīl; Hindi hāthī banner dhvaja, patākā ʿalam war-drum dundubhi, bherī naqqāra spy cara, gūḍhapuruṣa jāsūs envoy dūta ilchī, wakīl pay vetana, bhakta ṭalab, mawājib tribute kara, bali pīshkash, kharāj

The coexistence of these vocabularies is itself historical evidence. Sanskrit inscriptions of the Vijayanagara kings borrow Persian titles; Marathi documents of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries are full of Persian administrative terms; and the Persian chroniclers of the Mughals use Hindi words for Indian institutions. Military language, like military practice, was a meeting ground of traditions.

docs.title: 3.16 Manuscripts and Editions
docs.text:
Many of the texts discussed in this chapter survive in a small number of manuscripts, and several have never been critically edited. The Arthaśāstra itself was recovered only in the early twentieth century, when R. Shamasastry identified a palm-leaf manuscript of it at Mysore in 1905, and further manuscripts were found later that allowed Kangle to prepare his critical edition (Kangle 1960–1965). The dhanurveda texts are known mostly from late manuscripts and from printed editions of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, some of them based on single manuscripts and of uncertain reliability. The Mānasollāsa was edited in three volumes between 1925 and 1961 (Shrigondekar 1925–1961); the Hastividyārṇava was published with its illustrations and a translation in 1976 (Choudhury 1976).

Manuscript libraries in India — among them the Sarasvati Mahal Library at Thanjavur, the Oriental Research Institute at Mysore, the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute at Pune, and the Government Oriental Manuscripts Library at Chennai — and in Europe hold other works on arms, elephants, horses and statecraft, many of them unstudied. Their cataloguing, editing and translation would add considerably to our knowledge. Claims about the contents of unpublished manuscripts, however, should be treated with caution until the texts are edited and their dates established; several “ancient military treatises” cited in popular literature cannot be located at all.

docs.title: 3.17 Translation and Exchange
docs.text:
Texts on war, like other texts, moved between languages. At Akbar’s court the Mahābhārata was translated into Persian as the Razmnāma (“Book of War”) in the 1580s, and the Rāmāyaṇa was also translated; illustrated copies were made for the emperor and his nobles, showing the epic battles in the dress and arms of the Mughal age (Chapter 13). Persian works on horses and elephants drew on Sanskrit treatises, and Sanskrit and vernacular authors in turn borrowed from Persian. Kāmandaka’s Nītisāra travelled to Java, and the epics, with their battles and divine weapons, were retold in the languages of Southeast Asia and carved on the temples of Java and Cambodia. In the colonial period European scholars translated the Arthaśāstra, the epics and the dharmaśāstras, and their interpretations shaped how Indians themselves came to understand these texts.

The textual traditions of war were never closed. Military knowledge, like other forms of knowledge, circulated among courts, communities and languages, and was transformed in the process.

docs.title: 3.18 Reading the Sources in Translation
docs.text:
Most readers will meet the sources described in this chapter in translation, and the choice of translation matters. For the Arthaśāstra, R. P. Kangle’s critical edition and annotated translation remains the scholarly standard, and Patrick Olivelle’s translation adds a fresh study of the text’s composition and date; R. Shamasastry’s pioneering translation of 1915 is historically important but less reliable, and L. N. Rangarajan’s rearranged version is readable but should be checked against the others (Kangle 1960–1965; Olivelle 2013; Shamasastry 1915; Rangarajan 1992). For the Mahābhārata, K. M. Ganguli’s complete prose translation of 1883–96 is freely available, while the incomplete Chicago translation begun by J. A. B. van Buitenen and continued by James Fitzgerald is based on the critical edition and is more accurate (Ganguli 1883–1896; Buitenen 1973–1978; Fitzgerald 2004). The Mānava Dharmaśāstra is best read in Olivelle’s critical edition and translation (Olivelle 2005).

For the Tamil war poems, George Hart and Hank Heifetz’s translation of the Puṟanāṉūṟu is reliable and well annotated (Hart and Heifetz 1999). For the Mughal period, W. M. Thackston’s translation of Bābur’s memoirs and H. Blochmann’s translation of the first volume of the Āʾīn-i Akbarī are standard (Thackston 1996; Blochmann 1873). Readers should be cautious with anthologies and websites that print “verses” on war without precise references to edition, chapter and verse: many such quotations cannot be traced to any text, and several that circulate widely were composed in modern times.

Persian manual of war, Delhi Śārṅgadhara-paddhati 1363 Anthology with archery verses Kodaṇḍamaṇḍana 15th c. (attr. Maṇḍana) Archery Bāburnāma 1520s–1530 Campaigns of Bābur Āʾīn-i Akbarī c. 1598 Mughal army and administration Ājñāpatra 1716 Maratha forts and navy Hastividyārṇava 1734 Assamese treatise on elephants Vasiṣṭha-Dhanurveda uncertain, probably late medieval Archery compilation Nītiprakāśikā uncertain, medieval Weapons and arrays Śukranīti 19th c. (Gopal) Polity; mentions firearms

docs.title: 3.19 Reading Battle Narratives
docs.text: Battle narratives, whether in epic poetry, court chronicles or ballads, pose particular problems for the historian. They follow literary conventions: the hero’s single combat, the dramatic reversal, the omen, the heroic death. They use numbers to impress rather than to inform. They often concentrate on the deeds of a few leaders and ignore the mass of soldiers. And they were written after the event, often long after, by authors with reasons to praise or blame. The modern historian reads them alongside other evidence — inscriptions, documents, the accounts of the other side, archaeology, the geography of the battlefield — and asks what kind of truth each source can offer. A Persian chronicle may be reliable on the sequence of events and the names of commanders while exaggerating the size of the enemy; a Rajput ballad may be unreliable on facts but invaluable as evidence for how a battle was remembered; an inscription may record the outcome of a battle while saying nothing of how it was fought. Learning to read these sources critically is the beginning of military history.

docs.title: 3.20 How to Read the Texts
docs.text:
Three principles guide the use of these sources in this volume.

First, date the text, not the tradition. A text that claims to transmit the teaching of a Vedic sage must be dated by its language, its contents and its manuscripts, not by its claim. The Agni Purāṇa’s dhanurveda is evidence for what a learned compiler of the late first millennium thought about weapons, not for the Vedic period.

Second, distinguish norm from practice. Treatises tell rulers what they ought to do; chronicles, inscriptions and the accounts of observers tell us what rulers did. The two sometimes coincide, sometimes do not.

Third, beware of numbers and lists. Sanskrit technical literature loves enumeration — four arms, six measures, thirty-two arrays, sixty-four arts. Such lists organise knowledge and aid memory; they do not necessarily describe distinct practices that all existed. Troop and casualty figures call for the same caution (Section 1.8).

  • Rocher (1986): the Purāṇas and the problems of dating them.

  • Gangadharan (1984–1987): English translation of the Agni Purāṇa.

docs.title: Chapter 4: Dhanurveda: The Bow, the Archer and the Divine Weapons
4.1 Introduction
docs.text: The bow gave its name to the Sanskrit science of arms. In the epics the greatest warriors — Arjuna, Karṇa, Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Rāma — are archers first, and the bow is the weapon that defines the hero. Kings of the Gupta dynasty had themselves shown on their coins holding a bow; Rajput and Mughal princes were painted hunting with bow and arrow; and in many forest and hill communities the bow remained the everyday weapon of hunting and war into the twentieth century. This chapter considers what is known about Indian bows and arrows, what the texts of dhanurveda say about the archer’s training, how archery appears in the epics, and how the “divine weapons” of the epics should be understood.

docs.title: 4.2.1 The evidence
docs.text:
The Ṛgveda mentions the bow (dhanus), its string (jyā), the quiver and arrows with points of horn or metal. One hymn (RV 6.75), addressed to the weapons of the warrior, praises the bow and its string; with the bow, the poet prays, “may we win cows” (RV 6.75.2) (Jamison and Brereton 2014; Singh 1965). The Vedic chariot-fighter was primarily an archer.

The Greek writers who accompanied Alexander described the Indian infantry bow as equal in length to the man who carried it. Arrian reports that the archer rested the lower end on the ground and braced it with his left foot to draw it, and that its long arrows could pierce shield and breastplate (Chakravarti 1941). This was evidently a long self-bow, probably of bamboo, which grows abundantly in India and makes an effective bow. Such bows remained common among infantry and forest peoples throughout Indian history.

The composite bow — a short, recurved bow built of a wooden core with horn on the belly and sinew on the back, glued and bound — stores more energy for its length and is well suited to use from horseback or chariot. Composite bows were known in the ancient Near East and the steppe, and the Vedic warrior’s bow may have been of this kind, though the hymns do not describe its construction. What is certain is that the composite bow came to dominate Indian cavalry warfare with the arrival of Śaka, Kuṣāṇa and Hūṇa horse-archers and, later, of the Turkic cavalry of the Delhi Sultanate. Surviving Indian composite bows, most of them from the seventeenth to nineteenth centuries, are short, sharply recurved, and often lacquered and painted; examples of the Mughal and Rajput courts are preserved in many museum collections (Elgood 2004; Egerton 1880). Bows of steel are also found, but they appear to have been rare and in some cases ceremonial.

docs.title: 4.2.2 Names of bows
docs.text: Sanskrit has many words for the bow — dhanus, cāpa, kārmuka, kodaṇḍa, śarāsana, iṣvāsa — and the epics give personal names to the bows of gods and heroes: Śiva’s Pināka, Viṣṇu’s Śārṅga, Arjuna’s Gāṇḍīva. Popular books sometimes treat these names as a classification of bow types, describing the kodaṇḍa as a recurve bow or the kārmuka as a composite war-bow. The texts do not support these identifications. The Arthaśāstra does attach four of the words to materials — kārmuka to bows of palm, kodaṇḍa to bows of bamboo, drūṇa to bows of wood and dhanus to bows of horn (AŚ 2.18) (Kangle 1960–1965) — but in most literature the words are used as synonyms, and the named bows are attributes of particular deities and heroes, endowed in the stories with miraculous powers.

docs.title: 4.3 The Composite Bow of the Later Period
docs.text:
The composite bow that dominated Indian cavalry warfare from the medieval period onwards was a sophisticated object. Its core was a thin strip of wood, often in several pieces joined together; to the belly (the side facing the archer) were glued strips of horn, usually from the water buffalo, which resist compression; to the back (the side facing the target) were glued layers of sinew, which resist tension. The whole was bound, covered with birch bark, leather or lacquer, and often painted. The tips (“ears”) were stiff and angled forward, acting as levers when the bow was drawn. Such bows were short — often little more than a metre long — and powerful, and they could be shot from horseback in any direction. They required great skill to make, months or years to season, and careful protection from damp, which could weaken the glue; Indian armies in the rainy season had to keep their bows in cases.

In its later Indian forms the composite bow was closely related to the bows of Persia, Central Asia and the Ottoman empire, and the surviving courtly examples carry the painted and gilded floral decoration of that wider world (Elgood 2004). Bamboo self-bows and simpler bows continued to be used by infantry and by forest and hill peoples.

docs.title: 4.4 The Draw and the Thumb Ring
docs.text:
There are two main ways of drawing a bow. In the “Mediterranean” draw, the string is pulled with the first three fingers; in the “Mongolian” or thumb draw, the string is held by the bent thumb, locked by the forefinger, and the thumb is protected by a ring. The thumb draw was used by the horse-archers of the steppes and was adopted by the Turks, Persians and Mughals. Indian museums contain many thumb rings (Persian zihgīr, shast) of jade, agate, ivory, metal and other materials, some of them of great beauty (Figure 4.1); Mughal emperors and princes are often painted wearing them (Elgood 2004). Indian sculpture of earlier periods shows archers using finger draws, though the conventions of sculpture make it difficult to identify techniques precisely, and the Agni Purāṇa also describes a finger draw (Section 4.7.2). The more elaborate descriptions of a “classical” Indian draw and its anchor points found in some popular accounts are not in the early texts.

Figure 4.1. An archer’s thumb ring of pale green jade inlaid with gold and set with red and green stones, Indian, seventeenth or eighteenth century (Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York). The ring protected the thumb that held the string in the thumb draw. Photo: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, CC0 1.0, via Wikimedia Commons (cropped)

docs.title: 4.5 Arrows
docs.text:
Indian arrows were usually made of reed or bamboo, fletched with feathers and tipped with heads of bone, horn or, from the first millennium BCE, iron. The epics and later texts name many kinds of arrows by the shape of their heads: the nārāca, often described as made wholly of iron; the ardhacandra, with a crescent-shaped head; the kṣurapra, “razor-edged”; the bhalla, with a broad blade; and the vatsadanta, “calf’s tooth” (Hopkins 1889). The names suggest specialised heads for piercing armour, cutting and wounding, though the epic battle descriptions use them more for poetic variety than for technical precision.

Poisoned and barbed arrows were known. Vedic hymns mention arrows smeared with poison, and the Mānava Dharmaśāstra forbids their use in fair combat (MDh 7.90; see Chapter 12) (Olivelle 2005) — a prohibition which implies that they were sometimes used. Fire-arrows, carrying burning material, appear in descriptions of sieges.

docs.title: 4.6 Fire Arrows and Incendiaries
docs.text: Fire was a weapon in Indian warfare from early times. The Arthaśāstra describes incendiary mixtures and “fire-arrows” for setting enemy camps, forts and stores alight, and the use of birds, monkeys and other animals carrying burning material into enemy forts (AŚ 13.4) — a stratagem found in many ancient literatures, whose practicality is doubtful (Kangle 1960–1965). Fire-arrows and pots of burning oil were standard weapons of siege warfare throughout the medieval period. These incendiary weapons are sometimes cited as evidence that ancient India knew gunpowder; but they contain no explosive, and the evidence for gunpowder in India begins much later (Chapter 5).

docs.title: 4.7 What the Dhanurveda Texts Teach
docs.text: For a book that takes dhanurveda as half its title, the obvious question is what the texts of that name actually say. The answer depends on which texts are meant, and on dates that Chapter 3 has set out: the Arthaśāstra’s chapter on the armoury is the earliest systematic material, the four dhanurveda chapters of the Agni Purāṇa are the oldest connected account of training, and the works that call themselves dhanurveda are later still. This section summarises them in that order. The Agni Purāṇa is paraphrased here from the Sanskrit text of Rājendralāla Mitra’s edition, chapters 248–251, as given in the electronic text on the GRETIL site, which follows that edition; Gangadharan’s is the standard English translation (Mitra 1870–1879; Gangadharan 1984–1987). Its verses are cited as AP chapter and verse. The printed text is corrupt in places, and where its sense is uncertain this is said.

docs.title: 4.7.1 The Arthaśāstra
docs.text: The Arthaśāstra has no chapter on how to shoot. Its chapter on the armoury, besides naming bows by material (Section 4.2), lists kinds of bowstring and arrow, and requires the superintendent of the armoury to keep weapons in good repair and in sufficient numbers (AŚ 2.18) (Kangle 1960–1965; Olivelle 2013). In its discussion of battle it assigns archers to positions behind the front ranks or on raised ground, from which they could shoot over the heads of other troops. Its interest is in supply and deployment, not in the skill of the individual archer.

docs.title: 4.7.2 The Agni Purāṇa’s four chapters
docs.text:
The Agni Purāṇa, a compilation whose present form dates from roughly the eighth to the eleventh century (Rocher 1986), presents its dhanurveda as the god Agni’s instruction to the sage Vasiṣṭha. The four chapters move from classification to stance, from stance to the draw, from the stationary target to the mounted archer, and finally to the noose, the sword and the other weapons.

The first chapter begins by classifying. The science has four parts, matching the four kinds of fighter, on chariot, elephant, horse and foot, and fighting is of five kinds: with weapons released by a machine, such as the bow or the sling; released by the hand, such as stones and javelins; released and then recovered, such as the lance (prāsa); not released at all, such as the sword; and without weapons, that is, wrestling (AP 248.1–5). Fighting with the bow is ranked best, with the lance middling, with the sword lowest, and with the bare arms last (AP 248.6–7). This is not the fourfold scheme of “released”, “held”, “released and held” and “released by spell” (mantramukta) often attributed to the Agni Purāṇa in modern books; spell-weapons have no category of their own in these chapters. The text then says who may teach and fight: the teacher of dhanurveda is a brahmin, the pupils are of two of the classes, a śūdra may fight in an emergency, and the king may take the help of people of mixed classes (saṅkara) living in his country (AP 248.7–8; the wording of the last verse is uncertain in the printed text). The norm of a twice-born art, practised in fact by others, is already present (Chapter 13).

docs.title: 4.7.3 The archer’s stances
docs.text:
Ten stances (sthāna) follow, each defined by the placing of the feet and knees and, for most, by the distance between the feet in spans (vitasti), cubits (hasta) or finger-breadths (aṅgula) (Table 4.1). The archer is to make his first salutation in the last of them, then take the bow in the left hand and the arrow in the right, and shoot from vaiśākha, jāta or a long stance (AP 248.19–20).

Table 4.1. The archer’s stances in the Agni Purāṇa (AP 248.9–19), paraphrased Stance Description in the text Verse samapada Feet together, toes, ankles and heels touching 248.9 vaiśākha Knees held rigid, the feet three spans apart 248.10 maṇḍala Knees seen in line “like a row of swans”, the feet four spans apart 248.11 ālīḍha “Plough-shaped”: right knee and thigh rigid, five spans wide 248.12 pratyālīḍha The reverse of ālīḍha: the left leg turned aside, the right straight 248.13 jāta Ankles five finger-breadths apart, the stance twelve finger-breadths long 248.14 daṇḍāyata One leg stretched out “like a staff” with the knee, the other bent and still 248.15–16 vikaṭa A wide stance, the feet two cubits (hasta) apart 248.16 sampuṭa Knees doubled, both feet turned upward 248.17 svastika Feet slightly turned and set firm, sixteen finger-breadths apart; the stance of the first salutation 248.18–19

Several of these names, ālīḍha and pratyālīḍha above all, also belong to the vocabulary of sculpture and dance, where they describe the lunging postures of fierce deities and of the archer-gods in temple reliefs. Posture was a shared language of several arts, and the archer’s stances were named in it.

docs.title: 4.7.4 Drawing, aiming and loosing
docs.text: The account of the shot is the most technical part of the text (AP 248.20–35). The archer rests the lower end of the bow on the ground and balances it; he sets the bow at the level of the navel and the arrow at the hip, raises the hand to between eye and ear, and grips the bow with the leading fist. The leading arm is to be neither turned in nor out, neither high nor low, neither bent nor stiffly raised, but “even and steady, like a staff”; the fist covers the target. The chest is lifted, the shoulders lowered, the neck still, and the distance between chin and shoulder is measured in finger-breadths. The arrow is taken at its feathered end between forefinger and thumb and drawn with the middle and ring fingers as well, quickly, until it is fully drawn; after the loose the drawing hand is thrown back. This is a finger draw, not the thumb draw of the steppe archers and the Mughal courts (Section 4.4). The text ends the chapter with measures: the longest arrow is twelve fists (muṣṭi) long, the middle eleven, the shortest ten; the best bow is four cubits long, the middle three and a half, the least three, the same measures serving for the foot-soldier and for the archer on horse, chariot or elephant (AP 248.36–38). An earlier chapter, on the marks of royal insignia and weapons, adds the materials: bows of metal, of horn and of wood, the horn of the buffalo and of deer among others, and woods such as sandal, cane, sāl and arjuna; bowstrings of bamboo, hemp or bark; and four cubits again as the best length for a wooden bow (AP 244.4–10). The horn bows may have been composite bows, but the text does not say how any bow was built.

docs.title: 4.7.5 From the target to the battlefield
docs.text: The second chapter turns from the shot to practice (AP 249). The archer, armoured and composed, ties his quiver-belt on the right, draws an arrow from the quiver with the right hand and takes up the bow with the left, nocks the arrow, draws, and looses at a disc-shaped target (candraka) sixteen finger-breadths across. Practice begins at a square target and moves on to targets that are low, high, moving and turning; the targets are grouped as “firm”, “difficult” and “varied and difficult”, two of each, and they are to be shot with the right hand and with the left. Only when he has mastered the targets on foot may the archer mount, and then practise against targets that whirl, move or stand, striking, piercing and cutting them (AP 249.10–18). The chapter closes with a verse on the archer as a pupil in discipline (yoga) who masters mind, eye and sight (AP 249.19).

docs.title: 4.7.6 The noose, the sword and the other weapons
docs.text: The third chapter opens with the same rule — mastery of hand, mind and eye before mounting — and then describes the noose (pāśa): ten cubits long, made of cotton, muñja grass, hemp, sinew, arka fibre, hide or other strong material, carefully twisted, kept at the belt, whirled above the head in a ring and thrown at a man-shaped target covered in leather, and at targets that leap, jump and run (AP 250.1–6). The sword is worn at the waist on the left side, held firm with the left hand and drawn with the right, and practice is against a post six finger-breadths in girth and seven cubits high fitted with iron rods and pieces of armour (AP 250.7–10). The fourth chapter is a catalogue. It names thirty-two movements of sword and shield, eleven of the noose, and the actions proper to the discus, spear, javelin, mace, axe, hammer, bhindipāla, club, vajra, paṭṭiśa, sword and sling, and it gives a long list of holds and blows for mace-fighting and wrestling, among them pulls, neck-twists and a “back-breaking” throw (AP 251.1–30). It ends with the crews of war: two men with goads on an elephant, one on its neck, with two archers and two swordsmen; three horsemen to guard a chariot or an elephant, three archers to guard a horseman, and shield-bearers to guard the archers; and the worship of each weapon with its own mantra before battle (AP 251.31–34).

docs.title: 4.7.7 The later compilations
docs.text: Later works that deal with archery — the archery verses of the Śārṅgadhara-paddhati (1363), the Kodaṇḍamaṇḍana attributed to the fifteenth-century architect Maṇḍana, and the Dhanurveda attributed to Vasiṣṭha — elaborate the same material, often with overlapping verses. Their printed editions rest on few manuscripts, and their contents are not paraphrased here verse by verse. None of them can be shown to preserve a lost Vedic or Mauryan treatise. Popular books sometimes present lists of “twelve archery postures” or detailed instructions on wind correction and arrow selection as classical teaching; such lists are not found in the texts named and should be treated with suspicion.

docs.title: 4.7.8 What the texts do and do not tell us
docs.text: Read in this way, the dhanurveda of the Agni Purāṇa is neither a fragment of a lost Vedic science nor an empty formula. It is a compact syllabus: classification, stance, draw, measured equipment, a graded sequence of targets, the passage from foot to horse, and a list of the other weapons a fighting man should know. It shares with the epics the ranking of the bow above all other weapons, and with the dharmaśāstras the assumption that teaching belongs to brahmins. What it does not give is equally clear: no draw weights, no measured ranges, nothing on how a bow is made, and nothing on the composite bow and thumb draw that dominated the cavalry warfare of its own time (Section 4.14). It describes, in other words, the archery of the foot-soldier and the courtly pupil as a learned compiler of the late first millennium understood it, and it should be read as evidence for that, not for the battlefields of the Vedic or Mauryan periods.

docs.title: 4.8.1 Droṇa’s school
docs.text:
The Mahābhārata’s account of the education of the Pāṇḍava and Kaurava princes by Droṇa (Ādiparvan) contains the most famous archery stories in Indian literature (Buitenen 1973–1978). In one, Droṇa sets a wooden bird in a tree as a target and asks each pupil what he sees before allowing him to shoot. The others see the tree, the bird, their brothers and the teacher; Arjuna says that he sees only the bird’s head, and he alone is allowed to shoot. The story became a byword for concentration. In another, Arjuna practises in the dark after noticing that he can eat in the dark without missing his mouth. The epic describes Arjuna as ambidextrous (savyasācin), able to draw the bow with either hand.

The same section tells of Ekalavya, the Niṣāda archer refused by Droṇa and later made to give up his right thumb; the episode is discussed in Chapter 13 as evidence of how birth limited access to martial training.

docs.title: 4.8.2 Tests of skill
docs.text: At the self-choice ceremony (svayaṃvara) of Draupadī, suitors must string a great bow and hit a target set beyond a mechanical device (yantra); in later retellings the target becomes the eye of a revolving fish seen in reflection in water. Arjuna, disguised as a brahmin, succeeds. In the Rāmāyaṇa, Rāma wins Sītā by stringing and breaking Śiva’s bow, which no other suitor can lift. Such contests are literary motifs, but they show how central skill with the bow was to the image of the ideal prince.

docs.title: 4.8.3 The Upaniṣadic image
docs.text:
The bow also became a religious metaphor. A well-known verse of the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad compares meditation to archery:

Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.4

praṇavo dhanuḥ śaro hy ātmā brahma tal lakṣyam ucyate apramattena veddhavyaṃ śaravat tanmayo bhavet The syllable oṃ is the bow, the self is the arrow, and brahman is said to be the target. It is to be struck by one who is not distracted; one should become one with it, like the arrow.

docs.title: 4.9 The Bow in Religion and Kingship
docs.text:
The bow was a symbol of divine and royal power. Śiva, as Tripurāntaka, “destroyer of the three cities”, is shown in sculpture drawing a bow made of Mount Meru, with Viṣṇu as the arrow; Rāma is the archer-king par excellence, and his bow became his emblem; Kāma, the god of love, shoots arrows of flowers from a bow of sugarcane strung with bees; the goddess Durgā carries a bow among her weapons. In Buddhist art, Māra, the tempter, is sometimes shown with Kāma’s flowered bow. Kings were praised as archers in inscriptions and poetry, and Gupta gold coins of the “archer type” show the king standing with a bow, a type copied by later dynasties.

The bow also left a curious trace in Indian mathematics. In Indian trigonometry, the chord of an arc was called jyā or jīvā, “bowstring”, because the arc and chord resemble a bow and its string. The word passed into Arabic as jība, was misread as jayb (“fold”, “pocket”), and was translated into Latin as sinus, from which comes the English “sine”. The archer’s bowstring thus passed, through Indian astronomy and Arabic, into the vocabulary of European mathematics.

docs.title: 4.10 Hunting
docs.text: The bow was the hunter’s weapon as much as the warrior’s, and hunting was the commonest way in which kings and nobles practised archery. Sanskrit literature has many royal hunts; in Kālidāsa’s Abhijñānaśākuntala, King Duṣyanta first appears pursuing a deer with his bow. The Arthaśāstra and the dharmaśāstras list hunting among the vices of kings, but also recognise its value as exercise and as training in judging the movement of animals and men; the Arthaśāstra prescribes protected hunting parks for the king (Kangle 1960–1965). Medieval kings hunted with bow, spear and trained cheetahs, and Mughal emperors organised enormous ring-hunts (qamargha), in which thousands of soldiers drove game into a closing circle, as both sport and military exercise. Rajput, Mughal and Pahari painting shows princes hunting deer, boar, lions and tigers with the bow long after firearms had become common.

docs.title: 4.11.1 What the texts say
docs.text:
The battle books of the epics are full of weapons that no smith could make. Heroes obtain from the gods weapons (astra) that are activated by a spell and that, when released, produce fire, floods, storms, darkness, snakes or showers of arrows. The brahmāstra, āgneyāstra (fire weapon), vāruṇāstra (water weapon), nāgāstra (serpent weapon), pāśupatāstra (Śiva’s weapon) and nārāyaṇāstra are among the most often named. Each has its counter-weapon, so that duels between heroes become exchanges of spells. Arjuna wins the pāśupata weapon from Śiva after fighting the god disguised as a mountain hunter (kirāta), an episode retold in Bhāravi’s poem Kirātārjunīya.

The epic surrounds these weapons with rules. They are to be used only against those who also wield them, and the most powerful only in extremity. At the end of the war Aśvatthāman releases the brahmaśiras, a weapon of the same order as the brahmāstra, against the unborn heir of the Pāṇḍavas, an act condemned as among the gravest crimes of the war; he is cursed to wander the earth in suffering. The moral point is clear: the greater the power, the greater the obligation to restrain it.

docs.title: 4.11.2 Myths about ancient weapons and aircraft
docs.text:
These passages have been read by some modern writers as descriptions of nuclear weapons, guided missiles or aircraft, evidence of a lost advanced civilisation. There is no basis for such readings. The divine weapons are described in the language of magic and myth, they are obtained by austerities and prayer, and they belong to the same narrative world as talking animals, flying mountains and gods who take part in battle. No archaeological evidence of any kind supports the existence of such technology in ancient India.

Two particular claims are often repeated. The first concerns J. Robert Oppenheimer, director of the laboratory that built the first atomic bomb, who said in a television interview broadcast in 1965 that when he saw the first test explosion in 1945 he recalled a line of the Bhagavadgītā (11.32), in which Kṛṣṇa, revealing his cosmic form, says that he is time, the destroyer of worlds. Oppenheimer had studied Sanskrit and admired the Gītā; his remark expresses awe at the moral weight of the bomb, and is not a claim that the Gītā describes nuclear weapons. The second claim concerns ancient aircraft (vimāna). The text most often cited, the Vaimānika Śāstra, is a twentieth-century work, said to have been dictated by Pandit Subbaraya Shastry in the early decades of the twentieth century; a study by engineers of the Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore, published in 1974, found that its descriptions of aircraft were technically unworkable (Mukunda et al. 1974). The flying chariot Puṣpaka of the Rāmāyaṇa is a mythical vehicle.

The divine weapons are better understood in literary and religious terms. They express the idea that victory comes from the favour of the gods and from the hero’s spiritual discipline as well as from skill; they dramatise the moral danger of overwhelming force; and they allowed epic poets to stage duels of cosmic scale.

docs.title: 4.12 Archery in Legend and Memory
docs.text:
Indian legend is full of feats of archery. Arjuna hits a revolving target seen only in reflection; Rāma pierces seven sāl trees with a single arrow in the Rāmāyaṇa, to prove his strength to the monkey-king Sugrīva; and later stories attribute to heroes the ability to hit a target by sound alone (śabdavedhī). The Pṛthvīrāj Rāso, in its later versions, tells that the captive and blinded Pṛthvīrāja killed Muḥammad of Ghur by shooting at the sound of his voice. This story is a legend: Muḥammad of Ghur was killed in 1206, fourteen years after Pṛthvīrāja’s death, in his camp in the Punjab by assassins, and the contemporary sources say nothing of Pṛthvīrāja’s captivity in Ghazni (Talbot 2016). But the legend shows the place of the archer-king in popular memory.

The story of Ekalavya has also been retold by the communities with which it is concerned. Among some Bhil communities of western India, it is said that archers traditionally draw the bow without using the thumb, a practice explained by reference to Ekalavya’s sacrifice; whatever the origin of the practice, the story shows how a Sanskrit epic episode could be reinterpreted from the point of view of those it excluded. In modern India, Ekalavya has become a symbol both of dedication to learning and of the injustice of exclusion by birth, and his name has been given to a national scheme of residential schools for tribal children (the Eklavya Model Residential Schools).

docs.title: 4.13 Archery Games and Contests
docs.text: Archery contests were part of courtly and popular festivals. The Mahābhārata’s tournament of the princes and the svayaṃvara contests are literary examples. In later centuries, archery competitions were held at courts and fairs, and Mughal and Rajput painting shows princes shooting at targets and at birds. Among the hill peoples of Himachal Pradesh, the archery game ṭhoḍā, in which teams shoot blunt arrows at each other’s legs, is played at village festivals (Chapter 15). In Bhutan, across the Himalaya, archery is the national sport and a central part of festival life. These games preserve, in a peaceful form, the skills and the social meanings of the bow.

docs.title: 4.14 Horse-Archery
docs.text:
The great change in Indian archery came from the steppe. Mounted archers using composite bows, able to shoot while advancing or retreating, were the core of the Śaka, Kuṣāṇa and Hūṇa armies in the early centuries CE, and of the Ghaznavid and Ghurid armies that invaded north India from the late tenth century. The Turkic slave-soldiers (mamlūk) who founded the Delhi Sultanate in 1206 were trained horse-archers, and the sultans’ armies relied on large forces of mounted archers supplied with imported horses (Jackson 1999; Digby 1971).

Indian armies adapted. Rajput cavalry, though famous for close combat with lance and sword, used the bow; the armies of Vijayanagara recruited Muslim horse-archers; and the Mughal army of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries combined mounted archers with matchlockmen and artillery (Gommans 2002). The bow did not give way quickly to firearms (Section 4.16).

docs.title: 4.15 The Bow among the Peoples of the Forests and Hills
docs.text:
Archery was never only a royal or kṣatriya art. Hunters and forest communities — the people the Sanskrit texts called Niṣāda, Śabara, Kirāta or Bhilla — were renowned archers, and kings recruited them as soldiers; the Arthaśāstra lists forest troops (aṭavī) among the sources of an army (Kangle 1960–1965). For many of the peoples whom Indian law and administration later classed as “tribes” (ādivāsī), the bow has been central to hunting, warfare and identity. Bhil archers, from the hills of western and central India, served the Rajput states and the Marathas and fought against the Mughals and the British; the emblem of the state of Mewar shows a Bhil archer beside a Rajput warrior, in acknowledgement of the alliance on which the kingdom’s defence depended. In eastern India the bow was the weapon of three great risings against colonial rule and the landlords and moneylenders who came with it. The Kol rising of 1831–32 in Chota Nagpur, in which Munda and Ho villagers attacked the outsiders who had taken their lands, was put down by Company troops. The Santal rising (hul) of 1855–56, led by the brothers Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu, was fought largely with bows, arrows and axes and suppressed with heavy loss of life. And the ulgulān (“great tumult”) of 1899–1900, led by Birsa Munda, whose followers attacked police posts and missions with bows and arrows, ended when the rising was crushed and Birsa died in prison at Ranchi in 1900 (Singh 1983). These movements, and the forest peoples’ relations with the states around them, are treated in Volume 23, Jana–Jāti. In the north-east, the bow was a principal weapon of many hill peoples until the twentieth century, and among the Khasi of Meghalaya traditional archery (teer) survives as a popular sport, now also the basis of a licensed lottery.

The archery of these communities has its own rituals, techniques and lore, transmitted orally and only partly recorded. It is part of India’s martial heritage as much as the courtly archery described in Sanskrit texts, and its study, through ethnography and oral history, remains an important task.

docs.title: 4.16 The Decline of the Bow
docs.text: The bow declined slowly as a military weapon. In the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, Mughal and Deccani armies still relied heavily on archers, especially mounted archers; the matchlock was slow to load, inaccurate and unreliable in wet weather, and a skilled archer could loose several arrows in the time a musketeer fired once and, at moderate ranges, shoot as accurately. Over the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, as matchlocks improved and as infantry armed with them became more numerous, the bow lost ground. By the time of the Anglo-Maratha and Anglo-Sikh wars of the early nineteenth century, it had largely disappeared from the regular armies of Indian states, surviving among irregular troops, hunters and forest peoples. Its last major military use in India was in the risings of forest peoples against colonial rule described in Section 4.15.

docs.title: 4.17 Archery as Discipline and Sport
docs.text:
Popular writing often links Indian archery to yoga and meditation, citing the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad or Droṇa’s bird test. The link is real at the level of metaphor: Indian thinkers used the archer’s concentration as an image of the mind’s focus, and Buddhist and Jain texts use similar images. But claims that the dhanurveda texts prescribe systematic yogic breathing techniques for archers, or that classical archery postures were the source of modern yoga postures, go beyond the evidence. Many of the standing postures of modern yoga, including the “warrior” poses, were named and standardised in the twentieth century (Singleton 2010).

In modern India, archery has been reborn as an Olympic sport, with recurve and compound bows of modern materials. Its practitioners include many athletes from tribal communities of Jharkhand, Odisha and the north-east — a modern echo of the ancient importance of the bow outside the courts. Table 4.2 gathers some of the Sanskrit and later terms of archery used in this chapter.

Table 4.2. Some terms of archery Term Meaning dhanus, cāpa, kārmuka, kodaṇḍa Bow (largely synonymous in usage) jyā, guṇa, maurvī Bowstring iṣu, śara, bāṇa Arrow iṣudhi, tūṇa, tūṇīra Quiver nārāca Arrow described as wholly of iron ardhacandra Arrow with a crescent-shaped head kṣurapra Arrow with a razor-edged head bhalla Arrow with a broad head lakṣya Target sthāna Stance samapada, vaiśākha, maṇḍala Stances: feet together; feet three spans apart; feet four spans apart, knees in line (Table 4.1) ālīḍha, pratyālīḍha Wide lunging stances, each the mirror of the other savyasācin Ambidextrous archer (an epithet of Arjuna) śabdavedhin One who can hit a target by sound (legendary) kamān, tīr (Persian) Bow; arrow zihgīr, shast (Persian) Thumb ring for the thumb draw tarkash (Persian) Quiver

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Singh (1965): weapons of the Vedic period, including the bow.

  • Hopkins (1889): an exhaustive collection of epic material on weapons and fighting.

  • Mitra (1870–1879) and Gangadharan (1984–1987): the Sanskrit text and an English translation of the Agni Purāṇa, including its dhanurveda chapters.

  • Elgood (2004): arms and armour of the later period, with many bows.

  • Gommans (2002): horse-archery and cavalry in Mughal warfare.

docs.title: Chapter 5: Weapons, Armour and Military Technology
5.1 Introduction
docs.text:
The weapons of Indian armies changed greatly over three thousand years. The copper and bronze blades of the Harappans gave way to iron in the first millennium BCE; the chariot-archer of the Vedic hymns gave way to the elephant and then to the mounted archer and lancer; and from the fifteenth century gunpowder weapons gradually transformed warfare, until by the late eighteenth century the decisive arms were field artillery and drilled infantry with flintlocks. Through all these changes Indian smiths, armourers and gun-founders produced weapons of great quality, and Indian crucible steel was famous across Asia and Europe.

This chapter surveys the main categories of weapons and armour, the textual classifications, the metallurgy that supported them, and the coming of gunpowder, including the much-discussed rockets of Mysore. The evidence before about 1500 comes chiefly from texts, sculpture and a small number of excavated objects; for the period after 1500 the great museum collections of arms and armour, in India and abroad, are the main source (Elgood 2004; Egerton 1880).

docs.title: 5.2.1 The Arthaśāstra
docs.text: The chapter of the Arthaśāstra on the superintendent of the armoury (AŚ 2.18) is the earliest systematic Indian list of weapons (Kangle 1960–1965; Olivelle 2013). It divides them into fixed machines (sthitayantra), mounted on walls and gates; mobile machines (calayantra); weapons with pointed heads, such as various kinds of spear and javelin (śakti, prāsa, kunta, tomara, śūla and others); bows, bowstrings and arrows; swords; razor-edged weapons such as axes; “weapons of stone” (missiles and sling-stones); armour; and accessories such as the elephant goad and the chariot-banner. Several of the machine names are obscure. One of them, the śataghnī (“hundred-killer”), has attracted much speculation. The text gives no clear description, and commentators and modern scholars have interpreted it as a heavy spiked log or pillar dropped or rolled from a rampart onto attackers. There is no basis for the popular claim that it was a multi-barrelled gun or a multiple-arrow launcher.

docs.title: 5.2.2 The classes of the Agni Purāṇa
docs.text:
The Agni Purāṇa’s chapters on dhanurveda classify fighting by the way the weapon is used: released by a machine (yantramukta), such as the bow and the sling; released by the hand (pāṇimukta), such as stones and javelins; released and recovered (muktasandhārita), such as the lance; not released (amukta), such as the sword; and without weapons (AP 248.2–5; Section 4.7.2) (Mitra 1870–1879; Gangadharan 1984–1987). The “machine” here is first of all the bow itself, not a catapult or a rocket. Modern books often give instead a fourfold scheme in which the last class is weapons “released by spell” (mantramukta), the divine weapons of the epics (Chapter 4); that is not the scheme of these chapters. A simpler distinction, found in many texts, opposes śastra, a weapon held in the hand, to astra, a missile weapon or one released by spell.

These classifications are learned schemes. Actual armouries contained a variety of weapons that changed with fashion, supply and the influence of neighbours, and the names of medieval and early modern weapons are mostly not Sanskrit but Persian, Hindustani, Marathi and other vernacular terms.

docs.title: 5.3 A Guide to Weapon Names
docs.text:
Readers of Indian sources meet a bewildering variety of weapon names. Table 5.1 lists some of the most common, with their approximate meanings. Sanskrit names, mostly from the epics, the Arthaśāstra and the Purāṇas, cannot always be matched with surviving objects, and their translations are often conventional; the later names, mostly Persian and Hindustani, refer to weapons that survive in collections (Elgood 2004; Egerton 1880; Hopkins 1889).
