docs.title: 5.4 Weapons in Sculpture and Painting
docs.text:
For the period before about 1500, sculpture is the main visual evidence for Indian weapons. The reliefs of the early Buddhist monuments at Sāñcī and Bhārhut show soldiers with bows, swords, spears and shields; Gupta and post-Gupta sculpture shows the weapons carried by deities, which often reflect real weapons; and medieval temples in Karnataka, Odisha, Rajasthan and elsewhere have friezes of soldiers, cavalry and elephants. Hero-stones show the weapons of ordinary fighters — bows, swords, spears and shields — with considerable realism. The interpretation of this evidence requires care, because sculptors followed conventions and often represented weapons schematically, and because the weapons of gods were partly symbolic.

For the period after 1500, painting is a rich source. The illustrated manuscripts of the Mughal court, Rajput and Pahari painting, and Deccani painting show armies, weapons, armour and horse equipment in detail, and can sometimes be compared with surviving objects. Elgood and other specialists have used such comparisons to date and identify weapons in collections (Elgood 2004).

docs.title: 5.5.1 Early swords
docs.text: The Vedic word asi may refer to a knife or short sword; by the time of the epics the sword (khaḍga, asi, nistriṃśa) is a regular weapon of the warrior, used with a shield. Sculpture of the early centuries CE shows straight, broad, double-edged swords, often with a pointed or leaf-shaped tip. The Greek writers report that Indian swords were broad and long and wielded with two hands; and the first-century Periplus of the Erythraean Sea lists Indian iron and steel among the goods traded to the ports of the Red Sea, an early reference to the export of Indian metal.

docs.title: 5.5.2 Medieval and early modern swords
docs.text:
The best-known Indian sword types belong to the medieval and early modern periods (Figure 5.1) (Elgood 2004):

  • The khaṇḍā is a straight, broad, double-edged sword, often with a blade that widens towards a blunt or rounded tip and with a basket hilt. It is associated particularly with Rajput and Maratha warriors and with the Sikh emblem of the same name.

  • The talwār is a curved, single-edged sabre with a characteristic hilt ending in a disc-shaped pommel. Curved swords of this kind reached India with the Turkic and Persian cavalry of the medieval period, and the talwār became the most common sword of north and central India from the sixteenth century.

  • The shamshīr, a more sharply curved Persian sabre, was also used, especially at the Mughal and Deccan courts.

  • The firangī (“foreign”) is a long straight blade, often imported from Europe, mounted in an Indian basket hilt. Firangīs were popular with Maratha cavalry in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries.

  • The paṭā or daṇḍ-paṭṭā is a gauntlet sword: a long straight blade fixed to an iron gauntlet that encloses the hand and forearm (Figure 5.2). It is associated particularly with Maratha warriors.

  • The uṟumi, a long flexible blade of thin steel, coiled when not in use, belongs to the martial culture of Kerala (Chapter 15).

  • Regional forms include the heavy chopping knife of Coorg, the ayda katti, and the broad-bladed dhop and pattisa of the Deccan.

Figure 5.1. Two Indian swords in a museum display case: a curved talwār with a gilt hilt in the form of an animal head, and a straight, broad-bladed sword with reinforcing plates and a steel basket hilt, of the khaṇḍā type, above its red velvet scabbard (Mehrangarh Fort Museum, Jodhpur). The curved sabres of the later medieval and early modern periods show the influence of Turkic and Persian cavalry swords. (Photograph: Shitha Valsan; cropped.) Photo: Shitha Valsan, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Swords were more than weapons. Famous blades were named, inherited and given as gifts; a sword could stand in for an absent bridegroom at a Rajput wedding; and the presentation of a sword was a mark of honour at Mughal and Maratha courts. Śivājī’s sword, called Bhavānī, became a symbol of Maratha identity.

docs.title: 5.6 Daggers and Close-Combat Weapons
docs.text:
India produced an exceptional variety of daggers:

  • The kaṭār (also jamadhar) is a push-dagger with a triangular blade attached to a hilt of two parallel bars joined by cross-grips, so that the blade projects forward from the fist and is driven by a punching motion (Figure 5.2). Kaṭārs appear in sculpture of the Vijayanagara period and became widespread across India in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. Some later examples have blades that split into three when the grips are squeezed; others contain a small pistol. The kaṭār’s thick, stiff point was well suited to piercing mail.

  • The bichuā (“scorpion”) is a small curved dagger with a loop hilt; the khanjar and peshqabz are curved and straight daggers of Persian and Afghan type; the chilanum is a double-curved dagger of the Deccan.

  • The bāgh nakh (“tiger’s claws”) is a set of curved blades on a bar worn across the palm, concealed in the hand (Figure 5.3). By Maratha tradition it was the weapon with which Śivājī killed the Bijapur general Afzal Khān in 1659 (Section 9.16) (Sarkar 1919; Gordon 1993).

Figure 5.2. Left: a kaṭār (push-dagger) with a serrated blade, Indian, seventeenth or eighteenth century; the two side bars and the cross-grips form the hilt, so that the blade projects forward from the fist. Right: the hilt of a paṭā (gauntlet sword), its steel gauntlet covered with fine gold decoration, dated 1714–15 and fitted with a European blade. Both in the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York. Photo: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, CC0 1.0, via Wikimedia Commons Figure 5.3. A bāgh nakh (“tiger’s claws”), western India, eighteenth or nineteenth century: curved steel claws fixed to a bar with a ring at each end for the fingers, so that the weapon could be hidden in the hand (Higgins Armory Museum, Worcester, Massachusetts). Photo: Daderot, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons (cropped)

docs.title: 5.7 Spears, Maces and Axes
docs.text:
The spear was the commonest weapon of Indian infantry and an important cavalry weapon. Sanskrit texts distinguish many kinds of thrusting and throwing spears (śakti, prāsa, kunta, tomara, bhiṇḍipāla, śūla), though it is not always possible to match the names with surviving objects. Later armies used the long lance (barchhā, nezā) of the cavalry, the heavy spear (bhālā), and the all-iron spear (sāṅg). The Maratha light horseman’s long bamboo lance was famous, and Sikh and Maratha cavalry were feared lancers in the eighteenth century.

Maces (gadā, musala, parigha) appear in the epics as the weapons of Bhīma, Duryodhana and Balarāma. In the medieval period the flanged and spiked maces of Turkic and Persian armies (gurz, shashpar) were used against armoured opponents. The axe (paraśu, kuṭhāra) was a weapon of the god-hero Paraśurāma and of many infantrymen; the tabar (battle-axe) and the zaghnol (“crow’s beak”), a pick with a narrow armour-piercing point, were used by cavalry and infantry in Mughal times. The bhuj of Kutch and Sindh, a heavy knife-blade on a short haft, combined axe and dagger.

docs.title: 5.8.1 Shields
docs.text: The commonest Indian shield (dhāl, Sanskrit carman, phalaka, kheṭaka) was round, convex and of moderate size, made of hide — buffalo and rhinoceros hide were prized — or of steel, with bosses on the front holding the hand-grips behind. Lacquered and painted hide shields and steel shields inlaid with gold were made for the courts. Cane and wicker shields were used in eastern India and the north-east, and large standing shields protected archers and musketeers at sieges.

docs.title: 5.8.2 Body armour
docs.text: The Vedic and epic warrior wore armour (varman, kavaca) of some kind, but its form is not clear. In the hot climate of most of India, heavy armour was uncomfortable, and quilted cotton coats were widely worn; some were reinforced with plates or studs. Mail (Persian zirih) became common with the Turkic and Persian cavalry of the medieval period, and the Mughal and Rajput armour of the sixteenth to eighteenth centuries combined a mail shirt with the chār-āʾīna (“four mirrors”), four shaped plates protecting chest, back and sides, a domed helmet with a sliding nasal and mail neck-guard, and arm-guards (dastāna). Horses of heavy cavalry wore mail and plate, and elephants armour of plates or quilting (Section 5.11) (Elgood 2004).

docs.title: 5.9 The Makers of Arms
docs.text:
Weapons were made by specialised craftsmen whose skills were usually hereditary. Ironsmiths (Sanskrit karmāra, Hindi lohār, Tamil and Kannada kollar, kammāra) made blades, arrowheads and armour; bowyers, fletchers, leather-workers, carpenters, lacquer-workers and goldsmiths contributed to bows, shields, scabbards and hilts. The Arthaśāstra places weapon-making under the superintendent of the armoury, who was to employ artisans in state workshops and to test their products (Kangle 1960–1965). In south India, smiths and other artisans of the five metal and wood crafts formed the Viśvakarma (Kammāḷar) communities, which claimed descent from the divine architect Viśvakarman and a high ritual status, a claim disputed by other groups. Among the Sikhs, the Sikligar community of weapon-polishers and smiths became closely associated with the Khalsa in the eighteenth century.

Several regions were famous for particular products. South India and Sri Lanka produced crucible steel; Gujarat, Sindh, Lahore, Sialkot and Gwalior were known for sword blades and firearms; Rajasthan and the Deccan for decorated arms and armour; and Kutch and Kathiawar for shields. Arms were also imported: Persian and later European sword blades were prized, and the firangī sword was named after its European blade.

docs.title: 5.10 Armour in Practice
docs.text: How much armour did Indian soldiers actually wear? The answer varied with period, wealth and arm. Heavy cavalry of the Turkic and Mughal armies wore mail and plate and rode armoured horses; Rajput nobles wore mail coats and chār-āʾīna; infantry often wore quilted cotton coats or no armour at all. Climate limited the use of heavy armour: European observers in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries remarked on the light equipment of most Indian soldiers compared with European infantry of the previous century. As firearms improved, armour declined, though mail and helmets continued to be worn by cavalry into the nineteenth century, and Sikh Akālīs and some Rajput nobles still wore armour at the time of the Anglo-Sikh wars (Elgood 2004).

docs.title: 5.11 Armour for Horses and Elephants
docs.text:
Armour was not only for men. As the heavy cavalry of the Turkic and Persian traditions became the core of north Indian armies after about 1000, armour for horses became more common. Persian sources call it bargustuvān, and the Āʾīn-i Akbarī lists it among the equipment of the imperial cavalry (Blochmann 1873). Horse armour of the Mughal and later periods, surviving in museum collections, usually consists of a mail-and-plate trapper covering the neck, chest and flanks, with a shaffron of steel plates protecting the horse’s face. It was heavy and expensive, and only the richest horsemen could afford it for their mounts; most Indian cavalry fought on unarmoured horses, relying on speed rather than protection (Gommans 2002; Elgood 2004).

Elephants, the most valuable animals in the army, were also protected. The Mahābhārata and later poetry describe war elephants caparisoned and armoured, and Persian chroniclers describe elephants covered with plates of steel, with swords or blades fastened to their tusks and chains swung from their trunks. These descriptions are partly literary, but some elephant armour survives. A large elephant armour of mail and plates, thought to date from around 1600 and brought to Britain at the beginning of the nineteenth century, is now in the Royal Armouries at Leeds; it is one of very few such pieces to have survived anywhere (Figure 5.4) (Elgood 2004). Such armour protected the elephant’s head, trunk and flanks against arrows and spears, though not against the cannon and musket balls that made elephants increasingly vulnerable after the sixteenth century (Chapter 6).

Figure 5.4. The Mughal elephant armour of about 1600 in the Royal Armouries, Leeds, displayed on a model elephant. Small steel plates joined by mail protect the head, trunk and flanks; the two riders are modern display figures. Photo: Geni, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

The decline of animal armour followed the same path as that of human armour. Against firearms it gave little protection for a great deal of weight and cost, and by the eighteenth century it survived mainly as a feature of ceremonial display, worn by the horses and elephants of princes in processions rather than in battle.

docs.title: 5.12.1 The Iron Age
docs.text: Iron came into use in India in the late second and early first millennium BCE; the dates are debated, but iron objects are well attested in the Ganges valley and the Deccan by the early first millennium BCE. The megalithic burials of the south contain many iron weapons. The spread of iron tools and weapons was one of the conditions for the growth of kingdoms and cities in the Ganges valley (Thapar 2002).

docs.title: 5.12.2 The Delhi iron pillar
docs.text:
The most famous Indian iron object is the pillar now standing in the Qutb complex at Delhi (Figure 5.5), which carries an inscription of a king named Candra, generally identified with the Gupta ruler Candragupta II (c. 375–415 CE). It is over seven metres high and weighs about six tonnes, and it has resisted corrosion remarkably well for some sixteen centuries. R. Balasubramaniam’s studies attribute this to the composition of the iron, which contains a relatively high proportion of phosphorus and very little sulphur, and to the formation of a thin protective layer, including a crystalline iron hydrogen phosphate, on its surface, helped by the alternation of wet and dry seasons (Balasubramaniam 2002). The pillar was built up by forge-welding many lumps of iron, a technique requiring great skill. It is evidence of advanced craftsmanship; it does not show that ancient smiths possessed modern scientific knowledge.

Figure 5.5. The iron pillar in the Qutb complex at Delhi, with its modern railing, seen through an arch of the stone screen of the late twelfth-century mosque. It carries the inscription of a king Candra, generally identified with Candragupta II. Photo: Aiwok, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons (cropped)

docs.title: 5.12.3 Crucible steel
docs.text:
South India and Sri Lanka were centres of production of crucible steel, known in English as wootz, from the Kannada and Telugu word ukku. In this process iron was sealed in clay crucibles with carbonaceous material such as wood or leaves and heated for many hours, so that it absorbed carbon and melted, forming small cakes of high-carbon steel. Forged with great care at controlled temperatures, the steel developed a characteristic watered pattern. Sharada Srinivasan and Srinivasa Ranganathan have traced the archaeological and textual evidence for this industry in south India, with production sites in Telangana, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka, and its export to the Middle East, where steel cakes were forged into the blades that Europeans called “Damascus” swords (Srinivasan and Ranganathan 2004).

Scientific study of these blades has revealed their remarkable structure. In 2006 a team led by M. Reibold reported, from electron microscopy of a seventeenth-century Damascus sabre, the presence of carbon nanotubes and cementite nanowires in the steel (Reibold et al. 2006). This finding helps to explain the patterning and properties of such steel; it does not mean that historical smiths understood or intended nanostructures, which arose from the empirical process they had perfected.

The industry declined in the nineteenth century. Contributing factors included competition from cheap European steel, the collapse of the market for traditional swords as armies adopted firearms, the disarming of Indian society after 1857, and the loss of skilled lineages. The knowledge of the process was not entirely lost — it was recorded by European observers in the early nineteenth century — but production ceased, and modern attempts to reproduce the steel have relied on historical description and scientific analysis.

docs.title: 5.13 Machines and Siege Engines
docs.text: Early Indian texts refer to machines (yantra) for war, most of them for the attack or defence of forts. The Jain canonical tradition credits Ajātaśatru of Magadha with a stone-throwing machine (Chapter 2), the Arthaśāstra lists fixed and mobile machines, and Bhoja’s Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra discusses machines for defending a fort. Their construction is rarely described clearly. Medieval Persian chronicles describe sieges conducted with the counterweight trebuchet (manjanīq) and with protected approaches (sābāṭ) built up to the walls under cover; the trebuchet had spread across the Islamic world from the twelfth century and was used in the sieges of the Delhi Sultanate (Jackson 1999). Chapter 10 discusses sieges in more detail.

docs.title: 5.14.1 Origins and arrival
docs.text:
Gunpowder was invented in China, where it was in military use by the eleventh century and where guns developed in the thirteenth. Claims that it was known in ancient India rest on misreadings. Oppert’s arguments of 1880 relied heavily on the Śukranīti and similar texts (Oppert 1880), which are now known to be late; the Śukranīti in its present form is a nineteenth-century work (Gopal 1962). References to “fire” weapons in earlier texts concern incendiary arrows and pots of burning material, not explosives.

Iqtidar Alam Khan’s study of gunpowder in medieval India argues that knowledge of gunpowder reached India in the thirteenth or fourteenth century, probably through the Mongols, and that it was first used in fireworks and rockets; firearms in the proper sense appear in the fifteenth century, in the Deccan and in Gujarat and other regions, and spread widely after 1500 (Khan 2004). Firishta’s earlier date for Bahmanī artillery is discussed in Section 8.17. Portuguese and Ottoman gunners and founders served Indian rulers in the early sixteenth century, and both the Bahmanī successor sultanates and Vijayanagara used guns in their wars (Eaton 2005).

docs.title: 5.14.2 The Mughal artillery
docs.text:
Bābur’s victory at Pānīpat in 1526 owed much to his field guns and matchlocks, deployed behind carts chained together in the Ottoman manner and directed by his gunners Ustād ʿAlī-qulī and Muṣṭafā (Thackston 1996). Under Akbar and his successors the Mughal army maintained a large artillery establishment, from heavy siege guns drawn by elephants and oxen to light pieces carried on camels (shutarnāl) and swivel guns. The matchlock (tufang, bandūq) became the standard infantry firearm, and large numbers of matchlockmen (barqandāz) were recruited across north India (Gommans 2002; Kolff 1990).

The Deccan sultanates cast some of the largest guns of the age. The bronze gun called Malik-i Maidān (“lord of the battlefield”), cast in the mid-sixteenth century and now on a bastion at Bijapur, is over four metres long (Figure 5.6). Great guns of this kind were symbols of power as much as weapons; their weight made them difficult to move, and they were mainly used in sieges and fortress defence. The Jaivana gun at Jaigarh near Jaipur, cast in the eighteenth century, belongs to the same tradition.

Figure 5.6. The bronze gun Malik-i Maidān (“lord of the battlefield”), cast in the mid-sixteenth century, on its bastion at Bijapur, inside a modern railing. Photo: Rangan Datta Wiki, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 5.14.3 Firearms in the eighteenth century
docs.text: In the eighteenth century the flintlock musket, bayonet and light field artillery of European armies spread to Indian states. The Marathas, the Nizam, Mysore, the Sikh kingdom of Ranjit Singh and others raised infantry trained in European drill, often with European officers, and established foundries and arsenals (Roy 2011). Indian gun-founders produced artillery of high quality: British officers who captured Mysore and Sikh guns in the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries often remarked on it. The gap between Indian and Company armies by 1800 lay less in weapons than in finance, organisation, discipline and the regular payment of soldiers (Chapter 19).

docs.title: 5.15 Saltpetre and Gunpowder Production
docs.text: Gunpowder is a mixture of saltpetre (potassium nitrate), sulphur and charcoal, and saltpetre was its most important and most difficult ingredient. India, and especially Bihar and Bengal, was one of the world’s major sources of saltpetre, which formed naturally in the soils of the Ganges plain and was refined by specialised workers. From the seventeenth century, the Dutch and English East India Companies exported large quantities of Indian saltpetre to Europe, where it supplied the gunpowder of European armies and navies; control of the saltpetre trade was one of the Companies’ interests in Bengal and Bihar. Indian rulers produced their own gunpowder in workshops attached to their arsenals, and the quality of Indian powder varied. The abundance of saltpetre in India helps to explain the rapid spread of firearms and rockets in Indian warfare once the technology had arrived (Khan 2004).

docs.title: 5.16 Arsenals and the State
docs.text:
Large states maintained arsenals and workshops. The Mughal emperors’ household included many workshops (kārkhāna), among them the armoury (qūrkhāna) and the artillery establishment, and the Āʾīn-i Akbarī describes Akbar’s personal interest in weapons: it says that he devised improvements in the manufacture of matchlocks and in the cleaning of gun barrels, and that the imperial arsenal kept weapons graded by quality and weight (Blochmann 1873; Irvine 1903). Abū’l-Faẓl’s descriptions are courtly praise, but they show the importance attached to firearms at the Mughal court.

In the eighteenth century the successor states built arsenals and foundries on a larger scale. Tipu Sultan’s capital Srirangapatna had foundries for cannon, workshops for muskets and rockets, and stores of powder and shot; Tipu also tried to obtain craftsmen and machinery from France (Roy 2011). The Maratha powers, the Nizam and the nawabs of Awadh and Bengal employed European gun-founders and officers. Ranjit Singh established foundries at Lahore, where guns were cast under the direction of Indian and European specialists, and the Sikh army’s artillery was regarded by its British opponents as excellent. The East India Company built its own gun foundry at Cossipore near Calcutta, and powder works at Ishapore, in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries.

docs.title: 5.17.1 Infantry firearms
docs.text: The standard Indian infantry firearm from the sixteenth to the eighteenth century was the matchlock (toṛādār, from toṛā, the slow-match), a long-barrelled gun fired by bringing a smouldering cord into contact with the priming powder. Indian matchlocks were often very long, with slender stocks, and were fired from the shoulder or the chest; they were accurate in skilled hands but slow to load and vulnerable to rain. Matchlockmen (barqandāz, bandūqchī) were recruited in large numbers from the military labour market, especially in the eastern Ganges valley and Bundelkhand (Kolff 1990). The long Afghan matchlock or flintlock called jezail was famous on the north-western frontier. The flintlock, which fired by a spark from flint striking steel and was quicker and more reliable, spread among Indian armies in the eighteenth century, largely through the European companies.

docs.title: 5.17.2 Light artillery
docs.text: Light guns were mounted on camels (shutarnāl, zamburak) and fired from a kneeling camel, giving the Mughal, Persian and Afghan armies mobile firepower; Nādir Shāh’s camel guns were effective against the Mughal army at Karnal in 1739. Swivel guns were mounted on walls and boats, and small guns on elephants. Hand grenades (ḥuqqa) of pottery or metal were used in sieges, and rockets (bān) were carried by specialised rocket-men in Mughal and Maratha armies (Section 5.18).

docs.title: 5.17.3 Heavy artillery
docs.text: Heavy guns were used mainly in sieges and in the defence of forts. They were very heavy to move: great siege guns were drawn by teams of oxen and elephants, and an army with a large artillery train moved slowly. Gunners were often specialists from outside, at least at first: Ottoman (Rūmī) gunners served Bābur and the Gujarat and Deccan sultans; Portuguese and other Europeans (firangī) served many Indian rulers; and in the eighteenth century French and other European officers trained Indian artillerymen. By the eighteenth century, Indian gunners (golandāz) were numerous and skilled. Iqtidar Alam Khan’s study traces the adoption of these weapons and the debates among Mughal nobles about their value (Khan 2004).

docs.title: 5.18.1 Haidar Ali and Tipu Sultan
docs.text:
Rockets were used in Indian warfare from at least the fifteenth century, according to Khan’s evidence (Khan 2004); they were common in Mughal and Maratha armies, where they served mainly to frighten elephants and horses and to harass enemy formations. The rulers of Mysore, Haidar Ali (r. 1761–1782) and his son Tipu Sultan (r. 1782–1799), developed them into a more formidable weapon. Their rockets had cases of iron rather than paper or bamboo. The iron case could contain a more tightly packed and more powerful charge, giving greater range and power. The rockets were bound to long bamboo poles (Figure 5.7), sometimes fitted with blades, and fired in large numbers by specialised companies of rocket-men. The engineer Roddam Narasimha, in his study of Mysore rockets, estimates their range at up to a kilometre or more (Narasimha 1985).

Figure 5.7. A soldier of Tipu Sultan’s army lifting a rocket bound to a long bamboo pole and lighting its fuse: watercolour by Robert Home, late eighteenth century (Victoria and Albert Museum, London). He wears the purple jacket with white spots of Tipu’s infantry. Image: Robert Home (Victoria and Albert Museum, London), public domain, via Wikimedia Commons (cropped)

Mysore rockets were used against the East India Company’s armies throughout the Anglo-Mysore wars, from Pollilur in 1780 to the defence of Srirangapatna in 1792 and 1799 (Sections 18.5 and 10.15). British accounts record the alarm and casualties they caused, though they were not decisive weapons in themselves.

docs.title: 5.18.2 From Mysore to Congreve
docs.text: After the fall of Srirangapatna in 1799, rockets and rocket cases were taken to Britain. William Congreve, at the Royal Arsenal in Woolwich, began experiments from about 1804 and developed a series of iron-cased military rockets for the British army and navy. Congreve’s rockets were used against Boulogne and Copenhagen in the Napoleonic wars and against the United States in the war of 1812 (Narasimha 1985). The Mysore rockets thus influenced Congreve’s work: that is the precise and well-documented link. They were not the origin of rocketry, which goes back to medieval China, and the claim that “modern rocketry began in Mysore” overstates a real but specific contribution. The Mysore rockets deserve recognition as an effective adaptation of an existing weapon, and as one of the few cases in which an Indian military innovation was adopted by a European army.

docs.title: 5.19 Military Technology and Its Limits
docs.text:
It is sometimes argued that Indian states fell to the Europeans because their military technology was backward. The evidence reviewed in this chapter does not support so simple a view. Indian smiths made excellent steel and blades; Indian founders cast large and serviceable guns; Indian rulers adopted matchlocks, flintlocks and field artillery, and developed effective rockets. In the eighteenth century the armies of Mysore, the Marathas and the Sikhs were well equipped by the standards of the time (Roy 2011).

There were, however, real differences. European states had developed, over the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, methods of mass production of standardised muskets and cannon, systems of drill and tactics adapted to them, and military engineering and artillery schools; Indian states adopted these methods, but often depended on European specialists to apply them. More important than technology, as Chapter 19 argues, were finance, organisation and political cohesion. The history of Indian military technology is a history of skill and adaptation, not of backwardness — but technology alone did not decide the outcome of wars.

docs.title: 5.20 Decoration and Display
docs.text: Indian arms were often works of art. Hilts and blades were decorated with gold or silver wire inlaid into a cross-hatched steel surface (koftgarī), with enamel, with gems and with carved jade, ivory or rock crystal. Bidar in the Deccan gave its name to bidrī, an alloy of zinc inlaid with silver, used for hookahs and boxes more than for weapons. Inscriptions on blades recorded owners, prayers and verses in Persian, Arabic, Sanskrit and the vernaculars. Mughal and Rajput painting shows rulers and nobles with richly decorated swords, daggers and shields as emblems of rank (Elgood 2004). Such display weapons were often fully functional.

docs.title: 5.21 Indian Arms in Museum Collections
docs.text: Much of what is known about Indian arms and armour after 1500 comes from collections. In India, the National Museum in New Delhi, the Salar Jung Museum in Hyderabad, the City Palace Museum at Jaipur, the Mehrangarh Museum at Jodhpur and many other princely and state museums hold important collections. Abroad, the Royal Armouries at Leeds, the Victoria and Albert Museum and the Wallace Collection in London, and the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York hold large collections, many of them formed from objects taken during the colonial conquests or bought from princely families. Robert Elgood’s studies of Hindu arms and of the armoury of the Rathor court at Jodhpur, and Lord Egerton’s nineteenth-century catalogue, are the standard guides (Elgood 2004, 2017; Egerton 1880). The study of these objects — their metallurgy, inscriptions, decoration and provenance — is one of the most active fields of Indian military history.

docs.title: 5.22 Myths About Indian Weapons
docs.text: Several popular claims about Indian weapons have been examined in this chapter: that the śataghnī was a gun, that wootz steel was deliberate “nanotechnology”, that the Delhi pillar was made by techniques science cannot explain, and that the rockets of Mysore were the first rockets. Together with the older claim of ancient firearms and aircraft (Chapter 4), they are summarised in Table 20.1. Correcting these myths does not diminish the real achievements of Indian smiths, armourers and gun-founders, which are impressive enough without exaggeration.

docs.title: 5.23 Weapons as Trophies and Relics
docs.text: Weapons taken in war became trophies, and the weapons of famous warriors became relics. Indian rulers displayed captured guns and standards; Mughal chroniclers record the arms taken from defeated enemies; and Sikh shrines preserve weapons associated with the Gurus, which are shown to devotees. After the colonial conquests, large quantities of Indian arms were taken to Britain as trophies and souvenirs. After the fall of Srirangapatna in 1799, Tipu Sultan’s weapons, his throne and the mechanical organ known as “Tipu’s Tiger” (Section 18.5) were among the objects taken. Some of these objects have since been sold at auction and returned to India by private buyers, and the return of looted objects is now part of a wider international debate about colonial collections. The history of Indian arms is thus also a history of their movement, as gifts, trophies, loot and museum objects.

docs.title: 5.24 The Sword in Ritual and Symbol
docs.text: The sword acquired rich symbolic meanings in Indian culture. It was an emblem of sovereignty, carried before kings in procession and held by them in their portraits; it was worshipped as a form of the goddess, and it could stand for an absent Rajput bridegroom (Section 5.5). In Sikh tradition the double-edged sword (khaṇḍā) is used to stir the water of initiation into the Khalsa, and it gives its name to the Sikh emblem, which combines it with a quoit and two curved swords representing temporal and spiritual authority. The carrying of the kirpān by initiated Sikhs is a religious obligation. The sword’s symbolic importance long outlived its military usefulness and remains visible in ritual, art and politics today.

docs.title: 5.25 Weapons, Status and Ritual
docs.text: In pre-colonial India the right to carry weapons was widespread, and weapons were marks of status. Rajput and Maratha men of rank carried swords on all public occasions; peasants kept spears and matchlocks for defence and for service as seasonal soldiers; merchants travelled with armed guards (Kolff 1990). Weapons were also honoured in ritual. On the ninth day of the autumn festival of Navarātri, in many parts of India, weapons and tools are cleaned, decorated and worshipped (āyudhapūjā), and kings marked Daśahrā with displays of arms and armies (Chapter 13). The colonial Arms Act of 1878, which required licences to possess arms, therefore struck at social identity as well as at military capacity (Chapter 19).

docs.text:
• Elgood (2004): arms and armour from India, 1400–1865, with excellent illustrations.

  • Egerton (1880): a classic catalogue of Indian arms.

  • Srinivasan and Ranganathan (2004): the history and science of Indian crucible steel.

  • Balasubramaniam (2002): the Delhi iron pillar.

  • Khan (2004): gunpowder and firearms in medieval India.

  • Narasimha (1985): the rockets of Mysore and their influence in Britain.

docs.title: Chapter 6: Chariots, Elephants and Horses: The Animals of War
6.1 Introduction
docs.text:
Before the age of the railway and the motor engine, armies moved and fought with the help of animals. In India three animals shaped warfare above all: the horse, which drew the chariot and later carried the cavalryman; the elephant, which was India’s distinctive contribution to the warfare of the ancient world; and the ox, together with the camel in the arid west, which carried supplies and dragged guns. The availability of these animals depended on ecology and trade, and much of the military history of the subcontinent can be understood as the story of who controlled their supply.

Two scholars have been especially influential in developing this approach. Thomas Trautmann’s Elephants and Kings traces the history of the war elephant from its origins in India to its spread across Eurasia and its decline, and argues that the relationship between kings and wild elephants shaped Indian kingship and the preservation of Indian forests (Trautmann 2015). Jos Gommans and Simon Digby have shown how the supply of war-horses, mostly imported, determined the shape of medieval and early modern Indian armies (Gommans 2002; Digby 1971). This chapter draws on their work.

docs.title: 6.2.1 Origins and the Vedic chariot
docs.text: The light, horse-drawn chariot with spoked wheels developed on the steppes of Central Asia around the beginning of the second millennium BCE and spread rapidly across Eurasia, to Mesopotamia, Egypt, Anatolia, China and India. In the Ṛgveda it is the vehicle of gods and heroes. The hymns describe its wheels, felly, spokes, nave and axle, its pole and yoke, and the two horses that drew it, and they compare the making of a hymn to the work of a carpenter fashioning a chariot (Singh 1965; Jamison and Brereton 2014). The chariot carried two men, a driver and a fighter who was usually an archer. Chariot races were part of the great royal rituals of the later Vedic period, such as the vājapeya, in which the sacrificer wins a race run by seventeen chariots.

docs.title: 6.2.2 The epic chariot
docs.text: In the epics the chariot is the vehicle of the great warrior (rathin, mahāratha), and much of the poetry of battle consists of chariot duels. The charioteer (sūta) is a figure of ambiguous status: essential to victory and often the warrior’s confidant, yet socially inferior. Kṛṣṇa serves as Arjuna’s charioteer at Kurukṣetra, and the Bhagavadgītā is spoken on the chariot between the armies; Śalya drives for Karṇa and taunts him; Karṇa himself, believed to be the son of a charioteer, is mocked for his supposed birth. The epic grades warriors by their prowess as chariot-fighters — atiratha, mahāratha, ratha, ardharatha — and describes chariots with banners, multiple horses and quivers of arrows (Hopkins 1889).

docs.title: 6.2.3 Decline
docs.text: In historical warfare the chariot was already in decline by the time it was being celebrated in epic poetry. Porus fielded chariots at the Hydaspes in 326 BCE, but they were bogged down in the mud and achieved little. The Mauryan war office described by Megasthenes still had a board for chariots, and the Arthaśāstra describes their uses; but in the early centuries CE chariots disappear from the evidence of actual battles. Several reasons can be suggested: the rise of the war elephant as the elite heavy arm; the spread of cavalry using saddles and, later, stirrups, which could do what chariots did more cheaply and over rougher ground; the difficulty of using chariots in broken, forested or wet terrain; and the cost of keeping chariot horses in a country where good horses were scarce (Roy 2004). The chariot survived in literature, ritual and art — and in the great temple cars (ratha) drawn in processions — long after it had vanished from the battlefield.

docs.title: 6.3.1 An Indian invention
docs.text: Elephants were tamed and used in South Asia from an early period; the Harappan seals depict elephants, though not as war animals. The war elephant — an elephant trained to carry fighters and to charge in battle — appears in the evidence of the later first millennium BCE, and Trautmann argues that it was an Indian invention, perfected in the Ganges valley and especially in Magadha, whose rulers had access to the elephant forests of eastern and central India (Trautmann 2015). From India the war elephant spread westward: the Persian kings acquired Indian elephants, Alexander met them at Gaugamela and the Hydaspes, and Seleucus’s acquisition of five hundred elephants from Candragupta Maurya around 303 BCE made elephants a feature of Hellenistic warfare. The Ptolemies of Egypt and Carthage later used African forest elephants, captured and trained on the Indian model. Eastward, the war elephant spread to Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia, where it remained important into the nineteenth century.

docs.title: 6.3.2 Capture, not breeding
docs.text:
A central point of Trautmann’s argument is that war elephants were captured, not bred. Elephants take many years to reach maturity, a female gives birth to a single calf after a pregnancy of nearly two years, and a captive elephant must be fed and cared for during its long years of uselessness. It was far cheaper to capture adult or young elephants from the wild and train them. Indian kings therefore depended on the continued existence of wild elephant populations, and this gave them an interest in protecting forests. The Arthaśāstra prescribes elephant forests (nāgavana) under a superintendent and guards, with severe penalties for killing an elephant (AŚ 2.2) (Kangle 1960–1965; Trautmann 2015). The text also ranks elephants by region: those of the eastern forests of Kaliṅga and Aṅga were the best.

Capture was a skilled and dangerous operation, carried out by forest peoples with specialised knowledge. Methods included driving wild herds into stockades (the method later known in British India as kheddah), luring males with tame females, and trapping in pits. Captured elephants were tamed and trained by mahouts, who directed them with voice, feet and the goad (aṅkuśa).

docs.title: 6.3.3 The elephant in battle
docs.text:
Elephants served several purposes. They were a shock weapon, charging enemy lines and trampling men and horses unaccustomed to them; they carried archers, javelin-men and later musketeers in howdahs; they served as mobile command posts, raising the commander above the dust of battle so that he could see and be seen; they battered gates and walls; and they carried baggage and dragged heavy loads. Elephants were armoured with quilted cloth, leather or plates, and their tusks were sometimes fitted with metal sheaths or blades.

Their weaknesses were equally well known. Wounded or frightened elephants could panic and stampede through their own ranks, as happened at the Hydaspes; they were vulnerable to fire, missiles and noise; and disciplined infantry could open their ranks and let them through, or attack their legs and trunks. Over time, armies facing elephants developed counter-measures such as caltrops, fire, and later firearms and rockets, which were particularly effective in frightening them. The elephant’s value also depended on its mahout: if the mahout was killed, the animal often became uncontrollable. Ancient and medieval commentators were well aware of this, and the Arthaśāstra recommends the use of elephants only on suitable ground.

docs.title: 6.3.4 Elephants and kingship
docs.text: The elephant was a royal animal. Owning war elephants was a king’s privilege, and their numbers were a measure of his power; inscriptions and chronicles boast of elephants captured from defeated enemies, and the Aihoḷe inscription’s pun on Harṣa’s fallen elephants (Chapter 2) turns on the same idea. Medieval kings bore titles such as “lord of elephants” (gajapati); the Gajapati dynasty of Odisha took its name from it. The Delhi sultans, though their armies were built around cavalry, prized elephants and obtained many from Bengal and the eastern forests as tribute (Section 6.3.7) (Jackson 1999); the Mughal establishment is described in Section 6.5. Elephant fights were a royal spectacle at many courts.

docs.title: 6.3.5 The literature of elephants
docs.text: India developed a specialised literature on elephants (gajaśāstra, hastyāyurveda). The Hastyāyurveda attributed to the sage Pālakāpya deals with elephant medicine; the Mātaṅgalīlā, a Sanskrit text from Kerala, describes the marks, kinds and temperaments of elephants and their capture and care; the encyclopaedic Mānasollāsa discusses elephant sports and the royal elephant establishment (Shrigondekar 1925–1961). The Hastividyārṇava, an illustrated Assamese treatise completed in 1734 for the Ahom court, is one of the finest of these works (Choudhury 1976). Its paintings show elephants of different types, their capture, treatment and diseases (on its misdescription in popular books, see Section 3.8).

docs.title: 6.3.6 Decline
docs.text: The war elephant declined with the rise of effective artillery and musketry in the sixteenth to eighteenth centuries. Guns could kill or panic elephants at a distance, and the elephant’s size made it an easy target. Bābur, at Pānīpat in 1526, faced the elephants of Ibrāhīm Lodī with guns and archers, and they contributed to the confusion of the Lodī army (Thackston 1996). Elephants continued to be used to carry commanders, to haul artillery and baggage, and in the wars of the eighteenth century; the East India Company used them for transport well into the nineteenth century. But their role as the decisive shock weapon of Indian armies was over by about 1700.

docs.title: 6.3.7 The elephant trade
docs.text:
Elephants were traded as well as captured. Sri Lanka was a major source of war elephants for the kingdoms of south India; classical writers already mention the export of Sri Lankan elephants, and in the medieval period elephants were shipped from the island to the Coromandel and Malabar coasts. Elephants were also sent as tribute or gifts between rulers: Bengal and Odisha supplied many of the elephants of the Delhi sultans and the Mughals, and the capture of an enemy’s elephants was one of the main prizes of victory (Digby 1971; Trautmann 2015). Simon Digby showed that in the Delhi Sultanate the possession of elephants was a royal monopoly, and that the sultans’ control of the eastern elephant-bearing regions was one of the foundations of their military power.

Southeast Asian kingdoms, too, maintained war elephants on the Indian model; the bas-reliefs of Angkor Wat in Cambodia, of the twelfth century, show Khmer kings and commanders on elephants, and war elephants remained important in the wars of Burma, Siam and Cambodia into the nineteenth century.

docs.title: 6.4 The Classification and Training of Elephants
docs.text:
The elephant literature classifies elephants in elaborate ways. The Arthaśāstra and later texts distinguish types such as the bhadra, mandra and mṛga, by build and temperament, and a mixed type (saṅkīrṇa); they also distinguish elephants by age, by the region of the forest from which they came, and by their suitability for war, riding or carrying loads (Kangle 1960–1965; Trautmann 2015). The Arthaśāstra describes the stages of training: elephants were first accustomed to captivity and to their keepers, then trained to obey commands, to carry riders and loads, and finally to the special tasks of war — charging, breaking down gates and walls, trampling, and standing firm in the noise of battle (AŚ 2.31–32). Elephants were also trained to endure the sound of drums and the sight of fire.

The care of elephants was the work of skilled specialists: mahouts (hastipaka, mahāmātra), who rode and directed them; grooms and fodder-cutters; and elephant physicians, whose knowledge is recorded in texts such as the Hastyāyurveda. The mahout’s relationship with his elephant, often lifelong, was the foundation of the elephant’s usefulness, and the mahout’s craft was usually hereditary. In the forests, the knowledge of elephant-catchers from forest communities was indispensable to kings.

docs.title: 6.5 Elephants in the Mughal Empire
docs.text:
The Mughal emperors kept very large numbers of elephants, both in the imperial stables and in the establishments of their nobles. The Āʾīn-i Akbarī describes the imperial elephants in detail: their grading into classes according to size, temper and strength, their daily rations of grain, sugar and ghee, the number of attendants assigned to each, the fines imposed on keepers whose elephants grew thin, and the special elephants reserved for the emperor’s own use (Blochmann 1873). Elephants carried the emperor and his nobles in procession and in battle, drew heavy guns, carried baggage, served in hunts and fought in staged combats for the court’s entertainment. Akbar himself was celebrated by his chroniclers for his skill in mounting and controlling fierce elephants in musth, a dangerous display of courage that was also a demonstration of royal power (Figure 6.1). Although the military importance of the elephant declined in the age of firearms, its symbolic and logistical importance remained great.

Figure 6.1. Akbar riding the elephant Hawāʾī in pursuit of another elephant across a bridge of boats on the Yamuna at Agra; the boats give way beneath them and attendants fall into the river. From a double-page painting in the Akbarnāma, designed by Basawan, c. 1590 (Victoria and Albert Museum, London). Image: Basawan and Chitra, painters of Akbar's workshop (Victoria and Albert Museum, London), public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 6.6 Elephants in the Colonial Army and After
docs.text:
The decline of the war elephant did not end its military use. The East India Company and the later Indian Army kept elephants as transport animals, especially for heavy loads and difficult country, and in the nineteenth century heavy artillery was sometimes drawn by elephants on the march, with bullocks or horses taking over close to the enemy, where the elephants were too vulnerable and too easily frightened by gunfire (Trautmann 2015). Elephants were also used in the wars in Burma and on the north-eastern frontier, where roads were few and forests dense.

The last large-scale military use of elephants in the region came in the Second World War. During the Burma campaign the British army took over working elephants from the timber companies and used them to carry supplies, to build and repair bridges and to move through country impassable to vehicles. The work was described by J. H. Williams, a timber company officer who organised the army’s elephant companies, in his memoir Elephant Bill (Williams 1950).

After independence the elephant’s military role ended, but its ceremonial role continued. Caparisoned elephants still lead temple festivals in Kerala and the Daśahrā procession at Mysore, a ceremony that descends from the royal festival of the Vijayanagara and Mysore kings (Chapter 13). The capture of wild elephants, once a royal monopoly and a major military enterprise, gave way in the later twentieth century to conservation: the Asian elephant is now an endangered species, and its survival in India depends on the protection of the forests from which, for two thousand years, kings took their war elephants (Trautmann 2015).

docs.title: 6.7.1 A country short of good horses
docs.text:
The horse is not native to the subcontinent, and good war-horses were always scarce. The hot, humid climate of much of India, its diseases, and the lack of extensive dry pastures made it difficult to breed horses of the size and stamina needed for war. The most important horse-breeding regions within South Asia were in the arid and semi-arid zone running from the north-west through Sindh, Rajasthan and Gujarat into the western Deccan; elsewhere, horses had to be imported (Gommans 2002).

Imports came by two routes. Overland, horses from Central Asia and Afghanistan were driven through the passes of the north-west and sold at fairs in Punjab and the Ganges valley; early Sanskrit and Pali texts already praise horses from Kamboja and the Sindhu region in the north-west. By sea, Arab and Persian merchants shipped horses from the Persian Gulf and southern Arabia to the ports of Gujarat, the Konkan, Malabar and the Coromandel coast; the south, as Section 6.7.2 shows, depended on this sea trade most of all.

Some modern accounts claim that India had a flourishing indigenous horse-breeding tradition that made imports unnecessary. The evidence does not support this. Indian breeds did develop, especially in the arid west (Section 6.7.3); but the cavalry of the Delhi Sultanate, the Deccan states and the Mughals relied heavily on imported animals, and the horse trade was a major item of the subcontinent’s foreign trade for many centuries (Digby 1971; Gommans 2002).

docs.title: 6.7.2 Horses in the south
docs.text: South India depended especially heavily on imported horses. Marco Polo, visiting the Pāṇḍya country in the 1290s, reported that its kings bought thousands of horses every year from Arab and Persian traders, and that, because of the climate and their keepers’ ignorance, most of the horses died within a year, so that new ones had always to be bought — a complaint that suited the interests of the traders. Persian historians of the Mongol Ilkhanate also describe the great horse trade from the Persian Gulf to the ports of the south. The kings of Vijayanagara bought horses first from Muslim traders and then, after 1500, from the Portuguese at Goa, and Kṛṣṇadevarāya (r. 1509–1529), in his Telugu poem Āmuktamālyada, advised kings to improve their ports and to treat foreign merchants well so that the trade in horses and elephants would come to them and not to their enemies (Stein 1989). The Portuguese understood the importance of this trade and used it as a means of pressure on the Deccan states (Subrahmanyam 1993).

docs.title: 6.7.3 Indian horse breeds
docs.text: Although good war-horses were mostly imported, India did develop horse breeds of its own, especially in the arid west. The Kathiawari of Gujarat and the Marwari of Rajasthan, with their characteristic inward-curving ears, are hardy desert horses, bred over centuries from local and imported stock; they were prized by the Rajput states. The Marathas bred small, tough horses in the Bhīmā valley (the “Bhimthadi” horse), suited to the long, fast marches of their light cavalry. The Manipuri pony, small and agile, was used in the cavalry of the Manipur kingdom and in the game of polo, which the British learned in Manipur in the nineteenth century and spread throughout the world (Gommans 2002). These breeds supplemented, but did not replace, the import of larger horses from Central Asia and the Gulf.

docs.title: 6.7.4 The cavalry revolution
docs.text:
Horsemen are mentioned in the Vedic texts, but as a fighting arm cavalry became decisive in India only in the centuries around the turn of the era, with the Śakas, Kuṣāṇas and later the Hūṇas, mounted archers from the steppe. Gupta coins show the king on horseback, and Gupta-period sculpture shows cavalry. Cavalry became the dominant arm with the Turkic and Afghan armies of the eleventh to thirteenth centuries. Their mounted archers, highly mobile and supported by a constant supply of imported horses, defeated the elephant-and-infantry armies of many north Indian kings. The establishment of the Delhi Sultanate in 1206 was in large part a cavalry conquest (Jackson 1999).

The stirrup deserves a word. Loops for the big toe appear on riders in Indian sculpture from about the second or first century BCE (at Sāñcī and elsewhere), and some historians count them as the earliest stirrups; whether they were in general use, and whether they were stirrups at all rather than mounting aids, is debated. The rigid stirrup for the whole foot was developed in China and on the steppe by about the fifth century CE and seems to have reached India later, probably with Central Asian and Turkic horsemen. Its effect on Indian warfare is also debated; it gave the rider a steadier seat for archery and for lance and sword, but Indian cavalry did not change overnight because of it.

docs.title: 6.7.5 Cavalry in the Mughal and successor states
docs.text:
The Mughal army was above all a cavalry army. Each noble (manṣabdār) held a rank with two numbers, zāt (personal rank) and sawār (the number of horsemen he was obliged to maintain), and was paid, through salary or land revenue assignments, to keep a specified number of horsemen with horses of specified quality. To prevent fraud, horses were branded (dāgh) and descriptive rolls of the troopers (chehra) were kept, a system introduced under Akbar (Athar Ali 1966; Richards 1993; Irvine 1903). Mughal cavalry fought with bow, lance, sword and, increasingly, the matchlock.

The Marathas built their power on light cavalry, able to cover great distances, live off the land and avoid pitched battle; their troopers were either provided with horses by the state (bārgīr) or brought their own (śiledār) (Gordon 1993). The Sikh misls of the eighteenth century were also predominantly cavalry forces. The Pindaris, bands of irregular horsemen who served Maratha armies and lived by plunder, were suppressed by the East India Company in 1817–18. By the late eighteenth century, however, infantry trained in European drill and supported by field artillery had become the decisive arm, and Indian states that relied on cavalry alone were at a disadvantage against the Company’s armies (Chapter 19).

docs.title: 6.7.6 The literature of horses
docs.text: Sanskrit texts on horses (aśvaśāstra) are attributed to Śālihotra, a legendary authority on horse medicine, and to Nakula, the Pāṇḍava prince who was an expert horseman. They deal with the marks of good and bad horses, their colours, their diseases and remedies, and their training. The Arthaśāstra’s chapter on the superintendent of horses describes stables, rations, training, and the classes of horses by origin and quality (AŚ 2.30) (Kangle 1960–1965); the Mānasollāsa discusses horsemanship and polo (Shrigondekar 1925–1961). Persian works on horses (faras-nāma) circulated at the Mughal and Deccan courts and were sometimes translated or adapted from Sanskrit.

docs.title: 6.8 The Horse Fairs
docs.text: Horses imported overland and bred in the arid zone were sold at great fairs held at fixed times of the year, many of them attached to religious festivals. The fair at Sonpur on the Ganges in Bihar, held at the full moon of Kārttika (October–November), was one of the largest animal fairs in Asia, where horses, elephants and cattle were traded; the fair at Pushkar in Rajasthan and many others served the same purpose. Armies and their commanders bought remounts at these fairs, and the fairs were also places where soldiers could find employment. Gommans has shown how this network of fairs and trade routes linked the horse-breeding regions of Central Asia and the arid zone with the armies of the Ganges valley and the Deccan (Gommans 2002).

docs.title: 6.9 Oxen, Camels and the Logistics of War
docs.text:
Armies needed far more animals for transport than for fighting. Bullocks drew carts and carried packs; camels carried loads in the arid west and north; elephants carried heavy baggage and hauled guns. Perhaps the most important logistical institution of pre-colonial north and central India was the Banjārā, communities of itinerant grain-carriers who moved with large herds of pack oxen and supplied armies on campaign with grain bought in the countryside (Kolff 1990; Gommans 2002). Mughal, Maratha and later British armies depended on them, and the size and speed of an army were often limited by the number of Banjārā bullocks that could be hired.

Large armies moved slowly, accompanied by markets (bāzār), servants, families and camp followers who sometimes outnumbered the soldiers many times over. Contemporary descriptions of Mughal armies on the march compare them to moving cities. Their need for fodder and grain shaped the timing of campaigns, which normally began after the monsoon and the autumn harvest and ended before the next rains.

docs.title: 6.10 Camels and the Desert
docs.text: In the deserts of Rajasthan, Sindh and the north-west, the camel was indispensable. It carried supplies across country where oxen could not find water or fodder, carried riders on long, fast journeys, and in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries carried light swivel guns (shutarnāl, zamburak), which could be fired from the kneeling animal (Chapter 5). Nādir Shāh’s camel guns were among the weapons that defeated the Mughals at Karnal in 1739. The Rajput states of the desert, especially Bikaner and Jaisalmer, bred camels and maintained camel-mounted troops; the Bikaner camel corps, the Ganga Risala, served in the British imperial forces in China in 1900 and in Egypt and Palestine in the First World War. Where the camel mattered, the arid zone mattered, and the arid zone was the corridor of conquest for most of Indian history (Gommans 2002).

docs.title: 6.11 Draught Cattle and the Artillery
docs.text: The coming of heavy artillery increased the importance of draught animals. Siege guns were drawn by long teams of oxen, sometimes assisted by elephants pushing from behind. The rulers of Mysore developed a specialised breed of draught cattle, later known as the Amrit Mahal, for moving guns and supplies quickly; the East India Company, after the conquest of Mysore, took over the breeding establishments and used the cattle for its own artillery and transport. The speed of Haidar Ali’s and Tipu Sultan’s armies, which often outmarched their opponents, owed much to these animals and to the organisation of supply (Roy 2011).

docs.title: 6.12 The Care of Animals
docs.text: Armies that depended on animals needed people to care for them. The Arthaśāstra prescribes for the royal stables of horses and elephants a staff of trainers, grooms, cooks for the animals’ food, physicians and guards, specifies rations and exercise, and lists diseases and their treatment (Kangle 1960–1965). The veterinary literature of horses and elephants (Chapter 3) shows a detailed, if traditional, knowledge of animal diseases. The Mughal stables were organised in the same way on a vast scale, with officials responsible for the purchase, branding, feeding and inspection of horses, elephants and camels (Blochmann 1873). In the field, the need for fodder and water often determined the route and timing of campaigns, and the death of animals from overwork, heat, cold and disease was one of the commonest causes of military failure.

docs.title: 6.13 The Hunting Cheetah and the Royal Menagerie
docs.text: Kings also kept animals for display and for the hunt: trained cheetahs, hawks, hunting dogs, fighting rams and cocks, and wild animals in menageries. Animal fights — of elephants, buffaloes, rams and cocks — were staged at many courts as entertainments, and the Mānasollāsa describes several of them among a king’s recreations (Shrigondekar 1925–1961). These activities were closely linked to war: they displayed royal power over the natural world, trained men in handling dangerous animals, and provided the same kind of spectacle as the military parade.

docs.title: 6.14 Ecology and Empire
docs.text:
Taken together, the history of the chariot, the elephant and the horse suggests a broad pattern in Indian military history. The forests of eastern and central India supplied elephants, and the kingdoms that controlled them — Magadha, Kaliṅga, later Bengal and Odisha — were rich in this distinctive military resource. The arid zone of the north-west and the Deccan supplied horses, or controlled their import, and was the corridor through which cavalry armies from Central Asia entered India (Gommans 2002). Kings needed both, and much of the strategy of Indian states, from the Mauryas to the Mughals, can be understood as an effort to secure access to elephant forests on one side and horse markets on the other. The shift of military power from the elephant to the horse, and then to the gun, marks the main stages of the history narrated in the following chapters. Table 6.1 summarises the sources, uses and periods of importance of the principal animals of Indian warfare.

Table 6.1. Animals in Indian warfare Animal Principal sources Military uses Period of greatest importance Horse (chariot) Steppe and north-west Drawing war chariots 2nd–1st millennium BCE Elephant Forests of eastern and central India; Sri Lanka; south India Shock, command, siege, transport Late 1st millennium BCE to c. 1700 Horse (cavalry) Central Asia, Afghanistan, Arabia and the Gulf; the arid west of India Mounted archery, lance and sword; raiding From the early centuries CE; dominant c. 1000–1800 Camel Rajasthan, Sindh, the north-west Transport; swivel guns; desert raiding Medieval and early modern Ox Throughout India; Mysore draught breeds Transport; drawing artillery; grain trains Throughout; crucial in the age of artillery
