docs.title: Chapter 7: Strategy, Battle Arrays and Intelligence
7.1 Introduction
docs.text:
Indian political literature contains a sophisticated body of thought about war and peace. Its fullest statement is in the Arthaśāstra, which treats war as one instrument of policy among several, to be used when it serves the interest of the state and avoided when cheaper means are available. Kāmandaka’s Nītisāra, the Mahābhārata’s Śāntiparvan, the dharmaśāstras and later nīti works repeat and adapt this framework. The same literature describes the organisation of an army on the march, the laying out of a camp, the choice of a battlefield and the battle arrays (vyūha) in which the four arms were to be deployed. Finally, it gives a remarkable account of secret services and espionage.

This chapter examines these three subjects — strategy, battle arrays and intelligence — first as the texts present them and then, more briefly, in the light of what is known about actual warfare. The main sources are the Arthaśāstra in the translations of Kangle and Olivelle (Kangle 1960–1965; Olivelle 2013), and the studies of Chakravarti and Roy (Chakravarti 1941; Roy 2004).

docs.title: 7.2 The Theory of the State and Its Enemies
7.2.1 The seven constituents
docs.text: The Arthaśāstra and later texts analyse the state into seven constituents (prakṛti): the ruler (svāmin), the ministers (amātya), the territory and its people (janapada), the fort (durga), the treasury (kośa), the army (daṇḍa, bala) and the ally (mitra) (AŚ 6.1). The list is often called the saptāṅga, the “seven-limbed” theory of the state. It is worth noting that the army is only one of the seven, and that it depends on the treasury: the Arthaśāstra states that the army has its root in the treasury, and it devotes far more attention to revenue than to tactics. War, in this view, is an expensive activity whose outcome depends on the strength of the whole state. The strength of a king is further analysed into three powers (śakti): the power of counsel (mantraśakti), the power of might, that is of treasury and army (prabhuśakti), and the power of energy or personal drive (utsāhaśakti) (AŚ 6.2).

docs.title: 7.2.2 The circle of kings
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra’s theory of foreign relations is built on the figure of the “would-be conqueror” (vijigīṣu), a king who aims to extend his power. Around him lies a circle (maṇḍala) of other kings. The king whose territory adjoins his is his natural enemy (ari); the king beyond the enemy is his natural ally (mitra), since both have reason to fear the enemy between them; beyond that lie the enemy’s ally and the ally’s ally. Behind the conqueror lie the “rear enemy” who may attack him while he is engaged in front (pārṣṇigrāha), and the rear ally (ākranda) who can restrain him. To these the text adds a “middle” king (madhyama), strong enough to help or hinder both conqueror and enemy, and a neutral king (udāsīna), more powerful still and standing outside the circle (AŚ 6.2) (Kangle 1960–1965).

The theory is an abstraction. It is a way of thinking about the balance of power among neighbouring states, stating in schematic form the principle that “my neighbour’s neighbour is my friend”. It does not describe a particular historical situation, and it should not be pressed too far, but it shows a clear-eyed recognition that relations between states are governed by interest rather than sentiment.

docs.title: 7.2.3 The six measures and the four means
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra identifies six measures (ṣāḍguṇya) available to a king in his relations with others (AŚ 7.1; Table 7.1):

Table 7.1. The six measures of foreign policy (ṣāḍguṇya) Measure Meaning When advised (in brief) sandhi Peace, treaty When one is declining in relation to the enemy vigraha Hostility, war When one is growing stronger than the enemy āsana Remaining stationary When neither side can harm the other yāna Marching, attack When one’s strength is clearly superior saṃśraya Seeking shelter with a stronger king When one is weak dvaidhībhāva The double policy: peace with one, war with another When one needs help to fight

The general principle is that a king should choose the measure that will lead him from decline to stability and from stability to growth. War is one measure among six, appropriate only under certain conditions.

Alongside the six measures, Indian texts commonly list four means (upāya) of dealing with an opponent: conciliation (sāma), gifts or concessions (dāna), sowing dissension (bheda) and force (daṇḍa). The Manusmṛti and the epics recommend that force be used only when the other means fail (Olivelle 2005). The Arthaśāstra is more flexible, recommending whichever means is most effective in the circumstances, but it too treats force as the most costly option. Some modern writers describe this as an ancient theory of “graduated response”; the comparison is suggestive, but the four means were also a list of techniques for manipulating rivals, including bribery and subversion, not only a scale of moral restraint.

docs.title: 7.2.4 Kinds of conquest and kinds of war
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra distinguishes three kinds of conqueror (AŚ 12.1): the righteous conqueror (dharmavijayin), who is satisfied with the submission of the defeated king; the greedy conqueror (lobhavijayin), who wants land and wealth; and the demonic conqueror (asuravijayin), who wants the life, family and possessions of the defeated as well. A weak king is advised to submit to the first, buy off the second, and resist the third by every means. The idea of “righteous conquest”, in which a defeated king is restored as a tributary, is found in many inscriptions, for example in Samudragupta’s claim to have captured and then released the kings of the south.

The text also distinguishes three kinds of war (AŚ 7.6): open war (prakāśayuddha), fought at an agreed time and place; concealed war (kūṭayuddha), using surprise attacks, ambushes, feigned retreats and other stratagems in the field; and silent war (tūṣṇīṃyuddha), the use of secret agents to subvert or kill enemy leaders without open hostilities. The Arthaśāstra regards all three as legitimate instruments of the state. This frank acceptance of deception sits uneasily beside the rules of fair fighting in the dharmaśāstras, a tension examined in Chapter 12.

docs.title: 7.3 After the Arthaśāstra: Kāmandaka and Later Nīti
docs.text:
Kāmandaka’s Nītisāra (Chapter 3) restates the Arthaśāstra’s doctrines in verse, with a stronger emphasis on the king’s self-discipline and on the moral qualities of rulers and ministers. It treats the circle of kings, the six measures and the four means in much the same way as the Arthaśāstra, but it softens some of its harsher recommendations, and it gives more space to the conduct of envoys and to the arrangement of the army for battle. The Nītisāra became the standard handbook of statecraft for many centuries, cited by commentators and imitated by later authors, and its adaptation in Java shows how widely Indian political ideas travelled.

Later works on polity — the political chapters of the Purāṇas, the Nītivākyāmṛta of the Jain author Somadeva (tenth century), the Mānasollāsa, and the many anthologies of political maxims — repeat the same framework with variations. The Nītivākyāmṛta, written in short prose aphorisms, is notable for its practical tone and its emphasis on the king’s duty to protect his subjects; it shows that Jain authors, despite their commitment to non-violence, wrote frankly about the use of force by kings. This continuity of political vocabulary across a thousand years and more is striking, though its relation to the practice of particular states is difficult to establish.

docs.title: 7.4.1 Preparation
docs.text: The ninth book of the Arthaśāstra discusses the decision to march. The king should consider his own power, the place and the time; the seasons in which campaigns are possible (normally after the rains, when roads are passable and harvests stored); the strength and loyalty of the different kinds of troops — hereditary, hired, guild, allied, those won over from the enemy, and forest troops; and the dangers of revolt in the rear while the army is away (Kangle 1960–1965). It warns that the cost of a campaign in men, money and grain must be weighed against its expected gains, and that a march which gains little and costs much is a loss.

docs.title: 7.4.2 The march and the camp
docs.text:
The tenth book describes the camp (skandhāvāra). It should be laid out by experts on a suitable site, in a square, circular or rectangular plan, with the king’s quarters at the centre, surrounded by those of the treasury, ministers and household, and with the different arms, the stores and the market in assigned places. It should be protected by ditches, ramparts, palisades and guard posts, with roads running through it and gates on each side (AŚ 10.1) (Olivelle 2013). On the march (AŚ 10.2) the leader (nāyaka) goes in front, the king and his household in the centre, horses and picked troops on the flanks, and the commander-in-chief (senāpati) at the rear; the text discusses the speeds of march and the protection of the army at river crossings, in forests and in passes.

Later armies were organised in a broadly similar way. Persian sources describe the Mughal army’s camp as a carefully planned city, with the emperor’s tents at the centre and the encampments of the nobles laid out in fixed positions around it, so that each man knew where to go when the camp moved (Gommans 2002).

docs.title: 7.4.3 The choice of ground
docs.text: The Arthaśāstra gives detailed advice on suitable ground for each arm: firm, level ground for chariots, with few trees or ditches; open ground with some cover for cavalry; ground with trees and water for elephants, which could break through obstacles; and broken ground for infantry (AŚ 10.4). It lists the tasks of each arm. Cavalry is to scout, to attack the flanks and rear, to pursue and to cut off supplies; elephants to lead the advance, to break into enemy formations, to destroy fortifications and to protect the army; chariots to protect the army, to repel attacks and to break the enemy line; infantry to fight in all places and at all times. This division of labour shows an understanding of combined arms, even if the categories are schematic.

docs.title: 7.5 The Kinds of Troops
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra’s discussion of the kinds of troops available to a king (AŚ 9.2) is one of its most realistic passages, because it recognises that armies were assembled from many sources of differing reliability (Kangle 1960–1965; Olivelle 2013). Table 7.2 summarises its categories.

Table 7.2. The kinds of troops in the Arthaśāstra (AŚ 9.2), in brief Term Meaning Characteristics (as the text presents them) maula Hereditary troops Long attached to the king; the most reliable bhṛta Hired troops Paid soldiers; reliable while paid śreṇī Troops of corporations Bodies of armed men organised in guilds or associations mitra Allied troops Supplied by an ally; their reliability depends on the ally’s interest amitra Troops of the enemy Won over from the enemy; to be used with caution aṭavī Forest troops Forest peoples; useful in difficult terrain, but liable to plunder

The text discusses which kinds of troops to use against which enemies and in which circumstances: hereditary troops when the enemy also relies on such troops, or when the campaign is long; hired troops when the campaign is short and the treasury full; forest troops to clear the way through forests or to harass the enemy; enemy troops against other enemies, so that their losses do not matter. The armies of hired and allied contingents that Kolff describes in early modern Hindustan (Chapter 17) fit these categories well (Kolff 1990), but the fit shows that the text’s authors analysed a recurring problem accurately, not that later commanders learned from them.

docs.title: 7.6 The Weak King: Strategy for the Weaker Side
docs.text:
The twelfth book of the Arthaśāstra addresses a problem that every small state faced: what should a king do when attacked by a stronger enemy? Its answer is a catalogue of the means available to the weak (Kangle 1960–1965; Olivelle 2013). The weak king should first try to submit to a righteous conqueror, or buy off a greedy one with land or treasure. If the enemy is of the “demonic” kind, he should resist by all means. He should seek allies, especially the enemy’s rear enemy; send envoys to sow dissension among the enemy’s ministers and allies; use secret agents to stir up revolts in the enemy’s territory, to kill his commanders and to set his stores on fire; take refuge in forts and forests; and attack the enemy’s army when it is tired, scattered or divided. If all else fails, he should retreat to a strong fort and hold out until the enemy’s resources are exhausted.

This book is the most practical in the Arthaśāstra, and its catalogue covers, in general terms, the methods that weaker Indian states used against stronger ones in later centuries: the Ahom defence of Assam, the Maratha resistance to Aurangzeb, the guerrilla campaigns of rebels and chiefs (Section 7.15). It shows that the text’s authors understood that military power depends on the whole state — its forts, its alliances, its intelligence and its capacity to endure — and not only on the size of its army.

docs.title: 7.7.1 The Arthaśāstra’s arrays
docs.text: The word vyūha means an arrangement or disposition of troops. The Arthaśāstra describes the battle line as composed of a centre (uras, “chest”), two flanks (kakṣa) and two wings (pakṣa), with a reserve (pratigraha) behind (AŚ 10.5–6). It then describes four basic arrays (AŚ 10.6): the “staff” (daṇḍa), a line in which the troops are drawn up side by side; the “snake” (bhoga), in which the troops follow one another in column; the “circle” (maṇḍala), facing outwards on all sides; and the “dispersed” array (asaṃhata), in which units are placed separately. Each basic array has variants, defined by whether the wings, flanks or centre are advanced or held back and how strongly each part is manned (Kangle 1960–1965). The scheme is geometric and abstract, intended to give a commander a vocabulary for possible deployments.

docs.title: 7.7.2 The epic arrays
docs.text:
The Mahābhārata’s battle books name many arrays, often after animals or objects: the heron (krauñca), the sea-monster (makara), the hawk (śyena), the eagle (garuḍa), the thunderbolt (vajra), the needle (sūcī), the cart (śakaṭa), the circle (maṇḍala), the lotus (padma) and the wheel (cakra) (Hopkins 1889). Each day of battle begins with the commanders arranging their armies in one of these forms, and the poet describes which hero stood at the “beak”, “eyes” or “wings” of the bird. The most famous is the wheel-array (cakravyūha) formed by Droṇa on the thirteenth day of the battle, which Arjuna’s young son Abhimanyu breaks into but cannot leave; trapped inside, he is surrounded and killed by several warriors at once, in breach of the rules of fair fighting (Droṇaparvan).

The epic does not describe how these arrays were constructed in any detail, and modern diagrams showing the cakravyūha as a set of rotating concentric rings, or the padmavyūha as a flower with petals that close on attackers, are imaginative reconstructions. The Agni Purāṇa, Kāmandaka and later nīti works also list arrays, partly following the Arthaśāstra and partly the epic. Attempts to identify these arrays in historical battles — for example, to describe the deployment of Porus at the Hydaspes as a particular vyūha — are speculation, since no Indian account of those battles survives.

docs.title: 7.7.3 Arrays in practice
docs.text:
The armies of the Delhi Sultanate, the Mughals and their contemporaries drew up for battle in a form common to the Persian and Central Asian world: a vanguard (harāwal), a centre (qol) where the ruler stood, right and left wings (barānghār, juwānghār), flanking parties and a reserve (Gommans 2002). This arrangement — centre, wings and reserve — is not very different in principle from the Arthaśāstra’s centre, flanks, wings and reserve, which reflects the fact that the problems of deploying a large army on open ground have similar solutions everywhere. Bābur’s memoirs describe his use of the tulughma, a wide flanking movement by mobile cavalry around the enemy’s wings, combined with a centre protected by chained carts and guns (Thackston 1996).

One feature of Indian battles is repeatedly noticed in the sources: the importance of the commander’s visible presence. Commanders, often mounted on elephants, stood at the centre of the line where they could be seen, and the death, capture or disappearance of the leader frequently caused the collapse of the whole army. Ibrāhīm Lodī’s death at Pānīpat in 1526, the capture and execution of Rāma Rāya at the battle of Talikota (Rakshasa–Tangadi) in 1565, and the death of the Peshwa’s son Viśvāsrāv at the third battle of Pānīpat in 1761 each led to rout. Armies made up of the contingents of many chiefs, held together by loyalty to a single leader, were particularly vulnerable to this kind of collapse (Roy 2004).

docs.title: 7.8 Command, Signals and Morale
docs.text:
Armies were directed by signals. Drums, conch-shells and horns gave orders to advance, halt and retire; banners and standards marked the positions of commanders and units. The opening of the Bhagavadgītā describes the heroes of both armies blowing their named conches before the battle:

Bhagavadgītā 1.15

pāñcajanyaṃ hṛṣīkeśo devadattaṃ dhanaṃjayaḥ pauṇḍraṃ dadhmau mahāśaṅkhaṃ bhīmakarmā vṛkodaraḥ Kṛṣṇa blew the Pāñcajanya, Arjuna the Devadatta; Bhīma of terrible deeds blew the great conch Pauṇḍra.

The Arthaśāstra pays attention to morale. Before battle the king should address the troops; priests and astrologers should proclaim favourable omens; bards and panegyrists should describe the heaven that awaits the brave and the hell that awaits cowards; and a scale of rewards should be announced for killing enemy leaders and soldiers (AŚ 10.3) (Kangle 1960–1965; Olivelle 2013). The text recommends that the king himself remain in a protected position rather than expose himself to danger — advice that contrasts with the heroic ideal of the epics, in which kings fight in the front line.

The qualities of a commander (senāpati) are described in the Arthaśāstra and in the epics: knowledge of all arms and weapons, skill in riding elephants, horses and chariots, understanding of signals, terrain and seasons, and the ability to judge the right moment to advance or withdraw.

docs.title: 7.9 The Logistics of the March
docs.text:
The great problem of every pre-modern army was supply. An army of tens of thousands of men, with horses, elephants, oxen and camp-followers, consumed enormous quantities of grain, fodder, fuel and water every day, and it could not carry more than a few days’ supply with it. Indian armies solved this problem in several ways. They campaigned after the harvest, when grain was available; they bought supplies from the itinerant grain-carriers (Banjārā) and from the markets that travelled with the army (Chapter 6); they requisitioned or plundered the countryside; and they planned their routes along rivers and through fertile regions. The Arthaśāstra discusses the provisioning of an army on the march, the protection of supply convoys and the need to secure the support of the people of the territory through which the army passes (Kangle 1960–1965).

Logistics often determined strategy. The Mughal campaigns in the Deccan were limited by the difficulty of feeding armies in a dry region with poor communications; the Maratha strategy of cutting Mughal supply lines exploited this weakness; and the third battle of Pānīpat in 1761 was preceded by a long period in which the Maratha army, cut off from its supplies by Aḥmad Shāh Durrānī, was reduced to hunger before the battle (Gordon 1993; Gommans 2002). The East India Company’s success in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries owed much to its ability to organise supply, with contracts, depots, bullock trains and, later, river steamers and railways.

docs.title: 7.10 Roads, Rivers and Routes
docs.text:
Armies moved along routes shaped by geography. Invaders from the north-west came through the passes of the Hindu Kush and the Sulaiman range — the Khyber, the Kurram, the Gomal and the Bolan — into the Indus plains, and from there along the corridor between the Thar desert and the Himalaya towards Delhi and the Gangetic plain. This corridor explains why so many decisive battles were fought in the same small region around Tarain, Pānīpat and Karnal (Figure 1.1, inset). The Vindhya hills and the forests of central India divided north from south; armies crossed them by a few routes, of which the passage by Burhanpur on the Tapti, the “gate of the Deccan”, was the most important for the Mughals.

States that could build and maintain roads gained a military advantage. Megasthenes, as reported by the Greek geographer Strabo, mentions Mauryan officials responsible for roads, who set up pillars at intervals to mark distances and side-roads (Thapar 2002). In the sixteenth century Sher Shāh Sūr is remembered for building or improving a road from Bengal to the Punjab, with resting places (sarāʾī) at regular intervals, wells and trees; the Mughals maintained this route and marked the road between Agra and Lahore with brick milestones (kos mīnār), some of which still stand (Richards 1993). These roads served trade, the post and the movement of officials as well as armies.

Rivers were both barriers and highways. The great rivers of the north could be crossed in the dry season at fords, but during and after the monsoon they were impassable except by boat. Armies built bridges of boats lashed together: Bābur describes building such a bridge across the Ganga in 1528 to attack an Afghan army on the far bank, under fire from the enemy (Thackston 1996). The collapse of a bridge of boats could be catastrophic, as it was for the Sikh army at Sobraon in 1846 (Chapter 19). Rivers also carried heavy supplies and artillery, and control of river traffic — on the Ganga, the Indus and the Brahmaputra — was an important element of strategy (Chapter 11).

The seasons governed everything: campaigns ran from the end of the rains to the next monsoon, as Chapter 1 explained. The Marathas exploited this cycle by raiding after the harvest and returning home before the rains; the Mughals, whose armies could stay in the field for years, were nevertheless slowed by it (Gommans 2002; Gordon 1993).

The British transformed the geography of war by building metalled roads and, from the 1850s, railways. The railway allowed troops to be moved across India in days rather than months, and after 1857 the planning of the railway network took account of military needs, including the defence of the north-west frontier. In this, as in much else, the colonial state continued an old pattern — the use of communications to hold a large territory — with new technology.

docs.title: 7.11 Decision and Chance in Battle
docs.text:
Indian strategic literature recognised the role of chance. The Arthaśāstra distinguishes between human effort (mānuṣa) and fate or providence (daiva), and it advises the king to rely on human effort while taking precautions against misfortune. Kings consulted astrologers and omens before campaigns, and the timing of battles was often fixed by astrological calculation; the Arthaśāstra itself, though sceptical of those who rely only on the stars, allows the use of astrologers and omens to encourage the troops (Section 7.8).

The course of battles in Indian history often turned on accidents: an elephant that panicked, a commander struck by an arrow, a contingent that changed sides at the critical moment. Besides the cases noted above (Section 7.7), the second battle of Pānīpat (1556) and the battle of Samugarh (1658) were each decided by what happened to a commander on his elephant (Sections 9.2 and 9.8). The texts’ emphasis on the protection of the commander and on the maintenance of reserves, and Bābur’s and the Company’s reliance on disciplined, cohesive forces, were in part responses to this fragility.

docs.title: 7.12.1 The Arthaśāstra’s secret service
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra treats intelligence as a permanent function of government, directed as much at the king’s own officials and subjects as at foreign enemies. It describes two groups of secret agents (AŚ 1.11–12) (Kangle 1960–1965; Olivelle 2013). The first group are “establishments” (saṃsthā), agents placed in a fixed position:

  • the kāpaṭika, an agent posing as a student;

  • the udāsthita, an agent posing as a renouncer who has given up the ascetic life;

  • the gṛhapatika, an agent posing as a householder or farmer;

  • the vaidehaka, an agent posing as a trader;

  • the tāpasa, an agent posing as an ascetic with shaved head or matted hair.

The second group are roving agents (sañcāra):

  • the sattrin, “classmate” agents, usually orphans raised and trained by the state;

  • the tīkṣṇa, “fiery” agents, men ready to risk their lives, used for violent tasks;

  • the rasada, poisoners;

  • the parivrājikā, a wandering female ascetic, who could gain entry to the households of officials.

These nine types of agent, with variations, run through the whole Arthaśāstra. They report on the loyalty of officials, the mood of the people and the activities of foreign agents; they test the integrity of ministers; they spread rumours and sow discord in enemy states; and in time of war they gather information, mislead the enemy and, in “silent war”, kill its leaders. The text recommends that information be confirmed by three independent reports before it is believed.

docs.title: 7.12.2 Testing the ministers
docs.text: The Arthaśāstra describes four secret tests (upadhā) of a minister’s integrity (AŚ 1.10): the test of righteousness (dharmopadhā), in which an agent suggests that the king is unrighteous and should be replaced; the test of wealth (arthopadhā), an offer of gain; the test of desire (kāmopadhā), an approach by a woman agent; and the test of fear (bhayopadhā), a suggestion that the minister is in danger and should join a plot. Ministers are to be assigned to offices according to the tests they pass. The Arthaśāstra does not hide that the tests are entrapment.

docs.title: 7.12.3 Envoys
docs.text: Diplomacy and intelligence overlapped. The Arthaśāstra distinguishes three grades of envoy (AŚ 1.16): the envoy with full powers to negotiate (nisṛṣṭārtha), the envoy with limited powers (parimitārtha), and the bearer of a message (śāsanahara). An envoy should observe the enemy’s forts, army, treasury and allies, cultivate the disaffected at the enemy’s court, and report on everything he sees. The epic embassy of Kṛṣṇa to the Kaurava court, in the Udyogaparvan, combines a last attempt at peace with an assessment of the enemy’s resolve.

docs.title: 7.12.4 Myths and literary motifs
docs.text: Some popular accounts attribute to the Arthaśāstra the “poison maiden” (viṣakanyā), a woman supposedly made immune to poison from childhood so that her embrace would kill. The motif is found in later literature, notably in Viśākhadatta’s political drama Mudrārākṣasa, in which Cāṇakya is the hero, and in story collections; it has no basis in pharmacology and should be treated as a literary device. Equally, claims that ancient Indian spies used invisible inks, mirror signals or carrier pigeons as a regular system are not supported by the texts. The Kāmasūtra does list cipher-writing (mlecchita-vikalpa) among the sixty-four arts, and the Arthaśāstra describes the use of signs and codes by agents, but the details are sparse.

docs.title: 7.12.5 Intelligence in later states
docs.text: Later Indian states also maintained intelligence services. The Delhi sultans and, on a larger scale, the Mughals stationed news-writers in the provinces and with the armies, linked to the court by relays of runners (harkāra) and post-stations (ḍāk chaukī); the Mughal system is described in the next section (Bayly 1996; Richards 1993). The Marathas relied on networks of harkāras and local informants; Maratha tradition remembers Bahirjī Nāik as the chief of Śivājī’s spies.

docs.title: 7.13 The Mughal Information Order
docs.text:
The Mughal state developed an elaborate system for gathering and transmitting information, which C. A. Bayly has called the Mughal “information order” (Bayly 1996). News-writers (wāqiʿa-nawīs, akhbār-nawīs) attached to provincial governments, armies and cities sent regular reports to the court; the court circulated newsletters (akhbārāt) recording the emperor’s daily proceedings; and confidential reporters (sawāniḥ-nigār, khufiya-nawīs) watched the officials. Runners (harkāra) and relays of post-stations carried the reports across the empire. The system was used not only by the emperor but by nobles, bankers and merchants, who maintained their own news-writers and agents.

The successor states of the eighteenth century inherited and adapted this system, and the East India Company in turn took it over, employing Indian news-writers and runners. Bayly argues that the Company’s success depended in part on its ability to tap these networks, and that its failure to understand the information flowing through them contributed to its surprise at the rising of 1857 (Bayly 1996). Intelligence, as the Arthaśāstra had insisted, remained one of the foundations of power.

docs.title: 7.14.1 Envoys and embassies
docs.text: The exchange of envoys was a constant feature of relations between Indian states. Megasthenes at the Mauryan court, the Chinese envoys to Harṣa, the embassies exchanged between Indian kings and the rulers of Persia, China and Southeast Asia, the envoys of the Delhi sultans and of the Bahmanī and Vijayanagara courts, and the ambassadors of European powers to the Mughal court — among them Sir Thomas Roe, the English ambassador to Jahāngīr from 1615 to 1619 — are among the best known. Envoys carried letters and gifts, negotiated treaties, observed the strength of the host state, and sometimes acted as spies, as the Arthaśāstra expected (Section 7.12).

docs.title: 7.14.2 Treaties, hostages and marriages
docs.text: Treaties ended wars and defined new relationships. They often involved the surrender of territory or forts, the payment of tribute or indemnity, and the giving of hostages. In 1665, for example, Śivājī, besieged at Purandar by the Mughal general Jai Singh of Amber, agreed to surrender twenty-three of his forts and to send his son Sambhājī to serve the Mughals; the treaty led to his visit to Agra and his famous escape (Gordon 1993; Sarkar 1919). Marriage alliances were another instrument of policy: the marriages of Rajput princesses into the Mughal imperial family from the 1560s sealed the alliance between the Mughals and many Rajput houses, as earlier marriages had sealed alliances among Indian dynasties.

docs.title: 7.14.3 Tribute and subordinate alliance
docs.text: A recurring pattern of Indian statecraft was the conversion of defeated rivals into tributary allies rather than their elimination — the “righteous conquest” of the texts. This pattern can be seen in Samudragupta’s treatment of the southern kings, in the Cōḻa and Rāṣṭrakūṭa practice of receiving tribute from defeated kings, in the Mughal incorporation of Rajput rulers as manṣabdārs, and in the Maratha collection of cauth from territories they did not directly govern. The East India Company adapted it in the “subsidiary alliance” system, developed by Governor-General Wellesley around 1800, under which Indian rulers kept their thrones but paid for Company troops stationed in their territories and accepted British control of their foreign relations (Roy 2011). In each case, indirect rule allowed a conqueror to extend his power at a lower cost, though it also left potential rivals in place.

docs.title: 7.15 Strategy in Practice: Four Examples
docs.text:
The theory of the texts can be compared with the strategy of actual rulers. Four examples, discussed in more detail elsewhere in this volume, illustrate the range of Indian strategic practice. One caution applies to all of them, and to every comparison of this kind in the volume. When the practice of a later ruler resembles the advice of the Arthaśāstra, the resemblance is analytical, not genealogical: it shows that the text described the situation of a weaker or a stronger state accurately, not that the ruler had read it or inherited its teaching. There is no evidence that any of the rulers below consulted the text.

The Ahoms against the Mughals.

The Ahom kingdom of Assam faced a much larger and richer enemy in the Mughal empire. Its strategy, as described in the Ahom chronicles, combined defence of the narrow Brahmaputra valley with forts and stockades, the use of the river and of a strong fleet of boats, delay until the monsoon and disease weakened the invader, and counter-attack when the enemy was exhausted. The Mughal invasions of the 1660s and the battle of Saraighat (1671) are described in Section 9.11 (Gait 1906).

Śivājī and the Mughals.

Śivājī’s strategy relied on the strength of hill forts, the mobility of light cavalry, surprise attacks on enemy commanders and wealthy towns, and a willingness to negotiate and to submit temporarily when necessary, as at Purandar in 1665. His raids on Surat financed his state, and his escape from Agra in 1666 restored his freedom of action. This combination of military pressure and diplomacy is the course that the Arthaśāstra lays out for a weaker king (Gordon 1993).

The Mughal Deccan wars.

Aurangzeb’s strategy in the Deccan after 1681 was one of attrition: the capture of every fort and the destruction of every Maratha field army. It failed because the Marathas had no single centre whose capture would end the war, because the Mughal army’s enormous size made it slow and expensive, and because Mughal commanders in the Deccan could often be bought or persuaded to make private arrangements with the enemy (Richards 1993).

The East India Company.

The Company’s strategy in the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries combined military force with alliances, subsidiary treaties, the exploitation of succession disputes and the purchase of local support. Its wars were financed by the revenues of the territories it had already acquired, so that each conquest paid for the next (Roy 2011; Peers 1995).

These examples show that Indian rulers, like rulers everywhere, combined force, diplomacy, deception and money in the pursuit of their aims. The Arthaśāstra’s categories provide a useful vocabulary for analysing their choices.

docs.title: 7.16 A Comparison: The Arthaśāstra and the Sunzi
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra is often compared with the Chinese military classic attributed to Sunzi (The Art of War), compiled probably in the fifth or fourth century BCE. The two works share several ideas: that war is a matter of state that must be undertaken only after careful calculation; that it is best to win without fighting, by diplomacy, subversion or the threat of force; that deception is fundamental to war; and that intelligence about the enemy, gathered by spies, is essential. The Sunzi’s last chapter describes five kinds of spies, and the Arthaśāstra describes nine.

The differences are also significant. The Sunzi is a short work devoted to war; the Arthaśāstra is a long treatise on the whole of government, in which war is one subject among many. The Sunzi speaks to the general; the Arthaśāstra to the king and his ministers. The Arthaśāstra devotes much more attention to economics, administration and law, and its discussion of foreign policy through the circle of kings has no exact equivalent in the Sunzi. The comparison is illuminating, but it should not be taken to show that one work influenced the other; there is no evidence of contact. Both are products of states at war and of thinkers who had reflected on its nature.

docs.title: 7.17 Kauṭilya and Machiavelli
docs.text:
Since the rediscovery of the Arthaśāstra in the early twentieth century, its author has often been called “the Indian Machiavelli”. The sociologist Max Weber, in his lecture “Politics as a Vocation” (1919), remarked that compared with the Arthaśāstra, Machiavelli’s Prince seemed harmless. The comparison captures the Arthaśāstra’s frank acceptance of deception, espionage, assassination and the manipulation of religion for political ends.

It can also mislead. Machiavelli wrote a short work addressed to a particular political situation in Renaissance Italy; the Arthaśāstra is a long, systematic treatise on the whole of government, most of which concerns administration, revenue, law and economic management. Its ruthlessness serves an explicit end: the security and prosperity of the kingdom and its people, which it repeatedly identifies as the purpose of royal power. It also accepts the authority of dharma in many matters, and its methods include the welfare of subjects, the protection of the weak and the promotion of agriculture and trade. Scholars such as Mark McClish and Patrick Olivelle have emphasised that the Arthaśāstra should be read as a work of political economy and administration, not merely as a manual of intrigue (McClish and Olivelle 2012; Olivelle 2013).

docs.title: 7.18 Is There an Indian Strategic Tradition?
docs.text:
Since independence, scholars and officials have debated whether India possesses a tradition of strategic thought on which modern policy can draw. In 1992 George Tanham, an American analyst, published an influential essay arguing that Indian elites had historically shown little inclination to think systematically about strategy, an absence he attributed to geography, to the fragmentation of political authority before British rule, and to cultural factors (Tanham 1992). Indian writers objected that Tanham had ignored both the long textual tradition of statecraft, from the Arthaśāstra onwards, and the practical strategic achievements of Indian states, and that the absence of a modern body of published strategic theory did not mean an absence of strategic thinking. Stephen Rosen approached the question from another side, asking how the social structures of Indian societies, from caste to the organisation of the Mughal and colonial states, shaped the military power that their armies could generate (Rosen 1996).

Later scholarship has taken a more differentiated view. A collection edited by Kanti Bajpai, Saira Basit and V. Krishnappa examined Indian “grand strategy” through texts such as the Arthaśāstra and the Mahābhārata, the practice of the Mughals and the British, and the policies of independent India, and found not a single tradition but several, often in tension: a realist tradition of power and advantage, a moral tradition of restraint, and the Gandhian and Nehruvian emphasis on non-alignment and the limits of force (Bajpai et al. 2014). Historians such as Kaushik Roy have argued that Hindu, Islamic and colonial traditions of war interacted over centuries and should be studied together rather than as separate civilisational blocks (Roy 2012). Indian military academies now teach the Arthaśāstra alongside Sunzi, Clausewitz and modern strategic studies. Such teaching can enrich strategic education, provided the texts are read historically, as products of particular times and societies with their exceptions and contradictions, rather than mined for slogans or presented as anticipating modern doctrine.

docs.title: 7.19 Assessment
docs.text: The chapter suggests an answer to the question just posed. There was a tradition of strategic analysis in India, and its central text, the Arthaśāstra, is as clear-eyed as any classical work about the costs of war, the uses of deception and the dependence of armies on revenue. But the tradition was a tradition of analysis, not of doctrine. Its battle arrays were schematic, its lists of measures and means were frameworks for thought, and there is no evidence that later commanders fought by them. What continued was not the text but the problems it described — supply, the loyalty of hired and allied troops, the weakness of a coalition held together by one leader, the value of information — and the practical solutions that Indian rulers worked out for them, which the following chapters trace.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Kangle (1960–1965) and Olivelle (2013): the Arthaśāstra on foreign policy, war and espionage.

  • McClish and Olivelle (2012): selections with a helpful introduction.

  • Chakravarti (1941): battle arrays, camps and marches in ancient Indian texts.

  • Gommans (2002): the Mughal army on the march and in battle.

  • Bayly (1996): intelligence and information in late Mughal and colonial India.

  • Bajpai et al. (2014): essays on Indian grand strategy from the Arthaśāstra to the present.

docs.title: Chapter 8: War and State in Medieval India, c. 600–1526
8.1 Introduction
docs.text:
Between the seventh century and the early sixteenth, the political map of South Asia was redrawn many times. The early medieval centuries were dominated by regional kingdoms that fought each other for control of the Ganges valley, the Deccan plateau and the river deltas of the south. From the late tenth century, armies from Afghanistan and Central Asia raided and then conquered much of the north, and the Delhi Sultanate, established in 1206, became for a time the most powerful state in the subcontinent. In the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries power fragmented again among regional sultanates and kingdoms, among them Vijayanagara in the south, the Bahmanī sultanate and its successors in the Deccan, the Rajput states of Rajasthan, the Gajapatis of Odisha and the Ahoms of Assam.

Military history in this period has often been written in communal terms, as a struggle between “Hindus” and “Muslims”. The sources do not support such a simple picture. Kings of every faith fought rivals of their own faith at least as often as rivals of another; armies recruited across religious and caste lines; and rulers borrowed weapons, tactics and titles from their enemies. Conquests were also often brutal: temples and cities were plundered, captives enslaved and populations massacred, by many armies. This chapter tries to describe both the warfare and its consequences without either apology or blame (Eaton 2019; Jackson 1999).

docs.title: 8.2.1 Kings, lords and military service
docs.text:
The early medieval kingdoms were organised around a king and a hierarchy of subordinate lords (sāmanta), who held land, owed military service and attended court. Inscriptions record grants to warriors and the titles of military officers, and the elaborate courtly culture of the period, studied by Daud Ali, was closely tied to the ethos of service and loyalty on which armies depended (Ali 2004). Armies were assembled from the king’s own troops and the contingents of his vassals, and their cohesion depended on the vassals’ loyalty, which was often fragile.

Hero-stones are among the most abundant evidence for warfare in this period. Thousands survive in Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Andhra, Maharashtra, Gujarat and Rajasthan. Typically divided into panels, they show the hero fighting, his death and his ascent to heaven attended by celestial women, often with an inscription naming him and recording the occasion — a cattle raid, a battle, the defence of a village. They show that warfare was not only the business of kings: herdsmen, villagers and local lords fought and died in the countless small conflicts that the royal inscriptions ignore.

docs.title: 8.2.2 The great kingdoms
docs.text:
In the Deccan and south, the Cāḷukyas of Bādāmi fought the Pallavas of Kāñcī through the seventh and eighth centuries. Pulakeśin II, who had checked Harṣa, was defeated and killed around 642 by the Pallava king Narasiṃhavarman I, who captured the Cāḷukya capital Vātāpi; the Cāḷukyas later took Kāñcī in their turn. The Rāṣṭrakūṭas, who replaced the Cāḷukyas in the mid-eighth century, raided deep into north India and the far south.

In the north, the period from about 750 to 950 is often described in terms of a “tripartite struggle” for Kanauj, the symbolic capital of the Ganges valley, between the Gurjara-Pratihāras of western India, the Pālas of Bengal and Bihar, and the Rāṣṭrakūṭas of the Deccan; how two of these powers looked to Arab observers is described in Section 8.4 (Thapar 2002).

docs.title: 8.2.3 The Arabs in Sindh
docs.text: The Arab conquest of Sindh in 711–712 by Muḥammad ibn al-Qāsim, a general of the Umayyad caliphate, brought the first Muslim state to the subcontinent. The main narrative source, the Chachnāma, is a Persian work of the early thirteenth century based on earlier Arabic material, and must be used with care. The Arab advance beyond Sindh was checked in the eighth century by the Pratihāras, the Cāḷukyas of Gujarat and other kings, and Arab rule remained confined to Sindh and Multan for three centuries.

docs.title: 8.2.4 The Cōḻas
docs.text: In the far south, the Cōḻa kings Rājarāja I (r. 985–1014) and Rājendra I (r. 1014–1044) built the most powerful south Indian state of the age, which is conventionally and fairly called the Cōḻa empire; what the evidence does not support is the later claim of a lasting overseas empire in Southeast Asia (Chapter 11). They conquered the Pāṇḍya and Cēra countries and much of Sri Lanka, fought long wars with the Cāḷukyas of Kalyāṇa in the Deccan, and in about 1022 Rājendra sent an army north along the east coast to the Ganges — the expedition commemorated in the name of his new capital, Gaṅgaikoṇḍacōḻapuram (“the city of the Cōḻa who took the Ganges”). Their naval raids on Southeast Asia are discussed in Chapter 11. Cōḻa inscriptions name many regiments, some of them recruited from particular communities or attached to particular kings, and record the grants made to them (Nilakanta Sastri 1955b). The Cōḻa–Cāḷukya wars of the eleventh century were fought with great ferocity; at the battle of Koppam in 1054 the Cōḻa king Rājādhirāja was killed on his elephant, and the battle was won by his brother.

docs.title: 8.3 The Cōḻa Army
docs.text:
The Cōḻa inscriptions of the tenth to twelfth centuries are unusually informative about the army. They name dozens of regiments (paṭai), some called after the king who raised them, some after their function or their weapons, and some after the communities from which they were recruited; there were regiments of elephants, of cavalry, of archers and of infantry, and regiments of men from particular regions. The vēḷaikkārar regiments formed a royal guard whose members were bound by special vows of loyalty (Chapter 12). Regiments made gifts to temples and appear in temple inscriptions as corporate bodies with their own officers and property, suggesting that they were permanent institutions with a strong collective identity (Nilakanta Sastri 1955b).

The Cōḻa kings also used the military resources of their subordinate chiefs and of the merchant guilds, which maintained their own armed guards. The overseas expeditions to Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia (Chapter 11) and the long wars with the Cāḷukyas required large forces and substantial logistical organisation. The Cōḻa state’s military power rested, like that of other medieval kingdoms, on the rich agriculture of its core region in the Kaveri delta and on the revenues of temple-centred villages.

docs.title: 8.4 The Rāṣṭrakūṭas and Pratihāras in Arab Eyes
docs.text: Arab geographers and travellers of the ninth and tenth centuries provide an external view of the early medieval Indian kingdoms. They describe the Rāṣṭrakūṭa king, whom they call the Balharā (from his title vallabharāja), as the greatest king of India, friendly to the Arabs and Muslims, with a large army and many elephants; and the Gurjara-Pratihāra king, whom they call the king of Jurz, as possessing excellent cavalry and as the greatest enemy of the Muslims among the Indian kings. These accounts confirm the impression given by Indian inscriptions of powerful states with large armies, and they show that the Arabs of Sindh, the Rāṣṭrakūṭas and the Pratihāras were part of a single political world, in which alliances crossed religious lines (Thapar 2002).

docs.title: 8.5 Kashmir: War in the Rājataraṅgiṇī
docs.text:
Kalhaṇa’s Rājataraṅgiṇī (1148–49) makes Kashmir the best documented region of early medieval India for military history. Its early books contain legendary material, but from the eighth century onward its account becomes more reliable. It describes the campaigns of Lalitāditya Muktāpīḍa (eighth century), whose expeditions, magnified by later tradition into a conquest of the world, are partly confirmed by Chinese sources that record his embassy to the Tang court; and in great detail the civil wars of the eleventh and twelfth centuries, in which kings fought the landholding lords called ḍāmaras, who maintained armed retainers and fortified houses.

Kalhaṇa describes sieges of fortified places in the mountains, the hiring of mercenaries — including Turkic soldiers in the service of Kashmiri kings — the burning of towns, the plundering of temples by kings in need of money, and the famines caused by war. His account of King Harṣa (r. 1089–1101), a gifted but erratic ruler who despoiled temple images for their metal, is one of the most vivid portraits of a king in Sanskrit literature. Kalhaṇa’s frankness about the misdeeds of Hindu kings and his sympathy for the sufferings of ordinary people make his work invaluable, and a warning against idealised pictures of Indian warfare.

docs.title: 8.6 Bengal and the East
docs.text:
In eastern India, the Pāla kings of Bengal and Bihar (eighth to twelfth centuries) were great patrons of Buddhism and builders of monasteries; their inscriptions also boast of military campaigns as far as Kanauj and beyond, and they maintained large forces of elephants from the eastern forests. They were succeeded in Bengal by the Sena dynasty, which fell to Muḥammad Bakhtiyār Khaljī’s sudden raid on Nadia around 1204 — a famous episode in which, according to the Persian historian Minhāj, Bakhtiyār entered the city with a small band of horsemen disguised as horse-traders and the aged king Lakṣmaṇasena fled (Jackson 1999).

Bengal, with its rivers, marshes and monsoon, was difficult for the cavalry armies of Delhi to hold, and its governors repeatedly declared independence. In 1342 the Ilyās Shāhī dynasty established an independent sultanate, and Fīrūz Shāh Tughluq twice besieged its fortress of Ekdala, in 1353 and 1359, without taking it. The Bengal sultans developed a powerful river fleet and fought the Ahoms, the kings of Odisha and the Arakanese (Eaton 2019).

docs.title: 8.7 The Rajputs
docs.text:
The term “Rajput” (from Sanskrit rājaputra, “son of a king”) came to describe a range of warrior clans that rose to prominence in western and central India between the seventh and twelfth centuries: the Pratihāras, Cāhamānas (Chauhans), Paramāras, Caulukyas (Solaṅkīs), Candellas, Gahaḍavālas and others. Rajput genealogies traced their ancestry to the sun and the moon, or to a fire-sacrifice on Mount Abu, but historians see Rajput identity as something that formed gradually, as lineages of diverse origin, some of them pastoral or tribal, established themselves as rulers and adopted the ideals of the kṣatriya (Talbot 2016). How far “Rajput” remained an open status in later centuries is discussed in Section 17.3.

Rajput warfare emphasised the cavalry charge and close combat with lance and sword, the defence of hill forts, and a strong ethic of honour and loyalty to one’s lord. The bardic literature that grew up around Rajput courts in later centuries celebrates heroic death in battle and the defence of forts to the last man. That literature also records the darker side of this ethic, including the collective self-immolation (jauhar) of women in besieged forts, discussed in Chapter 16.

docs.title: 8.8.1 Maḥmūd of Ghazni
docs.text: From the late tenth century, the Turkic rulers of Ghazni in Afghanistan raided north India. Maḥmūd of Ghazni (r. 998–1030) led some seventeen expeditions between about 1000 and 1027. He defeated the Hindu Śāhī kings of the north-west, whose last stand near Waihind, around 1008–9, ended when their army broke — according to the Persian accounts, after the king’s elephant took fright — and he raided cities and temples as far as Mathura, Kanauj and, in 1025–26, Somnath on the coast of Gujarat. His aims were above all plunder, to finance his wars in Central Asia; apart from the Punjab, he made no lasting conquests in India. The scholar al-Bīrūnī, who came to India in Maḥmūd’s train, wrote an extraordinary description of Indian learning and society and noted the hatred that the raids had created (Eaton 2019).

docs.title: 8.8.2 The Ghurid conquest and the battles of Tarain
docs.text:
At the end of the twelfth century the Ghurid ruler Muʿizz al-Dīn Muḥammad (often called Muḥammad of Ghur) invaded north India with a different aim: conquest. In 1191 he met the Cāhamāna king Pṛthvīrāja III at Tarain (Taraori), north of Delhi (Figure 1.1), and was defeated and wounded. He returned the next year and in the second battle of Tarain (1192) defeated and killed Pṛthvīrāja. According to the Persian accounts, he used his mobile horse-archers to harass and tire the Rajput army before delivering a decisive attack (Jackson 1999). In 1194 he defeated the Gahaḍavāla king Jayacandra of Kanauj at Chandawar. Over the following decade his commanders took Delhi, Ajmer, Gwalior and Kalinjar, and one of them, Muḥammad Bakhtiyār Khaljī, overran Bihar and western Bengal around 1200–1205. In the course of these campaigns Buddhist monasteries in Bihar were attacked. Minhāj’s account of the storming of a fortified place whose inhabitants were shaven-headed “brahmins” and whose buildings held many books is usually identified with the monastery of Odantapurī, and Nālandā was probably also attacked (Jackson 1999); the Tibetan pilgrim Dharmasvāmin, who visited Nālandā in the 1230s, found it damaged and largely deserted but still inhabited by a few monks (Roerich 1959). Organised Buddhist monastic life in the region declined rapidly in the following decades.

The figure of Pṛthvīrāja later became the subject of a large literature. The Pṛthvīrāj Rāso, composed in its surviving forms centuries after his death, and modern nationalist writing turned him into “the last Hindu emperor”. Cynthia Talbot has traced how this image was constructed over eight hundred years (Talbot 2016).

docs.title: 8.8.3 Why did the conquerors win?
docs.text:
Historians have long asked why the armies of north Indian kings, often larger than those of the invaders, were defeated. Several explanations have been offered, and most historians would combine them.

  • Horses and horse-archers. The Ghaznavid and Ghurid armies were built around Turkic horse-archers mounted on Central Asian horses, highly mobile and able to harass and outflank armies that relied on elephants and heavier cavalry. Their access to the horse markets of Central Asia gave them a decisive advantage in the supply of remounts (Digby 1971).

  • Professional cohesion. The core of these armies was formed by slave-soldiers (ghulām, mamlūk) who had been bought young and trained as soldiers, loyal to their master and to each other, and paid from the treasury. Indian armies, in contrast, were often coalitions of the forces of many lords, each with his own interests (Jackson 1999).

  • Strategy and aims. The Ghurids came intending to conquer and hold territory; the north Indian kingdoms had long been accustomed to wars of raid and tribute among themselves.

Older writing sometimes added that Indian kings were defeated because they observed the rules of righteous war while their enemies did not. The evidence does not support this. Indian kings were quite capable of surprise attacks, stratagems and ruthlessness, as the Arthaśāstra recommends, and they used them against each other and against the invaders. Nor were the invaders always victorious: Muḥammad of Ghur was defeated at Tarain in 1191 and earlier in Gujarat, and later Indian rulers repeatedly defeated sultanate armies.

docs.title: 8.9 The Hindu Śāhīs and the Ghaznavid Frontier
docs.text: Before the Ghaznavid raids reached the Ganges valley, they fell on the Hindu Śāhī kingdom of the north-west, which ruled the region between Kabul and the Punjab from its capital at Udabhāṇḍa (Hund) on the Indus. The Śāhī king Jayapāla fought Sabuktigīn, the founder of Ghaznavid power, in the late tenth century, and was defeated by Maḥmūd near Peshawar in 1001; according to the Persian accounts, he committed suicide on a pyre after his release, feeling disgraced by his defeat. His successors Ānandapāla and Trilocanapāla continued the struggle, at times with the help of other north Indian kings, until the kingdom was destroyed in the 1020s. Al-Bīrūnī wrote with respect of the Śāhī kings, noting their noble character (Eaton 2019). The Śāhīs’ long resistance delayed the Ghaznavid advance into India for a generation.

docs.title: 8.10 Indian Soldiers in Ghaznavid Service
docs.text:
The wars between the Ghaznavids and the kings of north India are often described as a simple conflict between “Turks” and “Hindus”. The armies themselves were more mixed. Maḥmūd of Ghazni and his son Masʿūd recruited Indian soldiers, called simply Hindūs in the Persian sources, into their armies. These troops had their own commanders, lived in their own quarter at Ghazni, and fought for the Ghaznavids not only in India but also in Khurasan and Central Asia, against Muslim enemies (Bosworth 1963).

The best-known of their commanders is Tilak, a man of humble origin, the son of a barber according to the historian Bayhaqī, who rose through his skill as a secretary and interpreter to become commander of the Indian troops under Masʿūd. In the 1030s Masʿūd sent him to suppress the rebellion of the Ghaznavid governor of Lahore, Aḥmad Niyāltigīn, and he succeeded. Bayhaqī’s account of his career, written by a contemporary who knew the court, is one of the clearest pieces of evidence for the place of Indian soldiers in a Turkic Muslim army (Bosworth 1963).

The employment of Indian troops by the Ghaznavids is the first of many examples of the military labour market described elsewhere in this volume. Later sultans of Delhi, the Bahmanīs and the Mughals all recruited Hindu soldiers and commanders, and Hindu kings such as those of Vijayanagara recruited Muslim horsemen and archers (Section 8.18). Soldiers followed pay and service; the religious language of the chronicles, which describes wars as between believers and unbelievers, must be read alongside the evidence of armies that were in practice drawn from many communities (Kolff 1990; Eaton 2019).

docs.title: 8.11.1 The slave sultans
docs.text: After the death of Muḥammad of Ghur in 1206, his Turkic slave commander Quṭb al-Dīn Aybak became the first ruler of an independent sultanate at Delhi. Under Iltutmish (r. 1211–1236) and Balban (r. 1266–1287) the sultanate consolidated its hold on the Ganges valley, Punjab and parts of Rajasthan. Its rulers distributed the revenues of territories to their commanders as assignments (iqṭā), in return for which the assignees (muqṭī) maintained troops and governed their areas (Jackson 1999).

docs.title: 8.11.2 The Mongol threat
docs.text: The greatest threat to the sultanate in the thirteenth century came not from Indian kings but from the Mongols, who conquered Central Asia, Iran and the Afghan borderlands from the 1220s and repeatedly invaded the Punjab. The wars on this frontier are described in Section 8.13.

docs.title: 8.11.3 ʿAlāʾ al-Dīn Khaljī
docs.text:
ʿAlāʾ al-Dīn Khaljī (r. 1296–1316) built the largest army the sultanate had yet maintained. According to the historian Baranī, he paid his cavalry in cash from the treasury, introduced the branding of horses (dāgh) and descriptive rolls of soldiers (ḥulya) to prevent fraud, and controlled the prices of grain, horses and other goods in the markets of Delhi so that the soldiers could live on their pay. Whether his market regulations worked as Baranī describes is debated, but there is no doubt that he maintained a very large army (Jackson 1999).

With it he conquered much of Rajasthan and the Deccan. Ranthambhor fell in 1301 and Chittor in 1303, both after long sieges. His general Malik Kāfūr led expeditions into the Deccan and the far south between 1307 and 1311, against the Yādavas of Devagiri, the Kākatīyas of Warangal, the Hoysaḷas of Dvārasamudra and the Pāṇḍyas of Madurai, returning with great quantities of plunder. These kingdoms were at first made tributary; under the Tughluq sultans in the 1320s most of them were annexed.

docs.title: 8.11.4 Decline
docs.text: Muḥammad bin Tughluq (r. 1325–1351) briefly extended sultanate rule over almost the whole subcontinent, but rebellions broke out in the Deccan and the south, and by the mid-fourteenth century the Bahmanī sultanate and the kingdom of Vijayanagara had emerged as independent states. Fīrūz Shāh Tughluq (r. 1351–1388) made the iqṭās hereditary and the army’s discipline declined. In 1398 Tīmūr invaded India, defeated the sultan’s army outside Delhi — where, according to the accounts, his troops met the sultan’s elephants with caltrops, ditches and fire — and sacked the city. The sultanate survived under the Sayyid and Lodī dynasties, the latter of Afghan origin, until Bābur’s victory at Pānīpat in 1526.

docs.title: 8.11.5 Who fought for the sultans?
docs.text: The sultanate’s elite was largely of Turkic, Afghan and Persian origin, but its armies were not. They included large numbers of Indian infantry (pāyak, from Sanskrit padātika), Indian archers and, increasingly, Indian commanders. Hindu chiefs served the sultans as tributaries and allies, and some rose to high office (Jackson 1999; Kolff 1990). Conversely, Hindu kings employed Muslim soldiers. The boundaries between “sultanate” and “Indian” warfare were thus never sharp.

docs.title: 8.12 Slaves, Converts and Social Mobility in the Sultanate
docs.text: The Delhi Sultanate’s military elite was open to men of humble and foreign origin. Its first rulers were Turkic slave-soldiers, and the sultans continued to buy and train slaves who could rise to the highest offices. Among them were Indians. Malik Kāfūr, ʿAlāʾ al-Dīn Khaljī’s most successful general and the conqueror of the south, was a eunuch slave originally from Gujarat; after ʿAlāʾ al-Dīn’s death in 1316 he briefly controlled the government before being killed. Khusrau Khān, a convert from the Barwārī community of Gujarat who had risen in the favour of Sultan Mubārak Shāh, killed his master in 1320 and ruled briefly before being overthrown by Ghiyāth al-Dīn Tughluq (Jackson 1999). Under Muḥammad bin Tughluq, men of many origins, including Indian converts and Hindus, received high appointments, to the indignation of the historian Baranī, who complained of the promotion of low-born men. The sultanate thus offered avenues of mobility through military service that cut across the hierarchies of birth, even as it maintained its own hierarchies of race and religion.

docs.title: 8.13 The Mongol Frontier
docs.text:
The Delhi Sultanate’s wars against the Mongols deserve a fuller account, because they are among its most remarkable achievements. From the 1220s, when Chinggis Khan pursued the ruler of Khwarazm to the Indus, Mongol armies were a constant threat on the north-western frontier. Punjab and the frontier were raided repeatedly, Lahore was sacked in 1241, and much of the region west of the Beas passed under Mongol control. Under ʿAlāʾ al-Dīn Khaljī, Mongol armies of the Chaghatayid khanate invaded India several times. In 1299 a large Mongol army reached the outskirts of Delhi and was defeated at Kīlī; in 1303, while ʿAlāʾ al-Dīn was besieging Chittor, the Mongols besieged Delhi itself for two months before withdrawing; in 1305 and 1306 further invasions were defeated, and the captured Mongols were put to death in large numbers (Jackson 1999).

Peter Jackson argues that the sultanate’s ability to resist the Mongols, which few other states of the time achieved, owed much to its large professional cavalry, its fortified frontier towns and its supplies of horses, and that the Mongol threat was a major reason for the military reforms of ʿAlāʾ al-Dīn. Ironically, the sultanate itself was in some respects a product of the Mongol conquests, which drove soldiers and scholars from Central Asia and Iran to seek service in India.

docs.title: 8.14 Ranthambhor and the Rajput Sieges
docs.text: The sieges of Rajput forts by the Delhi sultans in the early fourteenth century became central episodes of later Rajput memory. Ranthambhor, held by the Cauhan ruler Hammīra, was besieged by ʿAlāʾ al-Dīn’s armies in 1301 and fell after a long siege. Hammīra was later celebrated in the fifteenth-century Sanskrit poem Hammīra-mahākāvya of the Jain poet Nayacandra Sūri and in Rajasthani and Hindi works, which made him an example of a king who kept his word to those who sought his protection, at the cost of his kingdom and his life. Chittor fell in 1303, and the story of its siege was later transformed into the legend of Padminī (Chapter 16). These sieges show the strength of the Rajput hill forts and the persistence of the sultan’s armies, which could sustain long sieges with the help of trebuchets, mining and blockade (Jackson 1999; Talbot 2016).

docs.title: 8.15 The Kingdoms of the Deccan before 1300
docs.text:
In the twelfth and thirteenth centuries the Deccan and the south were divided among the Yādavas of Devagiri, the Kākatīyas of Warangal, the Hoysaḷas of Dvārasamudra and the later Pāṇḍyas of Madurai. These kingdoms fought each other constantly, and their inscriptions record the campaigns of their kings and commanders and the deaths of heroes (Nilakanta Sastri 1955a). Cynthia Talbot’s study of Kākatīya Andhra shows how the Kākatīya kings built their power on a network of warrior lineages and military commanders, many of them of peasant or pastoral origin, who held lands in return for service (the nāyaṃkara system), and on the expansion of agriculture through tank irrigation in the dry uplands (Talbot 2001). Warangal, the Kākatīya capital, was protected by concentric circuits of earthen and stone walls; its siege by the armies of ʿAlāʾ al-Dīn in 1309–10 and its fall to the Tughluqs in 1323 ended the dynasty.

The southern campaigns of Malik Kāfūr in 1307–1311 brought these kingdoms under Delhi’s influence, and within two decades most of them had been annexed. Their fall was followed, in the 1330s, by revolts that led to the foundation of Vijayanagara and of the Bahmanī sultanate, both of which drew on the military personnel and traditions of the older kingdoms.

docs.title: 8.16.1 Vijayanagara and the Bahmanīs
docs.text:
Two states that emerged from the collapse of sultanate rule in the Deccan dominated the peninsula for two centuries: the kingdom of Vijayanagara, founded around 1336 on the Tungabhadra, and the Bahmanī sultanate, founded in 1347. They fought repeatedly over the rich Raichur doab between the Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers. Both used large cavalry forces and both depended on imported horses (Stein 1989; Eaton 2005).

The army of Vijayanagara was organised around military chiefs (nāyaka) who held territories in return for maintaining troops for the king — a system that Burton Stein compared with the iqṭā of the sultanates (Stein 1989). The kings recruited Muslim horse-archers and gave them land and freedom of worship; Devarāya II (r. 1424–1446) is said to have done so to match the Bahmanī cavalry. Phillip Wagoner has shown how the Vijayanagara court adopted the dress, titles and courtly culture of the Islamicate world, its kings styling themselves “sultan among Hindu kings” (hindūrāya-suratrāṇa) (Wagoner 1996). After 1500 the Portuguese at Goa became important suppliers of horses to Vijayanagara.

docs.title: 8.16.2 Rajasthan, Gujarat and Malwa
docs.text: In the fifteenth century the Sisodiya kings of Mewar, especially Rāṇā Kumbhā (r. 1433–1468), fought the sultans of Malwa and Gujarat and built or rebuilt many forts, including Kumbhalgarh. The tower of victory at Chittor commemorates his wars. His successor Rāṇā Sāṅgā (r. 1508–1528) was the most powerful ruler in north India when Bābur invaded. The sultanates of Gujarat and Malwa were wealthy states with strong armies; Gujarat was also a maritime power, and its fleet fought the Portuguese at Diu.

docs.title: 8.16.3 The east: Odisha and Assam
docs.text: The Gajapati kings of Odisha are treated in Section 8.19. In the Brahmaputra valley the Ahoms, a Tai people who had entered Assam in the thirteenth century under their leader Sukaphā, built a kingdom whose military strength rested on a system of compulsory service: every adult man (paik) was enrolled in a unit and served the state for part of the year, as soldier or labourer, in return for land (Gait 1906). In the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries the Ahom kings expanded at the expense of the Chutiya and Kachari kingdoms and repulsed invasions from Bengal; in the 1530s Suhungmung, known as the Dihingiya Rājā, defeated the Bengal sultan’s general Turbak, an event recorded in the Ahom chronicles. The paik system, river fleets and skill in building earthworks and stockades made the Ahom state one of the most durable in medieval India, and it later held off the Mughals (Chapter 9).

docs.title: 8.17 The Bahmanī Army
docs.text:
The Bahmanī sultanate of the Deccan (1347–c. 1527) recruited its nobility and soldiers from two main groups: the “Deccanis” (dakhnī), Muslims settled in the Deccan, many of them descendants of the soldiers who had come south with the Tughluqs, together with Ethiopian (ḥabshī) soldiers; and the “newcomers” (āfāqī), Persians, Turks and Arabs recruited from overseas. The rivalry between these two groups shaped Bahmanī politics and military affairs. The greatest Bahmanī minister, Maḥmūd Gāwān (c. 1411–1481), a Persian merchant who rose to become chief minister, led campaigns that took Goa and extended the sultanate to both coasts, reorganised the provinces and the army, and checked the power of provincial governors; he was executed in 1481 on the basis of a forged letter, and the sultanate soon broke into five successor states (Eaton 2005).

The later Persian historian Firishta states that the Bahmanīs used artillery against Vijayanagara as early as the 1360s. Iqtidar Alam Khan and other historians doubt this early date, arguing that Firishta, writing around 1600, projected the weapons of his own time back into the past; firearms are reliably attested in the Deccan only from the fifteenth century (Khan 2004). The case shows the care needed in using later chronicles as evidence for earlier technology.

docs.title: 8.18 Vijayanagara at War
docs.text:
Vijayanagara reached the height of its power under Kṛṣṇadevarāya (r. 1509–1529), who campaigned against the Gajapati kingdom of Odisha (Section 8.19) and defeated the sultan of Bijapur at Raichur in 1520. The Portuguese chronicler Fernão Nuniz, who was in Vijayanagara in the 1530s, gives a detailed account of the Raichur campaign: the enormous size of the king’s army, its contingents commanded by nāyakas, its elephants and cavalry, the Portuguese musketeers who helped in the siege, and the crowds of camp followers, merchants and women who accompanied it (Stein 1989). The figures he gives for the army — hundreds of thousands of men — cannot be taken literally, but his description conveys the scale of a great Indian army on campaign.

The Vijayanagara kings presented themselves as protectors of the southern Hindu traditions against the sultanates, but their wars were driven as much by competition for the Raichur doab, for ports and for horses as by religion; they allied at different times with different sultans, and they employed Muslim soldiers in large numbers (Wagoner 1996).

docs.title: 8.19 The Gajapatis of Odisha
docs.text: The Gajapati kings of Odisha, who ruled from the early fifteenth to the mid-sixteenth century, were among the most powerful rulers of eastern India. Kapilendra (r. c. 1434–1467) founded the dynasty and claimed conquests as far south as the Kaveri, and north against the sultans of Bengal and Jaunpur; his successors fought the Bahmanīs and Vijayanagara for control of the eastern Deccan and the Andhra coast. The Gajapatis drew on the military service of the paika peasant-soldiers (Chapter 15) and on the elephants of the Odisha forests, from which their title, “lord of elephants”, derived. Kṛṣṇadevarāya of Vijayanagara took the Gajapati forts of Udayagiri and Kondavidu in 1513–1515 and married a Gajapati princess as part of the peace settlement. The kingdom fell in 1568 to the Afghan sultan of Bengal, and Odisha later became a Mughal province.

docs.title: 8.20 The Western Coast and the Portuguese
docs.text: On the western coast, the arrival of the Portuguese in 1498 introduced a new kind of warfare. The sultan of Gujarat, in alliance with the Mamluk sultan of Egypt, fought the Portuguese at sea at Chaul (1508) and Diu (1509); the Portuguese seized Goa from Bijapur in 1510; and in 1538 a combined Gujarati and Ottoman force besieged the Portuguese fortress at Diu unsuccessfully. Chapter 11 discusses these wars. They mark the beginning of the European military presence that would transform Indian warfare over the next three centuries (Pearson 1987; Subrahmanyam 1993).

docs.title: 8.21 Gunpowder and the Military Labour Market
docs.text:
Two developments of the fifteenth century prepared the way for the warfare of the Mughal age. The first was gunpowder. Firearms began to appear in Indian warfare in the fifteenth century, first in the Deccan and Gujarat, and spread through the sixteenth (Khan 2004). Siege guns made forts more vulnerable and encouraged the building of thicker walls and bastions (Chapter 10).

The second was the growth of what Dirk Kolff calls the military labour market (Kolff 1990). In north India, especially in the eastern Ganges valley, large numbers of peasants took up soldiering as seasonal or permanent employment (naukarī), hiring themselves to any ruler or commander who would pay. Bands of armed men under their own leaders moved across north India in search of service; Afghan soldiers from the Lodī period onward and “eastern” (pūrbiyā) soldiers from Bihar and eastern Uttar Pradesh were among the best known. Kolff argues that identities such as “Rajput” and “Afghan” were often adopted by men who entered this market, and that the line between peasant and soldier was fluid. This vast reservoir of armed men shaped the politics of north India for four centuries and was later tapped by the Mughals and by the East India Company; Chapter 17 examines it in detail.

Table 8.1 lists some of the major battles and sieges of the period covered in this chapter. Dates are those generally accepted; for many early medieval battles only approximate dates are known. Several of the sites are shown in Figure 1.1, and the forts in Figure 10.10.

docs.title: 8.23 Assessment
docs.text: Two points from these nine centuries carry forward. The first is that the decisive variable was rarely courage or doctrine but access to horses and the means to pay the men who rode them: the states that controlled the horse trade and could pay their cavalry in cash or assignments — the Ghurids, the Khaljīs, Vijayanagara, the Bahmanīs — prevailed over those that relied on loose coalitions of semi-independent lords. The second is that the religious language of the chronicles is a poor guide to the composition of armies, which recruited across every line of faith and caste. The Mughals inherited both lessons.
