docs.title: 10.19 Forts, Power and Memory
docs.text: Forts were more than military installations. They were royal residences, treasuries, prisons and administrative centres; they were symbols of sovereignty, so that the capture of a fort meant the submission of its ruler; and they became sites of memory. The stories of heroic defence and jauhar at Chittor, the legends of Śivājī’s forts, the memorials of sieges in inscriptions and ballads, all show how forts entered regional identities. Today many of these forts are protected monuments and tourist sites, and six hill forts of Rajasthan are inscribed together on the World Heritage list. Their study, combining archaeology, architectural history and the military history of sieges, remains one of the most rewarding fields in the history of Indian warfare.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Deloche (2007): a detailed study of Indian fortification.

  • Toy (1957): a classic survey of Indian forts, with plans.

  • Kangle (1960–1965): the Arthaśāstra’s chapters on forts and sieges.

  • Gommans (2002): Mughal siege warfare.

  • Gordon (1993): the Maratha fort system.

docs.title: 11.1 Introduction
docs.text:
The subcontinent has a long coastline, great navigable rivers and some of the oldest maritime trade networks in the world. Ships from Gujarat, Malabar, the Coromandel coast, Bengal and Sri Lanka traded with the Persian Gulf, the Red Sea, East Africa, Southeast Asia and China for more than two thousand years. Yet naval warfare plays a smaller part in the history of Indian states than land warfare. Most Indian rulers drew their wealth from the land and fought their wars on land; sea power was usually left to merchants, coastal communities and specialised naval families. There were important exceptions — the Cōḻa raids on Southeast Asia, the navies of Gujarat, Calicut and the Marathas, the river fleets of Bengal and Assam — and the arrival of armed European ships after 1498 forced Indian states to confront the problem of naval power directly.

This chapter surveys the evidence for Indian maritime and naval activity, the Cōḻa expeditions, riverine warfare, the encounter with the Portuguese, and the Maratha navy of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Popular claims that India once possessed “the world’s first dockyard” or “a navy that ruled the Indian Ocean” are examined along the way.

docs.title: 11.2.1 The Harappans
docs.text: The Harappan civilisation traded by sea with Mesopotamia and the Gulf; Harappan seals and beads have been found in Mesopotamia and in Oman and Bahrain, and Mesopotamian texts of the late third millennium BCE refer to ships from Meluhha, probably the Indus region (Possehl 2002). Clay models and seal images show boats. At Lothal in Gujarat, a large brick-lined basin adjoining the town was identified by its excavator as a dockyard. This interpretation has been widely repeated, but it is disputed: other archaeologists have argued that the basin was a reservoir or tank for water. It is safest to say that Lothal had a large brick basin whose function — dock or reservoir — remains debated, and not to describe it as “the world’s first dockyard”.

docs.title: 11.2.2 Texts and early historic trade
docs.text:
The Ṛgveda refers to boats and to the sea, and one hymn tells of the Aśvins rescuing Bhujyu from the ocean in a ship; the extent of Vedic seafaring is uncertain. By the early historic period, Buddhist Jātaka stories tell of merchants sailing to Suvarṇabhūmi (probably lower Burma or the Malay peninsula), and the Arthaśāstra describes a superintendent of ships (nāvadhyakṣa, AŚ 2.28), responsible for ferries, ports, river and coastal traffic and the collection of tolls, and for suppressing pirates (Kangle 1960–1965). Megasthenes mentions a board of officials responsible for co-operation with the navy, probably meaning river transport.

In the first centuries CE, trade between India and the Roman empire flourished. The Greek Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (first century CE) describes the ports of western India and the monsoon winds that made the voyage across the Arabian Sea possible; it mentions pirates on the Konkan coast. Tamil Caṅkam poems describe the port of Puhār (Kāvirippūmpaṭṭiṉam) and the ships of the yavanas (westerners) at Muziris on the Malabar coast. The Sātavāhanas put ships on their coins. None of this amounts to a navy in the modern sense, but it shows a world of sea trade that states sought to tax and protect.

docs.title: 11.3.1 Sri Lanka and the Maldives
docs.text: The Cōḻa kings of the late tenth and eleventh centuries undertook the most ambitious overseas expeditions of any Indian state before the modern period. Rājarāja I (r. 985–1014) invaded Sri Lanka, sacked Anurādhapura and annexed the north of the island; his inscriptions also claim the conquest of “the twelve thousand ancient islands”, usually identified with the Maldives and Lakshadweep. His son Rājendra I (r. 1014–1044) completed the conquest of Sri Lanka for a time (Nilakanta Sastri 1955).

docs.title: 11.3.2 The raid on Śrīvijaya
docs.text:
Rājendra’s inscriptions record an expedition, around 1025, against the Southeast Asian maritime kingdom of Śrīvijaya, centred on Sumatra and controlling the Straits of Malacca. A long Tamil inscription at Tanjavur lists the places attacked: Kaḍāram (Kedah, on the Malay peninsula), Śrīvijaya itself, and a series of other ports in Sumatra and the Malay peninsula, among them Paṇṇai, Malaiyūr, Ilaṅgāśokam and Māyiruḍiṅgam, whose identifications are partly uncertain. The expedition seized the king of Kaḍāram and much treasure.

The purpose and scale of the expedition are debated. Older accounts described it as a conquest that made the Cōḻas masters of the Indian Ocean. The essays collected by Hermann Kulke, K. Kesavapany and Vijay Sakhuja show that it is better understood as a raid, possibly prompted by Śrīvijaya’s interference with the trade between south India and China, in which Tamil merchant guilds had a strong interest; the Cōḻas made no lasting conquest in Southeast Asia, and relations with Śrīvijaya were soon resumed (Kulke et al. 2009). A later Cōḻa king, Vīrarājendra, claims in his inscriptions to have conquered Kaḍāram around 1068 on behalf of a ruler who had sought his help, and to have restored it to him — a second intervention, but again not lasting rule (Nilakanta Sastri 1955). A Tamil merchant inscription at Takuapa in Thailand and other evidence show the presence of Tamil merchant guilds in the region. How the Cōḻa fleets were raised is not known: there is no clear evidence of a permanent fleet of warships, and the expedition may well have been carried in merchant ships requisitioned or provided by the guilds. It remains a remarkable feat of long-distance organisation.

docs.title: 11.4 The Eastern Coast and Southeast Asia
docs.text:
The eastern coast of India had long-standing maritime connections with Southeast Asia. Ports in Kaliṅga (Odisha), Andhra and the Tamil country sent merchants, monks and Brahmin priests to the kingdoms of Burma, Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam, the Malay peninsula and Indonesia from the early centuries CE, and Indian scripts, religions and political ideas spread in the region. The Pallava kings of Kāñcī, whose port was Māmallapuram, had close relations with Southeast Asian courts, and some Southeast Asian scripts derive from the Pallava script. In Odisha, the festival of Boita Bandāṇa, held at the full moon of Kārttika, when people float small boats on rivers and the sea, is popularly associated with the memory of voyages by Odia merchants (sādhaba) to Bali, Java and other lands.

These connections were mainly commercial and cultural, not military. Apart from the Cōḻa raids of the eleventh century, there is little evidence of Indian states conducting naval warfare in Southeast Asia, and claims of an Indian “maritime empire” in the region before the Cōḻas confuse cultural influence with political control. The spread of Indian culture in Southeast Asia was carried by traders, priests and local rulers who adopted Indian forms, not by conquest (Kulke et al. 2009).

docs.title: 11.5 Rivers and Deltas
docs.text:
In the great river valleys of the north and east, war was often fought on and across rivers. Armies crossed rivers on boats lashed together into bridges; the Arthaśāstra discusses ways of crossing rivers with boats, rafts, inflated skins and bridges (Kangle 1960–1965). In Bengal, whose delta is cut by countless channels, control of war-boats was essential. The sultans of Bengal, the Pāla kings before them and the chiefs of the delta (the bārah bhūyān) who resisted the Mughals in the late sixteenth century all maintained fleets of river boats. The Mughals, to conquer Bengal and hold it, built their own river fleet (nawwāra), which was maintained by revenue assignments in the province (Richards 1993).

The Ahom kingdom of Assam fought its decisive battle against the Mughals at Saraighat on the Brahmaputra in 1671 largely with boats (Section 9.11) (Gait 1906). Riverine warfare thus decided the fate of the eastern regions as decisively as cavalry did in the north.

docs.title: 11.6 The Western Ocean before the Portuguese
docs.text: On the west coast, the ports of Gujarat — Cambay, Broach, Surat, Diu — and of the Konkan and Malabar were centres of a trade in which Gujarati, Arab, Persian, Mappila Muslim, Jewish and other merchants took part. The rulers of these coasts levied customs and offered protection but rarely tried to control the sea itself. Piracy was common, and merchant ships carried armed men. The Zamorin (Sāmūtiri) of Calicut, the most powerful ruler of the Malabar coast, relied on the Mappila Muslim community for his maritime strength. The sultans of Gujarat had a fleet, which in alliance with the Mamluk sultanate of Egypt defeated a Portuguese squadron at Chaul in 1508, before being defeated in turn by the Portuguese off Diu in 1509 (Pearson 1987; Subrahmanyam 1993).

docs.title: 11.7.1 The cartaz system
docs.text: When Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498, he opened an era in which European ships, heavily armed with cannon, sought not merely to trade but to control the sea. The Portuguese seized Goa in 1510 and built a chain of fortified ports. They claimed the right to license all shipping in the Arabian Sea, requiring merchant ships to buy a pass (cartaz) and to call at Portuguese ports to pay duties, and they attacked ships that did not comply (Pearson 1987; Subrahmanyam 1993). Their naval superiority rested on the broadside-armed sailing ship and on their willingness to use violence at sea, which Indian rulers, for whom the sea had been a space of relatively free trade, did not at first match.

docs.title: 11.7.2 The Kuñjāli Marakkārs
docs.text: The most persistent resistance at sea came from the Kuñjāli Marakkārs, a lineage of Mappila Muslim naval commanders in the service of the Zamorin of Calicut. For most of the sixteenth century, successive Kuñjālis led fleets of small, fast, oared vessels that attacked Portuguese shipping along the Malabar coast and beyond, avoiding battle with the Portuguese galleons and exploiting their knowledge of the shallow coastal waters. The fourth Kuñjāli built a fortified base at Kottakkal, quarrelled with the Zamorin, and was besieged by a combined force of the Zamorin and the Portuguese; he surrendered in 1600 and was executed by the Portuguese at Goa (Malekandathil 2010). The Kuñjālis are remembered in Kerala as heroes of resistance to European domination, and the Indian Navy has named an establishment after them.

docs.title: 11.7.3 Rani Abbakka of Ullal
docs.text: On the Tulu coast north of Mangalore, the queen of the small principality of Ullal, Abbakka Chowta, resisted Portuguese attempts in the mid-sixteenth century to enforce their control over the trade of the coast, in alliance with the Zamorin. Portuguese sources record expeditions against Ullal; much of what is told of her comes from later local tradition (Chapter 16).

docs.title: 11.8 Calicut and Cochin
docs.text: The arrival of the Portuguese in Malabar quickly drew them into the rivalry between the Zamorin of Calicut, the most powerful ruler of the coast, and the rulers of Cochin, who were his tributaries. The Portuguese allied with Cochin, and in 1503–1504 a small Portuguese force under Duarte Pacheco Pereira, with Cochin’s troops, defended Cochin against a much larger army of the Zamorin for several months, exploiting the backwaters and fords of the region and the firepower of their guns and boats. The episode established the Portuguese on the coast. The Zamorins fought the Portuguese for most of the sixteenth century, on land and sea, with the help of the Kuñjāli Marakkārs and of Muslim merchants, and the coast remained a zone of chronic warfare (Pearson 1987; Malekandathil 2010).

docs.title: 11.9 The Gujarat Sultanate, the Ottomans and Diu
docs.text: The Gujarat sultanate was the most important Indian maritime state of the early sixteenth century. Its ports traded with the Red Sea, the Persian Gulf, East Africa and Southeast Asia, and its merchants were among the wealthiest in Asia. The Portuguese attempt to control the trade of the Arabian Sea brought them into conflict with Gujarat and with the Mamluk and then the Ottoman sultans, who were concerned with the Red Sea trade. After the defeat of the Gujarati–Mamluk fleet off Diu in 1509, the Portuguese sought to obtain Diu itself, and in 1535 the sultan Bahādur Shāh, pressed by the Mughal Humāyūn, allowed them to build a fort there. Relations soon broke down; Bahādur was killed in a confrontation with the Portuguese in 1537. In 1538 an Ottoman fleet under Süleyman Pasha, in alliance with Gujarat, besieged the Portuguese fort at Diu, but the siege failed, and the Ottomans withdrew. A second Gujarati siege in 1546 also failed. Diu remained Portuguese until 1961 (Pearson 1987; Subrahmanyam 1993).

docs.title: 11.10 Bengal: The Mughals, the Portuguese and Arakan
docs.text: In Bengal, the rivers and the Bay of Bengal were the scene of long conflicts in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries between the Mughals, the local chiefs, Portuguese adventurers and the kingdom of Arakan, on the coast of present-day Myanmar. The kingdom of Arakan, with its capital at Mrauk-U, was a significant naval power in this period. Its fleets, manned partly by Portuguese freebooters and by local sailors known in Bengal as Magh, raided the Bengal delta for slaves and plunder from bases at Chittagong and the island of Sandwip, carrying off large numbers of people to be sold or settled in Arakan. In 1632 Shāh Jahān’s governor besieged and took the Portuguese settlement at Hooghly. In 1666 the Mughal governor Shāyista Khān, having built up a large river and coastal fleet and won over many of the Portuguese, captured Chittagong from Arakan, ending the raids (Richards 1993). The campaign is one of the few significant naval operations undertaken by the Mughal empire, and it shows that the Mughals could build and use fleets when their interests required it. The Arakanese raids also show that maritime violence in the Indian Ocean was not only the work of Europeans; slaving and raiding by local powers were part of the history of these seas too.

docs.title: 11.11 The Siddīs of Janjira
docs.text:
The Siddīs (also called Ḥabshīs) were people of East African origin who came to India as soldiers, slaves and sailors and rose to high positions in the Deccan sultanates; the most famous of them, Malik Ambar (1548–1626), was regent of the Ahmadnagar sultanate and a leading commander against the Mughals (Eaton 2005). On the Konkan coast, a Siddī family held the island fortress of Janjira from the late fifteenth century (Figure 11.1), first as vassals of Ahmadnagar and Bijapur and later as admirals of the Mughal fleet on the western coast. The Siddīs were the principal naval rivals of the Marathas: Śivājī and his successors attacked Janjira repeatedly but never took it. In 1689 the Siddī admiral Yāqūt Khān, acting for the Mughals in a war with the English East India Company, occupied most of Bombay island and besieged the English in their fort until the Company made peace with Aurangzeb in 1690. The Siddīs of Janjira remained rulers of a small state until 1948.

Figure 11.1. The island fortress of Janjira off the Konkan coast near Murud, seen from the mainland. Photo: Amitabha Gupta, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (cropped)

docs.title: 11.12.1 Śivājī and the sea
docs.text: Śivājī was among the first Indian rulers of the period to build a navy of his own. His conquest of the Konkan coast in the 1650s and 1660s brought him into conflict with the Siddīs of Janjira (Section 11.11) and with the Portuguese and English. He built fleets of small and medium vessels at Kalyan and other ports, and fortified islands and headlands: Sindhudurg near Malvan was begun in the 1660s, and Vijaydurg, Suvarnadurg and Kolaba became important naval bases (Apte 1973; Gordon 1993). The Maratha fleet consisted mainly of gurābs, two- or three-masted vessels carrying guns, and gallivats, lighter oared vessels; it was suited to coastal warfare rather than battle in the open sea.

docs.title: 11.12.2 Kānhojī Āṅgre
docs.text:
The Maratha navy reached its height under Kānhojī Āṅgre, who became admiral (sarkhel) around 1698 and controlled much of the Konkan coast from his bases at Kolaba and Vijaydurg (Gheria) until his death in 1729. Āṅgre’s fleet levied passes on merchant ships, as the Portuguese did, and seized ships that refused, including vessels of the English East India Company, which called him a pirate. English expeditions against his bases in 1718 and 1720 failed, and a combined English–Portuguese attack on Kolaba in 1721 also failed (Apte 1973). After his death his sons divided his power, and in 1756 a combined force of the Company’s Bombay Marine, a Royal Navy squadron and the Peshwa’s army destroyed the fleet of his son Tulājī Āṅgre at Vijaydurg. The Peshwas, more interested in land campaigns, did not rebuild a strong navy.

Kānhojī Āṅgre was an able commander who built a formidable coastal power. Some popular accounts describe him as having “ruled the Arabian Sea” or “defeated the combined European navies”; his achievement was more limited but real: for three decades he made the Konkan coast dangerous for European shipping and forced the Company to negotiate.

docs.title: 11.13 Travancore and the Battle of Colachel
docs.text: On the Kerala coast, the Dutch East India Company, which had displaced the Portuguese from Cochin in 1663, sought to control the pepper trade of the small Malabar kingdoms. In 1741 Mārtāṇḍa Varma, the ruler of Travancore, defeated a Dutch force that had landed at Colachel, in the far south of Kerala. The battle was small in scale, but it was a rare defeat of a European company by an Indian army in the period, and it ended Dutch ambitions in the region. One of the Dutch officers captured, Eustachius De Lannoy, entered Travancore service and helped to train its army in European methods and to build its fortifications; the state that Mārtāṇḍa Varma built on this basis is described in Chapter 9.

docs.title: 11.14 Merchant Ships, Pirates and the Mughal Empire
docs.text: Indian merchant shipping in the seventeenth century was large and valuable. Ships owned by Mughal nobles and merchants of Surat sailed each year to the Red Sea, carrying pilgrims to Mecca and goods for sale. In 1695 the English pirate Henry Every captured the Ganj-i Sawāʾī, a great ship belonging to the Mughal emperor, returning from the Red Sea with pilgrims and treasure; the passengers were brutally treated. Aurangzeb’s government retaliated by holding the English Company responsible and threatening its trade, and the Company was obliged to provide armed escorts for Indian ships and to pay compensation. The episode illustrates both the wealth of Indian maritime trade and the Mughal empire’s dependence on others for its protection at sea (Subrahmanyam 1993).

docs.title: 11.15 The Bombay Marine
docs.text: The English East India Company’s own naval force on the western coast, later known as the Bombay Marine, grew from the armed ships the Company kept from the early seventeenth century to protect its trade. It fought the Portuguese, the Marathas under the Āṅgres and pirates of the Arabian Sea, and in 1756, together with a Royal Navy squadron, destroyed the Maratha fleet at Vijaydurg (Section 11.12). Its ships were largely built in India, at Surat and Bombay, by Indian shipwrights, and many of its sailors were Indian (Malekandathil 2010). The Bombay Marine was a forerunner of the Royal Indian Navy, and through it of the navies of India and Pakistan.

docs.title: 11.16 Indian Seamen in European Ships
docs.text:
The European companies that came to dominate the Indian Ocean depended from the start on Indian seamen. The Portuguese manned their ships in Asian waters largely with Asian sailors, and the English, Dutch and French companies did the same. The word by which the British came to call these men, lascar, comes from the Persian lashkar (“army”) and lashkarī (“soldier”), and its use shows the overlap between military and maritime labour in the Indo-Persian world (Jaffer 2015).

Lascars were recruited through intermediaries — the serang (boatswain or headman) and his subordinate tindals — who engaged crews from the coastal towns of Bengal, Gujarat, the Konkan and Malabar, and from further afield in the Indian Ocean, and who represented them to the European officers. They served on the Company’s merchant ships, in the Bombay Marine and other armed vessels, and from the late eighteenth century increasingly on ships sailing to Britain. Their pay was lower than that of European sailors, their conditions often harsh, and in British ports they were subject to legal restrictions that confined them to particular ships and lodgings; in the early nineteenth century reports of lascars stranded and destitute in London prompted official enquiries (Jaffer 2015).

In the age of steam the employment of Indian seamen grew. By the early twentieth century Indian crews — many from Sylhet and Chittagong in Bengal, from the Punjab and from the western coast — formed a large part of the workforce of British merchant shipping, especially in the stokeholds of steamships. They served in both world wars, and many were lost when their ships were sunk; Indian merchant seamen who died in the world wars are commemorated with other sailors on war memorials such as those at Bombay and Chittagong (Balachandran 2012).

The lascars belong to the military history of India in two ways. They were part of the maritime labour on which European naval power in the Indian Ocean rested, as the sepoys were part of the military labour on which the Company’s land power rested; and their experience — of recruitment through intermediaries, unequal pay, and service far from home — parallels in many respects that of the sepoys described in Chapter 19.

docs.title: 11.17 Tactics of the Coastal Navies
docs.text: The Indian navies of the early modern period generally avoided pitched battles with European sailing warships, whose broadsides they could not match. Instead they adopted tactics suited to their ships and their coasts. Fleets of light, oared vessels — the Malabar paraus, the Maratha gallivats — could move in calms when sailing ships were becalmed, enter shallow waters and river mouths where larger ships could not follow, and attack becalmed or isolated merchant ships by surrounding them and boarding. Larger vessels such as the Maratha gurāb, with a few guns firing from the bow, could engage at a distance. Coastal forts provided refuge and support, and the fleets operated close to them. These tactics made the Kuñjālis and the Āṅgres formidable in coastal waters but left them vulnerable when the Europeans concentrated superior force against their bases, as at Kottakkal in 1600 and Vijaydurg in 1756 (Apte 1973; Malekandathil 2010).

docs.title: 11.18 Mysore and the Sea
docs.text: Haidar Ali and Tipu Sultan, though primarily land powers, recognised the importance of the sea. After conquering the coast of Kanara and Malabar, Haidar built a small fleet, and Tipu planned to build a larger one with French help, establishing dockyards on the Kanara coast. His navy never became a serious force, but his efforts show the growing awareness among Indian rulers of the late eighteenth century that the East India Company’s power rested in part on its command of the sea, and that an Indian state that wished to resist it needed naval as well as land forces (Roy 2011).

docs.title: 11.19 Indian Ships and Shipbuilding
docs.text:
Indian ships of the western Indian Ocean were traditionally built with planks sewn together with coir rope rather than fastened with iron nails, a technique described by medieval travellers including Marco Polo. Sewn hulls were flexible and easily repaired, though less suited to carrying heavy guns. Later Indian shipbuilders adopted iron fastenings and European designs. By the eighteenth century the shipyards of Surat and Bombay, run by Parsi master builders such as the Wadia family, built large ships of teak for the East India Company and for the Royal Navy; teak was prized for its strength and resistance to rot and shipworm (Malekandathil 2010).

Texts such as the Yuktikalpataru, attributed to King Bhoja, classify ships by size and shape and discuss the woods suitable for their construction. The attribution and date of this text are uncertain, and its classifications are schematic. Claims sometimes made on its basis — that ancient Indian ships were built without iron to avoid interference with the magnetic compass, for example — are anachronistic. The magnetic compass was used in Indian Ocean navigation from the medieval period, but there is no evidence that it influenced shipbuilding in this way.

Indian pilots were skilled navigators who used the stars, the monsoon winds and detailed knowledge of coasts and currents. The name “Hippalus”, sometimes given to the south-west monsoon wind, comes from a Greek navigator to whom Greek sources attributed the discovery of the direct route across the Arabian Sea; it has nothing to do with Indian terminology.

The vessels used in war on the Indian coasts were mostly adapted from those used in trade and fishing. Table 11.1 lists some of the types mentioned in this chapter. The names were used loosely in European and Indian sources, and the same name could describe rather different vessels in different places and centuries (Apte 1973; Malekandathil 2010).

The naval and amphibious events discussed in this chapter are listed in Table 11.2, and the places where they occurred are shown in Figure 11.2. The naval history of India is often presented either as a story of forgotten greatness or as one of neglect. Neither picture is accurate. Indian merchants and seamen were central to the trade of the Indian Ocean for millennia, and coastal states taxed and protected that trade. A few states — the Cōḻas, Gujarat, Calicut, the Marathas, the Ahoms on their river — built fleets that were effective in their own waters. But most Indian states did not seek to control the sea, and they had no answer to the armed sailing ships of the Europeans, who used naval power to tax and then to dominate Indian trade. The East India Company’s command of the sea was one of the foundations of its victory on land.

docs.title: Chapter 12: The Ethics of War: Dharmayuddha in Text and Practice
12.1 Introduction
docs.text:
Indian traditions have thought long and hard about the morality of war. The Bhagavadgītā, perhaps the most widely read Indian text, is set on a battlefield and begins with a warrior’s refusal to fight. The dharmaśāstras and the epics set out rules for “righteous war” (dharmayuddha) that protect non-combatants, the wounded and those who surrender. Buddhist and Jain teachers, committed to non-violence (ahiṃsā), questioned whether war could ever be justified, while Buddhist and Jain kings fought wars. Later, Islamic legal thought, Sikh teaching and Rajput codes of honour added their own perspectives.

It is common in popular writing to present dharmayuddha as a humane code that Indian armies faithfully observed, and to contrast it with the conduct of their enemies. This chapter takes a more careful view. It sets out the rules as the texts state them; it notes the exceptions that the same texts allow; it considers the evidence of what armies actually did; and it places the Hindu texts alongside Buddhist, Jain, Islamic and Sikh thought. Kaushik Roy’s Hinduism and the Ethics of Warfare in South Asia and the essays collected by Torkel Brekke are useful modern guides (Roy 2012; Brekke 2006), and Upinder Singh’s Political Violence in Ancient India is now the fullest study of how early Indian texts and inscriptions, Brahmanical, Buddhist and Jain, thought about the violence of kings, from punishment and war to the treatment of forest peoples (Singh 2017).

docs.title: 12.2.1 The Mānava Dharmaśāstra
docs.text: The clearest statement of the rules of fair fighting is in the seventh chapter of the Mānava Dharmaśāstra (MDh 7.90–93) (Olivelle 2005). A king fighting in battle, it says, should not strike his enemies with concealed weapons, or with barbed, poisoned or fire-tipped arrows. He should not kill an enemy who is standing on the ground when he himself is mounted; one who is impotent; one who joins his palms in supplication; one whose hair has come loose; one who is seated; or one who says “I am yours”. Nor should he kill a man who is asleep, without armour, naked, unarmed, not fighting, merely watching, or engaged in combat with someone else; nor one whose weapon is broken, who is in distress or grievously wounded, who is frightened, or who is fleeing. The text adds that a king should keep in mind the duty of good men.

docs.title: 12.2.2 The epic rules
docs.text:
The Mahābhārata gives similar rules in several places. At the beginning of the Bhīṣmaparvan, the leaders of the two armies agree on conventions for the coming battle: warriors are to fight only equals — chariot-fighter against chariot-fighter, horseman against horseman, foot-soldier against foot-soldier; those who withdraw or surrender, who are disarmed or engaged with another, are not to be struck; charioteers, drummers, conch-blowers, porters and those who bring up weapons are not to be attacked. Bhīṣma’s teaching in the Śāntiparvan contains further rules, including the treatment of the wounded enemy, who should be cared for and released (Fitzgerald 2004; Brockington 1998).

These rules have three principal concerns. They protect those who are not, or are no longer, fighting — the unarmed, the wounded, the fleeing, those who surrender, and those who serve the army but do not fight. They require fair combat between equals. And they forbid certain weapons, especially poisoned and barbed arrows, that cause needless suffering. They have often been compared with the principles of modern international humanitarian law, and the comparison is illuminating, provided one remembers that similar rules were formulated in many ancient and medieval cultures, and that the Indian rules, like the others, applied in the first instance to warriors of a particular class fighting each other.

docs.title: 12.2.3 Righteous conquest
docs.text: The texts also counsel restraint once victory is won. In the Arthaśāstra the “righteous conqueror” is content with the submission of the defeated king (Chapter 7), and the Mānava Dharmaśāstra advises the conqueror to install a member of the defeated king’s family on the throne, to respect the customs of the conquered country, and to honour its gods and brahmins (MDh 7.201–203) (Olivelle 2005). Inscriptions confirm that many kings followed this practice, at least in part: Samudragupta’s Allahabad inscription boasts of capturing and then releasing the kings of the south, and medieval kings often reinstated defeated rivals as tributaries.

docs.title: 12.3 Restraint in the Tamil Tradition
docs.text: The Tamil war poems of the Caṅkam anthologies also express ideas of restraint. One poem of the Puṟanāṉūṟu (PN 9) praises a Pāṇṭiya king who, before attacking, proclaims a warning so that cows, brahmins, women, the sick and those who have no sons to perform their funeral rites may take shelter before the fighting begins (Hart and Heifetz 1999). The poem presents this as the king’s righteousness. It is a striking parallel to the Sanskrit rules protecting non-combatants, expressed in a different literary and cultural tradition, and it shows that ideas of protected persons in war were widespread in early India. The same anthology, however, also celebrates the burning of enemy lands and the destruction of enemy towns, and it would be a mistake to read the poem as a description of ordinary practice.

docs.title: 12.4.1 The Arthaśāstra
docs.text: The same tradition contains a very different voice. The Arthaśāstra accepts open war, concealed war and “silent war” as equally legitimate means to the king’s ends (Chapter 7). It recommends surprise attacks, night attacks, ambushes and feigned retreats; it describes the use of poisons and fire against enemy armies and forts; it advises the assassination of enemy kings and commanders by secret agents; and it recommends the subversion of enemy troops by bribery and rumour (Kangle 1960–1965; Olivelle 2013). The Arthaśāstra does not reject the rules of fair fighting so much as treat them as one option among many, to be followed when it is advantageous. The rule of thumb is victory at the least cost.

docs.title: 12.4.2 The dharmaśāstra itself
docs.text: Even the Mānava Dharmaśāstra does not confine war to fair duels. In its discussion of campaigns it advises the king, when he has invaded an enemy’s territory, to besiege him, to harass his country, and to spoil his fodder, food, water and fuel; to destroy his tanks, ramparts and ditches; and to attack him unexpectedly and at night (MDh 7.195–196) (Olivelle 2005). It also recommends winning over the enemy’s subjects and officials. The rules of fair fighting governed conduct between warriors on the battlefield; they did not protect the enemy’s land and resources, which were legitimate targets.

docs.title: 12.4.3 The Mahābhārata’s dilemmas
docs.text:
The Mahābhārata itself shows the rules being broken, repeatedly and by both sides, and it makes the breaking of them one of its central moral problems (Brockington 1998; Hiltebeitel 1976):

  • Abhimanyu, Arjuna’s son, is trapped in the wheel-array and killed by several warriors attacking him together, in breach of the rule of single combat.

  • Bhīṣma, who will not fight Śikhaṇḍin because Śikhaṇḍin was born a woman, is brought down by Arjuna shooting from behind Śikhaṇḍin.

  • Droṇa is induced to lay down his arms by the false report that his son Aśvatthāman is dead; Yudhiṣṭhira, famous for his truthfulness, confirms the report with an equivocation (an elephant named Aśvatthāman has been killed), and his chariot, which had ridden above the ground, sinks to earth. Droṇa is then killed while sitting in meditation.

  • Karṇa is killed by Arjuna while trying to free his chariot wheel from the mud, at Kṛṣṇa’s urging.

  • Bhīma defeats Duryodhana in the mace duel by striking him on the thigh, below the navel, a foul blow by the rules of mace-fighting.

  • After the battle, Aśvatthāman enters the Pāṇḍava camp by night and massacres the sleeping warriors and the sons of Draupadī.

Kṛṣṇa, who counsels several of these acts, justifies them by the impossibility of defeating the Kaurava champions by fair means and by the Kauravas’ own earlier wrongs. The epic does not simply endorse or condemn him. It shows the victors stricken with grief and doubt: Yudhiṣṭhira wishes to renounce the kingdom he has won, and the whole Śāntiparvan is in part an attempt to reconcile him to the duties of a king (Fitzgerald 2004). The epic’s treatment of āpaddharma, “law in time of distress”, acknowledges that ordinary rules may give way in extremity. Rather than a simple code, the Mahābhārata offers a tragic reflection on the difficulty of keeping ethical limits in war.

docs.title: 12.4.4 The Bhagavadgītā
docs.text:
The Gītā’s argument is not about the rules of war but about whether to fight at all. Arjuna, seeing his kinsmen and teachers in the opposing army, refuses to fight. Kṛṣṇa answers that the self cannot be killed, that Arjuna’s duty as a warrior (svadharma) is to fight a righteous war, and that he should act without attachment to the fruits of action. In the famous words of the second chapter:

Bhagavadgītā 2.47

karmaṇy evādhikāras te mā phaleṣu kadā cana mā karmaphalahetur bhūr mā te saṅgo ’stv akarmaṇi You are entitled to the deed alone, and never to what it yields. Let the result of the deed not be what moves you, and do not cling to not acting.

For the ethics of war, the force of the verse is that it moves the test of right conduct from outcome to motive. A few verses earlier Kṛṣṇa tells Arjuna to hold pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat as equal, and so to fight without incurring sin (BG 2.38). On this view a warrior is answerable for fighting from duty rather than from greed, hatred or fear; who wins the battle is not the measure of his righteousness.

The Gītā has been read in many ways: as a justification of the warrior’s duty, as an allegory of the inner struggle, and as a text on devotion. In the twentieth century B. G. Tilak read it as a call to action, including political action, while Gandhi read the battle as an allegory and drew from the Gītā a doctrine of non-violent, selfless action. Both readings have roots in the text’s long history of interpretation.

docs.title: 12.5 The Evidence of Practice
docs.text:
What did armies actually do? The evidence is mixed, and it does not support a picture of uniform restraint.

On the side of restraint, there are Megasthenes’ report that Indian farmers continued to work their fields while armies fought nearby — an idealised generalisation, but perhaps reflecting a real convention — and many inscriptions in which kings boast of restoring defeated rivals and protecting brahmins and temples. Treaties, truces and the ransoming of prisoners are well attested.

On the other side, kings of every period boasted of destruction. Aśoka’s Thirteenth Rock Edict records the death and deportation of hundreds of thousands in Kaliṅga (Hultzsch 1925). The inscriptions of the Pallavas, Cāḷukyas, Rāṣṭrakūṭas and Cōḻas celebrate the burning of enemy capitals; Cōḻa armies sacked Anurādhapura and the Cāḷukya capital, and their inscriptions record the capture of enemy women. Kalhaṇa’s Rājataraṅgiṇī describes King Harṣa of Kashmir (r. 1089–1101) appointing an officer to despoil temple images for their metal. Captives were frequently enslaved, and the women of defeated households were taken as spoils. Rajput and other armies raided and burned villages, and the Maratha cavalry of the eighteenth century, which lived by levying contributions, was feared in Bengal and elsewhere for its devastation. None of this was unusual among pre-modern armies anywhere in the world.

The Turkic and Afghan conquerors of the eleventh to thirteenth centuries were often extremely destructive: the Ghaznavid raids plundered cities and temples, and the Persian chronicles record massacres and the enslavement of captives. But the same chronicles show the sultans also making treaties, accepting the submission of Indian chiefs and protecting their Hindu subjects, whom Islamic law in its Ḥanafī form came to treat as protected non-Muslims (dhimmī) (Jackson 1999; Eaton 2019). Attempts to divide Indian warfare into a restrained “Hindu” type and an unrestrained “Muslim” type do not survive comparison with the evidence. Restraint and brutality were both found on all sides, shaped more by the circumstances of particular wars than by religion.

docs.title: 12.6 Aśoka’s Dhamma and the Limits of Remorse
docs.text:
Aśoka’s Thirteenth Rock Edict is the most famous Indian statement of remorse for war, and it deserves a closer reading (Hultzsch 1925; Thapar 1961). Aśoka records the conquest of Kaliṅga, the numbers deported, killed and dead, and says that he now feels intense regret, because the conquest of a country involves killing, death and deportation, and because those who suffer include brahmins, ascetics and householders who practise virtue, and their friends, relatives and kin. He declares that he now considers “conquest by dhamma” the chief conquest, and he lists the kings of the Hellenistic world — Antiochus, Ptolemy, Antigonus, Magas and Alexander — among those whom his dhamma has reached.

The edict also contains a warning. Aśoka tells the forest peoples (aṭavi) within his dominions that he is willing to forgive them as far as forgiveness is possible, but that he also has power, and that they should be ashamed of their wrongdoing so as not to be killed. He asks his descendants not to seek new conquests, or, if they do, to practise forbearance and light punishment. In the separate edicts inscribed in Kaliṅga itself, which omit the account of the war’s casualties (Figure 12.1), Aśoka instructs his officials to treat the people justly and to avoid arbitrary imprisonment and torture.

Figure 12.1. Part of Aśoka’s inscription cut in Brāhmī script into the rock face at Dhauli, near Bhubaneswar. The Dhauli version of the rock edicts leaves out the Thirteenth Edict, with its account of the Kaliṅga war, and adds the two Separate Edicts addressed to the officials of the region. Photo: Bhajish Bharathan, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Aśoka’s remorse was genuine and unusual, but it did not lead him to disband his army or to renounce coercion. His policy is better described as a renunciation of further conquest combined with an attempt to govern by moral persuasion, backed by the power of the state. Upinder Singh’s study places the edicts within this tension between the ideal of non-violence and the violence that kingship required (Singh 2017).

docs.title: 12.7 Protection of Refugees and Safe Conduct
docs.text:
One of the strongest norms of Indian warrior ethics was the protection of those who sought refuge (śaraṇāgata). The Rāmāyaṇa’s Rāma receives Rāvaṇa’s brother Vibhīṣaṇa when he comes to seek protection, declaring it his duty to protect anyone who seeks refuge. Medieval Rajput tradition celebrated Hammīra of Ranthambhor for refusing to surrender Mongol fugitives who had taken refuge with him, at the cost of his kingdom (Chapter 8). Islamic tradition, too, recognised the grant of safe conduct (amān), which bound the giver.

Promises of safe conduct were nevertheless often broken. The Sikh tradition remembers the oaths broken at Anandpur in 1704–5, when Guru Gobind Singh’s followers were attacked after leaving the town on a promise of safety. Kalhaṇa records similar betrayals in Kashmir, and the chronicles of every period contain examples of envoys seized, prisoners killed and agreements disregarded. The importance attached to such promises in literature is a sign both of their value and of their fragility.

docs.title: 12.8 The Treatment of Captives
docs.text: The texts prescribe the humane treatment of captured warriors: the rules in the Mahābhārata require that a wounded or captured enemy be cared for and eventually released. In practice the treatment of captives varied greatly. Defeated kings were often reinstated as tributaries; prisoners of rank could be ransomed or exchanged; ordinary captives, including women and children, were frequently enslaved, by the armies of the Delhi sultans, by Rajput and Maratha armies, and by the Portuguese. Rebels and enemies who had broken their submission were often executed with exemplary cruelty, as with the execution of the Maratha king Sambhājī by Aurangzeb in 1689 and of the Sikh leader Banda Singh Bahādur and his followers at Delhi in 1716. Such acts were intended to deter others, and they were remembered for generations as atrocities by the communities that suffered them.

docs.title: 12.9 War and the Common People
docs.text:
The sufferings of ordinary people in war appear only occasionally in the sources, which were written by and for elites. Yet there are glimpses. Kalhaṇa describes the famines and destruction caused by the civil wars of Kashmir. Persian chroniclers note the devastation of the countryside by passing armies. European travellers in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries describe villages abandoned at the approach of armies, crops trampled and requisitioned, and the miseries of the camp-followers. The Maratha cavalry raids into Bengal in the 1740s, known as the bargi raids, were remembered in Bengali poetry and lullabies for the terror they caused. The rules of righteous war, which protected cultivators and non-combatants in principle, were often ignored when armies needed to feed themselves or to punish a recalcitrant population.

Two episodes from the Mughal Deccan show how war and hunger combined. In 1630–32, when the rains failed in the Deccan and Gujarat, Shāh Jahān’s court and armies were encamped at Burhanpur for the war against Ahmadnagar and the rebel noble Khān Jahān Lodī. The official history of the reign describes the famine at length — the dead in the streets, the starving reduced to eating whatever they could find, the emperor’s soup kitchens and remissions of revenue — and the English and Dutch merchants at Surat reported mass mortality in their letters. Drought was the cause, but the presence of great armies, which bought up grain and fodder and moved through the stricken districts, deepened the disaster (Richards 1993). Seventy years later, the long war between Aurangzeb and the Marathas (Section 9.16) brought a different kind of ruin. Bhīmsen, a Kāyastha officer in Mughal service who wrote a Persian memoir of the war, the Nuskha-i Dilkushā, describes districts laid waste by both armies, cultivators who abandoned their fields because whatever they grew would be taken, roads made unsafe by raiders, and the hunger and disease of the imperial camp itself. His account, from an officer of the imperial side who was nevertheless appalled by what he saw, is one of the most direct statements in the sources of the cost of war to those who did not fight it.

The point is not that Indian armies were especially destructive. The armies of the Thirty Years’ War in Germany, which were also largely hired and often unpaid, did comparable damage. It is that the protection which the normative texts extend to cultivators depended on conditions — regular supply, paid soldiers, a short campaign — that were rarely met, and that the military labour market described in Chapter 17 made plunder a substitute for pay whenever the treasury failed.

docs.title: 12.10 Loyalty unto Death: Bodyguards and Self-Sacrifice
docs.text: A distinctive and disturbing feature of warrior ethics in medieval south India was the vow of personal loyalty unto death. Cōḻa inscriptions mention regiments called vēḷaikkārar, whose members were bound by a vow to protect the king and, according to some interpretations, to die with him (Nilakanta Sastri 1955). In Karnataka, inscriptions and hero-stones record retainers called garuḍa or leṅka, who vowed to share their lord’s fate and in some cases killed themselves on his death. Some hero-stones in Tamil Nadu and Karnataka depict men cutting off their own heads as an offering to the goddess, sometimes to fulfil a vow for the success of their lord. These practices express an ideal of absolute personal loyalty that was celebrated in inscriptions and poetry. They also show how warrior ethics could demand the sacrifice of the individual in ways that modern readers may find hard to accept, and they belong to the same complex of values as the Rajput sākā and jauhar (Section 12.15).

docs.title: 12.11 Temples, Images and the Politics of Conquest
docs.text:
The destruction and plunder of temples in war is one of the most emotive subjects in Indian history. The evidence shows that temples were attacked by conquerors of different faiths, and that their reasons were usually political as well as religious. Temples were rich, and plunder financed armies; royal temples were also symbols of the sovereignty of the dynasties that built them, so that their desecration signalled the end of a ruler’s authority.

Indian kings before the arrival of Islam carried off the images of defeated rivals’ temples as trophies: inscriptions and chronicles record that Cōḻa armies took images from the Cāḷukya country and installed them in their own territory, and Kalhaṇa records King Harṣa of Kashmir melting down temple images for their metal. The Ghaznavid raids of the eleventh century plundered temples on a large scale, and the Persian chroniclers praised them as acts of religious war. The Delhi sultans and later rulers destroyed temples in newly conquered territories, especially those associated with enemy dynasties, while generally leaving the temples of submissive subjects alone; Richard Eaton has argued that the destruction of temples by Indo-Muslim rulers was concentrated at moments of conquest and rebellion and was connected with the defeat of particular rulers (Eaton 2019).

Islamic law as applied in India, codified under Aurangzeb in the Fatāwā-yi ʿĀlamgīrī, recognised non-Muslim subjects as protected people who paid the poll-tax (jizya); in principle it forbade the destruction of existing places of worship of protected subjects, though it restricted the building of new ones. Practice varied greatly between rulers and periods: Akbar abolished the jizya in 1564, and Aurangzeb reimposed it in 1679. Neither the claim that Indo-Muslim rulers systematically destroyed all temples nor the claim that they never did so is supported by the evidence. The subject is best approached, as Eaton suggests, by examining particular cases in their political context.

docs.title: 12.12 The Ethics of Espionage
docs.text: The Arthaśāstra’s detailed instructions on secret agents, entrapment, poisoning and assassination (Chapter 7) raise a further ethical question: how did the Indian tradition regard covert action? The Arthaśāstra justifies its methods by their end, the protection of the king and the people, and it tends to recommend the harshest methods against those already guilty of treason or crime — the text speaks of using secret punishment against “thorns” who harm the kingdom. Later nīti works soften some of its recommendations, and the dharmaśāstras treat deceit as generally sinful, though permissible in certain emergencies. The literary tradition, in plays such as Viśākhadatta’s Mudrārākṣasa, celebrates the cleverness of Cāṇakya’s intrigues while also portraying their moral ambiguity. The tension between the needs of state security and the demands of morality, which modern democracies continue to face in the regulation of intelligence services, was thus already a subject of Indian political reflection.

docs.title: 12.13.1 Buddhism
docs.text: Buddhist teaching regards killing as a grave wrong and holds up non-violence as the ideal. The Pali discourses praise the righteous wheel-turning king (cakkavatti), who conquers the world through righteousness rather than force; in the Cakkavatti-sīhanāda Sutta of the Dīgha Nikāya (DN 26) the wheel-treasure rolls through the four quarters, and the kings of each region submit without battle and are told only to keep the moral precepts. The same discourse makes the decline of the world begin when a king fails to give wealth to the poor, so that poverty breeds theft, punishment and finally the slaughter of all against all. Aśoka’s “conquest by dhamma” reflects this ideal. The monastic code drew a practical line: the Vinaya forbids the ordination of a soldier in a king’s service, so that the order would not become a refuge from military duty. Buddhist kings fought wars nonetheless, and Buddhist chronicles sometimes justified them. The Sri Lankan Mahāvaṃsa, compiled in the fifth or sixth century, tells how King Duṭṭhagāmaṇī, after defeating the Tamil king Eḷāra, was troubled by the deaths he had caused, and was reassured by monks that the slaughter of unbelievers carried little demerit (Mahāvaṃsa 25) (Geiger 1912). Modern scholars have discussed this passage as an example of the tension between Buddhist ethics and the demands of kingship (Brekke 2006; Singh 2017).

docs.title: 12.13.2 Jainism
docs.text: Jainism holds the most rigorous doctrine of non-violence of any Indian tradition, extending it to all living beings. But Jain householders were not monks, and Jain teachers distinguished between kinds of violence: intentional violence was forbidden, but violence in the course of one’s occupation or in defence (virodhī hiṃsā) could be unavoidable for a householder. Jain kings, ministers and generals — among them Cāmuṇḍarāya, general of the Gaṅga kings in the tenth century, who commissioned the colossal image of Bāhubali at Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa, and the thirteenth-century Gujarati ministers Vastupāla and Tejaḥpāla — led armies and fought wars. Jain literature retells the story of Bāhubali, who at the moment of victory over his brother renounced the world, as an image of the conquest of the self. In the ninth-century Ādipurāṇa of the Digambara teacher Jinasena the story is also a reflection on war. Bharata, the first universal emperor, conquers the quarters of the world, but when his brother refuses to submit the ministers on both sides propose that, to spare the armies, the brothers fight each other alone, in contests of staring, of water-fighting and of wrestling; Bāhubali wins them all, the emperor’s discus will not harm a kinsman, and the victor renounces the kingdom he has won. The Jain imagination thus accepted the conquering king as part of the world’s order while turning the climax of his war into a lesson in the futility of victory. Jain authors also wrote frankly on statecraft, as in Somadeva’s Nītivākyāmṛta (Section 7.3), and Upinder Singh has traced how Buddhist and Jain thinkers, while condemning violence, accepted a measure of it as part of royal duty (Singh 2017).

docs.title: 12.14.1 Islamic law of war
docs.text: The Islamic law of war (siyar), developed in the eighth and ninth centuries, distinguishes combatants from non-combatants and forbids the killing of women, children, the old and monks who take no part in fighting; it regulates the treatment of prisoners, the division of spoils and the terms on which non-Muslims could submit and become protected subjects paying a poll-tax (jizya). In India, Persian works on statecraft such as Fakhr-i Mudabbir’s Ādāb al-ḥarb wa’l-shajāʿa discussed the conduct of war, combining Islamic legal norms with the Persian tradition of advice to kings. In the fourteenth century Ẓiyāʾ al-Dīn Baranī’s Fatāwā-yi Jahāndārī went further: it argued that a sultan must sometimes govern by state regulations (ẓawābiṭ) of his own making where the sacred law did not suffice, and urged him to humble the unbelievers, while Baranī’s own history shows sultans who in practice made treaties with Hindu chiefs and employed them (Jackson 1999). In India the Ḥanafī jurists’ acceptance of Hindus as protected subjects (dhimmī) who paid the jizya turned the law of conquest into a law of rule over a non-Muslim majority (Section 12.11). As with the Sanskrit texts, practice often diverged from the norms, and chroniclers praised sultans for both piety and ferocity.

docs.title: 12.14.2 The Sikh Gurus
docs.text: Sikh teaching took up arms reluctantly and with conditions. Guru Gobind Singh’s Persian letter to Aurangzeb, the Ẓafarnāma, written after the Mughal and hill chiefs’ forces had broken their oaths of safe conduct at Anandpur, contains a widely quoted couplet to the effect that when all other means have failed, it is right to take up the sword. The Khalsa’s codes of conduct (rahit) forbade the molestation of women and required protection of the weak (Grewal 1990; Dhavan 2011). Like other traditions, the Sikh one combined an ideal of just and limited war with the realities of a long and bitter conflict.

docs.title: 12.15 Honour, Death and Glory
docs.text: Another strand of Indian warrior ethics concerned not the protection of the enemy but the warrior’s own honour. The epics promise heaven to the warrior who dies facing the enemy; the Gītā tells Arjuna that if he is killed he will gain heaven, and if he wins he will enjoy the earth (BG 2.37). Hero-stones show the dead warrior ascending to heaven. Rajput bardic poetry exalted the warrior who fought to the death rather than retreat or surrender, and the custom of the last charge (sākā) of the men of a fallen fort, accompanied by the jauhar of the women, became the supreme expression of this ethic. Modern scholarship has examined how these customs were celebrated and how they were imposed: the jauhar, often presented as the free choice of women, took place under extreme duress and in a social order that valued women’s “honour” above their lives (Chapter 16) (Sreenivasan 2007).

docs.title: 12.16 Rajput Honour and Its Costs
docs.text: The Rajput ethic of honour, as celebrated in bardic literature and in later nationalist writing, emphasised loyalty to one’s lord, the refusal to retreat, the protection of those who sought refuge, and death rather than surrender. These values inspired remarkable acts of courage. They also had costs. The ideal of the last charge and the jauhar turned defeats into massacres; the emphasis on personal and clan honour made it difficult for Rajput rulers to co-operate with each other; and the code was applied selectively, since Rajput armies, like others, raided, plundered and took captives. Modern historians such as Ramya Sreenivasan have shown how the image of the honourable Rajput warrior was shaped over centuries by bards, by the needs of Rajput courts under Mughal and British rule, and by nationalist writers (Sreenivasan 2007; Talbot 2016). Understanding this history does not diminish the courage of individual warriors, but it helps to separate history from myth.

docs.title: 12.17 The Ethics of the Mercenary
docs.text: A large part of the soldiers who fought in Indian wars were paid professionals who served whoever employed them — the hired troops (bhṛta) of the Arthaśāstra, the peasant soldiers of Kolff’s military labour market, the Afghan, Rajput, Purbiya and Maratha bands of the medieval and early modern periods, the European adventurers of the eighteenth century, and the sepoys of the East India Company (Kolff 1990). Their ethic was one of service and loyalty to the employer who paid them and gave them his salt, rather than loyalty to a cause, a religion or a nation. Changes of side when pay was not forthcoming, or when a better offer came, were common and were not always regarded as dishonourable. This ethic of service helps to explain both the flexibility of Indian armies and the ease with which the East India Company recruited Indian soldiers to conquer India. The moral world of the Indian soldier was shaped as much by the realities of employment as by the ideals of the texts (Chapter 17).

docs.title: 12.18 Violence in 1857
docs.text: The rising of 1857 was marked by extreme violence on both sides. Rebels killed British officers, civilians, women and children at Meerut, Delhi and above all at Kanpur, where British women and children held captive were killed in the Bibighar in July 1857. The British response was ferocious: rebels and suspected rebels were hanged in large numbers, sometimes after summary trials or none at all; villages were burned; and some captured sepoys were executed by being blown from cannon. The violence of 1857 left deep scars on both British and Indian memory, and it shaped British policy in India for decades. Here, as in many wars before it, the laws of war, whether Indian or European, gave way once the conflict took on the character of rebellion and reprisal.

docs.title: 12.19 Non-Violence and War in Modern India
docs.text:
In the twentieth century, Mahatma Gandhi made non-violence (ahiṃsā) the basis of a mass political movement against British rule. His position on war was not simple. In the Boer War and the First World War he supported the British empire, organising an ambulance corps in South Africa and, in 1918, campaigning for Indian recruitment into the army, on the grounds that Indians who claimed the rights of citizens should accept its duties. Later he opposed participation in war and argued that non-violent resistance could be used even against invasion. His allegorical reading of the Bhagavadgītā (Section 12.4) was contested by other nationalists, including Tilak and Aurobindo (Roy 2012).

Independent India adopted a constitution and institutions that are not founded on any one religious tradition, and it ratified the Geneva Conventions of 1949. Its armed forces train their personnel in international humanitarian law. The traditions of dharmayuddha, Aśoka’s dhamma, Gandhian non-violence and the Sikh and Rajput codes of honour are frequently invoked in Indian military and political discourse, as sources of values and identity rather than as legal codes. Table 12.1 brings together the principal norms of war discussed in this chapter, with their sources and the exceptions or contrary evidence that the same traditions record.

Table 12.1. Norms of war in Indian traditions, with exceptions Norm Principal sources Exceptions and contrary evidence Do not strike the unarmed, fleeing, wounded, sleeping or surrendering MDh 7.91–93; Mahābhārata Epic killings of Abhimanyu, Droṇa and Karṇa; the night massacre No poisoned, barbed or fire-tipped arrows MDh 7.90 Arthaśāstra recommends poisons and incendiaries Fight only equals Mahābhārata (Bhīṣmaparvan conventions) Multiple attackers on Abhimanyu; practice of armies Protect non-combatants and those who serve the army Mahābhārata; PN 9 Plunder and enslavement recorded in inscriptions and chronicles Spare the enemy’s land and people Megasthenes (as an observation) MDh 7.195–196: spoil fodder, water and fuel; destroy tanks Restore the defeated king AŚ 12.1; MDh 7.202–203; inscriptions Annexations by many kingdoms; “demonic” conquerors Keep promises of safe conduct Epics; Islamic amān Broken oaths at Anandpur; betrayals in Kashmir Use force only after other means MDh 7; epics Arthaśāstra: use whichever means is most effective Protect refugees (śaraṇāgata) Rāmāyaṇa; Rajput tradition Refugees surrendered or killed in many wars Do not kill women, children, the old and monks Islamic siyar Massacres in conquests and sieges Take up arms only when other means fail Ẓafarnāma (Sikh tradition) Long cycles of reprisal in the eighteenth century Renounce conquest Aśoka, Rock Edict XIII Aśoka kept his army and warned the forest peoples

docs.title: 12.20 Indian Ethics of War in Comparative Perspective
docs.text:
Indian ideas about the ethics of war can usefully be compared with those of other traditions, provided the comparison is made with care (Brekke 2006).

The Christian just war tradition.

In Latin Christianity, Augustine (fourth to fifth century) and later Thomas Aquinas (thirteenth century) developed a theory of the “just war”, which required a legitimate authority, a just cause and a right intention; later writers added conditions such as last resort and proportionality, and rules for the conduct of war (jus in bello), including the protection of non-combatants. The Indian texts address many of the same questions: who may make war (the king), for what reasons (the protection of the people and of dharma), and by what means. The Indian tradition gives more attention than the early Christian one to the rules of combat between warriors, and less to the theory of legitimate authority, which it takes for granted in the figure of the king.

Islamic thought.

The Islamic law of war (siyar) distinguishes between kinds of war, regulates the treatment of non-combatants, prisoners and property, and defines the conditions under which non-Muslims could live under Muslim rule as protected subjects. Like the Sanskrit texts, it combines an ideal of regulated warfare with recognition of the needs of states, and like them it was applied variably in practice. Persian works on statecraft composed in India drew both on Islamic law and on the Persian tradition of advice to kings, which in many respects resembles the Indian nīti literature in its pragmatism.

Chinese thought.

Classical Chinese thinkers debated war from many perspectives: Confucians emphasised the moral authority of the ruler and the welfare of the people, Mohists condemned offensive war, and military writers such as Sunzi analysed war as an instrument of state. The range of Indian views — from the pragmatism of the Arthaśāstra to the rules of the dharmaśāstras and the non-violence of the Jains — is comparable in breadth.

The comparison shows that the questions raised by war were similar across civilisations and that many of the answers were too. It also highlights the distinctive features of the Indian tradition: its systematic treatment of the warrior’s duty (svadharma) in the Gītā, its tragic reflection in the Mahābhārata on the moral costs of victory, Aśoka’s public remorse, and the radical non-violence of the Jain tradition. These are contributions to the world’s moral reflection on war that deserve to be known on their own terms, without exaggerated claims of priority.

docs.title: 12.21 Indian Traditions and the Modern Laws of War
docs.text:
Since the nineteenth century, Indian scholars and statesmen have pointed to the rules of dharmayuddha as evidence that India possessed an indigenous tradition of humanitarian restraint in war. The comparison with modern international humanitarian law is legitimate and instructive. The protection of non-combatants, of the wounded and of those who surrender, the prohibition of perfidy and of weapons causing unnecessary suffering, and the idea that war must be declared and conducted under rules, all have parallels in the Indian texts.

The comparison should not be turned into a claim of priority or uniqueness. Ancient Greek, Roman, Chinese, Jewish, Christian and Islamic traditions also formulated rules restricting the conduct of war, and in none of them were the rules consistently observed. The Indian texts themselves, as this chapter has shown, also recommend deception, devastation and assassination. The value of the Indian tradition lies less in any claim to have anticipated the Geneva Conventions than in the depth and honesty of its reflection — above all in the Mahābhārata — on the moral costs of war, on the difficulty of keeping limits in extremity, and on the grief that follows even a just victory (Roy 2012).

  • Brekke (2006): essays on the ethics of war in Hindu, Buddhist, Islamic, Chinese and Japanese traditions.

  • Olivelle (2005): the Mānava Dharmaśāstra, with its rules of war.

  • Fitzgerald (2004): the Śāntiparvan in translation.

  • Hiltebeitel (1976): the battle books of the Mahābhārata and Kṛṣṇa’s role in them.

docs.title: Chapter 13: The Making of Warriors: Education, Society and Martial Culture
13.1 Introduction
docs.text: Armies are made of men — and occasionally women — who have to be recruited, trained, fed, paid, honoured and remembered. This chapter turns from the conduct of war to the warrior: how princes and soldiers were educated, who was allowed to bear arms and who was excluded, how warrior identities were formed and changed, and how martial values were expressed in art, literature, festival and ritual. It draws on the epics and the Arthaśāstra for the ideals of royal education, on the work of Dirk Kolff and William Pinch for the social history of soldiering, and on a range of art-historical and ethnographic evidence for martial culture (Kolff 1990; Pinch 2006).

docs.title: 13.2.1 The epic model
docs.text:
The epics give a vivid, idealised picture of the education of princes. In the Mahābhārata, the Pāṇḍava and Kaurava princes are taught first by Kṛpa and then by Droṇa, a brahmin master of arms, who trains them in archery, the use of the mace, sword and spear, chariot-driving and the riding of horses and elephants (Buitenen 1973–1978). Their training ends in a public tournament (raṅga) in which each displays his skill before the king and the people: Arjuna shows his mastery of the bow, Bhīma and Duryodhana fight with maces until the fight threatens to become real. Each prince has his specialism — Yudhiṣṭhira the chariot and spear, Bhīma and Duryodhana the mace, Nakula and Sahadeva the sword, Arjuna the bow.

In the Rāmāyaṇa, the young Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa are taken by the sage Viśvāmitra to protect his sacrifice from demons, and on the way he teaches them two spells against hunger and fatigue and gives them divine weapons. The figure of the brahmin or sage who teaches arms to princes — Droṇa, Kṛpa, Paraśurāma, Viśvāmitra — recurs throughout the epics.

docs.title: 13.2.2 The Arthaśāstra’s curriculum
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra lays down a curriculum for the prince that combines intellectual and military training (AŚ 1.5). After learning to write and count, he is to study the three Vedas, philosophy (ānvīkṣikī), economics (vārttā) and government (daṇḍanīti) under appropriate teachers. His day is to be divided: in the first part he should receive training in the arts of elephants, horses, chariots and weapons, and in the second he should listen to accounts of the past (itihāsa), including the Purāṇas, stories, examples, the law and the science of politics (Kangle 1960–1965; Olivelle 2013). The ideal prince is thus a soldier and a scholar, trained in self-discipline (vinaya), with control of his senses.

The Arthaśāstra and the Mānava Dharmaśāstra also warn kings against the vices of pleasure, among them hunting, gambling, sleeping by day, women and drink (MDh 7.47) (Olivelle 2005). Hunting nevertheless remained the favourite sport and military exercise of kings, training riders and archers and displaying royal power (Section 4.10).

docs.title: 13.2.3 Medieval courts
docs.text: Medieval courts maintained this ideal. Daud Ali has shown how early medieval courtly culture prescribed a disciplined life for princes and courtiers in which martial skills, courtly manners, literary taste and loyalty were combined (Ali 2004). The Mānasollāsa of the Cāḷukya king Someśvara III describes the recreations of a king, including wrestling, horsemanship, elephant-riding, archery contests and the hunt (Shrigondekar 1925–1961).

docs.title: 13.3 The Training of Princes in the Mughal and Successor States
docs.text:
Mughal princes learned war by practice as much as by instruction. They were taught riding, archery, swordsmanship and musketry from childhood, took part in royal hunts, and were given commands while still young: Aurangzeb, for example, was appointed governor of the Deccan at the age of eighteen and led a campaign against the Bundela chief Jujhār Singh in his teens. Akbar, who never learned to read, was nonetheless a skilled rider, hunter, marksman and commander, and personally took part in several battles and sieges. Princes commanded armies in the field as part of their training for rule, and their success or failure in war often determined their standing in the competition for the throne (Richards 1993).

Rajput princes were trained in a similar way in riding, hunting and the use of arms, and they too learned by commanding the contingents that their families supplied to the Mughals. Maratha tradition records that Śivājī was brought up at Pune under the guardianship of his father’s administrator Dādājī Koṇḍadev, learning riding and arms alongside the young men of the hill villages who later became his soldiers (Gordon 1993). These examples show that, in practice, the education of princes in early modern India combined formal instruction in literature and religion with an apprenticeship in war, conducted through hunting, service and command.

docs.title: 13.4 Birth, Caste and the Right to Arms
13.4.1 The norm
docs.text: In the theory of the four social classes (varṇa), the profession of arms belongs to the kṣatriya, whose duties are to protect the people, to make gifts, to sacrifice and to study the Veda (MDh 1.89) (Olivelle 2005). Brahmins and vaiśyas may take up arms in an emergency, when the social order is threatened (MDh 8.348), and the epics present brahmin warriors such as Droṇa, Kṛpa, Aśvatthāman and Paraśurāma. The normative texts say little about the arms-bearing of śūdras and of groups outside the four classes, but they generally assume that warfare is a matter for the higher classes.

docs.title: 13.4.2 Ekalavya and Karṇa
docs.text:
Two famous episodes of the Mahābhārata show how birth could limit access to martial training. Ekalavya, a prince of the Niṣāda forest people, asks Droṇa to teach him and is refused. He makes a clay image of Droṇa and trains before it until he becomes a better archer than Arjuna, Droṇa’s favourite pupil. When Droṇa discovers this, he demands as his teacher’s fee the thumb of Ekalavya’s right hand, and Ekalavya cuts it off and gives it, losing his skill. Karṇa, a great warrior raised by a charioteer, is barred from competing with Arjuna at the tournament when Kṛpa demands to know his lineage; Duryodhana makes him a king on the spot to give him the necessary status, and he remains loyal to Duryodhana for the rest of his life.

These stories have been read in many ways. In the epic they serve partly to explain Arjuna’s supremacy and Karṇa’s tragic loyalty. Modern readers, especially in the anti-caste movements of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, have seen in Droṇa’s demand an emblem of the exclusion of lower castes and forest peoples from learning, and Ekalavya has become a symbol of talent denied by birth. Both readings take the stories seriously as evidence of the social order that the epic assumes.

docs.title: 13.4.3 The reality of recruitment
docs.text:
In practice, Indian armies always recruited far more widely than the norm suggests. The Arthaśāstra lists hired troops, guild troops and forest troops among the sources of soldiers (Kangle 1960–1965). Medieval inscriptions record soldiers and heroes from many communities, including herdsmen, hunters and peasants. In early modern Hindustan peasants took up arms as paid soldiers in great numbers, and military service could change a man’s standing and even his caste identity; that argument is set out in Chapter 17 (Section 17.3). In the south, warrior identities such as Nāyar in Kerala and Kaḷḷar and Maṟavar in Tamil Nadu were tied to military service to chiefs and kings. In Maharashtra, Śivājī’s armies drew on peasant communities of the hills. The Mughal and Deccan armies included Turks, Persians, Afghans, Abyssinians (ḥabshī), Rajputs, Marathas and men of every region.

The right to bear arms was thus a matter of power, opportunity and pay as much as of birth. At the same time, rulers often tried to control it: by restricting the possession of horses and elephants, by recruiting from particular communities they trusted, and, in the colonial period, by legislation (Chapter 19).

docs.title: 13.5 Warrior Communities and Social Mobility
docs.text:
Many of the communities that today claim a martial heritage acquired it through the military opportunities of particular periods. A few examples show the range.

The Marathas.

The Maratha warrior elite emerged from the peasant communities of the western Deccan, especially the Kuṇbī cultivators, through service in the armies of the Deccan sultanates and of Śivājī. Successful families claimed Rajput descent and kṣatriya status, and Śivājī’s coronation in 1674 involved an elaborate ritual to confirm his kṣatriya standing (Gordon 1993). The boundary between “Maratha” and “Kuṇbī” long remained fluid.

The Nāyars.

In Kerala, the Nāyars were a matrilineal community whose men served as the soldiers of the Kerala principalities and were trained in the kaḷari (Chapter 15). Their military role ended in the late eighteenth century, and their social organisation was transformed in the nineteenth and twentieth (Zarrilli 1998).

The Kaḷḷar and Maṟavar.

In southern Tamil Nadu, the Kaḷḷar and Maṟavar communities supplied soldiers and local chiefs (pāḷaiyakkārar, poligars) under the Nāyakas of Madurai and their successors; the Maṟavar chiefs of Ramnad and Sivaganga became rulers of small states. After the poligar wars against the East India Company at the end of the eighteenth century, the British classified some of these communities as “criminal tribes”, a stigma that outlasted the repeal of the Criminal Tribes Act in 1952.

The Bedars.

In Karnataka and the Deccan, the Bedar (Boya) communities, traditionally hunters, supplied infantry and archers to Vijayanagara, the Deccan sultanates and the Mughals; some Bedar chiefs, such as the rulers of Shorapur, became local kings.

The Jats.

The Jat peasant communities of the Punjab and the Agra–Delhi region rose to power through revolt and service in the late seventeenth and eighteenth centuries (Section 9.18); the making of Rajput identity through service is discussed in Section 17.3.

These examples show that “martial” identities were made in history, through service, reward and the claiming of status, and were not simply inherited from antiquity. The colonial theory of “martial races” later froze some of these identities into fixed categories (Chapter 19). Table 13.1 summarises some of the communities and groups whose history is closely associated with military service, as discussed in this volume. The associations are historical, not inherent: members of these communities followed many occupations, and many other groups also supplied soldiers.
