docs.title: 13.6 Warrior Ascetics
docs.text: One of the most striking features of Indian military history is the role of armed ascetics. By the sixteenth century, orders of Śaiva renouncers (the nāgā or gosāīn sections of the Daśanāmī order) and Vaiṣṇava bairāgīs had armed wings, which fought each other for control of pilgrimage sites and were hired as soldiers by rulers. In the eighteenth century, bands of armed ascetics served the Mughals, the Marathas, the nawabs of Awadh and Bengal and the East India Company; the Gosāīn commanders Anūpgir and Umrāogir were powerful military entrepreneurs. William Pinch’s Warrior Ascetics and Indian Empires traces this history and shows that the armed ascetic, far from being a contradiction, was a familiar figure of the Indian military world (Pinch 2006). The “Sannyāsī and Fakīr” raids in Bengal in the 1760s and 1770s, which the Company suppressed, were a conflict between such armed mendicants and the new colonial state. The akhāṛās of the ascetic orders, which still parade at the Kumbh Melā, preserve the memory of this armed past.

docs.title: 13.7 Training Grounds
docs.text: Below the level of princes, training took place in village and town gymnasia — the akhāṛā of north India, the tālīm of Maharashtra, the kaḷari of Kerala, the silambak-kūṭam and other training grounds of the Tamil country — and in the households of military chiefs. Chapters 14 and 15 describe these institutions. Kolff notes that in north India young men trained in village akhāṛās in wrestling, stick-play and the use of arms, and that such training prepared them for service in the armies that recruited across the region (Kolff 1990). In this sense the military labour market rested on a widespread popular martial culture.

docs.title: 13.8 Rewards, Honours and Loyalty
docs.text:
Armies were held together by rewards and by ideals of loyalty. Kings rewarded soldiers with pay, land, titles, weapons, horses and robes of honour. In south India, grants of land were made to the families of men who died in battle, and some hero-stones record such grants. In the Indo-Persian world, the robe of honour (khilʿat) presented by a ruler to a servant created a personal bond; titles such as khān and bahādur (“brave”) marked the favour of the emperor; and the ideal of being “true to one’s salt” (namak-ḥalāl) — loyal to the master whose salt one has eaten — was one of the most powerful ideas in Indian military culture. The opposite, namak-ḥarām, was the worst of insults. British officers in the colonial army consciously cultivated this ethic of personal loyalty among their sepoys (Alavi 1995).

Loyalty was also owed to lineage and community. Rajput warriors fought for their clan and their lord; Sikh soldiers for the Khalsa; Maratha commanders for their own families as much as for the Peshwa. The tension between these loyalties and loyalty to the state was a constant feature of Indian warfare.

docs.title: 13.9 Banners, Drums and Music
docs.text: Banners, standards and music were essential to the life of armies. Each army and each great commander had banners; the capture of an enemy’s standard was a sign of victory. The Maratha armies carried the saffron banner (bhagvā jhenḍā); the Mughals had standards with the sun and other emblems; Rajput clans had their own flags. Kettle-drums (naqqāra, nagāṛā) were symbols of sovereignty: the right to beat the drum (naubat) at the palace gate at fixed hours was a royal privilege, and the drum-house (naqqār-khāna) stood at the entrance of Mughal palaces. In battle, drums, horns, trumpets and conches signalled orders and encouraged the troops. The Tamil Caṅkam poems already describe the war-drum kept in its own shrine, whose capture meant defeat (Chapter 2). Martial music survives today in the bands of the Indian army, in the drums of festivals, and in the musical traditions of many former courts.

docs.title: 13.10 Drill and the Regular Soldier
docs.text: The eighteenth century introduced a new kind of military training: drill. The infantry battalions raised by the European companies and, following their example, by the Nizam, the Marathas, Mysore, the Sikhs and others, were trained to march in step, to manoeuvre in formation and to load and fire their muskets in unison on command, under officers who were often European or Eurasian. Drill made soldiers interchangeable parts of a unit, able to fight in close order under fire; it required long training, regular pay and permanent units, and it changed the relationship between soldiers and their commanders (Roy 2011). Seema Alavi has described how the East India Company’s sepoys were shaped by this new discipline, while the Company also adapted to their customs (Alavi 1995). The older martial training of the gymnasium and the household, centred on individual skill, did not disappear, but it ceased to be the basis of military effectiveness.

docs.title: 13.11 Ranks and Titles across the Periods
docs.text:
Military ranks and titles changed with each political order, and many of them passed from one system to the next with altered meanings. The word nāyaka, “leader”, was the title of commanders in Sanskrit inscriptions, of the military lords of Vijayanagara, and finally, as nāik, of a corporal in the Company’s sepoy army. Table 13.2 gives a selection (Irvine 1903; Gordon 1993; Alavi 1995).

docs.title: 13.12 Soldiers’ Families and the Military Household
docs.text: Indian armies on campaign were accompanied by large numbers of non-combatants: the families of soldiers, servants, grooms, grass-cutters, water-carriers, merchants and entertainers. European observers in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries were astonished by the size of these camps. The presence of families reflected the long duration of campaigns and the fact that soldiering was a family enterprise: a soldier’s wages supported his household, and families followed the soldier when they could. In the military labour market described by Kolff, soldiers often served far from home for years, sending money back to their villages and returning between engagements (Kolff 1990). The colonial army later separated soldiers from their families on campaign but supported them through pensions and land grants in the recruiting districts (Omissi 1994). The social history of soldiers’ families — of the women who managed households in the soldiers’ absence, of widows, and of children brought up in camps — remains largely unwritten.

docs.title: 13.13.1 Sculpture
docs.text:
Indian sculpture is full of warriors and battles. The early Buddhist reliefs of Sāñcī show the armies of the kings who fought over the Buddha’s relics (Figure 13.1), with elephants, horses, chariots and archers. The seventh-century relief of the goddess Durgā slaying the buffalo-demon Mahiṣāsura at Māmallapuram shows the goddess riding a lion and drawing a bow against the demon’s army (Figure 13.2), one of the most dynamic battle scenes in Indian art. Medieval temples in Karnataka, Rajasthan and elsewhere carry friezes of soldiers, elephants and horsemen on their bases, and scenes from the epic battles. The goddess as warrior — Durgā, Mahiṣāsuramardinī, Cāmuṇḍā — became one of the most important images of the medieval period, and the goddess was the patron of many royal and warrior lineages.

Figure 13.1. The siege of Kuśinagara in the “war over the Buddha’s relics”, a detail of the south gateway of Stūpa 1 at Sāñcī (first century BCE). Townspeople watch from the balconies and towers of the city while archers and soldiers attack its walls. Photo: Photo Dharma from Sadao, Thailand, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons Figure 13.2. Durgā, riding her lion and drawing her bow, attacks the buffalo-headed demon Mahiṣa and his army: relief in the Mahiṣāsuramardinī cave at Māmallapuram, seventh century. Photo: Rainer Halama, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (cropped)

docs.title: 13.13.2 Hero-stones
docs.text:
Hero-stones are the most widespread memorials of warriors. They are found by the thousand in Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Andhra, Maharashtra, Gujarat and Rajasthan, and in smaller numbers elsewhere. Tamil literature already refers to them in the Caṅkam period (Hart and Heifetz 1999). A few hero-stones inscribed in Tamil-Brāhmī script, found in the Theni district of Tamil Nadu, are dated by their editors to the last centuries BCE, though their dating is debated; inscribed hero-stones become numerous from the middle of the first millennium CE. Typically they show in panels the hero in combat, his death, and his ascent to heaven (Figure 13.3), and some record his name and the occasion of his death. Some commemorate men who died defending cattle or villages, others soldiers who died in royal wars, and others women who died with their husbands. They were, and in many places still are, worshipped by local communities.

Figure 13.3. A hero-stone with an Old Kannada inscription of 1160, from the reign of the Kalacuri king Bijjala, at the Kedāreśvara temple, Baḷḷigāve (Shivamogga district, Karnataka). The panels read upwards: the hero fights his enemies, celestial women carry him to heaven, and at the top he worships the liṅga, with Nandi, the sun and the moon. Photo: Dineshkannambadi, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 13.13.3 Painting
docs.text: Rajput, Pahari, Deccani and Mughal painting of the sixteenth to nineteenth centuries includes many battle and siege scenes. The illustrated manuscripts of Akbar’s court — the Akbarnāma, the Bāburnāma and the Razmnāma, the Persian translation of the Mahābhārata made for Akbar in the 1580s — show armies, weapons and armour of the artists’ own day, so that the heroes of the epic fight with Mughal swords and shields. These paintings are valuable evidence for the equipment and appearance of armies in the period, though they follow pictorial conventions and should not be taken as photographs of particular battles.

docs.title: 13.14 Martial Values in Literature
docs.text: The Nāṭyaśāstra, the classical treatise on drama, counts the heroic (vīra) among the eight principal aesthetic moods (rasa), arising from energy and resolve; Sanskrit court poetry describes battles and royal victories at length, often with great artifice. Tamil Caṅkam poetry has a whole genre of war poems (puṟam), praising kings, mourning heroes and describing the mothers and widows of warriors with unflinching realism (Hart and Heifetz 1999). In later centuries, regional literatures developed heroic genres of their own: the Rajasthani rāso, vāt and dūhā, which celebrated Rajput heroes and their deaths; the Marathi povāḍā, ballads of Maratha warriors sung by itinerant bards; the heroic ballads of north Kerala, the vaṭakkan pāṭṭukaḷ, which tell of the feats of kaḷari-trained warriors such as Tacchōḷi Ōtēnaṉ and the woman warrior Uṇṇiyārcca; and Punjabi vārs celebrating Sikh warriors. These works shaped the self-image of warrior communities and are today important sources of regional identity, though as historical sources they must be used with caution.

docs.title: 13.15 Warrior Gods and Folk Heroes
docs.text:
Martial values were sustained by religion. Many royal and warrior lineages worshipped a form of the goddess as their protector: Tuljā Bhavānī was the patron goddess of Śivājī and the Marathas; the Rajput clans had their clan goddesses (kuldevī); Kerala’s kaḷaris honour the goddess as guardian. Hanumān is the patron of wrestlers (Chapter 14). Muslim soldiers venerated warrior saints and martyrs (ghāzī, shahīd); the shrine of Ghāzī Miyān at Bahraich, associated with a legendary eleventh-century warrior, attracted Hindu as well as Muslim devotees.

Folk epics celebrate local warrior heroes who became gods. In Rajasthan, the epic of Pābūjī, a Rathor hero who died defending the cattle of a woman who had sought his protection, is performed by bards (bhopā) before a painted scroll (paṛ); the epic of Devnārāyaṇ is performed in a similar way. In Bundelkhand and the Ganges valley, the Ālhā ballads, telling of the heroes Ālhā and Ūdal, warriors of the Candella court, in their wars with Pṛthvīrāja, are sung especially in the rainy season. In Kerala, some of the deities of the teyyam ritual dances of the north are deified warriors, among them heroes of the kaḷari ballads. In Tamil Nadu, Madurai Vīraṉ and other hero-gods are worshipped at village shrines. These traditions show how the memory of warriors, and especially of those who died defending cattle, women and village, became part of popular religion.

docs.title: 13.16.1 Daśahrā and Āyudhapūjā
docs.text: The autumn festival of Navarātri and Daśahrā (Vijayadaśamī) was the great martial festival of many Indian kingdoms. It celebrates the victory of the goddess over the buffalo-demon and of Rāma over Rāvaṇa, and it marked the end of the monsoon and the beginning of the campaigning season. On the ninth day weapons, tools and vehicles are worshipped (āyudhapūjā), and on the tenth day kings went in procession, inspected their armies and worshipped the śamī tree — the tree in which, according to the Mahābhārata, the Pāṇḍavas hid their weapons during their year in disguise. The Mahānavamī festival at Vijayanagara, described by Portuguese visitors in the sixteenth century, was an immense display of royal and military power; the Dasara of the Wodeyar kings of Mysore continues it in modern form. Maratha armies traditionally set out on campaign after Daśahrā.

docs.title: 13.16.2 Other festivals
docs.text: Many regional festivals include martial displays. At Hola Mohalla, held at Anandpur in Punjab the day after Holī, Nihang Sikhs and others display horsemanship and gatka, a tradition associated in Sikh memory with Guru Gobind Singh (Chapter 15). In Manipur, the Lai Haraoba festival includes ritual dances, and Manipuri martial arts and wrestling are displayed at festivals. In Kerala, the snake-boat races of the monsoon season are often said to preserve the memory of war-boats, and the kaḷari tradition has its own annual rituals. Across north India, wrestling tournaments (daṅgal) are held at fairs and festivals (Chapter 14).

docs.title: 13.17 Martial Culture and Caste Critique
docs.text: The celebration of the warrior in Indian culture was also criticised. Buddhist and Jain teachers rejected the glorification of killing, and the Buddhist tradition re-imagined the ideal king as a righteous ruler who conquers through dharma (Chapter 12). In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, anti-caste thinkers such as Jotirao Phule and B. R. Ambedkar criticised the way in which the ideology of varṇa had excluded the lower castes from arms and learning; Phule reinterpreted Indian history as a struggle between the Brahmins and the peasant and lower-caste majority, and Ambedkar emphasised the participation of the Mahār and other Dalit communities in the armies of the Marathas and of the East India Company, including the Mahār soldiers who fought for the Company at Bhima Koregaon in 1818. In these readings the history of Indian martial culture is also a history of exclusion and of struggles over who had the right to bear arms and to be honoured as a warrior.

docs.title: 13.18 Wounds, Medicine and the Care of Soldiers
docs.text:
What happened to soldiers who were wounded? The evidence is scattered but suggestive. The Arthaśāstra’s field physicians and the surgery of wounds in the Suśruta Saṃhitā are described in Section 2.18. Medieval inscriptions record grants to the families of men killed or maimed in battle, and some hero-stones record gifts of land to the families of the fallen.

In the Mughal period, surgeons (jarrāḥ) accompanied the armies, and the nobles employed physicians of the Greco-Islamic (yūnānī) tradition as well as Indian practitioners. Kerala’s kaḷari masters treated injuries with massage, medicated oils and bone-setting (Chapter 15), and village bone-setters throughout India treated fractures and dislocations, including those suffered in wrestling and in fighting. Most wounded soldiers, however, probably received little care beyond what their comrades and families could give, and many died of infection. Systematic military medical services, with hospitals, regimental surgeons and ambulances, were developed in India only in the colonial army of the nineteenth century; the Indian Medical Service, founded in the eighteenth century to serve the East India Company’s armies, became one of the main channels by which Western medicine spread in India.

Claims that ancient Indian military surgeons had knowledge equivalent to modern trauma surgery go beyond the evidence. Suśruta’s surgery was remarkable for its time, including procedures such as the reconstruction of the nose, but it operated without knowledge of infection or anaesthesia in the modern sense, and its outcomes cannot be compared with those of modern medicine.

docs.title: 13.19 Remembering the Dead
docs.text:
Societies remember their dead in war in characteristic ways. In early medieval India, the hero-stone was the principal memorial: a stone set up where the hero fell or near his village, carved with his image and sometimes his name, and worshipped with offerings by his family and community. In Rajasthan, memorial stones (pāliyā, devlī) show the hero on horseback, and in many places the sites became shrines. Rajput and Maratha ballads, Sikh accounts of martyrs (shahīd), Muslim shrines of warrior saints and the Tamil poems of the Caṅkam age all preserved the memory of those who died in war.

The colonial army introduced memorials of a European kind: obelisks and cenotaphs listing the names of the dead, regimental memorials in churches, and after the First World War great monuments such as the India Gate in New Delhi, inaugurated in 1931, which bears the names of Indian soldiers who died in that war. Independent India has added its own memorials, including the National War Memorial in New Delhi, inaugurated in 2019. These different forms of memorial — the hero-stone, the ballad, the shrine and the inscribed monument — reflect different ideas of the dead warrior: as a deified hero, as a martyr for a faith, or as a citizen who died for the nation.

docs.title: 13.20 Assessment
docs.text: The chapter’s central finding is a gap between ideal and recruitment. The texts imagined the warrior as a prince trained in arms and letters by a brahmin teacher, and they reserved the right to arms for the higher classes; armies drew instead on peasants, herdsmen, forest peoples and ascetics, trained in village gymnasia and in service. The ideal excluded many; the reality included them, though often on unequal terms, and the honours of the hero-stone, the ballad and the festival were the means by which ordinary fighters claimed a place in a culture that had not been written for them.

docs.title: Chapter 14: Mallayuddha and Kuśtī: Wrestling and Unarmed Combat
14.1 Introduction
docs.text: Wrestling is the most widespread and the best documented of India’s traditional combat arts. It appears in the epics as the art of heroes, in medieval courts as a royal entertainment, in the gymnasia of towns and villages as a training for soldiers and a discipline for young men, and in the modern world as both a living folk tradition and an Olympic sport in which Indian athletes have won many medals. This chapter traces its history, describes the institution of the akhāṛā and the culture of the wrestler (pahalvān), discusses related arts such as the armed boxing called vajramuṣṭi and the pole-gymnastics called mallakhamb, and considers the traditional knowledge of the body’s vulnerable points (marma). Joseph Alter’s ethnography of North Indian wrestling, The Wrestler’s Body, is the fundamental modern study (Alter 1992).

docs.title: 14.2.1 The epics
docs.text: The Sanskrit word for wrestler is malla, and wrestling is mallayuddha or niyuddha. The Mahābhārata contains several wrestling bouts. The most famous is the fight between Bhīma and Jarāsandha, king of Magadha, in the Sabhāparvan: the two fight for many days and nights until Bhīma, at Kṛṣṇa’s hint, tears his opponent in two. In the Virāṭaparvan, Bhīma, disguised as a cook at the court of King Virāṭa, defeats a champion wrestler at a festival and later kills the general Kīcaka with his bare hands (Buitenen 1973–1978; Hopkins 1889). In the stories of Kṛṣṇa told in the Harivaṃśa and the Purāṇas, the young Kṛṣṇa and his brother Balarāma kill the champion wrestlers Cāṇūra and Muṣṭika in the arena of the tyrant Kaṃsa at Mathurā. These narratives present wrestling as a heroic and royal art, and they made Bhīma, Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa patrons of wrestlers.

docs.title: 14.2.2 Early historic evidence
docs.text: Buddhist and Jain texts mention wrestlers and wrestling matches at festivals, and the name Malla was borne by one of the republican peoples of north Bihar in the Buddha’s time, though the connection with wrestling is uncertain. Sculpture of the early centuries CE occasionally shows wrestlers, and Tamil Caṅkam poetry refers to wrestlers and contests of strength. Claims that particular Harappan seals or figurines depict wrestlers are speculative.

docs.title: 14.3.1 The Mānasollāsa
docs.text: The most detailed early account of Indian wrestling is in the Mānasollāsa, the encyclopaedia compiled for the Cāḷukya king Someśvara III around 1129–1131 (Shrigondekar 1925–1961). Its section on the recreation of wrestling (mallavinoda) describes how the king should maintain wrestlers, classifying them by age and strength; how they should be fed, with milk, meat, ghee and other strengthening foods; their daily exercises; the arena in which they fight; and the conduct of bouts before the king, with holds and throws, rules of victory and the rewards for winners. It shows that by the twelfth century wrestling was an established courtly institution in the Deccan, with professional wrestlers supported by royal patronage.

docs.title: 14.3.2 The Jyeṣṭhīmallas and the Malla Purāṇa
docs.text:
In western India, a community of hereditary wrestlers called Jyeṣṭhīmallas (Gujarati Jeṭhīs) claimed brahmin status and maintained a tradition of wrestling and of vajramuṣṭi, a form of combat with a knuckle-weapon. The Malla Purāṇa, a Sanskrit text associated with this community, describes its origins and customs, the training of wrestlers, their diet and exercises, and the conduct of bouts. Its date is uncertain; it is generally regarded as a medieval work. The Jyeṣṭhīmallas served Rajput and Maratha courts in Gujarat and Rajasthan and later the court of Mysore, where wrestlers of this community still performed in the early twentieth century (Mujumdar 1950; Green and Svinth 2010).

Modern books on Indian wrestling often describe four classical styles, named after the epic and mythological heroes Hanumān, Jāmbavān, Jarāsandha and Bhīma, each with a characteristic emphasis — technique, holds, joint-breaking or strength. The source of this classification is unclear; it appears in modern writing but is not found in the Mānasollāsa, and it should be treated as a modern scheme rather than a classical one.

docs.title: 14.3.3 Vajramuṣṭi
docs.text: Vajramuṣṭi (“thunderbolt fist”) was a combat sport in which the fighters wore on one hand a knuckle-weapon of horn, ivory or metal, sometimes with projecting points, and struck and grappled until blood was drawn or a fighter was disabled. It was associated with the Jyeṣṭhīmallas and was performed at courts as a spectacle. Portuguese visitors to Vijayanagara in the early sixteenth century describe bloody wrestling and fighting contests at the Mahānavamī festival, which may have been of this kind. The art had become rare by the twentieth century (Green and Svinth 2010), though short ritual bouts are still staged by wrestlers of the Jetti community at the Mysore Dasara.

docs.title: 14.3.4 Persian wrestling and the Mughal court
docs.text: The arrival of Turkic and Persian elites from the eleventh century brought the Persian tradition of wrestling, with its heroic ideal of the pahlavān and its training house, the zūrkhāna. The words kuśtī (wrestling) and pahalvān (wrestler) are Persian. In India the Persian and Indian traditions merged. The Mughal emperors maintained wrestlers at court; the Āʾīn-i Akbarī lists wrestlers from Persia and Turan alongside Indian wrestlers and the fighters called mal, and describes their pay and their contests (Blochmann 1873). In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, the courts of Lucknow, Patiala, Kolhapur, Baroda, Indore, Datia and other states were great centres of patronage, and wrestlers of all communities, Hindu and Muslim, competed for princely support.

docs.title: 14.4.1 Space and ritual
docs.text:
The akhāṛā (or akhāḍā) is the North Indian wrestling ground and gymnasium. Its centre is a pit of soft, carefully prepared earth (Figure 14.1), dug and turned daily, mixed with substances such as oil, buttermilk and turmeric and kept free of stones. Around it are spaces for exercise, a well or water supply, and usually a shrine to Hanumān, the monkey-god of the Rāmāyaṇa, who embodies strength, celibacy and devotion and is the patron of wrestlers. Before training, wrestlers worship Hanumān and touch the earth of the pit with reverence; the earth itself is regarded as sacred and beneficial to the body (Alter 1992).

Figure 14.1. A kuśtī bout in an earthen pit, watched by a crowd. Traditional Indian wrestling is fought on soft, prepared earth, and a bout is won by pinning both of the opponent’s shoulders to the ground. Photo: MaximusPrasad, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

The akhāṛā is presided over by a master (guru or ustād), whose authority extends over the wrestlers’ training, diet and conduct. Alter’s fieldwork in Banaras in the 1980s showed that the akhāṛā was not merely a sports club but a moral community, in which young men were taught an ideology of self-discipline, devotion and service, and in which wrestling was understood as a way of life as well as a sport (Alter 1992).

docs.title: 14.4.2 The wrestler’s regimen
docs.text:
The traditional wrestler’s life is governed by a strict regimen. He rises early, exercises for hours, wrestles, bathes, eats a large and carefully chosen diet, rests, and trains again in the evening. The characteristic exercises (vyāyām) include the daṇḍ, a flowing push-up, and the baiṭhak, a deep knee-bend, performed in hundreds or thousands of repetitions; the swinging of heavy wooden clubs (jorī, mugdar) and the stone or iron mace (gadā); rope-climbing; and the turning of the earth of the pit. Indian club-swinging was adopted by British soldiers in India in the nineteenth century and spread to Britain and America as a form of gymnastics.

The diet traditionally emphasises milk, ghee, almonds and other foods believed to build strength, with vegetarian and non-vegetarian variants. Wrestlers are expected to practise celibacy (brahmacarya), in the belief that the conservation of semen builds strength and vitality; Alter discusses this belief and its place in the wrestler’s ideology (Alter 1992). It is a traditional belief, not an established physiological fact.

docs.title: 14.4.3 The bout
docs.text: A traditional bout is fought on the earth by two wrestlers wearing a loincloth (laṅgoṭ), and is won by pinning both of the opponent’s shoulders to the ground (cit). There are many named holds and throws, such as the dhobīpāṭ (a shoulder throw, “washerman’s throw”) and the kalājaṅg; the names and techniques vary by region and lineage. Bouts are held at tournaments (daṅgal), often attached to festivals and fairs and sponsored by local patrons; the winner of a major tournament may receive a title, a mace, money or a turban.

docs.title: 14.5 A Vocabulary of the Akhāṛā
docs.text:
Table 14.1 explains some of the Hindi and Urdu terms of north Indian wrestling used in this chapter, largely following the usage recorded by Alter (Alter 1992).

Table 14.1. Some terms of north Indian wrestling Term Meaning akhāṛā Wrestling ground and the community that trains there pahalvān Wrestler guru, ustād, khalīfā Teacher; senior master kuśtī Wrestling (from Persian) daṅgal Wrestling tournament dāṅv A move or hold; the repertoire of techniques jōṛ Sparring practice with a partner daṇḍ Dipping push-up exercise baiṭhak Deep knee-bend exercise jōṛī, mugdar Heavy wooden clubs swung for strength gadā Mace, swung in exercise; emblem of Hanumān nāl Heavy stone ring lifted in exercise laṅgoṭ Loincloth worn in training and bouts mālish Massage, part of the daily regimen

docs.title: 14.6.1 Gama and the international stage
docs.text: In the early twentieth century Indian wrestlers made their mark internationally. The most famous was Ghulam Muhammad, known as Gama (c. 1878–1960), wrestler to the Maharaja of Datia and later of Patiala, who was widely regarded as unbeatable. In London in 1910 he wrestled the Polish champion Stanisław Zbyszko; the long match was declared a draw, and when Zbyszko failed to appear for the deciding bout, Gama was awarded the title. In 1928, at Patiala, he defeated Zbyszko in a rematch within a minute. His career, and those of other Indian wrestlers who toured Europe, gave Indian wrestling an international reputation. After 1947 Gama lived in Pakistan; the wrestling traditions of Punjab are shared by both countries.

docs.title: 14.6.2 Olympic wrestling
docs.text:
Indian wrestlers adapted to the international freestyle style. Khashaba Dadasaheb Jadhav won a bronze medal at the 1952 Helsinki Olympics, the first individual Olympic medal won by independent India. In the twenty-first century Indian wrestlers, many of them trained in traditional akhāṛās in Haryana, Delhi and Uttar Pradesh before moving to the mat, have won a series of Olympic medals since 2008, and women’s wrestling has grown rapidly (Section 14.11). Table 14.2 lists the Olympic medals won by Indian wrestlers up to 2024; most of the medallists began their careers in traditional akhāṛās before turning to freestyle wrestling on the mat.

The shift from earth to mat has changed the traditional institution. Many akhāṛās have added mats and modern training methods, and some traditional wrestlers regret the decline of the earthen pit and of the ideology of the pahalvān. Alter’s later work and the experience of the wrestlers themselves show a living tradition negotiating between continuity and change.

docs.title: 14.7 Princely Patronage and Famous Wrestlers
docs.text:
In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, the princely states were the great patrons of Indian wrestling. Maharajas maintained wrestlers, paid for their diet and training, and organised great tournaments at which champions from across India competed for prizes and titles. Kolhapur, under Shāhū Mahārāj (r. 1894–1922), was a particularly important centre: the ruler, a keen supporter of wrestling and of the non-Brahmin movement, built a large wrestling stadium, and Kolhapur remains a centre of wrestling in Maharashtra. Patiala, Baroda, Indore, Datia, Gwalior and the courts of Punjab and Rajasthan were also important patrons (Alter 1992; Mujumdar 1950).

Wrestlers became popular heroes. Besides Gama, the most famous were his brother Imām Bakhsh; Ghulām of Amritsar, who toured Europe at the turn of the twentieth century; and Gobar Goho (Jatindra Charan Guha) of Calcutta, who wrestled professionally in the United States in the early 1920s and was billed there as a world champion in the light-heavyweight class. In independent India, Dārā Singh (1928–2012) became famous first as a wrestler in the professional circuit and then as a film actor, playing among other roles the god Hanumān in a television serial of the Rāmāyaṇa.

docs.title: 14.8 Wrestling Titles and Tournaments
docs.text: Wrestling culture is organised around tournaments and titles. At the village and district level, daṅgals are held at fairs, festivals and the anniversaries of saints and gods, often sponsored by local notables or politicians; spectators contribute prize money, and the bouts are accompanied by drums and commentary. At higher levels, titles such as Rustam-i Hind (“Rustam of India”, after the hero of the Persian epic), Bhārat Kesarī and Hind Kesarī (“lion of India”) and, in Maharashtra, Mahārāṣṭra Kesarī (“lion of Maharashtra”) are awarded to the winners of major championships. These titles carry great prestige in rural society, and successful wrestlers often become local leaders. Alter’s work describes how the ideology of the akhāṛā links personal discipline, the health of the body and the health of the nation in the thought of modern Indian wrestlers (Alter 1992).

docs.title: 14.9 Physical Culture and the Gymnasium
docs.text: The North Indian akhāṛā had counterparts throughout India: the Marathi tālīm, the gymnasia (vyāyāmśālā) of the physical culture movement, and the clubs founded by nationalists in Bengal and Punjab. In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries a number of physical culturists systematised Indian exercises, combining the daṇḍ, baiṭhak, club-swinging, mallakhamb and wrestling with European gymnastics and bodybuilding. In Baroda the physical culturist Manikrao and his circle, and later D. C. Mujumdar, whose Encyclopedia of Indian Physical Culture (1950) recorded many exercises and martial arts, were influential (Mujumdar 1950). In the same period the bodybuilder Eugen Sandow toured India (1904–5), and the ideal of the muscular, disciplined body spread through schools and clubs. Mark Singleton has shown that this movement also shaped the modern practice of postural yoga (Singleton 2010).

docs.title: 14.10 Wrestling, Religion and Community
docs.text:
Wrestling in north India has long crossed religious boundaries. The akhāṛā’s patron is Hanumān, and its rituals are Hindu, but many of the most famous wrestlers and masters of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries were Muslims, among them Gama and his brother Imām Bakhsh, and Muslim wrestlers had their own patron saints and rituals. Hindu and Muslim wrestlers trained in the same styles, competed in the same tournaments and were patronised by the same princes; wrestling lineages (gharānā) sometimes included members of both communities. Alter describes how the wrestler’s ideology, centred on the discipline of the body, celibacy and devotion, could be shared across religious lines, even as it was expressed in Hindu terms in the Banaras akhāṛās he studied (Alter 1992). The partition of India in 1947 divided the great wrestling centres of Punjab between India and Pakistan, and Pakistani wrestlers continued the traditions of Gama’s family.

Wrestling also had a place in the culture of particular castes and communities. In north India, Yādav (Ahīr) and Jāṭ communities, among others, have strong wrestling traditions, and in Maharashtra wrestling is closely associated with the rural Marāṭhā and other peasant communities. The akhāṛā could be a site of caste and community identity, but also, especially in towns, a place where young men of different backgrounds trained together under a common discipline.

docs.title: 14.11 Women’s Wrestling
docs.text: Until recently, wrestling in India was an almost exclusively male activity, and the ideology of the akhāṛā, with its emphasis on celibacy and the avoidance of women, excluded them. A few women wrestlers performed exhibition bouts, often against men, and attracted great curiosity; the best remembered is Hamida Banu, who in the 1950s challenged male wrestlers to bouts, although her career is known mainly from newspaper reports and later retellings rather than from any study. The entry of women’s wrestling into the Commonwealth Games and Olympic Games at the beginning of the twenty-first century changed the situation. In Haryana, Mahavir Singh Phogat trained his daughters as wrestlers against strong social disapproval, and their success — Geeta Phogat won the Commonwealth Games gold medal in 2010, and several of her sisters and cousins also won international medals — encouraged many other families, and the film Dangal (2016) made their story widely known. Sakshi Malik’s Olympic bronze medal in 2016 and the success of Vinesh Phogat confirmed the place of women in Indian wrestling. Indian women wrestlers’ public protests in 2023 over allegations of sexual harassment against the president of the national wrestling federation drew national attention to the conditions of women in the sport.

docs.title: 14.12 Mallakhamb
docs.text: Mallakhamb (“wrestler’s pole”) is a form of gymnastics performed on a vertical wooden pole, or on a hanging rope or cane, in which the athlete climbs, balances and holds postures. It was originally a training exercise for wrestlers, developing grip and strength for holds. Maharashtrian tradition attributes its systematisation to Bāḷambhaṭṭadādā Deodhar, a wrestling master in the service of the Peshwa Bājīrāv II in the early nineteenth century (Mujumdar 1950). In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries mallakhamb was taken up by the physical culture movement in Maharashtra and became a school and club sport. It is today a competitive sport with national championships, and was declared the state sport of Madhya Pradesh.

docs.title: 14.13 Regional Wrestling Traditions
docs.text: Many regions have their own styles of wrestling. In Manipur, mukna is a belt-wrestling style practised by the Meitei, with ritual associations and competitions at festivals. In Mizoram, inbuan is a traditional wrestling in which competitors grip a belt and try to lift the opponent off his feet within a circle. In Kerala and the coastal Karnataka region, forms of belt-wrestling were also practised. Punjab has its own styles of open wrestling and of kabaḍḍī, a team game of tag and wrestling now played internationally. These regional forms deserve fuller study; their histories are mostly undocumented before the twentieth century.

docs.title: 14.14 Kabaḍḍī
docs.text: Kabaḍḍī is a team game of tag and wrestling played across South Asia under many local names. A raider from one team crosses into the opponents’ half, holding his breath and chanting “kabaḍḍī” to show that he has not taken a new breath; he tries to touch one or more opponents and return to his own side, while the defenders try to hold him until his breath runs out. The game requires agility, strength and wrestling skill, and it was traditionally played in villages without equipment. Its origins are unknown; claims that it is mentioned in the epics are speculative. In the twentieth century it was standardised, with national rules adopted in the 1950s; it became an Asian Games sport in 1990, and the professional Pro Kabaddi League, launched in 2014, has made it one of the most watched sports in India. Punjab has its own “circle” style of kabaḍḍī, popular also in the Punjabi diaspora.

docs.title: 14.15.1 Unarmed striking arts
docs.text: Alongside wrestling, India had unarmed striking arts. Muṣṭiyuddha, “fist-fighting”, is mentioned in Sanskrit literature, and vajramuṣṭi combined striking and grappling. In the Tamil country, kuttu varisai (“sequences of blows”) is an unarmed art related to silambam; in Kerala, kaḷarippayaṟṟu includes unarmed techniques (Chapter 15). Many of these arts teach that blows to particular points of the body are especially dangerous.

docs.title: 14.15.2 Marma in Āyurveda
docs.text:
The idea of vital points (marma) comes from Indian medicine. The surgical treatise Suśruta Saṃhitā enumerates 107 marmas, sites where flesh, vessels, ligaments, bones and joints meet, injury to which is dangerous. It classifies them by structure and by the consequence of injury, as shown in Table 14.3. The purpose of the classification was surgical: the physician needed to know which parts of the body to avoid in operations and which wounds were most dangerous.

Table 14.3. The 107 marmas of the Suśruta Saṃhitā, classified by the consequence of injury Class Consequence of injury Number sadyaḥprāṇahara Death soon after injury 19 kālāntaraprāṇahara Death after an interval 33 viśalyaghna Death when the embedded object is removed 3 vaikalyakara Disability 44 rujākara Pain 8 Total 107

docs.title: 14.15.3 Marma and varmam in the martial arts
docs.text:
The martial arts of Kerala and Tamil Nadu developed their own traditions of vital points: marmmam in kaḷarippayaṟṟu and varmam in the Tamil art of varmakkalai, which is linked to the Siddha medical tradition. Their lists of points differ from Suśruta’s and from each other. Teachers of these arts claim that knowledge of the points can be used both to disable an opponent and to heal injuries and illnesses through massage and manipulation. Phillip Zarrilli’s study of kaḷarippayaṟṟu describes this dual tradition, in which the master (gurukkaḷ) was also a healer, and the secrecy with which knowledge of the points was guarded (Zarrilli 1998).

Modern promotional writing often claims that the vital points correspond to specific nerves or arteries and that neuroscience has “confirmed” the effects described by tradition. Such claims are not supported by published scientific research. Some vital points do lie over vulnerable structures — the temple, the throat, the groin — and blows to them can be dangerous, as anyone would expect; but the traditional systems of points, their effects and their remedies have not been validated as medical knowledge.

Health and Safety Note

This chapter describes vital-point traditions historically. It does not give, and should not be used as, instruction in striking the body. Blows to the head, neck, chest or abdomen can cause serious injury or death. Traditional marma and varmam treatments are described here as traditional practices; their therapeutic claims have not been established by clinical research, and they are not a substitute for medical care for injuries or illness.

docs.title: Chapter 15: Kaḷarippayaṟṟu, Silambam, Gatka and Other Regional Martial Arts
15.1 Introduction
docs.text:
India has a great variety of regional martial arts: systems of training in the use of weapons and the body, transmitted from teacher to student, often with their own rituals, medical knowledge and social settings. Some, such as kaḷarippayaṟṟu in Kerala, silambam in Tamil Nadu and gatka among the Sikhs of Punjab, are now widely known; others, such as the paika exercises of Odisha or the pari-khaṇḍā of Bihar, survive in local festivals and performance.

Writing about these arts faces two difficulties. The first is evidence: most of them are documented in detail only from the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, and their earlier history must be reconstructed from scattered references. The second is the weight of modern claims. Since the late twentieth century these arts have been promoted as national heritage, as sports, as tourist spectacles and as wellness practices, and their promoters often claim for them great antiquity and unique powers. This chapter tries to describe each art as it is practised, to set out what is known of its history, and to identify claims that go beyond the evidence. It describes techniques in general terms only; it is not a manual.

docs.title: 15.2.1 Name and history
docs.text:
Kaḷarippayaṟṟu (often written kalaripayattu) takes its name from the Malayalam kaḷari, a training ground, and payaṟṟu, exercise or practice. It is the martial art of Kerala, historically practised by the Nāyar warrior communities who served the rulers and chiefs of the Kerala coast, and also by some Christian, Muslim and other groups, including the Tiyya (Īḻava) community in the north.

The tradition of kaḷarippayaṟṟu attributes its origin to Paraśurāma, the axe-wielding avatar of Viṣṇu, who in Kerala legend reclaimed the land from the sea and established 108 kaḷaris to teach the art; other lineages trace it to the sage Agastya. These are origin myths. Phillip Zarrilli’s historical study argues that kaḷarippayaṟṟu developed its characteristic form in the period of the wars between the Cēra kingdom of Mahodayapuram and the Cōḻas in the eleventh century and the subsequent fragmentation of Kerala among many small principalities, each relying on Nāyar retainers trained in local kaḷaris; the art as we know it is documented from about the twelfth century onwards (Zarrilli 1998). The claim, common in popular writing, that kaḷarippayaṟṟu is “the oldest martial art in the world” or “the mother of all martial arts” has no historical basis.

Portuguese writers of the early sixteenth century, notably Duarte Barbosa, described the training of Nāyar boys, who from about the age of seven were placed under masters to learn the use of weapons and to make their bodies supple (Zarrilli 1998). The north Kerala ballads of the following centuries are discussed in Section 15.3.

docs.title: 15.2.2 The kaḷari
docs.text: A traditional kaḷari is a rectangular area, often sunk below ground level and roofed, oriented east–west. In its south-west corner stands a seven-stepped altar (pūttaṟa) dedicated to the guardian deity of the kaḷari, frequently a form of the goddess; other deities and the lineage’s past masters are honoured at other points. Students begin and end each session with salutations to the deities, the earth and the master (gurukkaḷ). The kaḷari is thus a sacred space as well as a gymnasium (Zarrilli 1998).

docs.title: 15.2.3 The training
docs.text:
Training traditionally proceeds through stages:

  • Body exercises (meyppayaṟṟu): sequences of kicks, steps, jumps, turns and poses (vaṭivu), several of them named after animals such as the elephant, horse, lion, boar, serpent, cat, cock and fish, designed to make the body supple, strong and balanced. Zarrilli emphasises that their aim is a state in which “the body becomes all eyes”, fully aware and responsive.

  • Wooden weapons (kōlttāri): the long staff, the short stick, and the curved stick (ottakkōl), which in some lineages is associated with training in vital points.

  • Metal weapons (aṅkattāri; Figure 15.1): dagger, sword and shield, spear, and the flexible sword (uṟumi), a long, thin, flexible blade that is coiled when not in use.

  • Empty-hand techniques (verumkai), often taught last, to advanced students.

Two broad styles are usually distinguished: the northern style (vaṭakkan) of Malabar, with its emphasis on body exercises and weapons, and the southern style (teṟkan) of the old Travancore region, closer to the Tamil arts of varmakkalai and with more emphasis on empty-hand techniques; there are also intermediate traditions. Lineages differ considerably.

Figure 15.1. Kaḷarippayaṟṟu practitioners in a staged sword-fighting demonstration outdoors; their shields lie on the ground. Practice with metal weapons follows years of body exercises and training with wooden weapons. Photo: Ginu Plathottam, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons (originally Pexels)

docs.title: 15.2.4 Healing and vital points
docs.text: A distinctive feature of kaḷarippayaṟṟu is its association with healing. The traditional master was also a physician, who treated injuries with massage, medicated oils and knowledge of the vital points (marmmam). Students undergo oil massage (uḻiccil), often during the monsoon season, to make the body supple; in some lineages the master massages with his feet while holding a rope for balance. Knowledge of the vital points, believed to allow both disabling an opponent and healing, was guarded and taught only to trusted students (Zarrilli 1998). As explained in Chapter 14, these are traditional systems whose therapeutic claims have not been established by clinical research.

docs.title: 15.2.5 Decline and revival
docs.text:
Kaḷarippayaṟṟu declined in the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, as the Kerala principalities were absorbed by Mysore and then by the British, and the military role of the Nāyars ended. The disarming of Malabar after the revolt of Pazhassi Raja (suppressed in 1805), colonial restrictions on carrying weapons, and the social changes that broke up the Nāyar joint family all contributed. Some writers state that the British formally banned kaḷarippayaṟṟu; the evidence is better described as the collapse of its military function together with restrictions on arms.

The revival began in the 1920s in north Kerala, as part of a wider interest in Indian physical culture. C. V. Narayanan Nair (d. 1944), a student of Kottakkal Kaṇāran Gurukkaḷ, did much to popularise the art through public demonstrations, and his students later founded the C.V.N. Kalari in Thiruvananthapuram. A Kerala Kalarippayattu Association was formed in the late 1950s. Since the 1970s, kaḷarippayaṟṟu has influenced Indian and international theatre and dance — Zarrilli himself used it in actor training — and Indian cinema, and it has become a competitive sport with standardised events.

docs.title: 15.3 Duels, Champions and Ballads in Kerala
docs.text:
The north Kerala ballads (vaṭakkan pāṭṭukaḷ) give a picture of the social world of kaḷarippayaṟṟu in the sixteenth to eighteenth centuries. In this world, disputes between chiefs could be settled by a formal duel (aṅkam) fought to the death by champions on a specially built platform, after elaborate preparations and negotiations; the champions were often men of the Tiyya community known as cēkavar, trained in the kaḷari and hired for the purpose. The ballads tell of heroes such as Ārōmal Cēkavar and Tacchōḷi Ōtēnaṉ, and of the woman warrior Uṇṇiyārcca, famous for her skill with the flexible sword, who appears in the ballads as a bold and witty heroine. Zarrilli discusses these ballads as evidence for the practice and ideals of the kaḷari in the period before colonial rule (Zarrilli 1998). They became immensely popular in the twentieth century through Malayalam films based on their stories.

A form of judicial combat, in which the outcome of a duel decided a dispute, is also recorded elsewhere in medieval India, but the Kerala aṅkam is the best documented. It reflects a society in which political authority was fragmented among many chiefs, each with his own retainers, and in which professional fighters could sell their skills.

docs.title: 15.4 Women in Kaḷarippayaṟṟu
docs.text: The ballads show women trained in the kaḷari, and Portuguese and later observers mention women’s martial training among some Kerala communities. In the twentieth-century revival women took up the art in growing numbers, and some became masters. Meenakshi Amma of Vatakara, who learned kaḷarippayaṟṟu as a child and has taught it for decades, was awarded the Padma Shri, one of India’s highest civilian honours, in 2017, in recognition of her role in preserving and teaching the art. Women’s participation has made the art more widely accessible, though in some lineages the most advanced and secret knowledge was traditionally restricted.

docs.title: 15.5 Myths of the Flexible Sword
docs.text: The flexible sword (uṟumi) of Kerala, a long, thin, flexible steel blade that can be coiled like a belt, has attracted much exaggeration. Popular accounts claim that it was the ultimate weapon of Kerala’s warriors, that it could be used against many opponents at once, or that it was a secret weapon of assassins. In fact, the uṟumi was a specialised weapon, difficult to master and dangerous to its user, taught only to advanced students in some lineages; its effectiveness in battle, against armoured opponents or in the press of a crowded fight, is doubtful. Multi-bladed versions, now popular in demonstrations, are of uncertain antiquity. The uṟumi is best understood as a weapon of display and of the individual duel, whose dramatic appearance has made it a favourite of demonstrations and films, rather than as a weapon of war.

docs.title: 15.6 Silambam and the Tamil Martial Arts
15.6.1 Silambam
docs.text:
Silambam (cilampam) is the staff-fighting art of Tamil Nadu. The practitioner wields a bamboo staff, usually reaching to about the forehead, in rapid circular and figure-of-eight movements, combined with footwork patterns, to strike, block and disarm. The art also includes training with other weapons, such as the short stick, the paired deer-horns (māṭu) and the sword. Tamil tradition traces silambam to the Caṅkam period and to the sage Agastya, and points to references in early Tamil literature to staves and to martial training; but the specific art, with its terminology and forms, is documented mainly from later centuries, and its earlier history is uncertain.

Silambam was practised especially among the Kaḷḷar, Maṟavar and other communities of southern Tamil Nadu who served the Pāṇḍya, Nāyaka and Maṟavar rulers and the pāḷaiyakkārar (poligars), local military chiefs, whose wars with the East India Company are described in Section 15.7. Tamil migrants carried silambam to Malaysia and Sri Lanka, where it is also practised. In the twentieth century silambam was organised as a sport, with federations and competitions.

docs.title: 15.6.2 Kuttu varisai and varmakkalai
docs.text: Kuttu varisai is an unarmed art associated with silambam. Varmakkalai (“the art of vital points”) is a tradition of combat and healing found especially in the far south of Tamil Nadu, in Kanyakumari district, and connected with the Siddha medical tradition. Its practitioners attribute it to the sage Agastya and maintain texts, mostly in Tamil verse, on the vital points (varmam), their locations, the effects of striking them and the means of reviving a person struck. The same caution applies here as to kaḷarippayaṟṟu: the healing claims of varmam therapy are traditional and have not been validated by clinical research.

docs.title: 15.7 The Poligars and the Tamil Martial Tradition
docs.text: In southern Tamil Nadu the pāḷaiyakkārar (poligars), local chiefs who held fortified villages and territories under the Nāyakas of Madurai and their successors, maintained bands of armed retainers drawn largely from the Maṟavar, Kaḷḷar and related communities, trained in the use of the staff, spear, sword and musket. In the late eighteenth century the East India Company, acting at first for the Nawab of Arcot, sought to collect revenue from them and to dismantle their forts. The resulting poligar wars ended with the defeat and execution of Vīrapāṇḍiya Kaṭṭabomman of Panchalankurichi in 1799 and the suppression of a wider rising led by the Marutu brothers of Sivaganga in 1801. The Company then destroyed the poligars’ forts and disarmed their followers. These events, celebrated in Tamil ballads and later in films, are part of the background to the decline of the Tamil martial arts and to their later revival as symbols of Tamil identity.

docs.title: 15.8 Gatka and the Sikh Martial Tradition
15.8.1 Gatka
docs.text: Gatkā originally referred to a form of stick-fencing, in which the players use a wooden stick (soṭī) and a small shield (phari) to practise sword technique. It became associated above all with the Sikhs, whose martial tradition began with Guru Hargobind in the early seventeenth century and was formalised with the creation of the Khalsa by Guru Gobind Singh in 1699 (Chapter 9). Today gatka is practised in Punjab and in the Sikh diaspora as a display art, performed at religious festivals and processions with swords, sticks, spears and the throwing quoit (cakkar), and as a competitive sport with rules and federations (Grewal 1990).

docs.title: 15.8.2 The Nihangs and “shastar vidya”
docs.text:
The Nihangs (also called Akālīs) are an order of Sikh warriors, distinguished by their blue robes, tall turbans and the weapons they carry, often including steel quoits (cakkar) worn on the turban. They trace their origin to the time of Guru Gobind Singh, and they formed a fighting force in the Sikh armies of the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries. European observers in the nineteenth century described Akālī warriors throwing the steel quoit with considerable range and accuracy (Egerton 1880). Today the Nihangs are prominent at the Hola Mohalla festival at Anandpur, held the day after Holī, with its displays of horsemanship and arms.

In recent decades some teachers, notably Nidar Singh Nihang, have presented an art they call shastar vidiā (“science of weapons”) as an older and more complete Sikh martial system, distinct from the sporting gatka; Nidar Singh and Parmjit Singh have also written on the Sikh community of Hazur Sahib in Nanded, where old Sikh martial and ritual practices survive (Singh and Singh 2008). The history and status of this system are debated within the Sikh community and among scholars, and its claims to represent an unbroken pre-modern tradition are difficult to verify.

docs.title: 15.9 The Akālīs in the Sikh Kingdom
docs.text: The Akālīs or Nihangs played a distinctive part in the Sikh kingdom of Ranjit Singh. They were irregular warriors, fiercely independent and devoted to the Khalsa, who acknowledged no authority but the Guru and the Panth; their leader in Ranjit Singh’s time, Akālī Phūlā Siṅgh (d. 1823), was the custodian of the Akal Takht at Amritsar and on occasion rebuked the Maharaja himself for breaches of Sikh conduct. The Akālīs fought as shock troops in Ranjit Singh’s campaigns against the Afghans, and Phūlā Siṅgh was killed leading an assault at the battle of Nowshera in 1823. British observers of the Sikh kingdom regarded the Akālīs as the most fanatical and the most dangerous of the Sikh soldiers (Grewal 1990; Cunningham 1849).

docs.title: 15.10 Huyen Langlon (Thang-ta) of Manipur
docs.text: The Meitei of the Manipur valley have a martial tradition called huyen langlon, which includes an armed art, thang-ta (“sword and spear”), and an unarmed art, sarit sarak. Thang-ta is practised with sword, spear and shield, both in combat forms and in ritual and dance forms, and it is closely associated with Meitei religion and with festivals such as Lai Haraoba. The arts declined after the kingdom came under British control in 1891 (Section 15.11); they were revived in the twentieth century and today have competitive forms and organisations. Manipur also has its own wrestling, mukna (Chapter 14).

docs.title: 15.11 The Meitei Kingdom and Its Warriors
docs.text: The Meitei kingdom of the Manipur valley had a long military history. Its chronicles record wars with the Shan states and with Burma, and in the eighteenth century, under kings such as Garib Niwaz (r. 1709–1748), Manipuri cavalry raided deep into Burma. In the early nineteenth century Burma conquered Manipur, and the period of Burmese occupation (1819–1825), remembered in Manipur as the “seven years’ devastation”, drove much of the population into exile. Gambhir Singh, a Manipuri prince, raised a force known as the Manipur Levy with British support and recovered the kingdom during the first Anglo-Burmese war (1824–26). In 1891, after a succession dispute and the killing of British officials, a British expedition defeated the Manipuri forces at the battle of Khongjom, which is commemorated in Manipur, and the kingdom came under British control. The martial arts of Manipur — thang-ta, sarit sarak and mukna wrestling — were part of the training of the kingdom’s soldiers, and their twentieth-century revival was linked to the assertion of Meitei identity.

docs.title: 15.12.1 Maharashtra: mardānī khel
docs.text: Mardānī khel (“manly games”) is the name now given to the weapon arts of Maharashtra, associated with the Maratha military tradition. They include the use of the gauntlet sword (paṭā), the stick (lāṭhī), the vīṭā (a short spear attached to a cord, which can be thrown and pulled back) and other weapons, practised in the tālīms and at festivals, especially in Kolhapur. In the twentieth century, physical culture institutions in Maharashtra and Baroda documented and taught these arts (Mujumdar 1950).

docs.title: 15.12.2 Odisha: the paika
docs.text: The paikas were the peasant militia of the kingdom of Khurda in Odisha, who held land in return for military service. In 1817, after the British annexation of Khurda and the loss of their lands, the paikas rose in revolt under Bakshi Jagabandhu Bidyadhar; the rising was suppressed, but it is remembered in Odisha as an early revolt against British rule. The paika akhāḍās preserve their martial exercises and displays with sword, shield and stick, performed to drums.

docs.title: 15.12.3 Bengal: lāṭhi khelā
docs.text: Lāṭhi khelā, stick-fighting with the bamboo staff (lāṭhi), was widely practised in rural Bengal, where landlords employed armed retainers (lāṭhiyāl). In the early twentieth century nationalists, including Sarala Devi Chaudhurani and members of revolutionary societies such as the Anushilan Samiti (founded in 1902), promoted stick-fighting and physical culture as means of building courage and strength among young men, in reaction to colonial stereotypes of the “effeminate” Bengali (Chapter 19).

docs.title: 15.12.4 Bihar and Jharkhand: pari-khaṇḍā
docs.text: Pari-khaṇḍā is a sword (khaṇḍā) and shield (pari) art of Bihar and Jharkhand. Its movements are closely related to the Chhau dance of Seraikela and the surrounding region, in which dancers perform martial themes; the relationship between martial training and performance here, as in Kerala and Manipur, is close.

docs.title: 15.12.5 Kashmir: sqay
docs.text: Sqay is a sword-and-shield fencing art from Kashmir, organised as a modern sport with a national federation since the late twentieth century. Its promoters describe it as an ancient Kashmiri art; its earlier history is not well documented.

docs.title: 15.13 Other Arms Traditions
docs.text:
Many other regional arms traditions deserve mention, though their histories are less fully documented.

  • In Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, kaṟṟa sāmu (stick exercise) and katti sāmu (sword exercise) were taught in village gymnasia and displayed at festivals.

  • In Tamil Nadu, besides silambam, there are traditions of exercise with heavy clubs (kaṟlakkaṭṭai) and of the deer-horn weapon (māṭu); aṭimuṟai, an unarmed art of the far south, is related to varmakkalai.

  • In Himachal Pradesh, ṭhoḍā is a ritual archery game in which teams of archers shoot blunt-headed arrows at the legs of their opponents, accompanied by dancing and music, at village festivals.

  • In Assam and the north-east, many hill communities had their own traditions of sword and spear fighting, often expressed in war dances that survive today as cultural performances (Chapter 13).

docs.title: 15.14 Martial Arts and Performance
docs.text:
In many parts of India martial training and performance were closely connected. In Kerala, the training of actors in the dance-drama kathakaḷi uses intensive body exercises and oil massage similar to those of the kaḷari, and many early kathakaḷi actors came from families with martial traditions. In the twentieth century Indian and international theatre makers drew on kaḷarippayaṟṟu: Phillip Zarrilli developed a method of actor training based on it, and the dancer Chandralekha incorporated its movements into contemporary dance. In eastern India the masked chhau dances of Purulia, Seraikela and Mayurbhanj draw on martial movements and themes, and their training includes exercises related to sword-and-shield play. In Manipur, the martial and the ritual are intertwined in the dances associated with Meitei religion. These connections show that the boundary between martial art and performing art was always permeable, and they help explain why many martial traditions survived as performance after their military functions disappeared.

Table 15.1 summarises the principal regional martial arts discussed in this chapter and in Chapter 14. The “documented from” column gives the period from which the art, in a recognisable form, is attested in dated sources; many practitioners claim much greater antiquity.

docs.title: 15.15 Teachers, Lineages and the Transmission of Skill
docs.text:
The martial arts of India were transmitted, like many other crafts, from teacher to pupil within lineages. In Kerala the teacher of kaḷarippayaṟṟu is the gurukkaḷ or āśān; in the akhāṛā of north India the wrestlers’ teacher is the guru or ustād; in the Sikh tradition the teacher of gatkā is often called ustād as well. In each case the relationship is personal and hierarchical. The pupil is admitted after a ritual of entry, owes the teacher obedience and gifts, and learns by imitation and repetition under the teacher’s eye rather than from written instruction (Zarrilli 1998; Alter 1992).

Lineage gave each tradition its identity. In Kerala, Zarrilli distinguishes northern, central and southern styles of kaḷarippayaṟṟu, which differ in their forms, weapons and emphasis, and within each style there are the particular lineages of individual kaḷaris, each claiming descent from a founding master (Zarrilli 1998). In north India wrestlers identify themselves with the akhāṛā in which they trained and the guru who trained them, and rival akhāṛās compete for prestige. Such lineages preserve knowledge, but they can also restrict it: teachers have often kept the most valued techniques, or the knowledge of healing and vital points, for a few trusted pupils.

Some lineages kept written texts. Kerala families of teachers hold palm-leaf manuscripts in Malayalam that record sequences of movement, lists of vital points and recipes for medicines; in Tamil Nadu, texts on varmam circulate among practitioners. These manuscripts are usually brief and allusive, written as reminders for those who already know the practice, and few have been edited or dated. They should not be confused with modern printed books that present “ancient” material without manuscript evidence.

In the twentieth century the transmission of the martial arts changed. Associations were formed to organise competitions and register teachers, syllabuses were written, and the arts began to be taught in schools, colleges and urban studios to pupils with no hereditary connection to them. These changes widened access, including to women and to pupils of all castes, and helped the arts to survive; but they also standardised practices that had been diverse, and shifted authority from the individual teacher to the association. The tension between lineage and organisation runs through the modern history of every tradition described in this chapter.

docs.title: 15.16 Sport, Rules and Safety
docs.text: The transformation of regional martial arts into sports has required the invention of rules for safe competition. Silambam competitions score strikes with padded or marked staffs; gatka competitions use sticks and shields with scoring by judges; kaḷarippayaṟṟu competitions judge the performance of forms (payaṟṟu) and controlled sparring; thang-ta competitions use padded sticks. Protective equipment, weight classes and medical supervision have been introduced. These changes make the arts safer and more accessible, especially for children and for women, but they also change their character. Practitioners and federations continue to debate how much of the traditional curriculum can or should be preserved in competitive formats.

docs.title: 15.17 The Politics of Revival
docs.text:
The twentieth-century revival of regional martial arts was closely connected with regional and national identities. In Kerala, the revival of kaḷarippayaṟṟu in the 1920s and 1930s was part of a broader Malayali cultural renaissance and of nationalist interest in Indian physical culture (Zarrilli 1998). In Tamil Nadu, silambam became associated with Tamil cultural pride. In Punjab, gatka was promoted by Sikh religious organisations as part of Sikh heritage, especially after the political turmoil of the 1980s. In Manipur, thang-ta was revived in the 1950s as part of the assertion of Meitei culture. In Maharashtra, mardānī khel was associated with the memory of Śivājī.

These connections gave the arts new energy and new audiences, but they also shaped the way their histories were told, often emphasising antiquity, purity and heroic resistance. The task of the historian is to recognise the importance of these arts for the communities that practise them while examining the evidence for their history with care.

docs.title: 15.18 Who Practised the Martial Arts?
docs.text:
The social basis of the regional martial arts was broader than the image of an exclusive warrior caste suggests. In Kerala, kaḷarippayaṟṟu was practised not only by Nāyars but by the Tiyya (Īḻava) community, from which many of the cēkavar champions of the ballads came; by Mappila Muslims, whose own martial traditions were associated with resistance to the Portuguese and later to the British; and by Syrian Christians, some of whose families maintained kaḷaris (Zarrilli 1998). In Tamil Nadu, silambam was associated with several communities, including those of the Maṟavar and Kaḷḷar country but also many others. Gatka was open to all initiated Sikhs, regardless of caste origin, in keeping with the Khalsa’s rejection of caste distinctions, though in practice caste persisted in Sikh society. In Manipur, thang-ta was part of Meitei culture as a whole. The paikas of Odisha were peasants of several castes who held land for military service.

At the same time, access to martial training was shaped by caste, gender and class. Certain lineages guarded their knowledge closely; some communities were excluded from carrying arms; women’s participation was limited in most traditions. The modern revival has opened most of these arts to all, a change that practitioners themselves often celebrate as a return to the inclusive spirit of their traditions, and that historians would more cautiously describe as a new development.

docs.title: 15.19 Martial Arts and Modern India
docs.text:
Three themes emerge from this survey. First, most of India’s regional martial arts were closely tied to particular military and social systems — Nāyar retainers in Kerala, poligar armies in Tamil Nadu, the Sikh misls, the Meitei kingdom, the paika militia — and declined when those systems were dismantled in the colonial period. Second, their revival in the twentieth century was part of a broader movement of physical culture and cultural nationalism, and it changed them: arts that had been transmitted within lineages were taught publicly, standardised, made into sports, and adapted for the stage and the screen. Third, the revival has been accompanied by claims of antiquity and of unique power that often go beyond the evidence. Historians such as Zarrilli have shown that it is possible to respect these arts as living traditions while examining their history critically (Zarrilli 1998).

Health and Safety Note

Martial arts training with weapons or striking techniques should be undertaken only under qualified supervision. Nothing in this chapter is intended as instruction. Traditional massage and vital-point therapies are described here as cultural practices; they are not a substitute for medical diagnosis and treatment.

docs.text:
