  • Green and Svinth (2010): encyclopaedia entries on Indian and other martial arts.

  • Mujumdar (1950): Indian physical culture and weapon arts in the mid-twentieth century.

  • Singh and Singh (2008): the Sikhs of Hazur Sahib and their martial and ritual traditions.

  • Grewal (1990): the history of the Sikhs.

docs.title: Chapter 16: Women and War: Vīrāṅganās, Rulers and Victims
16.1 Introduction
docs.text:
War in South Asia, as elsewhere, was overwhelmingly the business of men, and the texts that describe it were written by men. Yet women appear in the history of Indian warfare in many roles: as rulers and regents who commanded armies, as defenders of besieged forts, as guards and soldiers, as patrons of warriors, as the mothers and widows celebrated in war poetry, and, very often, as the victims of war — captured, enslaved, or driven to death to avoid capture. The figure of the vīrāṅganā, the “heroic woman” who takes up arms, has a special place in Indian popular culture, from the folk theatre of north India to modern cinema (Hansen 1988).

This chapter surveys the evidence. It tries to avoid two distortions. One presents Indian women as having been uniformly passive and secluded until modern times; the other presents a long tradition of women warriors as though women’s military participation had been normal. The truth lies between: women who fought and commanded were exceptional, usually members of ruling families acting in the absence of men, and their exceptional status is precisely why they were remembered.

docs.title: 16.2.1 The Vedic hymns
docs.text: The Ṛgveda contains a few references that later writers have read as evidence of women fighters. One hymn (RV 1.116.15) praises the Aśvins for giving Viśpalā an iron leg when her leg was cut off “in the contest”, so that she could run again. Viśpalā is usually taken to be a woman warrior; some scholars, however, interpret her as a racing mare, and the passage is too brief to settle the question (Jamison and Brereton 2014). Another hymn (RV 10.102) describes Mudgalānī, the wife of Mudgala, driving her husband’s chariot to victory in a race or contest. These passages show that women could be imagined in martial roles, but they do not establish a tradition of women’s military service.

docs.title: 16.2.2 Women guards
docs.text: Greek and Sanskrit sources agree on one practice: the king was guarded by armed women. Megasthenes reported that the Mauryan king was protected in his palace by women bodyguards, and the Arthaśāstra prescribes that the king, on rising, should be surrounded by women armed with bows (AŚ 1.21) (Kangle 1960–1965; Olivelle 2013). Women guards of the inner palace are mentioned in Sanskrit drama and in accounts of later courts, including those of Vijayanagara and the Mughals; the Mughal harem was guarded by armed women, some of them from Central Asia and Abyssinia.

docs.title: 16.2.3 The epics and the goddess
docs.text: The epics have few women fighters. Draupadī, wife of the Pāṇḍavas, is a fierce advocate of war after her humiliation at the dice game, but she does not fight; Kaikeyī in the Rāmāyaṇa is said to have driven her husband’s chariot in a battle of the gods and demons; Citrāṅgadā, princess of Maṇipūra and wife of Arjuna, is a ruler’s heir. Later traditions, such as Satyabhāmā’s part in Kṛṣṇa’s battle with the demon Naraka, told in the Harivaṃśa and the Purāṇas, expand women’s martial roles. The most powerful image of female martial power is divine: the goddess Durgā, who in the Devīmāhātmya (c. fifth to sixth century) receives the weapons of all the gods and slays the buffalo-demon Mahiṣa and his armies. The warrior goddess was the patron of many royal lineages, but her worship did not imply that human women should fight.

docs.title: 16.2.4 Tamil war poetry
docs.text: The Tamil Caṅkam poems of war give a particularly vivid picture of women’s relation to war — not as fighters but as mothers, wives and widows of warriors. In one famous poem of the Puṟanāṉūṟu, a mother who hears that her son fled from battle goes to the battlefield intending to punish herself if the report is true, finds him dead with his wounds in front, and rejoices more than on the day she bore him (Hart and Heifetz 1999). Poems by women poets such as Auvaiyār, who was also an envoy between kings, express the heroic ethic, and others lament its cost. These poems show how women participated in, and were bound by, a culture that exalted death in battle.

docs.title: 16.3.1 Raziya
docs.text: Raziya (r. 1236–1240), daughter of Iltutmish, is the only woman to have ruled the Delhi Sultanate. Her father designated her as his heir, and after a struggle she took the throne. She appeared in public, rode an elephant and led her armies in person; the historian Minhāj al-Sirāj, who served her, praised her as a just and capable ruler who lacked only the qualification of being a man. She was overthrown by a faction of Turkic nobles and killed in 1240 (Jackson 1999).

docs.title: 16.3.2 Rudramā Devī
docs.text: Rudramā Devī ruled the Kākatīya kingdom of Warangal in the Telugu country from about 1262 to 1289. She took the masculine title Rudradeva Mahārāja in her inscriptions, faced revolts by subordinate chiefs and attacks by the Yādavas of Devagiri, and maintained her rule through a network of military commanders loyal to her. The Venetian traveller Marco Polo, who visited the coast of her kingdom, described it as ruled by a wise queen. Cynthia Talbot’s study of medieval Andhra places her reign in the context of the Kākatīya state’s military and social organisation (Talbot 2001).

docs.title: 16.3.3 Durgāvatī
docs.text: Rāṇī Durgāvatī of the Gond kingdom of Garha-Katanga in central India was born into the Chandela dynasty and married into the Gond royal house; after her husband’s death she ruled as regent for her young son. In 1564 the Mughal governor Āṣaf Khān invaded her kingdom. Durgāvatī led her forces in person, mounted on an elephant; after initial resistance her army was defeated near Narhi, and, wounded, she killed herself rather than be captured. Abū’l-Faẓl, Akbar’s historian, recorded her courage. She became a heroine of the Gond people and of Indian nationalism.

docs.title: 16.3.4 Chand Bībī
docs.text: Chand Bībī (d. 1600), a princess of Ahmadnagar who married into the ruling family of Bijapur, acted as regent in both sultanates. In 1595–96, as regent of Ahmadnagar, she organised the defence of the city against a Mughal army led by Akbar’s son Murād. When the besiegers blew a breach in the wall with a mine, she is said to have directed its repair under fire; the Mughals withdrew after a negotiated settlement. She was killed in 1600, during factional conflict in the city, shortly before Ahmadnagar fell to the Mughals (Eaton 2005). Her career shows that the figure of the woman ruler-commander was not confined to any one religious tradition.

docs.title: 16.3.5 Abbakka of Ullal
docs.text: Abbakka Chowta, queen of the small Tulu principality of Ullal near Mangalore in the mid-sixteenth century, resisted Portuguese attempts to control the trade of the coast, in alliance with the Zamorin of Calicut and others. Portuguese sources record expeditions against Ullal; much of what is now told of her, including her death in captivity, comes from later tradition, which has made her one of the best-known resisters of European expansion in coastal Karnataka.

docs.title: 16.4 Cennabhairādevī of Gersoppa
docs.text: Cennabhairādevī, queen of the small Jain-ruled principality of Gersoppa (Nagire) in the hinterland of the Kanara coast, is said to have ruled for several decades in the second half of the sixteenth century. Her territories produced much of the pepper exported from the Kanara ports, and later writers report that the Portuguese called her the “pepper queen”. She traded with the Portuguese but resisted their attempts to control the pepper trade. Her reign has not received a critical study in English, and the details commonly given, including the length of her rule and her conflicts with the Portuguese, rest on regional histories and tradition that this volume has not been able to check against the Portuguese records or the Kannada inscriptions; they are given here with that caution.

docs.title: 16.5 Women at the Mughal Court
docs.text: The Mughal court offers several examples of women’s involvement in war and politics. The imperial harem was guarded by armed women, known in Persian sources as urdubegī, many of them from Central Asia or Africa, who were trained in the use of the bow and other weapons. Women of the imperial family were active in politics: Nūr Jahān, the wife of Jahāngīr, issued orders and coins in her own name and was a skilled hunter, reported to have shot tigers from an elephant. In 1626, when the general Mahābat Khān seized Jahāngīr in a coup at a crossing of the Jhelum, Nūr Jahān led an attempt to rescue him, directing the attack from an elephant; it failed, but she later outmanoeuvred Mahābat Khān and secured the emperor’s release (Richards 1993). Women of noble families managed estates and sometimes defended them, and the widows of commanders sometimes kept their husbands’ troops together.

docs.title: 16.6.1 Tārābāī
docs.text: Tārābāī (1675–1761), widow of the Maratha king Rājārām, led Maratha resistance against Aurangzeb after her husband’s death in 1700. As regent for her young son, she directed the war against the Mughals, appointed commanders and kept the Maratha state alive through the hardest years of the Deccan wars (Gordon 1993). After Aurangzeb’s death, the release of her nephew Shāhū by the Mughals led to a civil war that she lost; she remained a powerful figure in Maratha politics for decades.

docs.title: 16.6.2 Keladi Cennammā and Ahilyābāī Holkar
docs.text: Cennammā, queen of the Nāyaka kingdom of Keladi in Karnataka (r. 1672–1697), gave refuge to Rājārām when he fled south from the Mughals in 1690 and successfully resisted the Mughal forces sent against her. Ahilyābāī Holkar (r. 1767–1795), ruler of the Maratha state of Indore, is remembered mainly as a just administrator and a builder of temples and pilgrim facilities across India, but she also maintained the Holkar army and directed its affairs through her commander Tukojī Holkar.

docs.title: 16.6.3 Velu Nācciyār and Kuyili
docs.text: Velu Nācciyār, queen of Sivaganga in Tamil Nadu, lost her husband and her kingdom in 1772 when the forces of the Nawab of Arcot and the East India Company attacked Sivaganga. According to the accounts now current, she took refuge with the poligar of Virupachi and, with the support of Haidar Ali of Mysore and of the Marutu brothers (Section 15.7), recovered her kingdom in 1780. Tamil tradition tells that her woman commander Kuyili set herself on fire and destroyed an enemy powder magazine; the story, as told today, rests on oral tradition and later writing. No critical study of the queen’s career is cited here, and the details should be taken as those of regional history and tradition. Both women are now honoured in Tamil Nadu as early resisters of colonial rule.

docs.title: 16.7 Women Rulers in the South
docs.text: In south India, several women ruled as regents and directed military affairs. Rāṇī Maṅgammāḷ, regent of the Nāyaka kingdom of Madurai from 1689 to about 1704, conducted the kingdom’s relations with the Mughals, who were then advancing into the south, and with the neighbouring Tanjavur and Mysore kingdoms; she is remembered for her public works and for her diplomacy. The queens of the Keladi and other Nāyaka kingdoms, the queens of Kerala’s matrilineal ruling houses and the women rulers of small Maṟavar and poligar states all played military roles at times. Their histories, recorded partly in inscriptions and court chronicles and partly in local tradition, show that women’s rule was not exceptional in the south Indian political world.

docs.title: 16.8 Sikh Women in Tradition
docs.text: Sikh tradition remembers women who took part in the wars of the Gurus’ time. The best known is Māī Bhāgo, who, according to tradition, led a band of Sikhs who had deserted Guru Gobind Singh back to his side and fought with them at the battle of Muktsar (Khidrana) in 1705. The Khalsa’s ideals of equality and of the duty to defend the faith gave women a place in Sikh martial memory, and today Sikh women perform gatka at festivals and in competitions (Dhavan 2011).

docs.title: 16.9 Begum Samrū
docs.text: One of the most remarkable figures of eighteenth-century north India was Begum Samrū (c. 1750s–1836), the ruler of the small principality of Sardhana near Meerut. Born in obscure circumstances, she became the companion and later the wife of Walter Reinhardt, known as Sombre or Samrū, a European mercenary commander who had served several Indian rulers and received Sardhana as a jāgīr. After his death in 1778 she inherited command of his mercenary army of infantry and artillery, which she led in the service of the Mughal emperor Shāh ʿĀlam II and others; she is reported to have taken part in campaigns in person. She converted to Catholicism and built a large church at Sardhana. After the British conquest of the region in 1803 she made terms with the East India Company and kept her principality until her death. Her career illustrates the world of the eighteenth-century military entrepreneurs, in which a woman of humble origins could command an army (Roy 2011).

docs.title: 16.10.1 Cennammā of Kittūr
docs.text: Cennammā of Kittūr (1778–1829), widow of the ruler of the small state of Kittūr in north Karnataka, refused to accept the East India Company’s decision not to recognise her adopted son as heir. In October 1824 her forces resisted the Company’s attempt to take control; the collector of Dharwar, St John Thackeray, was killed. A larger force took Kittūr in December, and Cennammā died in captivity in 1829. She is commemorated in Karnataka as one of the earliest Indian rulers to fight the Company.

docs.title: 16.10.2 The rising of 1857
docs.text:
The rising of 1857 produced the most famous of India’s women warriors. Lakṣmībāī, Rāṇī of Jhānsī (d. 1858), was the widow of the ruler of Jhānsī, whose state the Company had annexed under the “doctrine of lapse” after it refused to recognise her adopted son. When the rising broke out she at first negotiated with the British, and then, accused of complicity in the killing of Europeans at Jhānsī, took command of its defence. Sir Hugh Rose besieged and stormed Jhānsī in March and April 1858; the Rāṇī escaped by night and joined the rebel forces under Tātyā Ṭope. She was killed in battle near Gwalior in June 1858. Her British opponents acknowledged her courage. Joyce Lebra-Chapman’s study separates the historical Rāṇī from the legend that grew around her in songs, novels and nationalist history (Lebra-Chapman 1986).

Other women of 1857, at Jhānsī and Lucknow, are described in the next section. Kathryn Hansen has traced how the figure of the vīrāṅganā became part of north Indian popular theatre and print culture, admired but also contained as an exception to normal womanhood (Hansen 1988).

docs.title: 16.11 The Women of Jhānsī and Lucknow
docs.text: The defence of Jhānsī in 1858 involved many women besides the Rāṇī. Contemporary British accounts and later Indian tradition mention women carrying ammunition, food and water to the defenders on the walls and working the guns. Among the Rāṇī’s companions, tradition remembers the attendants Sundar and Mundar and Jhalkārībāī, a woman of the Kolī community who is said to have disguised herself as the Rāṇī to cover her escape. At Lucknow, Begum Hazrat Mahal, who led the resistance in the name of her young son, issued proclamations answering the British, and continued to resist after the fall of the city; she eventually took refuge in Nepal, where she died in 1879. The British accounts of the fighting at Sikandar Bagh in November 1857 mention a woman sniper killed in a tree, whom later tradition identifies with Ūdā Devī, a Pāsī woman. Jhalkārībāī and Ūdā Devī have become heroines for Dalit communities in north India (Section 16.15). These women came from very different social backgrounds — royal, courtly and humble — and their memory has been taken up by different communities in modern India.

docs.title: 16.12 The Begums of Bhopal
docs.text: The princely state of Bhopal in central India was ruled by women for most of the period from 1819 to 1926 — an unusual succession of four women rulers. Qudsia Begum governed as regent after her husband’s assassination in 1819; her daughter Sikandar Begum ruled from the 1840s to 1868, reformed the administration and the army, and supported the British during the rising of 1857, for which she was rewarded; Shāh Jahān Begum and Sultān Jahān Begum followed her. The Begums of Bhopal commanded the state’s forces in a formal sense, reviewed troops and, in Sikandar Begum’s case, were known for their skill in riding and their interest in military affairs. Their rule shows that the role of the woman ruler with military responsibilities continued into the colonial period, within the limits set by British paramountcy.

docs.title: 16.13 Women as Victims of War: Jauhar and Captivity
16.13.1 Jauhar
docs.text:
The darkest chapter of women’s relation to war in India is the jauhar, the collective death by fire of the women of a besieged fort to avoid capture, usually followed by a last charge of the men. Contemporary or near-contemporary sources record jauhars at Chanderi in 1528, during Bābur’s siege, and at Chittor in 1535 and 1568; Amīr Khusrau’s account of ʿAlāʾ al-Dīn’s capture of Ranthambhor in 1301 describes the burning of the women of the fort, which suggests that similar events occurred earlier (Sreenivasan 2007).

The best-known story of jauhar, that of Rāṇī Padminī of Chittor, whose beauty is said to have drawn ʿAlāʾ al-Dīn Khaljī to besiege the fort in 1303, comes from Malik Muḥammad Jāyasī’s Sufi poem Padmāvat, written in 1540, more than two centuries after the siege. Ramya Sreenivasan’s study shows how the story was retold and transformed by Rajput bards, colonial writers and nationalists, each giving it new meanings (Sreenivasan 2007). Padminī is a literary heroine whose historical existence cannot be established.

The jauhar has been interpreted in opposite ways. Rajput tradition celebrates it as the supreme expression of honour and courage; feminist historians have pointed out that it was the product of a social order that valued women chiefly as bearers of family honour, and that the women’s “choice” was made under the most extreme pressure. Both perspectives recognise the reality of the fear of capture: women captured in war were enslaved, given to the victors or sold, by armies of every religion. A history of Indian warfare that celebrates heroism without acknowledging this suffering is incomplete.

docs.title: 16.13.2 Captivity and enslavement
docs.text: Inscriptions and chronicles from many periods record the capture of women as spoils of war: Cōḻa and Cāḷukya inscriptions boast of seizing enemy queens, the chronicles of the Delhi Sultanate record the enslavement of captives in great numbers, and Rajput, Maratha and other armies took captives in their turn. The suffering of women in war was one of the realities that the rules of dharmayuddha (Chapter 12) addressed, at least in principle, by forbidding the harming of non-combatants.

docs.title: 16.14 Women against Colonial Rule
docs.text:
In the twentieth century women took part in armed resistance to colonial rule in several ways. In the hills of Manipur and the Naga country, Gaidinliu (1915–1993), a young Rongmei Naga woman, led a religious and political movement against British rule in the early 1930s; she was captured in 1932 and imprisoned until 1947; Jawaharlal Nehru, who met her in prison in 1937, called her “Rani”, the title by which she is remembered. In Bengal, women joined revolutionary societies: Pritilata Waddedar led an attack on a European club in Chittagong in 1932 and took her own life to avoid capture, and Bina Das fired at the Governor of Bengal at a university convocation in the same year. These women were few, but they broke with the assumption that political violence was a male domain, and they are remembered as heroines in Bengal and the north-east.

The women’s regiment of the Indian National Army, named after the Rāṇī of Jhānsī, is discussed below (Section 16.17). Its existence shows how the memory of the vīrāṅganā was mobilised by nationalists in the struggle for independence.

docs.title: 16.15 Representing the Vīrāṅganā
docs.text: The figure of the woman warrior has been represented in many ways in Indian culture. In north Indian folk theatre and popular print, as Kathryn Hansen has shown, the vīrāṅganā was a figure of admiration who took on male roles in a crisis — often after the death of her husband — and returned to female roles afterwards, so that her heroism confirmed rather than challenged the normal order (Hansen 1988). Nationalist writers made the Rāṇī of Jhānsī a symbol of the nation, as in Subhadra Kumari Chauhan’s Hindi poem “Jhānsī kī Rānī” (1930), one of the most widely memorised poems in Hindi. In recent decades, Dalit writers and activists have recovered figures such as Jhalkārībāī and Ūdā Devī as heroines of their own communities. Feminist historians have asked what these representations reveal about the constraints on women’s lives and about the uses of women’s images in politics. The study of the vīrāṅganā is thus as much a study of memory and representation as of military history.

docs.title: 16.16 Women in Hero-Stones and Memorial Stones
docs.text:
The memorial stones of medieval India give a glimpse of women’s relation to war at the local level. Most hero-stones commemorate men, but some commemorate women who died fighting, often in defence of cattle or village. Far more numerous are the memorial stones of women who died with their husbands, by self-immolation on the husband’s funeral pyre or otherwise; in Karnataka these are called mahāsatī stones, and they usually show a raised right arm with bangles, the sign of the married woman, sometimes alongside the hero’s image. In Rajasthan, satī memorials are found at many villages and forts. These stones were worshipped, and some satī sites became places of pilgrimage.

The memorial stones show how the ideology of the heroic death extended to women, and they are evidence of the practice of widow immolation, which was more common in some regions, communities and periods than others. The practice was criticised by some Indian thinkers long before the nineteenth century, and it was prohibited in British India by Lord William Bentinck’s regulation of 1829, after a campaign in which the Bengali reformer Rammohun Roy played a prominent part. Its glorification in modern times, as in the controversy that followed the death of Roop Kanwar in Rajasthan in 1987, led to further legislation. A history of women and war in India must include these stones and the lives they commemorate, alongside the stories of queens and commanders.

Queen; resisted the Portuguese Cennabhairādevī, Gersoppa later 16th c. docs.title: 16.17 The Twentieth Century and After
docs.text:
In the twentieth century, women entered military roles in new ways. In 1943 Subhas Chandra Bose’s Indian National Army, formed from Indian prisoners of war and civilians in Southeast Asia, created a women’s unit named the Rani of Jhansi Regiment, commanded by Lakshmi Swaminathan (later Sahgal) — a deliberate evocation of the vīrāṅganā tradition. After independence, women served in the Indian armed forces first as doctors and nurses; from the 1990s they were commissioned in other branches, from 2016 as fighter pilots, and following a Supreme Court judgment in 2020 they became eligible for permanent commissions in the army. Advocates of women’s military service have often invoked historical figures such as Lakṣmībāī; but the modern changes owe more to changing ideas of citizenship and equality than to any continuity with the past.

Table 16.1 summarises some of the women rulers, regents and commanders discussed in this chapter. It is not a complete list, and for several figures the details rest partly on later tradition, as noted in the text. Read together, the entries bear out the argument with which the chapter began: almost every woman in it before the twentieth century held command as a widow, a regent or the heir of a ruling house, in a moment of crisis, and was remembered because her role was exceptional.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:

  • Lebra-Chapman (1986): the Rāṇī of Jhānsī in history and legend.

  • Sreenivasan (2007): the Padminī story and its many retellings.

  • Talbot (2001): medieval Andhra and the Kākatīya state.

  • Hart and Heifetz (1999): Tamil war poems, including those on mothers and widows.

docs.title: Chapter 17: Soldiers for Hire: The Military Labour Market, c. 1450–1857
17.1 Introduction
docs.text:
Earlier chapters have followed kings, commanders and campaigns. This chapter follows the men who did the fighting. Between the fifteenth and the mid-nineteenth century most of them were neither hereditary warriors bound to a single lord nor conscripts. They were hired. They came from villages in particular regions, travelled long distances to find employment, served one master and then another, and returned home with savings, wounds or nothing. Dirk Kolff called this world the “military labour market” of Hindustan, and his book Naukar, Rajput and Sepoy (1990) changed the way historians think about Indian armies (Kolff 1990). Jos Gommans extended the argument to the Afghan horse-traders and soldiers of the eighteenth century and to the Mughal army as a whole (Gommans 1995; Gommans 2002). Stewart Gordon and André Wink showed how the same logic worked in the Maratha Deccan (Gordon 1994; Wink 1986). Seema Alavi traced how the East India Company tapped the market and reshaped it (Alavi 1995), and Gommans and Kolff’s reader collects essays on soldiering and weaponry across the whole period from 1000 to 1800 (Gommans and Kolff 2001).

The idea has already appeared in this volume in brief: in the outline of the fifteenth century (Section 8.21), in the discussion of caste and recruitment (Section 13.4), and in the ethics of the mercenary (Section 12.17). Here it is examined in detail. The chapter asks where soldiers came from, how they were recruited and paid, why they changed sides, what they lived on when pay failed, and how the market was absorbed and finally closed by the colonial state. The sepoy armies of the Company and the rising of 1857 are described in Chapter 19; this chapter is concerned with the soldiers who filled them and with the world those soldiers came from.

docs.title: 17.2 Sources for the Soldier’s History
docs.text:
The history of ordinary soldiers has to be pieced together from records kept by those who employed, paid and fought them. Persian sources are the richest for the Mughal period. The chronicles describe recruitment, musters, mutinies over pay and changes of side, usually from the point of view of the court; the Āʾīn-i Akbarī gives the statistical survey of the empire’s armed manpower discussed below; and the Mughal newsletters (akhbārāt) and the reports sent by Rajput agents at the imperial court, many of which survive in the archives of the former Rajput states, record day-to-day events such as the arrival of contingents, quarrels over arrears and the desertion of troops. The registers (bahī) of the Rajput courts record grants, service obligations and payments.

For the Maratha state the Peshwa’s records at Pune, written mostly in Marathi in the Modi script, include accounts of troops, horses, pay and debts on a scale unmatched elsewhere in India before the Company; Stewart Gordon and André Wink built their studies on them (Gordon 1993; Wink 1986). From the late eighteenth century the Company’s records — muster rolls, pension and invalid lists, recruiting returns, courts of inquiry into mutinies, and the correspondence of officers and political agents — allow individual soldiers to be followed in a way that earlier records rarely do. Alongside these documents stand literary sources: the heroic ballads of north India and the Deccan (Section 13.15), the Hindi romances in which a prince leaves home in the guise of a wandering ascetic, and a few memoirs, discussed later in this chapter, whose authenticity is itself a historical problem.

Each kind of source has its bias. Court histories treat soldiers as numbers and their protests as disorder; Company records describe them through the categories of caste and loyalty that the Company used to manage them; ballads celebrate heroes and forget the rank and file. Kolff’s achievement was to read these sources together, and against each other, to recover the outlines of a social world that none of them describes directly (Kolff 1990).

docs.title: 17.3 Naukarī: Service as a Way of Life
17.3.1 The armed peasantry
docs.text:
The basic fact about the countryside of early modern north India is that it was armed. Peasants kept swords, spears, bows and, from the sixteenth century, matchlocks; villages had walls, watchtowers or thorn hedges; and local landholders (zamīndār) maintained retainers who could be called out against rivals, bandits or the revenue officials of the state. Abū’l-Faẓl’s survey of the Mughal provinces, compiled in the 1590s, lists the forces of the zamīndārs district by district. Its totals run to more than four million men, the great majority of them foot-soldiers. Kolff treats this figure, which is certainly incomplete, as a minimum measure of the armed manpower of the countryside (Kolff 1990; Blochmann 1873). Mughal chronicles repeatedly describe districts as “refractory” (mawās): tracts in forest or ravine country whose villages refused revenue and fought the troops sent to collect it.

For a ruler, this armed peasantry was at once a danger and a resource. It made the collection of revenue a permanent small war, and it meant that any rival with money could raise an army quickly. It also meant that the state did not need to train soldiers from scratch. Young men learned to wrestle, to fence with sticks and to use arms in the village akhāṛā (Section 13.7); what they sought from a ruler was employment.

docs.title: 17.3.2 The seasons of service
docs.text:
The Persian word naukar means servant, and naukarī service; in the vocabulary of north India it came to mean above all military employment. Kolff describes naukarī as a regular part of the peasant economy. In many families of the eastern Ganges valley, Bundelkhand and Rajasthan, one or more sons left home after the harvest to look for service, while the others worked the land. Some returned for the next sowing; others stayed away for years, sending money home. The campaigning season, which opened after the rains (Section 1.5), was also the season of recruitment. Soldiering in this sense was a form of labour migration, like the later migration of men from the same districts to the jute mills of Calcutta or, under indenture, to the plantations of Mauritius and the Caribbean, and it was governed by similar calculations of wage, risk and distance.

The relationship between a naukar and his master was personal and contractual at once. It was sealed by acceptance of pay and by the ethic of loyalty to the salt (Section 13.8), but both sides knew that it could end. A master who did not pay could expect his men to leave; a soldier who left an employer who had paid him was dishonoured. Most of the time the system worked on this understanding, and the moral language of salt and loyalty served to make a market relationship durable.

docs.title: 17.3.3 An open status
docs.text:
Kolff’s most influential argument concerns identity. In the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, he suggests, the word “Rajput” in Hindustan often described not a closed descent group but a way of life: that of the man who had left his village with his weapons in search of service and fortune. Men of many peasant and pastoral origins became Rajputs by living as soldiers, and Kolff draws attention to the image of the wandering warrior in the popular literature of the period, which has much in common with the image of the ascetic who has left home. Only in the seventeenth century, under Mughal patronage, did a more exclusive “Rajput great tradition” take shape, centred on the courts of Rajasthan, their genealogies and their bards, which tied Rajput status to descent from a recognised lineage (Kolff 1990).

The argument has been debated. Critics have pointed out that lineage and clan mattered in Rajput identity long before the Mughals, as the early medieval inscriptions and later genealogies show (Talbot 2016). But the central point, that military service could change a man’s social standing and that martial identities were made in history, is now widely accepted, and it is supported by the histories of the Marathas, Jats and other communities summarised in Section 13.5. The same was true of the identity “Afghan”, which in Hindustan could be acquired by men who joined Afghan bands and adopted their dress and loyalties.

docs.title: 17.4 The Recruiting Grounds of Hindustan
docs.text: Soldiers could come from anywhere, but some regions supplied far more than others. They were usually regions of dense peasant population, limited opportunities for advancement at home, and a tradition of service that made the road to employment familiar.

docs.title: 17.4.1 Bhojpur and the Purbiyas
docs.text: The most famous of these regions lay in the eastern Ganges valley: the country of Awadh, the districts around Banaras, and above all Bhojpur, the region of western Bihar between the Ganges and the Son. To soldiers and rulers in Malwa, Rajasthan and the Deccan these men were pūrbiyā, “easterners”, and the word became almost a synonym for hired infantry. The dominant landholding lineage of Bhojpur, the Ujjainiya Rajputs, who traced their descent from the Paramāras of Ujjain, were at once local lords, occasional rebels against the Afghan and Mughal rulers of Bihar, and suppliers of fighting men to them; Kolff uses their history to show how a lineage could prosper by managing the flow of soldiers out of its territory (Kolff 1990). In the eighteenth century, matchlockmen from the town of Baksar (Buxar) on the Ganges were so common in the armies of Bengal and Bihar that “Buxerry” (from baksariyā, “man of Baksar”) became a common word for a matchlockman or armed guard in the English of the Company’s servants.

docs.title: 17.4.2 The Purbiyas in Malwa
docs.text: The power of these soldiers is shown most dramatically by events in Malwa in the early sixteenth century. Sultan Maḥmūd II Khaljī of Malwa came to rely on a Purbiya chief, Medinī Rāy, and his followers to secure his throne against his own nobles. For some years Medinī Rāy’s men dominated the sultanate, until the sultan escaped to Gujarat and was restored with Gujarati troops in 1518, after which the Purbiyas were driven out of the capital at Mandu with great slaughter. Medinī Rāy held the fortress of Chanderi under the protection of Rāṇā Sāṅgā of Mewar and joined Sāṅgā against Bābur at Khanua in 1527. Bābur besieged Chanderi in January 1528; his memoirs describe the storming of the fort and the defenders’ last stand (Thackston 1996). The episode shows a body of hired soldiers acting as a political force in its own right, able to make and unmake rulers, and it shows how quickly the fortunes of such a force could turn.

docs.title: 17.4.3 Bundelkhand
docs.text: South of the Yamuna, the rugged country of Bundelkhand was another nursery of soldiers. Its Bundela chiefs, based at Orchha from the 1530s, built their power by recruiting and leading the men of the region, and by placing them at the disposal of the Mughals when it suited them. Bīr Siṅgh Deo, who killed Akbar’s minister Abū’l-Faẓl in 1602 at the instigation of Prince Salīm, was rewarded when Salīm became the emperor Jahāṅgīr, and used his rank and revenues to build the palaces of Orchha and Datia. His successors alternated between high Mughal service and rebellion; the rebel Campat Rāy and his son Chhatrasāl (Section 9.18) drew on the same reservoir of fighting men (Kolff 1990). Bundelkhand matchlockmen served in armies across north and central India well into the nineteenth century.

docs.title: 17.4.4 Afghans and Rohillas
docs.text:
Afghan soldiers formed a market of their own. The Lodī sultans of Delhi (1451–1526) drew Afghans into Hindustan with offers of land and employment, and Afghan histories written in Mughal times describe how their clans settled in the towns and villages of the Ganges plain. The career of Sher Shāh Sūr shows how this world worked. Born Farīd, the son of a minor Afghan holder of revenue rights at Sasaram in Bihar, he made his name in the service of an Afghan ruler of Bihar, gathered a following of Afghan soldiers by paying them promptly and treating them as comrades, and used that following to defeat Humāyūn in 1539–40. His biographer ʿAbbās Khān Sarwānī, writing for Akbar, dwells on his care in recruitment, in the inspection of men and horses, and in regular payment (Richards 1993). After the Mughal restoration the Afghans lost their empire but not their place in the market: they served the Mughals, the Deccan sultans and later the Marathas.

In the eighteenth century, Gommans has argued, Afghan horse-traders, soldiers and settlers formed an “Indo-Afghan” network that linked the horse markets of the north-west with settlements in Rohilkhand and Farrukhabad and with the armies of the Durrānī kings of Afghanistan (Gommans 1995). The Rohilla state of ʿAlī Muḥammad Khān (d. 1748) and his successors grew out of this network; its leaders were at once horse-dealers, landholders, military contractors and rulers. Its last independent ruler, Ḥāfiẓ Raḥmat Khān, was killed in 1774 fighting the combined army of Awadh and the East India Company.

docs.title: 17.4.5 The Punjab misls
docs.text:
In the Punjab of the mid-eighteenth century the market took a form shaped by religion as well as by pay. As Mughal authority collapsed under the Afghan invasions, Sikh fighting bands (jathā) gathered around leaders of proven ability and, from 1748, acted together in the Dal Khālsā, a loose federation that met at Amritsar to decide on common action (Section 9.20). The bands that crystallised out of this federation, the misls, were not hereditary armies. A horseman, usually a Jat peasant who had taken initiation into the Khalsa, chose the leader (sardār) under whom he would serve and could, in principle, leave him for another; he supplied his own horse and arms; and he received a share of the plunder and, as the misls settled down, of the land they conquered. Historians describe this system of shares in conquered territory as pattīdārī (Grewal 1990).

The misls paid for themselves in part through rākhī, “protection”: villages and towns placed themselves under a misl’s protection in return for a share of their produce, traditionally a fifth, and the misl undertook to defend them against other raiders and against the Afghan armies. Rākhī was at once a tax, a contract and a form of political allegiance, and it allowed the misls to turn the protection business of the armed countryside into territorial power. Purnima Dhavan has shown how, in the same decades, Sikh writers worked to define the conduct of the Khalsa warrior, so that the misl horseman was bound not only by pay and plunder but by a code of religious discipline (Dhavan 2011). When Ranjit Singh united the Punjab, he absorbed the misl cavalry into the ghoṛcaṛhā horse of his kingdom and built a regular army alongside it (Chapter 18).

docs.title: 17.5.1 Bārgīr and śiledār
docs.text: In the Deccan the market took a different form, because the dominant arm was light cavalry. The Maratha armies distinguished two kinds of trooper. The bārgīr rode a horse and carried arms supplied by the state or by his commander and received a lower wage; the śiledār (from Persian silāḥdār, “bearer of arms”) owned his horse and equipment and hired them out together with his own service at a higher rate. The household cavalry of the Peshwas and the great chiefs (pāgā) consisted of bārgīrs; the larger part of a Maratha army consisted of śiledārs and their leaders, who were in effect small contractors. A horse was capital, and its loss could reduce a śiledār to a bārgīr or to a foot-soldier. Stewart Gordon has shown how a successful śiledār family could rise, over two or three generations, from village service to command and to the holding of revenue assignments (Gordon 1993, 1994). The Bengali word bargī, used for the Maratha raiders of the 1740s, comes from bārgīr.

docs.title: 17.5.2 Ḥabshīs and Arabs
docs.text: The Deccan market also drew men from overseas. Ethiopian and other East African soldiers (ḥabshī), many of whom had come to India as slaves, served the Bahmanī and later sultanates, and some rose to the highest commands (Section 9.15). From the second half of the eighteenth century Arab soldiers, many of them from the Hadhramaut in southern Arabia, became prominent in the armies of the Nizam, the Maratha chiefs and the Gaikwads of Baroda. They had a reputation for steadiness in the defence of forts, and Arab garrisons in Khandesh were among the last to resist the Company in 1818. In Hyderabad, Arab commanders (jamādār) lent money to the state and to nobles and took the revenues of districts as security, becoming a political force that the Nizam’s ministers and the British Resident had to reckon with in the early nineteenth century. Their descendants remain a distinct community in the city, notably in the quarter called Barkas.

docs.title: 17.5.3 Peons, poligars and forest archers
docs.text:
In the south, the infantry of the Vijayanagara successor states and of the poligars (pāḷaiyakkārar) consisted largely of armed retainers known in English records as “peons”, drawn from communities such as the Kaḷḷar, Maṟavar and Bedar (Section 13.5). Kerala’s Nāyar soldiers stood somewhat apart, being bound by birth and kaḷari training to particular lords, but they too could be hired.

Across central and western India the forest and hill peoples — Bhils, Kolis, Mīṇās, Gonds and others — served as archers, scouts and guards, and also raided the settled country when they were not employed. Their relationship with the Rajput states was old and close; the arms of the Mewar state show a Bhil archer beside a Rajput warrior as supporters of the shield. The East India Company drew them into its own forces in the 1820s: the Khandesh Bhil Corps raised by James Outram in 1825 was intended both to employ the Bhils and to end their raiding. In this way the colonial state used the logic of the market against those who had lived from it.

docs.title: 17.6 Contractors, Credit and Arrears
docs.text:
Armies were assembled through a chain of contracts (Figure 17.1). At the top, the ruler granted a commander a rank, a salary and, very often, the revenue of a territory from which to pay it. The commander raised his contingent not man by man but through band leaders, called jamādārs (from jamʿ, a body of men) or by local titles, who brought followers recruited from their own villages and kin and negotiated their pay. The ordinary soldier therefore served the band leader who had recruited him, through him the commander, and through the commander the ruler. Each link was a bargain, and each could break.

Figure 17.1. The chain of military contracting in an early modern Indian army (schematic). Service ran up the chain and pay down it; bankers bridged the gaps, and the villages supplied both men and the revenue that paid them.

Pay was the heart of the system, and it was chronically late. In the Mughal empire the salary attached to a rank was a nominal figure; the revenue assignments (jāgīr) from which it was paid often yielded less. By the reign of Shāh Jahān the administration had recognised this formally, grading assignments by the number of months’ pay they could be expected to produce in a year and reducing the commander’s obligations accordingly (Athar Ali 1966; Richards 1993). A commander who received less than he expected passed the shortfall down the chain. Soldiers were paid in instalments, often months in arrears, and settled accounts at the end of a campaign, when deductions were made for advances, for horses lost or for absence.

Credit filled the gaps. Soldiers borrowed from the merchants and sutlers who followed the camp; commanders borrowed from bankers against the revenue of their assignments; rulers borrowed against future collections. In the Maratha state of the eighteenth century the great commanders were permanently in debt, and the bankers of Pune and other cities were indispensable partners in war (Gordon 1993; Wink 1986). C. A. Bayly has shown how in north India the same commercial families that financed the armies of the successor states later transferred their services to the Company (Bayly 1983). The military labour market was thus also a credit market, and the solvency of an army depended as much on the confidence of bankers as on the skill of its commanders.

When pay failed, soldiers had recognised ways of protesting. They might refuse to march, surround their commander’s tent, hold him or his officials until arrears were paid, or seize the revenues of the district in which they were quartered. Irvine collected many such cases from the Persian histories of the later Mughal period, some involving the most senior nobles of the empire (Irvine 1903). These were not mutinies in the European sense, aimed at overturning authority, but forms of collective bargaining within a system that both sides understood. They became dangerous when a rival offered the soldiers better terms.

docs.title: 17.7 Fitna: Changing Sides as Politics
docs.text:
Indian battles were often decided by defection, and Western observers, from the Portuguese to the British, took this as evidence of treachery or of a lack of national feeling. André Wink has proposed a different reading. Taking the Persian word fitna, “sedition” or “discord”, he argues that in the political culture of the Deccan and of Mughal India the winning over of an opponent’s followers was a normal and expected technique of statecraft, to be preferred to costly battle wherever possible (Wink 1986). Rulers expanded by drawing rival lords and their soldiers into their own service with offers of rank, land and pay; the enemy’s army was a pool of potential employees.

Seen from the soldier’s side, fitna was the political face of the labour market. A commander who brought his contingent over to the winning side, at the right moment, did what his men expected of him: he secured their future employment. A ruler who could not pay could not count on loyalty; one who could pay well could count on attracting soldiers from his enemies. The Arthaśāstra had already treated the winning over of the enemy’s disaffected officers and subjects, by gifts and dissension, as a central method of statecraft (Section 7.2), and the Mughal practice of granting generous terms to those who surrendered followed the same logic (Section 9.4). The decisive defections at Plassey and in the Anglo-Sikh wars (Chapter 19) belong to this pattern, although by then the party offering better terms was the Company.

docs.title: 17.8 Military Entrepreneurs
docs.text:
At the top of the market stood men whose business was war: commanders who raised, paid and led their own forces and hired them to rulers, and who could become rulers themselves. Historians call them military entrepreneurs, borrowing a term from the study of the Thirty Years’ War in Europe, where colonels and generals likewise raised regiments on credit and sold their services to princes. Two careers of the eighteenth century show how such men operated in India.

Muḥammad Khān Bangash (c. 1665–1743) began as the leader of a band of Afghan soldiers who hired themselves to local chiefs in Bundelkhand. He joined the prince Farrukhsiyar in the war of succession of 1712–13, was rewarded with rank, and founded the town of Farrukhabad, named after his patron, as the seat of his family. As a Mughal governor of Allahabad and later of Malwa he fought the Bundelas and the Marathas; in 1729 he was himself besieged at Jaitpur in Bundelkhand, when the Peshwa Bājīrāv I came to the aid of Chhatrasāl. His followers were Afghans of many clans, bound to him by pay and by the shared identity of the Afghan soldier, and his descendants ruled Farrukhabad as nawabs until the Company absorbed their territory. Gommans treats the Bangash state as a characteristic product of the Indo-Afghan world of horse-trading, soldiering and town-founding (Gommans 1995).

Anūpgiri Gosāīn, known by his Mughal title Himmat Bahādur (d. 1804), was the most successful of the armed ascetic commanders whose general history is outlined in Section 13.6. With his brother Umrāogiri he led a force of Nāgā ascetic soldiers, together with cavalry and artillery, which served in turn the Nawab of Awadh Shujāʿ al-Daula, the Mughal court in Delhi, Mahādjī Shinde and the Maratha commanders in Bundelkhand. In 1803, as the Company advanced against the Marathas, he came to terms with the British and helped them take Bundelkhand, receiving lands in return. William Pinch, who reconstructed his career, uses it to show that the ascetic regiments were part of the ordinary military economy of their time, recruited, paid and bargained for like any other troops (Pinch 2006). Bayly has shown that the Gosāīn orders were also important traders and bankers in the cities of the middle Ganges valley, so that the same networks could supply soldiers, credit and goods (Bayly 1983).

Such men were indispensable and dangerous. A ruler who hired them gained an army at once, without the expense of raising it; he also gained a partner with interests of his own, who would make terms with a stronger rival if the balance turned. The Company’s own success in India owed much to its ability to buy such partners, and then to dispense with them once its own armies were sufficient.

docs.title: 17.9.1 Booty and the soldier’s share
docs.text:
Every army plundered, and in many armies plunder was understood as part of the soldier’s reward. Islamic law reserved a fifth of the booty taken in war for the ruler and assigned the rest to the soldiers who took it, and the chronicles of the Delhi sultans and the Mughals record the distribution of horses, cloth, cash and captives after victories; the taking of captives is discussed in Section 12.8. Indian rulers of every tradition allowed their troops to sack a town taken by storm. Plunder was also a way of paying soldiers when the treasury was empty, and armies that could not be paid were set to plunder the enemy’s territory, or anyone’s.

The burden fell on the peasantry, who were also the families from whom soldiers came. A village that supplied men to one army could be sacked by another, or by the same army in a different season. Kolff observes that the line between the soldier and the bandit was thin: the same armed men could be employed, disbanded and turned to raiding within a year, and the same villages could shelter raiders and suffer from them.

docs.title: 17.9.2 The bargī raids in Bengal
docs.text: The raids of the Maratha cavalry of the Bhosales of Nagpur into Bengal in the 1740s show how plunder could become a strategy. Between 1742 and 1751 Maratha forces, at first under the general Bhāskar Paṇḍit, entered western Bengal almost every year to extract tribute from the Nawab ʿAlīvardī Khān, plundering the countryside to force him to pay. ʿAlīvardī had Bhāskar Paṇḍit and his officers killed at a meeting in 1744, but the raids continued until the Nawab ceded the revenue of Orissa and agreed an annual payment in 1751. The raids left a deep mark on Bengali memory (Section 12.9); the poet Gaṅgārām’s Mahārāṣṭra Purāṇa (1751) describes the flight of villagers before the raiders and the cruelties they suffered. The episode shows that the mobile warfare celebrated in Maratha memory as ganimī kāvā (Section 9.16) was experienced very differently by those on whose land it was fought.

docs.title: 17.9.3 The Pindārīs
docs.text:
The Pindārīs were the military labour market in its most extreme form. In the eighteenth century the term described irregular horsemen who accompanied the Maratha armies without pay, living by plunder in enemy territory and giving a share to the chiefs who protected them; there were bands attached to Shinde and to Holkar. After the Company’s victories of 1803–05 broke up the large Maratha armies, many disbanded soldiers joined the Pindārī bands, which grew into large independent forces under leaders such as Cītū, Karīm Khān and Wāṣil Muḥammad. Their raids reached deep into central India and, in 1816, into the Company’s territories on the east coast.

The Company’s campaign against them in 1817–18, which merged with the Third Anglo-Maratha War (Chapter 19), was one of the largest it ever mounted. Its methods are revealing. Armies converged on the Pindārī bases in Malwa from several directions, while political officers negotiated with the leaders. Karīm Khān surrendered and was given land in Gorakhpur; Cītū fled into the jungle and was killed there by a tiger in 1819. Amīr Khān, a Pathan commander whose large army of infantry and artillery had served Holkar and plundered Rajasthan, was recognised as Nawab of Tonk in return for disbanding most of his troops and surrendering his guns, and the state of Tonk survived until 1948. Gordon has argued that the Pindārīs should be understood not simply as robbers but as one end of a spectrum of military entrepreneurship that included the founders of states (Gordon 1994); Amīr Khān’s career, from freebooter to prince, illustrates his point.

docs.title: 17.10.1 Recruiting the Hindustani sepoy
docs.text:
The East India Company entered the market as one employer among many, and it recruited in the same places and in the same ways. Its early Bengal battalions, raised after 1757, included Muslims and Hindus of many castes, recruited partly from soldiers who had served the nawabs. From the 1770s, however, the Bengal army recruited more and more from the high-caste peasantry of Awadh and Bhojpur, the Brahmins and Rajputs whom it came to regard as the ideal soldiers. Seema Alavi has shown that this choice was deliberate. The Company constructed a model of the “Hindustani” sepoy, tall, high-caste and respectable, and made concessions to secure his loyalty: it accommodated his rules of diet and purity, granted pensions and leave, and even used its Resident at the Nawab’s court in Lucknow to press the sepoys’ family claims in the courts of Awadh (Alavi 1995). The sepoy became a man of standing in his village, and service in the Company’s army became the most desirable form of naukarī.

The Madras and Bombay armies recruited more widely, and they were less marked by the high-caste culture of the Bengal regiments. The Madras army of the late eighteenth century drew on Telugu and Tamil peasant communities, on Muslims of the Carnatic and on castes regarded as low, including Paraiyars, many of them Christians; its sepoys lived with their families in the regimental lines and were often accompanied by them on campaign. The Bombay army recruited Marathas and Kuṇbīs from the Konkan and the Deccan, Muslims, Purbiyas, Mahārs — whose part in the defence of Koregaon is described in Section 19.4 — and members of the Bene Israel Jewish community of the Konkan, several of whom rose to be Indian officers. For communities excluded from the dignity of arms by caste, service in these armies offered pay, rank and a measure of social standing, which is why the later exclusion of Mahārs and similar groups from recruitment, as the army reorganised itself in the late nineteenth century around the “martial races” (Section 19.9), was felt as a loss. Mahār leaders petitioned against it in the 1890s, and B. R. Ambedkar, whose father had served as an Indian officer in the Bombay army, later made the Mahārs’ military record part of his case against untouchability (Omissi 1994; Cohen 1971). The differences between the three armies also mattered in 1857, when the Bengal army rose and most of the Madras and Bombay regiments did not.

docs.title: 17.10.2 Pay, batta and the bargain
docs.text:
What distinguished the Company from its rivals was not the kind of soldier it hired but the regularity with which it paid him. Pay was monthly and usually on time; there were pensions for the wounded and for long service; and the families of men killed in service could receive support. The Company’s army thus offered what the older market rarely could: security. In return it demanded continuous service, drill and obedience to rules that the soldier had not negotiated.

Disputes arose where these rules touched pay or caste. The most frequent concerned batta, the extra allowance paid for service in the field or outside the Company’s own territories. When an allowance was withdrawn — as happened when a territory in which troops were serving was annexed and became “home” service — the soldiers saw a breach of the bargain. In 1844, after the annexation of Sindh, several Bengal regiments refused to march there when the Sindh allowance was ended, and one, the 34th Native Infantry, was disbanded. Service overseas, which threatened the caste status of high-caste soldiers, was another source of conflict, from Barrackpore in 1824 to the General Service Enlistment Act of 1856 (Section 19.7). In each case the soldiers’ protest followed the older pattern of collective bargaining; what was new was the Company’s insistence on treating it as mutiny.

docs.title: 17.10.3 The silladar cavalry
docs.text:
In one arm the older market survived inside the Company’s army almost unchanged. The regular cavalry of the Company was expensive, and from the early nineteenth century it relied increasingly on irregular regiments raised on the silāḥdār (in British spelling “silladar”) system, the same system as that of the Maratha śiledār (Section 17.5). The trooper joined with his own horse, or paid for one provided by the regiment, and with his own arms and equipment; he received a higher monthly wage than an infantry sepoy, out of which he maintained horse and kit. A man who could not afford a horse might ride one owned by another (often an officer or a better-off trooper) and share his pay with its owner. The regiments were commanded by a small number of British officers and run in large part by their Indian officers, who often recruited from their own families and districts.

The best-known of these regiments was raised by James Skinner (1778–1841), the son of a Scottish officer and a Rajput mother, who had served in the Maratha brigades until the war of 1803 forced British subjects to leave (Section 18.3). He brought a body of horsemen over to the Company and commanded them for the rest of his life; “Skinner’s Horse”, known from their coats as the Yellow Boys, became a permanent regiment. Skinner himself, who wrote in Persian and built St James’s Church in Delhi, embodied the mixed world of the late eighteenth-century military market. The silladar system lasted in the Indian cavalry until the early twentieth century, long after the infantry had become a fully state-equipped force, and it shows how closely the colonial army remained tied to the institutions of the market it had replaced.

docs.title: 17.10.4 The sepoy’s voice
docs.text: Ordinary soldiers of the Indian armies left few records of their own before the letters of the First World War. The best-known exception is a problem in itself. From Sepoy to Subedar, published in English in 1873 and translated, according to its title page, by Lieutenant-Colonel James Norgate from the Hindi memoirs of a Brahmin named Sītārām Pāṇḍe, describes a career in the Bengal army from 1812 to 1860, including the Pindārī campaign, the Afghan and Sikh wars and the rising of 1857 (Lunt 1970). Its accounts of recruitment, of the village’s pride in a son in the Company’s service, of the dangers of caste pollution and of the growing distance between sepoys and British officers have often been quoted. But no Hindi original has been found, and some historians regard the text as substantially the work of its British editor. It is best read as a mid-Victorian account of what a loyal sepoy was thought to feel, which may preserve genuine experience but cannot be taken as an unmediated voice.

docs.title: 17.11 The Closing of the Market
docs.text:
Kolff ends his account in 1850, and the date is apt. Over the first half of the nineteenth century the Company destroyed the conditions that had sustained the military labour market. It defeated the states that had employed soldiers in large numbers, and imposed treaties that limited the armies of those that survived (Chapter 18); it disbanded the Maratha armies and the Pindārīs; it absorbed some of the disbanded men into local corps and contingents paid for by Indian rulers; and it extended its own revenue and police administration into the countryside, where it began, slowly and incompletely, to disarm the villages. Large numbers of soldiers found employment in the remaining independent army of the Sikh kingdom, which recruited Purbiyas alongside Punjabis, until it too was defeated in 1846–49.

The rising of 1857 was in part the last great act of the market. Its core was the mutiny of the Bengal army, whose sepoys came from the old recruiting grounds of Awadh and Bhojpur; it was joined by the armed retainers of the landholders of Awadh, by disbanded soldiers of the annexed kingdom, and by contingents raised by the Company in the princely states, such as the Gwalior Contingent. Eric Stokes’s study of the rising in the countryside, published after his death under the title The Peasant Armed, showed how the military connections of particular districts shaped their response (Stokes 1986). Rudrangshu Mukherjee has shown how in Awadh the landholders and their followers fought together against the British (Mukherjee 1984). Kunwar Siṅgh, the elderly Ujjainiya chief of Jagdishpur in Bhojpur, who led a long campaign in Bihar and the eastern Ganges valley in 1857–58, was the heir of the lineage whose history Kolff had used to explain the military labour market.

After 1857 the Crown’s army turned away from these recruiting grounds (Section 19.9), and the Arms Act of 1878 (Section 19.12) completed the disarming of the countryside. The men of Bhojpur and Awadh continued to migrate for work, but now to the docks, mills and plantations of the empire rather than to the camps of rival kings.

The market did not vanish entirely; it was channelled. The princely states kept irregular forces, and in Hyderabad Arab and other irregular troops remained part of the Nizam’s establishment into the twentieth century. Armed watchmen and retainers continued to be hired by landholders and merchants. And the empire created new outlets for the old skills. Sikh and Punjabi Muslim men, recruited through the same networks of family and village that had once supplied the misls and the Lahore army, served as police and guards in Hong Kong, Singapore, the Malay states and East Africa from the later nineteenth century, and men from the hills of Nepal served the Company and the Crown as Gurkhas from 1815 onwards (Section 18.9). In this sense the history of Indian soldiering for hire continued well beyond 1857, but within limits set by the colonial state rather than by the competition of many employers that had defined the market at its height.

docs.title: 17.12 Assessment
docs.text:
The military labour market is one of the most important ideas in the modern study of Indian warfare, because it explains so much that older accounts treated as failures of character. Large armies could be raised quickly because the countryside was full of armed men seeking employment. Battles were decided by defection because soldiers and their commanders were contractors whose first concern was their next employer. Armies plundered because they were unpaid, and they were unpaid because the revenue that should have paid them passed through a long chain of assignments and loans. The same features made Indian armies flexible, cheap to raise and dangerous to the states that raised them.

The idea also has limits. It describes Hindustan and the Deccan better than Kerala, Assam or the far south, where service was more often tied to birth or to compulsory obligation (Section 9.12). It can make loyalty seem merely a matter of pay, whereas the sources show soldiers dying for lords, lineages and faiths when it would have been profitable to do otherwise. And it should not be romanticised: the open market in soldiers was also a market in violence, whose costs were borne by peasants in their fields. What it makes clear is that the sepoy of the Company was not a new creation but the latest form of the north Indian naukar, and that the colonial army was built from the labour, skills and expectations of a much older military world.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Kolff (1990): the classic study of the military labour market of Hindustan.

  • Gommans (1995): the Afghan horse-traders, soldiers and states of the eighteenth century.

  • Gordon (1994) and Wink (1986): soldiers, marauders and the politics of the Maratha Deccan.

  • Alavi (1995): the Company’s recruitment and management of the Hindustani sepoy.

  • Stokes (1986) and Mukherjee (1984): the rural dimension of 1857.

docs.title: Chapter 18: Drill, Guns and Treasure: Regular Armies of the Indian States, c. 1740–1849
18.1 Introduction
docs.text:
In the century between the Carnatic wars and the annexation of Punjab, almost every Indian state of any size tried to build an army of a new kind: infantry battalions armed with flintlocks and bayonets, drilled to manoeuvre and fire together, supported by field artillery of standard calibres and paid every month. Chapter 9 has described how the lesson was learned in the Carnatic in the 1740s (Section 9.24) and has noted the debate about an Indian “military revolution” (Section 9.25); Chapter 5 has described the foundries and arsenals (Section 5.16), and Chapter 13 the new discipline of drill (Section 13.10). This chapter looks at the armies themselves, state by state: who built them, who led them, how they were paid, how well they fought, and why most of them were finally defeated or absorbed by the East India Company.

The older view, still common in popular writing, was that Indian rulers failed to modernise, or modernised only superficially, and that their armies collapsed before the disciplined troops of the Company. Recent historians have overturned this picture. Randolf Cooper’s study of the Anglo-Maratha campaigns argues that the Maratha infantry and artillery of 1803 were among the most formidable opponents the British faced anywhere, and that the Company won by controlling the “military economy” of credit, cattle and grain rather than by superior fighting (Cooper 2003). Pradeep Barua and Kaushik Roy have surveyed the adoption of European methods by Indian states and concluded that the transfer was rapid and in many respects successful (Barua 2005; Roy 2011). The question is no longer why Indian states could not build modern armies, but why armies that were in many ways a match for the Company’s could not save the states that built them.

docs.title: 18.2 What Made an Army Regular
docs.text:
The words used at the time show what was new. Indian rulers spoke of “regular” troops in contrast to the older “irregular” forces; the Sikh kingdom called them the fauj-i-āʾīn, the army of rules, as against the fauj-i-be-qawāʿid, the army without regulations. A regular army had five features. Its infantry was organised in permanent battalions (palṭan, a word usually traced to the English “battalion”, though “platoon” has also been proposed) and its cavalry in regiments (risāla), with a fixed establishment of officers and men. Its soldiers wore uniform and carried standard weapons supplied by the state. They were trained in drill, which made it possible to manoeuvre large bodies of men under fire and to deliver volleys. They were paid monthly in cash, directly or through their officers, rather than through the revenue assignments of their commanders. And they were supported by artillery organised in batteries, with trained gunners, draught animals and ammunition supplies.

The vocabulary of the new armies travelled with them. Ranks borrowed from English and French appeared in Indian languages: kumedān for commandant, ajūṭan for adjutant, karnail and jarnail for colonel and general in the Sikh army; words of command were given in English or, in some units, French. The red or blue coat, the cross-belt and the drum became familiar in courts from Lahore to Srirangapatna. These borrowings are sometimes taken as signs of mere imitation. In fact they marked the adoption of a complete system, whose parts depended on one another: drill needed permanent units, permanent units needed regular pay, and regular pay needed a reliable flow of cash.

That last requirement was the hardest to meet. A cavalry army of the older type could be paid by assigning the revenue of districts to its commanders, who collected it themselves and paid their men when they could (Chapter 17). An infantry battalion could not wait. Its men had no horses to sell and no lands to fall back on, and if they were unpaid they would desert or mutiny. Every Indian state that built a regular army therefore faced a fiscal problem, and the way each state solved it — or failed to solve it — shaped its fate.

docs.title: 18.3 Officers from Abroad
docs.text:
Most Indian states hired European officers to raise and train their regular troops. The first wave came from the French: officers and soldiers left without employment when French power in India collapsed after the fall of Pondicherry in 1761, and adventurers who came out in the following decades. The second wave, after 1815, consisted largely of veterans of Napoleon’s armies, for whom peace in Europe meant unemployment. Alongside them served Britons, Irishmen, Germans, Italians and Americans, and a growing number of Eurasians born in India. Herbert Compton’s account of the “military adventurers of Hindustan”, published in 1892 and based on the memoirs and records available to him, remains the starting point for their biographies (Compton 1892). Table 18.1 lists some of the best known.

Table 18.1. Some European officers in the service of Indian states Officer Origin Employer Service and fate Michel Raymond France Nizam of Hyderabad Raised the Nizam’s French-officered corps from the 1780s; died 1798; corps disbanded the same year Benoît de Boigne Savoy Mahādjī Shinde Raised the Shinde brigades from 1784; retired 1795; later settled at Chambéry Pierre Cuillier-Perron France Shinde Commanded the brigades after de Boigne; left Shinde’s service in 1803 Anthony Pohlmann Hanover Shinde Commanded Shinde’s infantry at Assaye, 1803 George Thomas Ireland Begum Samrū; Maratha chiefs Built a short-lived principality at Hansi; defeated by Shinde’s brigades, 1801–02 Jean-François Allard France Ranjit Singh Arrived 1822; raised the cavalry of the Fauj-i-Khāṣ; died at Peshawar, 1839 Jean-Baptiste Ventura Italy Ranjit Singh Arrived 1822; commanded the infantry of the Fauj-i-Khāṣ Claude-Auguste Court France Ranjit Singh From 1827; artillery and foundry work Paolo Avitabile Italy Ranjit Singh From 1827; governor of Wazirabad and later of Peshawar

The value of these men lay less in battlefield command than in organisation: they knew how to raise, train, equip and administer a battalion, and how to establish a foundry or an arsenal. Their weakness was loyalty. They served for pay, and most had no stake in the survival of their employer’s state. The danger became plain in 1803. When war with the Company began, the Governor-General Richard Wellesley issued a proclamation calling on British subjects in Maratha service to leave it, with the promise of pensions; many British and Eurasian officers did so, and Perron himself left Shinde’s service and passed into Company territory early in the campaign. Not all deserted — Pohlmann commanded at Assaye — but the Maratha brigades entered the war with gaps in their command at every level (Cooper 2003; Compton 1892). The lesson was not lost on Ranjit Singh. As the usual terms are reported in the secondary literature, he bound them by written undertakings to serve him faithfully, even in a war with a European power and if need be against their own countrymen, required them to wear beards and to abstain from beef and tobacco, and encouraged them to marry and settle in the Punjab (Lafont 2002).

It is easy to exaggerate the role of these Europeans. They were few — a few dozen at most in any one army — and the soldiers, the junior officers and most of the gunners and craftsmen were Indian. Indian commanders such as Ilāhī Bakhsh, who led the Sikh artillery, or the Maratha officers of the Shinde brigades, learned the new methods and commanded with them. By the 1830s the Sikh regular army was largely officered by Punjabis.

docs.title: 18.4 Bengal and Awadh after Plassey
docs.text:
The first Indian rulers to attempt a regular army in direct response to the Company were the nawabs of the east, who had seen its effects at close quarters. Mīr Qāsim, whom the Company made Nawab of Bengal in 1760, moved his capital from Murshidabad up the Ganges to Monghyr in Bihar, further from Calcutta, and set about building an army that could stand against the Company’s sepoys. He raised infantry battalions drilled in the European manner, under an Armenian commander, Gurgīn Khān, and a number of European adventurers, among them the German Walter Reinhardt, known as Sombre, later the husband of Begum Samrū (Section 16.9); and he established workshops at Monghyr that made flintlock muskets and cast guns, whose quality British observers acknowledged. He also tried to put his finances in order, which brought him into conflict with the Company’s servants, who were trading in Bengal free of the duties that Indian merchants paid.

War broke out in 1763. Mīr Qāsim’s new army was defeated in a series of engagements in Bengal, at Katwa, Giria and Udhua Nala, and retreated into Bihar; Gurgīn Khān was murdered in his own camp, and at Patna Reinhardt, on the Nawab’s orders, killed the British prisoners held there. Mīr Qāsim fled to Awadh, and his forces joined those of the Nawab of Awadh and the Mughal emperor in the campaign that ended at Buxar in 1764 (Section 19.3). The experiment had lasted barely three years. It showed that battalions could be raised and equipped quickly, but also that a few years of drill could not create the cohesion, the officers and the confidence of a long-established force.

Shujāʿ al-Daula of Awadh (r. 1754–1775), defeated at Buxar, kept his throne by the treaty of Allahabad in 1765 and spent the following decade rebuilding his army at his new capital of Faizabad. He raised battalions of regular infantry, enlarged his artillery and employed French officers, among them Jean-Baptiste Gentil, alongside Gosāīn and Afghan contingents (Section 17.8). The Company watched this growth with suspicion, and a treaty of 1768 limited the size of the Nawab’s forces. With these troops, and a Company brigade, Shujāʿ al-Daula conquered Rohilkhand in 1774 (Section 17.4). After his death the Company pressed his successors to reduce their own armies and to pay for Company troops instead, the pattern that Wellesley later made general (Section 18.7).

docs.title: 18.5 Mysore under Haidar and Tipu
docs.text:
Haidar ʿAlī (c. 1720–1782) learned the value of European methods early. As a commander in the service of the Mysore state in the 1750s, stationed at Dindigul, he set up an arsenal with the help of French specialists and began to train infantry on the European model. After he took power in 1761 he built an army that combined the fast-moving cavalry traditional in the Deccan with growing numbers of disciplined infantry and a powerful artillery. In the First Anglo-Mysore War his cavalry ravaged the country around Madras, and in 1769 he dictated terms almost at its gates. In the Second, in September 1780, his army and that of his son Tipu surrounded and destroyed a Company column under William Baillie at Pollilur, near Kanchipuram, as it marched to join the main army; under the fire of the Mysore guns and rockets the column’s ammunition carts exploded and its square broke, and Baillie and the survivors were taken prisoner to Srirangapatna. It was one of the heaviest defeats the Company suffered in India (Figure 19.2).

Tipu Sultan (r. 1782–1799) carried the reform further. He organised his infantry into brigades (kushūn), each with its own artillery; gave his officers Persian titles of his own devising; issued detailed regulations for the army, of which a Persian manual, the Fatḥ al-Mujāhidīn, compiled at his order by his secretary Zayn al-ʿĀbidīn Shūshtarī and usually dated 1783, is the best known; and kept close personal control of appointments, supplies and discipline, as his surviving letters show (Kirkpatrick 1811). Srirangapatna became a centre of arms production, with foundries for guns, workshops for muskets and the iron-cased rockets that made Mysore famous (Section 5.18). Tipu sent embassies to the Ottoman sultan and to Louis XVI of France in the later 1780s, and corresponded with the French Republic, seeking officers, craftsmen and an alliance against the British.

The tiger was the emblem of this army. Tiger stripes (babrī) decorated uniforms, weapons and cannon, tiger heads formed the finials of his throne, and the mechanical organ known as “Tipu’s Tiger”, which shows a tiger mauling a European soldier and is now in the Victoria and Albert Museum in London (Figure 18.1), became the most famous object taken from Srirangapatna. Kate Brittlebank has shown that Tipu’s use of the tiger, and of a range of Islamic and local Hindu symbols, was part of a deliberate effort to establish the legitimacy of a new dynasty in a kingdom whose old ruling house he had displaced (Brittlebank 1997).

Figure 18.1. “Tipu’s Tiger”: a painted wooden tiger mauling a European soldier, made for Tipu Sultan in the 1790s, with an organ inside its body worked by a handle in its flank (Victoria and Albert Museum, London). Photo: Sourabh.biswas003, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (cropped)

The Mysore army fought well, but its state was outmatched. In the Third Anglo-Mysore War (1790–92) the Company, under the Governor-General Lord Cornwallis in person, allied with the Marathas and the Nizam, took Bangalore and advanced on Srirangapatna; Tipu made peace in 1792 by surrendering half his territory, paying a large indemnity and handing over two of his sons as hostages. In 1799 the Company, now free of the French threat in Hyderabad (Section 18.7), invaded again and stormed Srirangapatna, where Tipu was killed. His army had been reduced by the loss of territory and revenue in 1792; his search for French help had given Wellesley the pretext he sought; and his neighbours had joined his enemies. The fate of Mysore illustrates the general point of this chapter: an army could be modern and still be defeated by the diplomacy and finance of a stronger state.

docs.title: 18.6 The Maratha Brigades
docs.text:
The Marathas’ first experience of regular infantry came a generation before the Shinde brigades.
