Ibrāhīm Khān Gārdī, a Muslim commander who had learned the new methods in the French service in the Deccan under the Marquis de Bussy — the name gārdī is usually derived from the French garde — served the Nizam and then, from about 1760, the Peshwa, bringing with him battalions of musketeers and a train of artillery. At the third battle of Pānīpat in January 1761 his battalions, on the Maratha left, attacked the Rohilla contingent of the Afghan army and inflicted heavy losses before the collapse of the Maratha centre decided the day; he was captured and put to death after the battle (Gordon 1993). Gommans has pointed out that the Afghan victory owed much to its own mixture of heavy cavalry, camel-mounted swivel guns and an efficient supply system, which kept the Afghan army fed while the Maratha camp starved (Gommans 1995). Pānīpat thus showed both the promise of regular infantry and its dependence on the army around it.

The most powerful regular army built by an Indian state in the eighteenth century was that of the Shinde (Scindia) family of Gwalior. Mahādjī Shinde (d. 1794), who had survived the third battle of Pānīpat and rebuilt Maratha power in the north, engaged Benoît de Boigne in 1784 to raise two battalions of regular infantry. The force grew over the following decade into several brigades, each of infantry battalions with artillery and some cavalry, known in the Persianised military vocabulary of the north as kampū, a word usually derived from the Portuguese campo (“camp”), though a borrowing from the English “camp” or “company” has also been suggested (Compton 1892).

The brigades proved themselves in the wars of the north. At Lalsot in 1787, when Mahādjī’s army faced the combined forces of the Rajput kingdoms of Jaipur and Jodhpur and many of his own Mughal troops went over to the enemy, de Boigne’s battalions held their ground, though Mahādjī was forced to withdraw. In 1790 the brigades won decisive victories at Patan and Merta in Rajasthan against the Mughal noble Ismāʿīl Beg and the Rathors of Jodhpur, and in 1793 at Lakheri they defeated the army of the rival Maratha house of Holkar, whose own regular battalions were commanded by the French officer Dudrenec. These battles established the Shinde brigades as the strongest force in north India and made Mahādjī the protector of the Mughal emperor in Delhi.

The brigades were paid in an unusual way. Instead of drawing on the Maratha treasury, they were assigned the revenue of a block of districts in the Ganges–Yamuna Doab around Aligarh (a jaidād, or assignment for the support of troops), which de Boigne and later Perron administered directly. Pay was therefore regular, and the brigades were well equipped. But the arrangement turned the commander into a territorial ruler with his own revenues, fort and court at Aligarh, and his own interests. To the British, Perron’s position looked like the beginning of a French state in Hindustan, and this fear was one of the reasons Wellesley gave for war in 1803.

The campaign of 1803 showed both the quality of the brigades and the weakness of their political foundations. In the north, Gerard Lake stormed the fort of Aligarh, the brigades’ headquarters, on 4 September and defeated the remaining northern forces near Delhi and at Laswari; in the Deccan, Arthur Wellesley defeated Shinde and the Bhosale ruler of Nagpur at Assaye and Argaon (Section 19.4). British officers who fought at Assaye and Laswari wrote of the steadiness of the Maratha infantry and the accuracy of their gunners, and the casualty lists bear them out. Cooper argues that the brigades lost not because they fought badly but because the Company had already bought, through its proclamation and its agents, much of their officer corps; because their commanders could not agree on a common plan; and because the Company’s control of credit, grain and draught cattle in the Deccan allowed its armies to move and fight while the Marathas could not concentrate (Cooper 2003).

Yashwantrāv Holkar, who had stood aside in 1803, fought the Company in 1804–05 and showed what a mixed army of cavalry and regular infantry could still achieve. In 1804 his forces drove a Company column under Colonel Monson into a disastrous retreat through central India, and in early 1805 Lake’s army failed in four assaults on the mud fortress of Bharatpur, defended by its Jat ruler in alliance with Holkar (Section 9.18). The Company made peace with Holkar on relatively generous terms.

The last Maratha armies took the field in 1817–18, when the Peshwa Bājīrāv II, the Bhosale ruler of Nagpur and the Holkar court rose, separately and without a common plan, against the Company during its campaign against the Pindārīs (Section 17.9). The Peshwa’s army was defeated at Khadki outside Pune in November 1817 (Section 19.4). At Sitabuldi, outside Nagpur, later the same month, the Bhosale’s troops, among whom Arab soldiers fought with particular determination, attacked the Company’s small force on the hill above the Residency and were driven off only after two days of fighting. At Mahidpur in December 1817 the Holkar army, whose artillery was served with great skill, was defeated after a hard battle. The Peshwa’s best commander, Bāpū Gokhale, was killed in a cavalry action at Ashti in February 1818, and the Peshwa surrendered in June. The fortress of Asirgarh, whose garrison held out into 1819, was the last Maratha stronghold to fall. These battles show that the Maratha courts still commanded brave and skilful soldiers; what they lacked after 1803 was the money, the allies and the political unity to use them together.

The Shinde army survived the defeat of 1803 in reduced form. In December 1843, after a succession dispute at Gwalior, a Company army fought the Gwalior troops at Maharajpur and Panniar on the same day, 29 December, and defeated them after hard fighting. The Gwalior army was then reduced, and a “Gwalior Contingent” under British officers, paid by the state, was raised in its place; in 1857 that contingent joined the rising (Section 17.11).

docs.title: 18.7 Hyderabad, Awadh and the Subsidiary System
docs.text:
In Hyderabad the Nizam built his regular infantry around the French corps raised by Michel Raymond from the 1780s. By the 1790s it was the largest and best-trained part of the Nizam’s army, with its own arsenal and foundry, and it gave Hyderabad an independent military capacity that the Company regarded as a threat, the more so because its officers were French at a time when Britain and France were at war. Raymond died in 1798. In the same year the new Governor-General, Richard Wellesley, concluded a treaty with the Nizam under which the Company enlarged the force it stationed in Hyderabad and the French corps was disbanded; Company troops surrounded the corps’ camp, and its officers were sent to Europe as prisoners.

The treaty was an example of the subsidiary alliance, which Wellesley turned into the principal instrument of Company expansion. Its terms were broadly the same everywhere. The Indian ruler accepted a permanent force of Company troops in his territory and paid for it, first in cash and, when he could not pay, by ceding territory; he dismissed Europeans of other nations from his service; and he conducted his foreign relations through the Company. In 1800 the Nizam ceded the districts south of the Tungabhadra that became known as the Ceded Districts to pay for his subsidiary force. In 1801 the Nawab of Awadh, under pressure, ceded about half of his kingdom, including Rohilkhand and the lower Doab, to meet the cost of the Company troops stationed there, and agreed to reduce his own army. The Peshwa accepted a subsidiary alliance in 1802, the event that led to the war of 1803.

The subsidiary system was a means of disarmament as well as of expansion. It transferred the military power of Indian states to Company battalions paid with Indian money, and it required those states to cut their own forces. In Hyderabad, a further force, raised from 1813 under British officers and paid by the Nizam, became the Hyderabad Contingent; its cost led in 1853 to the assignment of the revenues of Berar to the Company. The soldiers dismissed from the armies of subsidiary states did not disappear. They joined the Pindārī bands, the armies of states still independent, or the turbulent retinues of local chiefs (Section 17.9), and the problem of the “unemployed soldiery” became one of the Company’s arguments for further annexation.

The burden of the subsidy could provoke armed resistance. Travancore, whose army had been reformed by Mārtāṇḍa Varma (Section 9.21), accepted a subsidiary treaty in 1805. The payments it required fell heavily on a state already burdened by debt, and the Company pressed for the reduction of Travancore’s own troops, whose allowances had already been cut. In 1808 the Dalawa (chief minister) Vēlu Tampi, who had himself negotiated the treaty, rose against the Company together with the minister of Cochin. His forces attacked the British Resident’s house at Cochin, and in January 1809 he issued a proclamation at Kundara calling on the people to resist. Company troops defeated the Travancore forces within a few months, and Vēlu Tampi took his own life to avoid capture; the British exposed his body in public. Travancore’s army was then largely disbanded, leaving only a small Nāyar brigade, and the state remained a subsidiary ally until 1947. In neighbouring Malabar, Kēraḷa Varma, the Pazhassi Rājā, had already fought a long forest war against the Company from the hills of Wayanad until his death in 1805; together, the two risings marked the end of independent armed power in Kerala.

docs.title: 18.8 The Army of the Sikh Kingdom
docs.text:
Ranjit Singh (r. 1799–1839) inherited an army of misl cavalry, brave and mobile but loyal to its own chiefs (Section 9.20). From the first decade of the nineteenth century he began to build regular infantry on the Company’s model. His first drill instructors were deserters from the Company’s sepoy regiments, and his early battalions were recruited largely from Purbiyas, Gurkhas and Punjabi Muslims, because Sikh horsemen at first regarded fighting on foot as beneath them. Over the following decades, helped by regular pay and by the prestige of the new battalions, Sikhs came to form the majority of the infantry (Grewal 1990; Bajwa 1964). The Nepali word lāhure, later applied to Gurkhas in British and Indian service, is usually derived from the name of Lahore, where Nepali soldiers served in Ranjit Singh’s army.

The arrival of the French and Italian officers Allard and Ventura in 1822, and of Court and Avitabile a few years later, gave the regular army its most famous unit, the Fauj-i-Khāṣ or “special army”, a brigade of infantry, cavalry and artillery trained on French lines, carrying its own standards and said to have used French words of command (Lafont 2002). Its officers’ careers have attracted much attention, but the army’s development was directed by the Maharaja himself, who attended parades, inspected recruits and horses, and followed the details of pay and equipment closely. The administrative records of the Lahore court, which survive in large numbers and were catalogued in the early twentieth century by Sita Ram Kohli, include muster rolls, pay accounts and orders that allow historians to reconstruct the army’s growth in unusual detail; Fauja Singh Bajwa’s study of the military system is based on them (Bajwa 1964). Beside the regular army the kingdom kept the irregular horse (ghoṛcaṛhā) of the Sikh landed families and the old misl contingents (Section 17.4), and the Akālīs, who acknowledged no commander but the Panth (Section 15.9); its soldiers included Hindus, Muslims and Gurkhas as well as Sikhs.

The artillery was the arm that most impressed the army’s opponents. The Lahore foundries cast guns of several calibres (Section 5.16), and the artillery was organised in batteries of foot, horse and camel guns. Its commander for much of the period, Ilāhī Bakhsh, was a Punjabi Muslim who had risen in the Maharaja’s service. In the Anglo-Sikh wars the Sikh gunners served their guns to the last at Ferozeshah and Sobraon (Section 19.4).

The regular army made possible the expansion of the kingdom beyond the plains of Punjab. Multan was taken in 1818 after a hard siege, Kashmir in 1819, and the trans-Indus territories in a series of campaigns against Afghan and tribal forces. At Nowshera in 1823 the Sikh army defeated a large Afghan and tribal force, in a battle in which the irregular Akālīs fought beside the new battalions (Section 15.9). Peshawar was annexed in 1834, and in 1837 the Sikh commander Harī Siṅgh Nalwā was killed defending the new fort at Jamrud at the mouth of the Khyber Pass against an Afghan attack. The north-western frontier that the British inherited in 1849 was, in large part, the frontier the Sikh army had won.

The regular army’s dependence on regular pay was its weakness after Ranjit Singh’s death. As the court at Lahore fell into a sequence of murders and short reigns, pay fell into arrears and the regiments formed elected committees (pañc) that negotiated with, and soon dominated, the court. The crossing of the Sutlej in December 1845, which began the First Anglo-Sikh War, owed something to the wish of court factions to turn an army they could neither pay nor control against the British. The army that fought at Ferozeshah, Sobraon and Chillianwala was as good as any the Company had faced; it was let down by commanders, some of whom were in contact with the enemy, and by a state that had lost its centre.

docs.title: 18.9 Armies of the Himalaya
docs.text: Two mountain states built regular armies in this period and used them in campaigns that took Indian soldiers into the high Himalaya and Tibet: the Gorkha kingdom of Nepal and the Dogra state of Jammu.

docs.title: 18.9.1 The Gorkha state
docs.text:
Pṛthvī Nārāyaṇ Śāh (r. 1743–1775), king of the small hill state of Gorkha, spent a quarter of a century conquering the Kathmandu valley, whose three Newar kingdoms fell in 1768–69. An expedition sent by the East India Company in 1767 to help the king of Kathmandu was turned back in the foothills. Pṛthvī Nārāyaṇ’s army was organised in companies on the Company’s model, with firearms, uniforms and drill, recruited from the hill peoples of his kingdom — Khas, Magar, Gurung and others — and paid by assignments of land. His advice to his successors, preserved as the Divya Upadeśa, describes the kingdom as a yam between two boulders, China and the Company, and recommends caution in dealing with both (Stiller 1973).

His successors carried Gorkha arms west along the Himalaya, taking Kumaon in 1790 and Garhwal in 1804 and besieging the Kangra fort of the Katoch ruler Saṃsār Cand from 1806 until Ranjit Singh’s intervention forced them back across the Sutlej in 1809. To the north, a dispute with Tibet over trade and coinage led to wars in 1788–92. After Gorkha troops plundered the monastery of Tashilhunpo at Shigatse in 1791, the Qing emperor sent an army that advanced across the Himalaya to within a short distance of Kathmandu in 1792; Nepal made peace and agreed to send missions to Beijing every five years.

docs.title: 18.9.2 The Anglo-Nepal war
docs.text:
Expansion along the foothills brought Nepal into conflict with the Company, and the war of 1814–16 was one of the hardest the Company fought in India (Pemble 1971). The Gorkha forces held stockaded hill forts in difficult terrain. At Kalunga (Nalapani), near Dehra Dun, a small garrison under Balbhadra Kũvar repulsed two assaults in October and November 1814 — the Company’s general, Rollo Gillespie, was killed in the first — before abandoning the fort; the British later erected two memorials on the site, one to their own dead and one in tribute to their opponents. In the west, David Ochterlony manoeuvred the veteran commander Amar Siṅgh Thāpā out of a chain of ridge-top forts around Malaun, and Amar Siṅgh surrendered in May 1815. A treaty was signed at Sugauli in December 1815; when the Nepalese court hesitated to ratify it, Ochterlony advanced towards the Kathmandu valley in 1816, and Nepal accepted the treaty, ceding Kumaon, Garhwal and much of the Tarai.

The war had a long sequel. Even before it ended, the Company began to enlist Gorkha soldiers taken prisoner or released after the surrender at Malaun, forming the first battalions of what became the Gurkha regiments of the Indian and British armies (Section 19.5). In Nepal, the minister Bhīmsen Thāpā, who dominated the court from 1806 to 1837, maintained and enlarged the army after the defeat; it remained the basis of the state’s power and, through the “Gurkha” connection, a source of employment for hill men in foreign service that continues today. In 1857–58 Jaṅg Bahādur Rāṇā, who had seized power in Nepal in 1846, led a Nepalese army to help the British recover Awadh, and was rewarded with the return of part of the western Tarai lost at Sugauli.

docs.title: 18.9.3 The Dogras in Ladakh and Tibet
docs.text:
The Dogra Rajput Gulāb Siṅgh, made Raja of Jammu by Ranjit Singh in 1822, built a state of his own on the northern edge of the Sikh kingdom. His general Zorāwar Siṅgh led a series of campaigns that are among the most remarkable in Indian military history. Between 1834 and 1840 his small armies crossed the high passes from Kishtwar into Ladakh, defeated the Ladakhi forces and brought the kingdom under Dogra control; in 1840 he conquered Baltistan, taking the fort of Skardu. In 1841 he invaded western Tibet, taking Rudok and Gartok and advancing to Taklakot near Lake Mānasarovar. As winter set in, his army, far from its bases and short of supplies, was attacked by Tibetan forces reinforced from Lhasa; Zorāwar Siṅgh was killed in battle in December 1841, and most of his army died in the fighting or of cold. Tibetan forces then advanced into Ladakh, but were driven back, and a treaty agreed at Chushul in 1842 restored the old frontier and the trade between Ladakh and Tibet (Datta 1973).

These campaigns were fought at altitudes of four thousand metres and more, in conditions that tested every arm. Supplies were carried by porters and pack animals over passes closed for months by snow; firearms and artillery had to be light enough to carry; and cold killed more men than battle. The Dogra soldiers were recruited from the hill peoples of Jammu and the neighbouring states, and their officers combined the methods of the Sikh regular army with long experience of mountain warfare. After the First Anglo-Sikh War, by the Treaty of Amritsar of 1846, the British recognised Gulāb Siṅgh as ruler of Jammu and Kashmir in return for a payment of seventy-five lakh rupees, and the Dogra army became the army of the princely state of Jammu and Kashmir.

docs.title: 18.10 Camps That Became Cities
docs.text:
Regular armies needed permanent quarters, and their camps left a lasting mark on the map of India. The older armies had lived in moving camps (Section 9.6); a regular battalion, with its parade ground, magazine, hospital, lines for the men and their families, and bazaar, was better kept in one place. The clearest Indian example is Gwalior. In 1810 Daulatrāv Shinde fixed his permanent camp below the fort of Gwalior, and the settlement that grew up around it is still called Lashkar, from the Persian word for an army or camp; it became the capital of the Shinde state and the core of the modern city.

The Company’s own cantonments, laid out in the decades after 1760, became the largest of these military towns: Barrackpore near Calcutta, Kanpur and Meerut in the Ganges plain, Secunderabad beside Hyderabad, where the subsidiary force was stationed from the early 1800s and which was named after the Nizam Sikandar Jāh, and Bangalore in Mysore. Each had its grid of barracks and bungalows, its parade ground, and a sadar bāzār that supplied the troops and soon housed a population of traders, artisans, servants and soldiers’ families many times larger than the garrison. Douglas Peers has described the colonial state of this period as a “garrison state” (Section 19.3); the cantonments were its physical form. Mhow in central India, founded by John Malcolm after the battle of Mahidpur in 1818 and later the birthplace of B. R. Ambedkar, is a typical example. The popular explanation of its name as an acronym for “Military Headquarters of War” is a modern invention; the name belonged to the village beside which the cantonment was built.

The Sikh kingdom too kept its regular army in fixed cantonments around Lahore, and the British, after annexing the Punjab, built their own at Mian Mir nearby. The cantonments of the regular armies, Indian and British, thus formed a new kind of settlement, at once military camp, market town and enclave of a distinctive mixed society, and many of them remain military stations today.

docs.title: 18.11 An Army of the Older Kind: Sindh, 1843
docs.text:
Not every state built a regular army, and the fate of one that did not shows by contrast what the new armies offered. Sindh was ruled from the 1780s by the Talpur Mīrs, a Baluch family that had overthrown the previous dynasty, the Kalhoras. The Mīrs divided the country among branches of the family at Hyderabad, Khairpur and Mirpur, and their military power rested on the Baluch tribes settled in Sindh, whose chiefs brought out their followers when called. These were brave and well-armed fighters, with matchlocks, swords and shields, supported by some artillery, but they had no permanent units, no drill and no regular pay.

The Company forced treaties on the Mīrs in 1838–39 to secure the passage of its armies to Afghanistan, and in 1843 its commander in Sindh, Charles Napier, provoked a war that ended in annexation. At Miani, on 17 February 1843, Napier’s small army of British and Bombay sepoy troops attacked a much larger Baluch force drawn up behind the high bank of a dry river bed. The Baluch fought hand to hand with sword and shield for several hours and suffered very heavy losses before they broke; a second battle at Dubba, near Hyderabad, in March completed the conquest. The story that Napier announced his victory with the one-word Latin pun peccavi (“I have sinned”, that is, “I have Sindh”) is a joke first published in the London magazine Punch, not a message he sent. The annexation was criticised at the time, even in Britain, as an unprovoked aggression; militarily, Miani showed how far the gap had opened between an army of the older kind and a regular force with drilled infantry and field artillery.

docs.title: 18.12 Paying for Regular Armies
docs.text:
The histories reviewed in this chapter all turn, in the end, on money. Regular infantry and artillery were more effective than the cavalry armies they replaced, but they were also more expensive, and their costs had to be met every month. Historians call the resulting competition among eighteenth-century states, each forced to extract more revenue to pay for larger and costlier armies, “military fiscalism” (Roy 2011); it drew rulers into dependence on bankers and revenue farmers, and armies whose pay fell into arrears mutinied, plundered or deserted (Sections 9.26 and 17.6). Indian states met these costs in different ways, each with its own risks.

The Shinde solution, the assignment of a block of territory to the commander of the brigades, secured regular pay at the cost of creating a semi-independent power within the state. Mysore under Tipu centralised revenue collection, took over trade in valuable commodities and kept tight control of expenditure, which gave the state a strong army but made enemies among the landholders and merchants whose income it squeezed. The Sikh kingdom paid its army from the revenues of a rich province and the tribute of its dependencies, and did so successfully while Ranjit Singh lived; after his death the arrears that accumulated turned the army into a political force. Hyderabad and Awadh, under subsidiary alliances, paid for an army that was not their own.

The Company was the most successful practitioner of military fiscalism, and its advantages went beyond the revenues of Bengal. It could borrow in India and in London at lower rates than any Indian ruler; Indian bankers increasingly preferred it as a debtor, because it was more likely to pay; and its commissariat could buy grain and hire draught cattle, often through the same Banjārā carriers who supplied Indian armies (Section 6.9), on a scale and with a reliability that its opponents could not match. Cooper’s phrase for what was at stake, the “military economy” of South Asia, captures the point: the wars of 1790–1849 were contests for control of the credit, animals, grain and soldiers of the subcontinent, and the Company won that contest before it won the battles (Cooper 2003).

docs.title: 18.13 Assessment
docs.text:
The regular armies of the Indian states were not failures. Within two generations Indian rulers raised infantry and artillery that destroyed a Company force at Pollilur, repulsed it at Bharatpur, made it pay heavily for its victories at Assaye, Laswari, Ferozeshah and Chillianwala, and won wars against other Indian powers and in the Himalaya. They adopted European methods selectively and quickly, as Indian armies had earlier adopted the horse-archer and the gun, and Indian soldiers, gunners and officers learned to use them well.

What the regular army changed was the relationship between the soldier and the state. The older armies of the labour market could be raised quickly and dissolved cheaply; the new ones were permanent, expensive and dependent on a steady flow of cash. They strengthened the states that could pay for them and endangered those that could not. They made Indian rulers dependent on foreign officers whose loyalty was conditional, and they offered the Company, through the subsidiary system, a means of taking control of Indian armies without fighting them. When the Company finally prevailed, it did not abolish the regular armies of India but took them over: the Gurkha battalions, the Sikh regiments raised after 1849, the Hyderabad and Gwalior contingents and the forces of the princely states became parts of the colonial military order described in Chapter 19.

  • Barua (2005) and Roy (2011): surveys of military change in South Asia.

docs.title: Chapter 19: Conquest, Sepoys and Disarmament: The Colonial Era
19.1 Introduction
docs.text:
Between the 1740s and the 1850s the English East India Company, a trading corporation, conquered most of the Indian subcontinent. It did so with armies composed overwhelmingly of Indian soldiers — the sepoys (from Persian sipāhī, soldier) — recruited from the same military labour market that had supplied the Mughals and their successors, drilled and officered in the European manner, and paid regularly from the revenues of the territories the Company acquired. After the great rising of 1857, the British Crown took over the Company’s territories and its armies, reorganised recruitment around the idea of “martial races”, and disarmed Indian society through the Arms Act of 1878. The Indian Army of the colonial state fought across the world in two world wars, and its officer corps was slowly Indianised before independence in 1947.

This chapter outlines that history, which ended the independent military traditions described in earlier chapters and shaped the modern armies of South Asia. It draws on the work of Seema Alavi, Douglas Peers, Kaushik Roy, Heather Streets, David Omissi and C. A. Bayly (Alavi 1995; Peers 1995; Roy 2011; Streets 2004; Omissi 1994; Bayly 1996).

docs.title: 19.2 The European Companies and the Sepoy
docs.text:
The Portuguese, Dutch, English and French trading companies that arrived in India in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries maintained small garrisons of European soldiers and hired Indian guards and auxiliaries. The decisive innovation came in the Carnatic wars of the 1740s and 1750s (Section 9.24), when the French governor Dupleix and the English commanders found that locally recruited Indian infantry, drilled in the European manner and led by European officers, could defeat much larger Indian armies built around cavalry. Both companies raised such units, and by the 1750s the English Company’s settlements at Madras, Calcutta and Bombay each had an army of sepoys (Roy 2011).

The sepoys were not a new kind of soldier socially. They were recruited from the peasant communities that had long supplied soldiers to Indian rulers — in the case of the Bengal army, largely from the high-caste peasants (Brahmins and Rajputs) of Awadh and Bihar, the “eastern” (pūrbiyā) soldiers of the north Indian military labour market (Chapter 17) (Kolff 1990). What was new was the regularity of their pay, their uniform drill and discipline, and the permanence of their units. Seema Alavi has shown how the Company, to secure the loyalty of these soldiers, accommodated their caste and religious practices, granted them pensions and privileges, and created a distinctive “sepoy” culture that combined Indian and European elements (Alavi 1995).

docs.title: 19.3.1 Bengal: Plassey and Buxar
docs.text:
The Company’s political power began in Bengal. In 1757 Robert Clive, with an army of about three thousand men, two-thirds of them sepoys, defeated the Nawab Sirāj al-Daula at Plassey (Palāśī). The battle was decided less by fighting than by the defection of the Nawab’s commander Mīr Jaʿfar, whom the Company had promised to make Nawab (Figure 19.1). The real military test came in 1764 at Buxar, where the Company defeated the combined armies of Mīr Qāsim, the deposed Nawab of Bengal, Shujāʿ al-Daula of Awadh and the Mughal emperor Shāh ʿĀlam II. In 1765 the emperor granted the Company the dīwānī, the right to collect the revenues of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa. With these revenues the Company could pay large armies (Roy 2011).

Figure 19.1. Robert Clive meeting Mīr Jaʿfar after the battle of Plassey, 1757: oil painting by Francis Hayman, c. 1760 (National Portrait Gallery, London). Painted for display in London, it shows the alliance on which the victory rested rather than the battle itself. Image: Francis Hayman (National Portrait Gallery, London), public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 19.3.2 Mysore, the Marathas and the Sikhs
docs.text:
The Company’s other wars were harder. Haidar Ali and Tipu Sultan of Mysore fought four wars against it between 1767 and 1799, and the Maratha powers three: in the first (1775–1782) they held their own; in the second (1803–1805) they were defeated at Assaye and Laswari; in the third (1817–1818) the Company destroyed the Pindari bands and the remaining Maratha powers, and the Peshwa’s territories were annexed (Gordon 1993). The last great independent Indian army, that of the Sikh kingdom of Punjab, was defeated in the two Anglo-Sikh wars of 1845–46 and 1848–49, and Punjab was annexed in 1849. The armies that the Company met in these wars are described in Chapter 18, and the most important battles in Section 19.4; Figure 19.2 shows where they were fought.

Figure 19.2. Some battles and sieges of the East India Company’s wars in South Asia, 1746–1849, discussed in Chapters 9, 18 and 19, plotted by latitude and longitude. One marker serves for the three battles of 1845–46 on the Sutlej, and one for Chillianwala and Gujrat; the positions of these markers and of Laswari, Malaun, Kalunga, Miani, Pollilur and Assaye are approximate. The frame is that of the map in Volume 12, extended northward to 35\(^\circ\)N; the coastline is simplified, islands other than Sri Lanka are omitted, and no rivers or political boundaries are shown.

docs.title: 19.3.3 Why did the Company win?
docs.text:
Historians have offered several explanations for the Company’s success, and most would combine them (Roy 2011; Peers 1995; Bayly 1996):

  • Finance. The Company could pay its soldiers regularly from the land revenues of Bengal and other territories, and borrow from Indian bankers and in London; Indian states, whose revenues were often assigned to commanders and nobles, struggled to pay their armies (Section 18.12).

  • Discipline and organisation. The Company’s infantry and artillery were trained and organised for sustained, coordinated action, and its officers formed a cohesive corps.

  • Sea power. The Company could move troops and supplies by sea and could not be cut off from Britain.

  • Alliances and divisions. The Company exploited rivalries among Indian rulers, made subsidiary alliances in which Indian states paid for Company troops stationed in their territories, and benefited from succession disputes and defections.

  • Information. The Company built up intelligence networks, often taking over those of Indian states (Bayly 1996).

The older claim that Indian armies were simply technologically backward does not survive scrutiny: Indian states had excellent artillery, they raised European-style infantry, and they employed European officers (Chapter 18). The difference lay in the institutions that sustained armies over long wars. Douglas Peers has described the resulting colonial state as a “garrison state”, in which military needs dominated government and revenue (Peers 1995).

docs.title: 19.4 The Great Battles of the Conquest
docs.text: The Company’s conquest of India was not a series of easy victories. Several of its battles were close-run, and some were defeats. A few are worth describing in more detail, because they show both the strengths of the Company’s armies and the capacity of Indian armies to resist them.

docs.title: 19.4.1 Assaye, 1803
docs.text: In the Second Anglo-Maratha War, Major-General Arthur Wellesley, later Duke of Wellington, found the combined armies of Daulatrāv Shinde and the Bhosale ruler of Nagpur encamped at Assaye in the Deccan on 23 September 1803. His own force was much smaller — by his own account fewer than ten thousand men, many of them sepoys — facing an army several times larger, with a strong artillery and infantry battalions trained by European officers in Shinde’s service. Wellesley crossed the river Kaitna at an unguarded ford and attacked. The Maratha infantry and gunners fought well, changing front to meet the attack, and their artillery inflicted heavy casualties; but the Maratha army was defeated after hard fighting, and its guns were captured. The Company’s losses were very heavy for so small a force. Later the same year Gerard Lake defeated Shinde’s northern army at Laswari, where the Maratha infantry again fought with great determination (Gordon 1993; Roy 2011; Cooper 2003). Why these well-trained brigades lost is discussed in Section 18.6.

docs.title: 19.4.2 The Third Anglo-Maratha War, 1817–18
docs.text: The final Maratha war began when the Peshwa Bājīrāv II attacked the Company’s residency at Pune in November 1817. He was defeated at Khadki (Kirkee) and pursued across the Deccan. At Koregaon on the Bhīmā river, on 1 January 1818, a small Company force of about eight hundred men, largely sepoys of the Bombay army, many of them from the Mahār community, under Captain Francis Staunton, held the village through a day of fighting against a much larger Peshwa army. The Peshwa’s forces broke off the action and moved away on the approach of a relieving Company force under General Smith, and Staunton’s detachment, its losses heavy, returned to Shirur the next day. The engagement was commemorated by the British with an obelisk, and in the twentieth century B. R. Ambedkar made it a symbol of Dalit courage; it remains a site of commemoration and of controversy. The Peshwa surrendered in June 1818, and his territories were annexed.

docs.title: 19.4.3 The Anglo-Sikh wars, 1845–49
docs.text: The Sikh army of Punjab, built up by Ranjit Singh, was the most formidable opponent the Company met in India. In the First Anglo-Sikh War, the battle of Ferozeshah (21–22 December 1845) was nearly a British defeat: after a day and night of fighting, the British army was short of ammunition and its commanders considered retreat, but the Sikh commanders, divided and some of them in secret contact with the British, withdrew. At Sobraon (10 February 1846), the British stormed the Sikh entrenchments on the Sutlej, and many Sikh soldiers drowned when the bridge of boats behind them broke. In the Second Anglo-Sikh War, the battle of Chillianwala (13 January 1849) cost the British heavy casualties for an indecisive result, causing consternation in Britain; the war was decided at Gujrat (21 February 1849), where British artillery overwhelmed the Sikh army (Cunningham 1849; Grewal 1990). Joseph Davey Cunningham, a British officer who wrote a history of the Sikhs in 1849, was dismissed from his post for criticising the conduct of the war and the treachery of some Sikh leaders who had aided the British.

docs.title: 19.5 Wars on the Frontiers
docs.text: The East India Company’s armies fought not only Indian states but also the neighbours of India. The war with Nepal (1814–1816) was hard fought (Section 18.9); the Gurkha soldiers of Nepal impressed their opponents, and from 1815, after the surrender at Malaun and even before the treaty of Sugauli, the Company began to recruit Gurkhas into its service, beginning a tradition that continues in the Indian and British armies today. The Anglo-Burmese wars (1824–26, 1852, 1885) led to the annexation of Burma in stages. The First Anglo-Afghan War (1839–1842) ended in disaster: the British force that had occupied Kabul was destroyed during its retreat in January 1842, one of the worst defeats suffered by a British army in Asia. In the decades after 1849, the north-western frontier with Afghanistan became the scene of almost continuous campaigning against the Pashtun tribes, culminating in the Tirah campaign of 1897–98, and the frontier became the training ground of the Indian Army (Omissi 1994). Inside India, too, the Company and the Crown fought the forest and hill peoples whose lands they took over, from the Kol rising of 1831–32 and the Santal hul of 1855–56 to Birsa Munda’s ulgulān of 1899–1900 (Section 4.15), and the hill peoples of the north-east into the twentieth century.

docs.title: 19.7 The Sepoy Army
docs.text:
By the 1850s the Company’s three armies of Bengal, Madras and Bombay together numbered over 250,000 men, of whom the great majority were Indian. Indian soldiers could rise only to the rank of subedār, below the most junior British officer. The relationship between the Company and its sepoys rested on a bargain: regular pay, pensions, honour and respect for caste and religion in exchange for loyal service. When the Company seemed to break this bargain, the sepoys resisted. At Vellore in 1806, new regulations on dress and appearance, which the soldiers believed threatened their religion, provoked a mutiny that was suppressed with heavy loss of life (Figure 19.3). At Barrackpore in 1824, sepoys ordered to serve in Burma, which required crossing the sea, refused, and were fired on. The General Service Enlistment Act of 1856, which required new recruits to serve overseas if ordered, was one of the grievances of 1857 (Alavi 1995).

Figure 19.3. A sepoy of the Madras Native Infantry and his wife: watercolour by a Company artist, 1810 (National Army Museum, London). Caste marks on the forehead were among the things forbidden by the dress regulations of 1806 that provoked the Vellore mutiny. Image: Unidentified Company artist (National Army Museum, London), public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 19.8 The Rising of 1857
docs.text:
In May 1857 sepoys of the Bengal army mutinied at Meerut and marched to Delhi, where they proclaimed the aged Mughal emperor Bahādur Shāh as their ruler. The immediate cause was the rumour that the cartridges of the new Enfield rifle, which had to be bitten open, were greased with the fat of cows and pigs; the deeper causes included the annexation of Awadh in 1856, the home of many sepoys, grievances over pay and service, and wider discontent among landholders and princes. Kim Wagner has shown how rumours of a plot against the sepoys’ religion spread through the Bengal army in early 1857 and turned scattered grievances into a mutiny (Wagner 2010). The rising spread across north and central India, joined by civilians, peasants and dispossessed rulers such as the Rāṇī of Jhānsī, Nānā Sāhib and Begum Hazrat Mahal of Awadh (Chapter 16). Delhi, Kanpur and Lucknow saw prolonged fighting and atrocities on both sides; the British recaptured Delhi in September 1857, and the rising was suppressed by 1859 with great brutality, including mass executions.

The Madras and Bombay armies, and the newly raised regiments of Punjab, remained largely loyal and were used against the rebels. This fact shaped British policy for the next ninety years.

docs.title: 19.8.1 The suppression of 1857
docs.text: The military campaigns of 1857–58 were the largest the British fought in India. The British besieged Delhi, held by the rebels, from June to September 1857, and finally stormed it after bitter street fighting. At Lucknow, the British Residency, with its garrison and civilians, was besieged for months and relieved only after two attempts, in September and November 1857. In central India, Sir Hugh Rose’s campaign of 1858 took Jhānsī and defeated the forces of Tātyā Ṭope and the Rāṇī of Jhānsī at Kalpi and Gwalior. Tātyā Ṭope continued a guerrilla campaign across central India until his capture and execution in 1859. The rebels, many of them former Company sepoys trained in the same methods as their opponents, lacked unified leadership, a common plan and reliable supplies of ammunition, and the British could draw on reinforcements from Britain and on the loyal armies of Madras, Bombay and Punjab.

docs.title: 19.9 Martial Races
docs.text:
After 1857 the Crown took over the government of India and its armies. The army was reorganised: the proportion of British to Indian troops was increased, artillery was kept largely in British hands, and recruitment shifted away from the high-caste peasants of Awadh and Bihar who had formed the core of the old Bengal army. Recruitment came to be concentrated in Punjab, the North-West Frontier, Nepal and a few other regions, among Sikhs, Punjabi Muslims, Pathans, Dogras, Jats, Gurkhas and some other communities.

This policy was justified by the theory of “martial races”, which held that some Indian communities were naturally warlike and others were not. The theory was given its most influential form by Lord Roberts, commander-in-chief in India from 1885 to 1893, and was later expounded in books such as George MacMunn’s The Martial Races of India (1933) (MacMunn 1933). Heather Streets has shown that the theory was a product of British imperial culture, combining ideas of race, masculinity and loyalty after 1857, and that it was used to justify recruitment from communities considered loyal and to exclude others, notably educated Bengalis and many of the communities of the south that had supplied the old Madras army (Streets 2004). David Omissi’s study of the Indian Army from 1860 to 1940 shows how recruitment, pay, honour and religion bound the “martial” soldiers to the army (Omissi 1994).

The theory had lasting effects. It reshaped the identities of the communities it favoured, which came to see military service as their tradition, and it stigmatised others as unmanly. The colonial stereotype of the “effeminate” Bengali provoked a nationalist response in the form of physical culture, wrestling and stick-fighting clubs (Chapter 15).

docs.title: 19.10 The Sepoy’s World
docs.text:
The Indian Army of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries was a world of its own. Its soldiers were recruited from particular districts and communities, often through family and village networks; they served in regiments organised by “class” (community), with their own religious teachers, festivals and customs, which the army supported. Pay, pensions and land grants made military service an attractive career for peasant families in Punjab, the Himalayan hills and other recruiting grounds, and soldiers’ remittances and pensions became an important part of the rural economy of these regions (Omissi 1994). Indian soldiers could rise to the rank of subedār or risaldār (later called Viceroy’s Commissioned Officers), but command remained in British hands until the gradual Indianisation of the officer corps after the First World War. Indian soldiers became eligible for the Victoria Cross, the highest British award for gallantry, in 1911; Sepoy Khudadad Khan, a Punjabi Muslim, was the first Indian to receive it, for his bravery at Ypres in 1914.

The relationship between the army and the soldiers rested on a mixture of material reward, honour, religion and personal loyalty to officers, which British officers consciously cultivated. When this relationship was disturbed — by religious grievances, by unfamiliar conditions of service, by political propaganda — mutinies could occur, as at Singapore in 1915, when Indian soldiers of the 5th Light Infantry mutinied amid rumours of being sent to fight the Ottoman empire.

docs.title: 19.11 The Princely States and Their Forces
docs.text: About a third of the subcontinent remained under the rule of Indian princes who accepted British paramountcy. Their armies were reduced and restricted by treaty, and many became ceremonial forces. From the late 1880s some princely states were encouraged to maintain “Imperial Service Troops”, trained to the standard of the Indian Army and available for imperial service. These forces fought in the First World War; the Jodhpur and Mysore lancers took part in the capture of Haifa in Palestine in 1918, an action still commemorated in India. Princely forces were absorbed into the armies of India and Pakistan after 1947.

docs.title: 19.12.1 The Arms Act of 1878
docs.text: In 1878 the Government of India passed the Indian Arms Act (Act XI of 1878), which required a licence to manufacture, sell, possess or carry firearms and other weapons, including swords. The Act exempted Europeans and certain other categories of person, and licences were granted to Indians at the discretion of officials. The Act remained in force, with amendments, until it was replaced by the Arms Act of 1959; the political controversy it provoked is described in Section 19.13.

docs.title: 19.12.2 Effects on martial traditions
docs.text: The Arms Act, together with the disbandment of the armies of conquered states, the end of princely patronage of many martial communities, and the creation of a professional colonial army recruited from selected groups, transformed the place of arms in Indian society. Communities whose status had rested on military service — the Nāyars of Kerala, the poligar soldiery of Tamil Nadu, the paikas of Odisha, many Rajput and Maratha families — lost their role. Traditional arts that depended on weapons declined, while those that did not, such as wrestling, survived more easily. Earlier disarmament campaigns, such as those in Malabar after the Pazhassi revolt and in the south after the poligar wars, had already begun this process. It would be wrong, however, to attribute the decline of the martial arts to the Arms Act alone. The arts also declined because the kind of warfare they served had ended, and because new forms of sport and physical culture, many introduced through schools and the army, offered other models.

docs.title: 19.13 The Politics of the Arms Act
docs.text: The Arms Act of 1878 became a political issue almost at once. Indian critics pointed out that it exempted Europeans and Eurasians while subjecting Indians, including men of rank, to the need for licences and to police searches; they argued that it humiliated Indians and left villages defenceless against wild animals and bandits. The Indian National Congress repeatedly passed resolutions from the 1880s onward calling for the Act’s reform and for the opening of military careers to Indians, linking disarmament to the wider exclusion of Indians from the defence of their own country. Some of the racial distinctions in the rules were modified in the early twentieth century, but the system of licences remained, and the possession of arms remained a privilege granted by the state. Independent India retained the principle of licensing in the Arms Act of 1959, while removing the racial distinctions of the colonial law.

docs.title: 19.14 Policing and the Lāṭhī
docs.text: Disarmament went together with the creation of a colonial police. The police forces organised in the provinces after 1861 were armed mainly with the bamboo staff (lāṭhī), often tipped with iron, and with a smaller number of firearms. The lāṭhī, the traditional weapon of village watchmen and landlords’ retainers, thus became the instrument of colonial crowd control, used against peasant protests, strikes and nationalist demonstrations; the “lāṭhī charge” became a familiar feature of Indian political life and remains so. In the 1930s, the beating of non-violent protesters with lāṭhīs, as at the Dharasana salt works in 1930, was reported internationally and became a symbol of colonial repression. At the same time, nationalist and revolutionary clubs trained young men in lāṭhī play as a form of self-defence and physical culture (Chapter 15). The same weapon thus served both the colonial state and those who resisted it.

docs.title: 19.15 Indian Responses
docs.text: Indian nationalists responded to the colonial image of Indians as unwarlike and to the experience of disarmament in several ways. In Maharashtra, B. G. Tilak promoted public festivals of Gaṇeśa (from 1893) and of Śivājī (from 1895), which included displays of physical culture. Swami Vivekananda called on young Indians to build “muscles of iron and nerves of steel”. Gymnasia and physical culture societies spread in Maharashtra, Bengal and elsewhere, combining wrestling, club-swinging, mallakhamb, stick-fighting and European gymnastics; in Bengal, revolutionary societies such as the Anushilan Samiti used such clubs to recruit and train young men (Mujumdar 1950). These movements laid the foundations of the twentieth-century revival of Indian martial arts (Chapter 20).

docs.title: 19.16 Indian Soldiers Overseas before 1914
docs.text: Long before the world wars, Indian soldiers served the British empire outside India. Sepoys of the East India Company fought in the Dutch East Indies, in Egypt against the French in 1801, and in the Anglo-Burmese wars; Indian troops formed part of the British expeditions to Abyssinia in 1868, to Malta in 1878, to Egypt in 1882 and to Sudan; they fought in China during the Opium Wars and against the Boxer rising in 1900; and they garrisoned British posts from Aden to Hong Kong. Indian soldiers and police were also recruited for service in British colonies in East Africa and Southeast Asia. The Indian Army thus became, in the words often used by contemporaries, an imperial reserve, paid for largely by Indian revenues (Omissi 1994). Indian nationalists criticised the use of Indian money and Indian lives in imperial wars that, in their view, served British rather than Indian interests.

docs.title: 19.17 The Indian Army in the First World War
docs.text: About 1.3 million Indians served in the First World War, which made the Indian Army one of the largest armies of the British empire. In 1914 Indian divisions were sent to France, where they arrived in time to help hold the line at Ypres and fought in the battles of 1914 and 1915 in conditions of cold, mud and trench warfare for which they were ill prepared. Indian cavalry remained on the Western Front until 1918. Most Indian troops, however, served in the campaigns against the Ottoman empire: in Mesopotamia, where an Indian force was besieged and forced to surrender at Kut al-Amara in 1916 before the British and Indian armies took Baghdad in 1917; in Egypt and Palestine; at Gallipoli; and in East Africa. The letters written by Indian soldiers from France, examined by the British censors, provide a rare record of the experiences and feelings of ordinary sepoys (Omissi 1994); Santanu Das has read them alongside soldiers’ songs, photographs and the writings of Indian civilians to recover the war’s place in Indian culture (Das 2018). The war brought new demands from Indian politicians for constitutional reform and for the Indianisation of the officer corps.

docs.title: 19.18 The Indian Army in the Second World War
docs.text:
The Second World War transformed the Indian Army. From a force of under two hundred thousand in 1939, it grew to about two and a half million by 1945, the largest volunteer army in history; recruitment spread far beyond the “martial races” to communities previously excluded (Cohen 1971; Omissi 1994). Indian divisions fought in East Africa, where they took part in the hard-fought battle of Keren in Eritrea in 1941; in the Western Desert of North Africa; in Iraq, Syria and Iran; and in Italy, including the battles around Monte Cassino in 1944. In Southeast Asia, Indian troops suffered defeat in Malaya and Singapore in 1942, where many were taken prisoner, and then formed the largest part of the army that fought the Japanese in Burma. The battles of Imphal and Kohima in 1944, in which the Japanese invasion of north-eastern India was defeated, and the reconquest of Burma in 1945 were fought largely by Indian divisions (Cohen 1971). Srinath Raghavan’s history of India’s war argues that the mobilisation of men, money and production for the war transformed the Indian economy and state and helped to make the post-war settlement of South Asia (Raghavan 2016).

The war also produced the Indian National Army, recruited largely from Indian prisoners of war in Malaya and Singapore, organised under Japanese auspices and led from 1943 by Subhas Chandra Bose, which fought alongside the Japanese in the Imphal campaign. The war’s demands on India — for men, money, food and materials — were immense, and they contributed to economic hardship and, in Bengal, to the catastrophic famine of 1943. The experience of the war, the expansion and Indianisation of the officer corps, and the political impact of the INA trials helped to bring British rule to an end. Table 19.2 summarises the main theatres in which Indian troops fought in the two world wars; it is intended as a guide to further reading rather than a complete record.

docs.title: 19.19 The Indian Army and Indian Nationalism
docs.text:
The relationship between the Indian Army and the nationalist movement was complex. Many nationalists regarded the army as an instrument of colonial power, paid for by Indian taxes and used to suppress Indian protest and to fight Britain’s wars abroad. The Indian National Congress demanded the Indianisation of the officer corps and the reduction of military expenditure. Indianisation proceeded slowly: Indians were first admitted to King’s commissions after the First World War, and the Indian Military Academy at Dehradun opened only in 1932. At the same time, Indian soldiers’ service in the world wars strengthened the case for Indian self-government, and the rapid expansion of the army in the Second World War brought many Indians into the officer corps.

In the last years of British rule, the army’s loyalty came into question. The trials of officers of the Indian National Army in 1945–46 at the Red Fort in Delhi aroused widespread sympathy, and in February 1946 ratings of the Royal Indian Navy mutinied at Bombay and other ports, with support from parts of the population. These events convinced many British officials that the armed forces could no longer be relied upon to maintain British rule. In 1947 the army was divided between India and Pakistan, a process accompanied by the violence of Partition, in which soldiers were deployed to protect refugees and were sometimes accused of taking sides. Stephen Cohen’s study traces the army’s development from colonial institution to national army (Cohen 1971).

docs.title: 19.20 The Colonial Legacy
docs.text:
The colonial period left a deep imprint on the military institutions of South Asia. The regimental system, the recruitment of particular communities, the military academies, the traditions of the officer corps and the separation of the army from politics in India (though not in Pakistan) all have colonial roots (Cohen 1971). Several infantry regiments of the Indian Army trace their origins to the sepoy battalions of the Company: the Madras Regiment claims descent from units raised in the 1750s, among the oldest in the army. Regiments named after communities and regions — the Sikh, Rajput, Jat, Dogra, Garhwal, Kumaon, Mahar, Maratha Light Infantry and Gorkha regiments, among others — preserve the legacy of colonial “class” recruitment, adapted to a national army.

Regimental war cries recall older martial traditions. The Sikh Regiment’s cry is the Sikh affirmation Jo bole so nihāl, sat srī akāl; the Rajputana Rifles’ Rājā Rāmcandra kī jai; the Maratha Light Infantry’s Bol Śrī Chatrapati Śivājī Mahārāj kī jai; the Gorkha regiments’ Jai Mahākālī, āyo Gorkhālī. Many units worship their weapons at Daśahrā, regimental museums display the arms and memorabilia of earlier wars, and some units demonstrate kaḷarippayaṟṟu, gatka or mallakhamb. The regiments are institutions of a modern state, governed by modern law, but they draw on the symbols of older martial cultures to create cohesion and pride.

The colonial period also left a body of myth: the “martial races” theory, the idea of an unwarlike India redeemed by British discipline, and, in reaction, nationalist narratives of an ancient Indian military genius suppressed by colonialism. The history traced in this volume suggests a more complex picture, in which Indian soldiers, commanders and states were neither uniquely heroic nor uniquely weak, but participants in the long and shared history of war.

docs.title: Chapter 20: Legacies: Revival, Myth and Memory
20.1 Introduction
docs.text: The colonial conquest ended the independent military traditions of the subcontinent, and the armed forces that succeeded the colonial army have been described in Chapter 19 (Section 19.20). This final chapter follows what happened to the warrior’s arts outside the army. It falls into three parts. The first traces the revival of Indian martial arts and physical culture since the late nineteenth century, which turned arts tied to vanished military systems into sports, performances, health practices and symbols of identity, and the claims that have grown up around them. The second examines the question of Indian influence on the martial arts of other Asian countries, which has produced some of the most persistent myths in the field, above all the story of Bodhidharma and Shaolin kung fu. The third gathers the popular claims examined throughout the volume, points readers to the sources, and sets out the questions that remain open and the conclusions the volume has reached. Chess, the board game of the four-limbed army, is treated with its ancestor caturaṅga in Section 2.20, and the debate over an Indian strategic tradition at the end of Chapter 7.

docs.title: 20.2 The Revival of Indian Martial Arts
20.2.1 Physical culture and nationalism
docs.text: As Chapter 19 explained, the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries saw a movement of physical culture in India, inspired partly by the desire to answer colonial stereotypes of Indian weakness and partly by the international vogue for gymnastics and bodybuilding. Gymnasia (vyāyāmśālā, tālīm, akhāṛā) were founded in Maharashtra, Bengal, Punjab and elsewhere; wrestling, club-swinging, mallakhamb, stick-fighting and Indian forms of exercise were combined with European gymnastics and drill. Institutions such as the Hanuman Vyayam Prasarak Mandal at Amravati, founded in 1914, and the Baroda physical culture circle around D. C. Mujumdar, whose Encyclopedia of Indian Physical Culture appeared in 1950, documented and promoted Indian exercises and martial arts (Mujumdar 1950). Mark Singleton has shown how the same milieu contributed to the formation of modern postural yoga (Singleton 2010).

docs.title: 20.2.2 From combat to sport and performance
docs.text:
After independence the regional martial arts were reorganised as sports, with associations, federations, standardised rules and competitions; as performing arts, used in dance, theatre and film; and as heritage, promoted by state governments and tourism departments. Kaḷarippayaṟṟu associations were formed in Kerala from the late 1950s, silambam and gatka federations later; the Sports Authority of India, established in 1984, and the Khelo India programme, launched in 2018, have included indigenous martial arts such as gatka, kaḷarippayaṟṟu, thang-ta and mallakhamb in national competitions. Kaḷarippayaṟṟu has influenced experimental theatre and dance in India and abroad, and the action choreography of Indian cinema draws on kaḷarippayaṟṟu, silambam and gatka.

This transformation has been both a rescue and a change. Arts that might have disappeared are now practised by many thousands of people, including women and members of communities once excluded from them. But sport and performance select and standardise: the healing knowledge of the kaḷari, the ritual of the akhāṛā, the lineage-specific forms of silambam, are hard to fit into competitive formats. Practitioners and scholars debate how to preserve the depth of the traditions while widening participation (Zarrilli 1998; Alter 1992).

docs.title: 20.2.3 Wrestling and archery
docs.text: Traditional wrestling has had the most visible modern success, through the Olympic medals won by Indian freestyle wrestlers since 2008, many of them trained in akhāṛās (Chapter 14). Modern archery, though using modern equipment, has produced Indian champions, many of them from tribal communities with their own traditions of the bow (Chapter 4).

docs.title: 20.3 Martial Arts and Yoga
docs.text: The revival also produced a common claim that yoga and the Indian martial arts were once a single discipline, or that yoga postures derive from combat stances. There are genuine connections. Both share a vocabulary of posture and breath; armed ascetics, including Nāth yogis and the nāgā orders, were soldiers as well as renouncers (Pinch 2006); kaḷarippayaṟṟu incorporates exercises that resemble yoga postures; and the physical culture movement of the early twentieth century helped shape both modern yoga and the revived martial arts (Singleton 2010). But the specific claims often made — that the “warrior” poses of modern yoga preserve ancient battle stances, or that classical yoga texts teach martial techniques — are not supported by the sources.

docs.title: 20.4 Science and the Claims Made for Martial Arts
docs.text:
Promoters of Indian martial arts often claim scientific support for their effectiveness or their health benefits: that marma and varmam points correspond to nerve centres, that traditional exercises produce exceptional fitness, that traditional diets are optimal, or that particular arts cure specific diseases. Some of these claims are plausible in general terms — regular, vigorous exercise is good for health, and traditional exercises such as the daṇḍ and baiṭhak are effective forms of strength training — but many are not supported by published research, and some are contradicted by it. Studies of martial arts training as exercise exist, but they do not validate the traditional theories of vital points or of the body’s “energy” channels.

The responsible course is to distinguish three kinds of statement: historical statements about what traditions taught and practised, which can be checked against sources; general statements about the benefits of exercise, which are well supported; and specific medical or physiological claims, which need clinical evidence. Indian martial arts are valuable cultural traditions and forms of physical education whether or not their traditional theories are scientifically validated. Their value does not depend on exaggerated claims, and such claims, when they are shown to be false, can damage the credibility of the traditions themselves.

docs.title: 20.5 Martial Arts in Cinema and Popular Culture
docs.text:
Cinema has been a powerful medium for the representation of Indian martial traditions. The stunt films of the 1930s and 1940s, including those of the actress Fearless Nadia, popularised sword fights and acrobatics; the mythological films of all periods staged the battles of the epics; and historical films have dramatised the lives of Śivājī, the Rāṇī of Jhānsī, Pṛthvīrāja, Rāṇā Pratāp and many others. Malayalam cinema made the heroes of the Kerala ballads famous; Tamil cinema used silambam in fight scenes; and recent big-budget films have used kaḷarippayaṟṟu and other traditional arts in their action sequences. Television serials of the Rāmāyaṇa and Mahābhārata in the late 1980s reached hundreds of millions of viewers and shaped popular ideas of epic warfare.

Cinema has also spread myths: films have presented Bodhidharma as the founder of Chinese martial arts, epic weapons as ancient technology, and historical battles with little regard for evidence. The historian’s task is not to condemn popular culture, which has its own purposes, but to make the evidence available so that viewers can distinguish history from legend.

docs.title: 20.6 Heritage, Tourism and Documentation
docs.text:
Indian martial arts are now promoted as cultural heritage by central and state governments, tourism departments and cultural organisations. Kaḷarippayaṟṟu demonstrations are a regular feature of tourism in Kerala; gatka and mallakhamb are performed at national events; the Hola Mohalla festival and the Mysore Dasara attract large audiences. Such promotion has brought support and recognition, but it can also encourage spectacle at the expense of depth, and it often repeats unverified claims of antiquity.

Serious documentation of these arts — recording their techniques, terminology, lineages, rituals and oral traditions, and the life histories of their masters — has been undertaken by scholars such as Zarrilli and Alter, by cultural institutions and by practitioners themselves (Zarrilli 1998; Alter 1992). Much remains to be done. The palm-leaf manuscripts of kaḷari and varmam lineages, the oral epics of warrior heroes, the arms and armour in princely and private collections, and the memories of elderly practitioners are all valuable sources that are at risk of being lost. Their careful study, using the methods of history, ethnography and conservation, is one of the most important tasks for the future of the field.

docs.title: 20.7 The Diaspora
docs.text: Indian martial arts have also travelled with the Indian diaspora. Silambam is practised by Tamil communities in Malaysia, Singapore and Sri Lanka; gatka by Sikh communities in Britain, North America and elsewhere, where it is performed at religious festivals and processions; kaḷarippayaṟṟu is taught in schools in Europe, North America and East Asia, often by teachers trained in Kerala; and Punjabi wrestling and kabaḍḍī tournaments are held in Britain and Canada. In the diaspora these arts often serve as markers of community identity and as ways of transmitting culture to new generations, as well as forms of exercise and self-defence (Green and Svinth 2010).

docs.title: 20.8.1 The legend
docs.text: A widely repeated story holds that the Indian Buddhist monk Bodhidharma, the legendary founder of Chan (Zen) Buddhism in China, came to the Shaolin monastery in Henan in the early sixth century, found the monks too weak to sit long in meditation, and taught them exercises from which Shaolin kung fu, and through it the martial arts of China, Korea and Japan, developed. In Indian versions of the story Bodhidharma is a Pallava prince from Kāñcī who was trained in kaḷarippayaṟṟu or another Indian martial art, so that Indian martial arts become the source of all East Asian ones. The story has been popularised in films and books in India and elsewhere.

docs.title: 20.8.2 The evidence
docs.text:
Historical research has shown that the story has no basis in the early sources. The earliest Chinese references to Bodhidharma, from the sixth and seventh centuries, describe him as a foreign meditation master — a brahmin from south India in one account, a monk from Persia in another — and say nothing of martial arts, or indeed of Shaolin (Broughton 1999). His association with Shaolin developed later in Chan hagiography. Meir Shahar’s study of the Shaolin monastery shows that Shaolin monks are first recorded as fighters in the early seventh century, when they helped the future Tang emperor Li Shimin, and that the monastery’s famous martial arts — first staff-fighting and later bare-handed styles — developed mainly in the Ming and Qing periods (fourteenth to nineteenth centuries), drawing on Chinese military practice, Daoist gymnastics (daoyin) and Chinese medicine (Shahar 2008).

The attribution of martial arts to Bodhidharma first appears in the Yijin jing (“Sinew-Changing Classic”), a manual of exercises composed in the early seventeenth century (around 1624), whose forged prefaces, attributed to famous generals of the Tang and Song periods, claim that Bodhidharma left the text at Shaolin. Shahar shows that its author was a Daoist and that its exercises derive from the Chinese tradition. The legend became widespread in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries through popular fiction and martial arts manuals (Shahar 2008).

The Bodhidharma story is therefore a legend, not history. This does not mean that India had no influence on Chinese culture — the transmission of Buddhism from India to China was one of the great cultural exchanges of history — but there is no evidence that Chinese martial arts derive from Indian ones.

docs.title: 20.9 India and Southeast Asia
docs.text:
Claims of Indian influence on the martial arts of Southeast Asia are more plausible in general terms, because Indian cultural influence on the region is well documented. The “Indianised” kingdoms of the first and early second millennia CE — Funan, Champa, Angkor, Śrīvijaya, Majapahit and others — adopted Sanskrit as a language of court and religion, Indian political ideas, the epics (the Rāmāyaṇa became the Thai Ramakien, the Khmer Reamker and the Javanese Kakawin Rāmāyaṇa), and the war elephant (Trautmann 2015). Sanskrit military terms entered Southeast Asian languages, and the Nītisāra of Kāmandaka was adapted in Old Javanese.

The martial arts of the region — Thai muay and krabi krabong, Malay and Indonesian silat, Filipino arnis, Khmer bokator — are, however, local developments with their own histories, documented mostly from recent centuries. Claims that they descend directly from kaḷarippayaṟṟu or silambam rest on general resemblances, which can be explained by common human solutions to the problems of fighting, and on a few shared terms, not on historical evidence of transmission. The clearest case of Indian martial arts in Southeast Asia is modern: silambam was carried to Malaya by Tamil migrants in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries and is practised there today (Green and Svinth 2010).

docs.title: 20.10 Claims and Evidence: A Summary
docs.text:
Throughout this volume, popular claims about Indian military traditions have been compared with the evidence. Table 20.1 summarises the most common of them, with the conclusion reached and the chapter in which each is discussed. The purpose of the table is not to diminish Indian achievements, many of which are real and remarkable, but to help readers distinguish what is supported by evidence from what is not.

docs.title: 20.11 Studying Indian Military History: Sources and Resources
docs.text:
Readers who wish to pursue the subjects of this volume further will find a wide range of sources and resources.

Texts in translation.

The Arthaśāstra is available in the translations of Kangle, Rangarajan and Olivelle (Kangle 1960–1965; Rangarajan 1992; Olivelle 2013); the Mahābhārata in the complete translation of K. M. Ganguli and the partial critical translations of the Chicago project (Ganguli 1883–1896; Buitenen 1973–1978; Fitzgerald 2004); the Mānava Dharmaśāstra in Olivelle’s edition (Olivelle 2005); the Agni Purāṇa in Mitra’s Sanskrit edition and Gangadharan’s translation (Mitra 1870–1879; Gangadharan 1984–1987); the Mahāvaṃsa in Geiger’s translation (Geiger 1912); the Tamil war poems in the translation of Hart and Heifetz (Hart and Heifetz 1999); Bābur’s memoirs in Thackston’s translation (Thackston 1996); and the Āʾīn-i Akbarī in Blochmann’s (Blochmann 1873).

Archives.

The archives of the Indian states and of the colonial government are vast. The National Archives of India in New Delhi, the state archives — among them the Maharashtra State Archives at Pune, which hold the records of the Peshwas’ government, and the Tamil Nadu Archives at Chennai — and the India Office Records at the British Library in London hold military records, correspondence and reports, much of which has been little studied. Persian, Marathi, Rajasthani and other documentary collections offer further material.

Museums and monuments.

The arms and armour collections mentioned in Chapter 5, the regimental museums of the Indian Army, the forts and battlefields protected by the Archaeological Survey of India and the state archaeology departments, and the many hero-stones preserved in museums and villages are all primary sources for the study of Indian warfare.

Modern scholarship.

The bibliography of this volume lists the principal modern studies. Among them, the works of Chakravarti and Sarva Daman Singh on early India, Olivelle and McClish on the Arthaśāstra, Upinder Singh on political violence in ancient India, Jackson on the Delhi Sultanate, Gommans and Kolff’s reader on the period 1000–1800, Gommans and Irvine on the Mughals, Gordon on the Marathas, Kolff on the military labour market, Trautmann on elephants, Roy on warfare and ethics, Alavi, Peers, Streets and Omissi on the colonial armies, and Zarrilli and Alter on martial arts provide a foundation for further study.

docs.title: 20.12 Open Questions
docs.text: Many questions in the history of Indian warfare remain open. How were armies actually recruited, paid and supplied in the early historic and early medieval periods, beyond the prescriptions of the texts? When and how did the Indian traditions of crucible steel develop? What was the real scale of the Cōḻa overseas expeditions? How did the military labour market of the Ganges valley operate before the fifteenth century? How did forest and hill peoples fight, and how did their military traditions interact with those of the states around them? What can the thousands of unpublished hero-stones and inscriptions tell us about local warfare? How did women experience war, beyond the few queens whose names are recorded? And how much of the technical knowledge of the martial arts is genuinely old, and how much is the product of the modern revival? These questions can be answered only by patient research in texts, inscriptions, archives and the field. The traditions described in this volume deserve that research.

docs.title: 20.13 Conclusion: Reading the Military Traditions of India
docs.text:
This volume has surveyed more than three thousand years of warfare and martial culture in South Asia, from the walled towns of the Indus civilisation to the sepoy armies and the modern revival of the martial arts. A few conclusions may be drawn.

First, Indian military history is rich and varied, and much of it is well documented. It deserves to be studied with the same critical care as the military history of other civilisations, using inscriptions, chronicles, archaeology and the comparative perspective of historians such as Gommans, Kolff, Trautmann and Roy.

Second, the Indian textual tradition of war is impressive in its range: the Arthaśāstra’s realism, the Mahābhārata’s moral depth, the dharmaśāstras’ rules of war, the technical literatures on elephants, horses and arms, and the Persian, Tamil, Rajasthani, Marathi and Assamese writings on war. But these texts must be dated and read for what they are. The idea of a complete ancient “science of war” preserved from Vedic times is a modern construction, and claims of ancient super-weapons are myths.

Third, Indian warfare was shaped by exchange and adaptation. The chariot, the war elephant, the mounted archer, gunpowder and the drilled infantry of the eighteenth century each transformed it, and Indian rulers and soldiers adopted new methods quickly. Rulers of every religion and region fought each other, recruited across communities and borrowed from their enemies.

Fourth, the ethics of war in Indian traditions combined a real concern for restraint with a frank acceptance of deception and force, and practice often fell short of the ideals. The most valuable part of this inheritance may be its honesty about the costs of war.

Finally, the martial arts that survive today are living traditions, transformed by colonialism and revival, which carry real knowledge of the body and of combat, and real cultural meaning. They are best served not by exaggerated claims but by careful documentation, critical history and safe practice.

500 elephants sent west c. 261 BCE Aśoka’s conquest of Kaliṅga (Rock Edict XIII) c. 50 BCE–300 CE Arthaśāstra (Olivelle’s dating) c. 1st–3rd c. CE Tamil Caṅkam war poetry (core) c. 2nd c. CE Mānava Dharmaśāstra 4th–5th c.  Gupta empire;
